REPORT
            The University of Delhi, a premier university of the country, is known for its high standards in teaching and 
research and attracts a  large number of students not only from all over  India but also several other countries.  
Established in February, 1922 under the provisions of the Delhi University Act, 1922 as a unitary and residential
university with a nucleus of three colleges, two faculties and about 750 students, it has grown  over the years into one of
the largest universities in the country. 
2.         The Delhi University (Amendment) Bill, 2000 provides for deletion of sub-section (2) of section 5 of the Delhi
University Act, 1922.  The aforesaid provision  prohibits the affiliation of any educational institution or college with a
university other than the Delhi University within the limits of the National  Capital Territory of Delhi, unless it is
specifically permitted by an order of the  Central Govt.    As per the Statement of Objects and Reasons attached to the
Bill, the Delhi University  already has a large number of institutions/colleges affiliated with it and may  not be in a
position to take on the continuous  additional burden of  new institutions/colleges as well as  increasing student
population.
3.         The Committee was  given to understand that  the Govt. of India was already contemplating for setting up of
self-financing universities  (private universities) to cater to the needs of the ever increasing demand of higher education. 
However, section 5 (2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922 had been causing difficulties/restraints in affiliation of
different colleges/institutions being set up in Delhi with any other university to cope up with the increased influx of
students.   
4.         The Committee was informed that the Indraprastha Vishwavidyalaya Bill was passed by the Legislative
Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi in 1998 and while the Bill was being examined in the Ministry of
Home Affairs for presidential assent, the Department of Legal Affairs brought to the notice of the  Ministry of Home
Affairs the implication of Section 5 of the Delhi University Act, 1922.
5.         The Committee was given to understand that the proposed deletion of  Section 5,  if passed by the Parliament,
would help the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya in its extension and also avoid complications regarding affiliation of
institutions/colleges with the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya within the jurisdiction of Delhi University.   It was also
submitted that the necessary  Cabinet approval had already been obtained for the proposal relating to deletion of Section
5 (2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922 before the Bill was moved in the Parliament.
6.         The Committee in its meeting held on the 12
th June, 2000  had a detailed discussion on the  proposed
amendment  in the Delhi University Act, 1922 with the  representatives of the Department of Secondary Education and
Higher Education, Chairman, UGC and also representatives of the Delhi University and Indraprastha Vishwavidyalaya.
7.         On a specific query about the number of colleges affiliated to the  Delhi University, the Committee was

97th Report of Committee On HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/97threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:14]
informed that so far 68 colleges had been affiliated to the Delhi University, out of which 8 colleges were maintained by
the Central/State Govt., 10 by the Delhi University and 1 by the Govt. of Bhutan. 21 colleges were sponsored by Private
Trusts and 28 were sponsored by the Delhi Govt.  The Committee was given to understand that the Delhi University was
in a position to attend to the requirements/conditions as laid down in the relevant Act and rules made thereunder so far
as its affiliated institutions/colleges were concerned.
8.         So far as Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya  was concerned, 8 teaching departments had been established and 35
colleges had been affiliated to the University   under the relaxation provided in  proviso to Section 5(2) of the Delhi
University Act, 1922. The Committee was also informed that with the exception of 2 Govt. aided colleges,  rest were
self financing private institutions.  
9.         Very strong apprehensions were raised about the implication of the resultant situation with  the deletion of sub-
section 5 (2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922.  It was clarified by the representatives of the Department   that even
after the proposed deletion, only such of the universities which were to be set up  by the Delhi Govt. would have the
power to affiliate colleges.  Attention of the Committee in this context was drawn to the Statement of Objects and
Reasons of the Amendment Bill which clearly stated that in order to facilitate the affiliation of institutions and colleges
with the Indraprashta Vishwavidyalaya or any other university that may be set up in Delhi, sub-section 2 of section 5 of
the Delhi University Act, 1922 was required to be omitted.  It was further clarified that no Govt.  or Union Territory
where there was a legislature would set up universities in the territorial jurisdiction of another State or Union Territory. 
10.       In contrast, the contention  of the  Delhi University was that this kind of blanket deletion of the provision would
have an adverse effect on the quality of education in Delhi. It was  pointed out that the Bill did not clearly reflect the
objectives mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Reasons but went beyond that.  With the deletion of Section 5(2),
not only control of the Central Govt. would be removed but there would also be no barrier for any university outside
Delhi to affiliate colleges set up in Delhi. The Committee was given to understand that a university outside Delhi had
already been given permission by the Central Govt. to affiliate a college in Delhi.  It was suggested that  the objective of
the proposed amendment namely to enable the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya to give affiliation to colleges could be
achieved through an amendment in the Delhi University Act. 
11.       The Committee noted that as per the provisions of Section 4 of the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya Act, 1998, no
college or institution situated within the jurisdiction of the University shall be compulsorily affiliated to the University
and affiliation shall be granted by the University only to such college or institution as may agree to accept its statutes
and ordinances.   However, in view of  section 5 (2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922, direct affiliation was being
granted by the Central Govt. to such colleges/institutions, opting for  affiliation to the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya. 
On a specific query whether there was any conflict so far as AICTE and other councils were concerned in view of the
direct affiliation being granted by the Central Govt. to such colleges, it was clarified to the Committee that  recognition
by the concerned council was  a mandatory provision and affiliation could only be granted thereafter.
12.       The Committee voiced its concern about a number of universities functioning in different parts of the country
which had been established  without any permission from the  Govt. and were running professional courses or granting
affiliation to institutions/colleges without the required approval from the concerned council.   The Committee was
informed that 20 such fake universities were functioning in different parts of the country which were  being approached
by the UGC for fulfilling the norms from time to time.  State Govts. were also being asked to take action against them. 
It was also mentioned that some of the fake universities had  moved the courts against the UGC.   Under the existing 
provisions of the UGC Act, only a fine of Rs. 10,000 could be imposed against them.   The Committee was, however,
given to understand that more punitive action had been proposed against fake universities under the new UGC Act
which was under contemplation at present.
13.       Doubts were also raised about the future status of Delhi University in view of the proposed deletion of section
5(2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922. The Committee was of the view that deletion of section 5(2) would lead to
commercialisation of education particularly in Delhi.  There was a need for a safeguard in  the form of  Govt. control,
specially in view of the existing fake universities and likelihood of more such universities coming up in future.  
Continuance of   section 5(2) was very much required as there was genuine apprehension that there would be ample
opportunities for some unscrupulous elements to start universities and colleges which would hamper the prospects of
Delhi University and in the larger perspective, of higher education in the country.
14.       The Committee was not in agreement with the contention of the representatives of the Department and UGC that
with the deletion of section 5(2), all institutions would have a free choice to get affiliated either to the Indraprashtha

97th Report of Committee On HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/97threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:14]
Vishwavidyalaya or to the Delhi University or to any other university to be set up in future by the Govt. of Delhi or by
the Central Govt. The Committee noted that it had been duly clarified in the Statement of Objects and Reasons to the
Delhi University (Amendment) Bill 2000 that only the Indraprastha Vishwavidyalaya or any other University that may
be set up in Delhi would have the power to affiliate institutions and colleges.  However, the Committee felt that  with
the Bill becoming an Act, Statement of Objects and Reasons would not have any relevance.  This would result in not
only the removal of the Govt. control but also there would be no bar for universities from other states from affiliating
institutions and colleges in Delhi.
15.       Attention of the Committee was also drawn to a difficult situation which may arise with the omission of section
5 (2). It was felt that with the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya  being given the authority to affiliate self-financing
institutions, it may happen that the colleges already affiliated with the  Delhi University may opt for affiliation with
some other university. There was,  therefore, a need for having checks and balances so that only future institutions could
be affiliated to any university established in Delhi. 
16.       In its meeting held on the 10
th July, 2000, the Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Secondary
Education and Higher Education and Vice-Chancellors of  Delhi University and Indraprastha Vishwavidyalaya. 
Secretary of the Department informed the Committee that in view of the many apprehensions raised by the Committee 
with regard to the deletion of section 5(2),   particularly the loss of control of the Central Govt. in regulating the
affiliation of Delhi colleges and also the  establishment of  self-financing/private institutions in Delhi, the Department
of  Secondary Education and Higher Education held wider consultations with the Vice-Chancellors of Delhi University
and Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya and also  other stake-holders concerned with the amendment of Delhi University
Act, 1922 on the 23
rd June, 2000.
17.       The Committee was given to understand that there were conflicting views on the issue whether colleges already
affiliated to Delhi University might shift their affiliation to Indraprastha Vishwavidyalaya.   After much deliberations, it
was felt that    this issue should be better left open specially as a ban may not be really required and called for. There
already was an empowering element in section 5(2) which gave the Central Government the authority to direct
affiliation  of an institution/college with some other university.  It was also felt that the amendment would not result in
any dilution of status so far as the Delhi University was concerned.  There was little likelihood of any college leaving
the Delhi University for joining an infant university in future in view of  the fact that the  Delhi University  was a central
university and  was getting very liberal grants from the Central Govt.   Not only this, from the academic point of view,
Delhi University enjoyed a unique status, having 82 departments in different disciplines.  Any college affiliated to the
Delhi University would have access to all its departments engaged in the teaching of graduate/post-graduate/
professional courses, research etc.   
18.       It was, therefore, unanimously decided in the aforesaid meeting that section 5(2) of the Delhi University Act,
may be retained and the following proviso may be added to section 5(2):-
‘Provided that the provision of the above sub section shall not apply in the case of Guru Gobind Singh
Indraprashtha University incorporated by the Government of NCT of Delhi.’
19.       It was explained that the above cited proposed amendment in the Delhi University Act, 1922 would obviate the
need for Central Govt. orders in case of institutions/colleges seeking affiliation to the State Govt. created Indraprashtha
Vishwavidyalaya which had been set  up with an objective of catering to the increasing needs of higher education in
Delhi.  The Committee was also informed that  the proposed change in the legislation had been approved by the 
Minister for Human Resource Development.
20.       The Committee  after a detailed  discussion on the  various aspects connected with the proposed deletion of
section 5(2)  of the Delhi University Act, 1922  recommends that  section 5(2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922  
should not be deleted so as to    prevent the loss of control of the Central Govt.   in regulating the establishment of self-
financing/private institutions  in Delhi which may seek affiliation  to the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya or any other
university within or outside the National Capital Territory of Delhi.  The Committee also  recommends the addition of
the following proviso to section  5(2) of the Delhi University Act, 1922 so as to  obviate the need for  Central Govt.
orders in case of institutions/colleges seeking affiliation to the Indraprashtha Vishwavidyalaya :-
 ‘Provided that the provision of the above sub section shall not apply in the case of Guru Gobind Singh
Indraprashtha University incorporated by the Government of NCT of Delhi.’

            I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Ninety –eighth Report of the Committee on Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the
54th Report on National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), Bangalore.
2.         The Seventy-third Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 27 th February, 2001.  Replies of the
Government on the recommendations contained in the Report, received from the Department of Health, Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare were considered by the Committee.  Clarifications were also sought by the Committee from
the representatives of the Department.  .
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same at its meeting held on 22nd January, 2001.
 
NEW DELHI;
January 22, 2001
Magha 2, 1922 (Saka)
 
 
 
 
 
S.B. CHAVAN
Chairman
Department-related

 REPORT
            The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained
in its Fifty-fourth Report on the Functioning of National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS),
Bangalore which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 25th February, 1997.
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in
the Report.  They have been categorized as follows:-
(i)                  Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 3, 5, 5.1, 5.2, 11 (Chapter
I)
(ii)                Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government’s replies: 8, 9, 9.1, 10, 10.2, 10.3, 12, 13.1 (Chapter II)
(iii)               Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted by
the Committee: 4, 6, 7, 10.1, 13, 13.2, 13.3 (Chapter-III)
(iv)              Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been received – Nil
(Chapter – IV)
 CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNEMNT
III        Recommendation
3.         When the Committee sought to know as to whether the Institute is equipped with latest technology and sufficient
equipments in all the departments, the Director stated that efforts have always been made to equip all the departments
with the advanced technology and equipments.  However, due to lack of funds they are not able to keep pace with latest
improvements in technology, he added.  The Committee was also informed that if a special grant is made available to
the Institute then it would be possible to acquire the necessary equipments.  The Committee feels that the Institute is in
need of sophisticated equipments for diagnosis, treatment & research and the Department of Health may consider
making available sufficient funds for the purpose.
Action Taken
            Government of India has released the entire funds and the equipment has been purchased by the Institute.

98th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/98threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:14]
V         Recommendation
5.         One of the three important objectives of the Institute is manpower development in the field of mental health and
Neuro Sciences.  The Committee notes that the Institute offers Post Graduate Courses including M.Phil, Post-certificate
courses in nursing i.e. (Diploma in Psychiatric Nursing DPN and Diploma in Neurological Nursing DNN) are also
offered in the Institute.  Facilities to pursue PH.D Programmes are also available, it was added.
Action Taken
            The Institute has introduced new courses:
a)                  Post Doctoral Certificate course in Neuroanaesthesia
b)                  M.Phil course in Speech Language Pathology.
Recommendation
5.1       The Committee was informed by the Director that the courses conducted by the Institute are always in great
demand due to the limited intake capacity of the Institute.  When asked to explain the steps taken to meet the demand,
the Director replied that recently it has been proposed to increase the number of seats in the following courses:
                        MD-Psychiatry                         8 to 14 seats
                        DM-Neurology                                    4 to 6 seats
                        M.CH Neurosurgery                4 to 6 seats
                        M.Phil Clin. Psychology            12 to 15 seats
                        M.Phil in PSW                         12 to 15 seats
5.2       The Committee desires that this proposal may be finalized as early as possible.  For increasing the seats, the staff
strength is also required to be increased.  Necessary steps may therefore, be taken to sanction additional posts.
Action Taken
            Medical Council of India has agreed to increase the number of seats as proposed by the Director, NIMHANS,
Bangalore and the Institute has also increased the M.Phil Clinical Psychology and M.Phil in PSW as proposed.
11.       Recommendation
            To overcome the problems occurring due to accidents and epilepsy, prevention is required for which public
awareness is essential.  To a question as to whether the Institute is publishing any literature for the awareness of the
common public on the mental health related problems, the Director of the Institute responded that they are planning in
this direction.  One of the faculty members of the Institute has published nearly forty books in Kannada.  The Institute is
also planning to publish them in the regional languages, he added.  The Director also stated that the Health Education
Bureau in the Institute is working on it.  He also stated that the Institute is in a position to supply posters on mental
health in case any State is in need of it.  The Committee is of the opinion that there is need to publish the materials about
mental health and related problems in all the regional languages so that people of all the regions/states can be benefited. 
Necessary steps may be taken in this direction.  The Department should take the responsibility of publishing the material
in various regional languages in a time-bound manner.
Action Taken
            State Health Secretaries have been informed about the IEC materials developed by NIMHANS and have been
requested to make use of these materials after getting it translated into local languages for generating public awareness. 
The Central Health Education Bureau has also been asked for the same.
 CHAPTER-II
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATINS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN
VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLY
Recommendation
8.         The Committee has learnt that a sixty bedded drug dependence unit is functioning in the Institute and funds are
not being given for this by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare while similar centres established in PGI
Chandigarh, AIIMS, Delhi etc. are funded by the Govt. of India under the National Drug De-Addiction programme. 

98th Report of HRD

The unique feature of the Centre in this Institute is, it has been started with community based activity.  The Committee
was also informed that the Ministry has been approached for providing additional funds for De-Addiction programme. 
The Committee, however, feels that the Institute should not over-burden itself with the Drug De-addiction programme,
particularly when sufficient funds are not being received.
Action Taken
            Ministry of Health has approved the inclusion of existing Drug De-addiction Centre of NIMHANS under
National Drug De-addiction programme and sanctioned Rs. 517 lakhs in the 9 th Five year plan and to make it a
Regional Centre.
Recommendation
9.         The Committee has noted that a survey conducted on more that one lakh population on neurological disorders
showed that approximately 31 people out of 1000 suffer from neurological disorders, the commonest being headache
and epilepsy.  Considering the gravity of the situation, the Committee feels that there is need for evolving a national
strategy on epilepsy and other neurological disorders.
Action Taken
            Under National Mental Health Programme, epilepsy is also included as one of the disorders and NIMHANS has
taken up training of PHC doctors in the management of  Mental disorders including epilepsy.
Recommendation
9.1       The Committee also learnt that basic research studies on Yoga have helped in the application of Kriya Yoga in
the successful treatment of patients with depression.  Since yoga treatment does not require any medicines and is free
from side effects, it needs to be extensively used.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps should be taken by
the Institute to involve more yoga experts in treating the patients who suffer  from depression.  The yoga unit may be
further developed.
Action Taken
            The proposal for establishment of advanced centre in Ayurveda at NIMHANS has been agreed to by Deptt.of
ISM&H and  has released amount for providing infrastructure.
Recommendation
10.       The Institute caters to the needs of Patients suffering from Psychiatric and neurological disorders.  The Institute
has a bed capacity of 805.  Besides this, the Institute also offers a combined neuro psychiatric out-patient service to
impart better co-ordinated patient care.  When the Committee sought to know as to whether the bed capacity is proposed
to be increased, it was stated that they propose to increase the beds in casualty unit by 50 beds.  They also propose to
increase bed capacity in head injury unit and stroke unit, it was added.  The Committee desires that necessary steps may
be taken to increase the beds at the earliest.
Action Taken
            Providing emergency care in the city is a State responsibility and NIMHANS being an apex referral Hospital
should normally not be handling emergency cases which can detract from their primary focus which is aimed at
evolving the best standards for teaching clinical research and patient care.  However, subject to receiving State Govt.’s
financial support the proposal for establishing a 50 bedded casualty will be taken forward in the IX  Plan.
Recommendation
10.2     To save a number of lives from head injuries the Director apprised the Committee that by making wearing of
helmets compulsory for two wheeler drivers all over the country, this problem can be solved to a large extent.  The
Committee feels that the suggestion is good and it should be looked into.
Action Taken
            Ministry of Surface Transport has reiterated instruction to all States/UTs Transport Commissioners for imposing
compulsory wearing of helmets by Two Wheeler drivers/pillion riders as prescribed under Section 129 of the Motor
Vehicles Act, 1988.

98th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/98threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:14]
Recommendation
10.3     The Committee has noted that the Institute does not get sufficient kits for HIV testing.  The Director informed
that National Aids Control Organisation (NACO) has been requested to increase the number of HIV kits supplied.  The
Committee feels that the Institute is in need of HIV Kits and NACO may increase the supply of HIV Kits.  The
Committee is, however, of the view that the Institute should not over-burden itself with treating HIV cases.
Action Taken
            NACO has provided sufficient HIV Kits to NIMHANS through State Government.  Further, patients of
HIV/AIDS having neurological and Psychiatric disorders are treated in NIMHANS.  Other AIDS patients are not treated
in NIMHANS.
            Recommendation
12.       There is a small unit under the control of Central Council of Ayurveda functioning in the Institute which is not a
part of NIMHANS.  The Committee was informed by the Director that there is a proposal to establish an advanced
centre of Ayurveda in the Institute.  The Committee, is, however,` of the opinion that the opening of advanced centre of
Ayurveda is an additional burden for the Institute.  Such a centre could be located elsewhere in an Ayurvedic Institute
and the patients requiring treatment in Ayurveda could be referred there.
Action Taken
            The proposal for setting up of advanced centre in Ayurveda at NIMHANS has been sanctioned by the
Department of ISM&H.  It is felt that patients should get the benefit of both the Ayurvedic System of medicine and the
Modern Allopathic system of Medicine.
Recommendation
13.1     The Committee was also informed that aid for development plans is received from many foreign countries such
as Germany, Japan, U.S.A. etc.  The Director pleaded that such aid should be made available to NIMHANS also.  The
Committee recommends that the Department of Health may look into the matter.
Action Taken
As and when such assistance is available all efforts would be made to make NIMHANS also a recipient of such
assistance.
 CHAPTER-III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
4.         Recommendation
            The Committee has noted that the Institute proposes to have collaboration with foreign universities and when
asked as to how far they are able to finalise the proposal, the Director informed the Committee that it has already
developed collaboration with a renowned University and for making further efforts in this direction the active support of
the Ministry of Human Resource Development is required.  The Committee feels that it is a premier Institute of its kind
in the country and collaboration with eminent and renowned foreign universities would further strengthen the Institute. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department  of Health should take up the matter with the Ministry of
HRD in this regard.
Action Taken
            The matter regarding collaboration with foreign  universities has been taken up with Ministry of Human
Resource Development.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee feels that collaboration with foreign universities  is very important because it provides additional
funds for being spent on plan-programmes.  The Committee is not satisfied with the effort of Department of Health in
this regard and strongly recommends that it should vigorously pursue the matter of foreign collaboration with the
Ministry of Human Resource Development.

98th Report of HRD

6.        Recommendation
            The Committee has noted that the Staff Position in the Institute is as under:-
                                               
 Sanctioned Working Vacant
Teaching 143 122 21
Non-teaching 830 737 93
            As regards the vacancies on teaching side it was stated that for five faculty posts, interviews were already held. 
It was also stated that 14 posts are reserved for SCs/STs and recruitment is under process under special recruitment
drive.  Action is being taken to fill up the remaining posts, it was added.  The Committee recommends that immediate
steps may be taken to fill up the posts reserved for SCs/STs.  The Committee also desires that the vacancies on the non-
teaching side also may be filled up at the earliest.  The Director also informed the Committee that some posts have to be
kept vacant due to paucity of funds.  The Committee views this with concern and strongly recommends that in future no
post should be kept vacant just because of paucity of funds.
Action Taken
            All reserved posts on the non-teaching side have been filled up.  As regards the faculty posts, the  Institute is
facing difficulties in filling up the reserved posts  even after resorting to a special recruitment drive.  The  Institute has
re-advertised the posts and is in the process of conducting interviews.
Further Comments
            The Committee specifically wanted to know whether the teaching posts in the reserved category were vacant due
to paucity of funds or non-availability of qualified candidates.  The Additional Secretary clarified that paucity of funds
was not the reason for vacancies in the teaching category.  It was the non availability of qualified candidates due to
which these posts were vacant.  It was informed that out of 21 vacant posts on the teaching side, 14 posts were reserved
for SCs/STs and candidates with adequate qualifications were not available in spite of repeated advertisements.  The
Secretary subsequently informed the Committee that as per the reservation policy they had to keep attempting, by way
of advertisements, to fill up the reserved posts.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee is anguished to note that in a prestigious institute like NIMHANS, which is a deemed university
and only one of its kind in the country, teaching has been allowed to be affected adversely for long because of non-
availability of suitable candidates from reserved category.  The Committee observes that such a situation cannot be
allowed to continue indefinitely, specially in a teaching institution.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that if
suitable candidates from reserved category are not available, the vacant posts should be filled up immediately on ad-hoc
basis, as per the guidelines laid down by Government of India.  The Committee may also be kept informed in the matter.
7.         Recommendation
            Research activity encompasses a large spectrum from cellular mechanisms to social systems associated with
various neurological and behavioural disorders.  However, the Committee learnt that it has not been possible to spend
adequate time for research in the Neuro-surgery Department.  When the Committee sought to know the reasons for this,
it was stated that the Department’s faculty are fully occupied with the operations and follow-up of the neuro-surgical
patients leaving them with very little time for research.  The gap can be bridged by increasing the staff strength, it was
added.  Neuro-surgery Department is a very important Department and research needs to be developed.  The
Department of Health may take necessary action to ensure that research activities are not hampered in the Neuro-surgery
Department.
Action Taken
            NIMHANS is initiating action to create posts by putting up proposals before the competent authorities.
Further Comments
            The Director General of Health Services was of the opinion that the operational type of research, namely, which
treatment is suited to what patient should be done by the surgeons themselves but basic research should be done by the

98th Report of HRD

Physiologists and Pathologists.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee was earlier informed that neuro-surgeons, being very busy with the operations and the follow up
of the neuro-surgical patients, generally did not find much time for research.  Therefore,  some research issues were
incorporated in the training programme of the Institution.  The Committee, however, is of the view that a surgeon due to
his or her direct exposure in handling neuro-surgical operations, has got lot of first hand practical experience which
ought to be put to optimum use while carrying out basic research.  The Committee expresses its reservations for creation
of posts for such purpose.
Recommendation
10.1     The Committee also learnt that people with even small accidents come from long distances for treatment  in the
hospital.  This would only increase the burden of the Institute.  For this, some kind of screening should be done at the
local level General Hospitals from where a case should be referred to NIMHANS only if it requires specialized
treatment.  For this,  the Committee feels that the matter should be taken up with the State Government requesting them
to issue necessary circular to the general hospitals stating that whenever head injury cases come, they have to examine
and admit unless it needs a special neuro-surgical intervention.  The Director assured the Committee that needful would
be done in the matter.  The Committee desires that it should be pursued by the Institute at regular intervals.
Action Taken
            The matter regarding reducing the patient load on NIMHANS by screening the patients in the General Hospitals
of the State Government has been taken up with the Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare, Govt. of
Karnataka, Bangalore.  They are in the process of establishing super-specialty hospital at Raichur.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee feels that NIMHANS should function as a referral Institute.  The matter should be taken up with
all the State Govts. that only such cases should be referred to the Institute which require special-neuro surgical
intervention.
13.       Recommendation
            The Committee noted that NIMHANS has been provided with Rs. 21.08 crores for 1996-97.  On being asked as
to whether this amount is sufficient to meet the requirements of the Institute, it was stated that a minimum of Rs. 30
crores was required.  The Director also informed the Committee that the main problem faced by the Institute is the lack
of funds for development.  The Institute needs special grants for this purpose, he stated.  Presently, the Institute is not
getting any grants from UGC and the Director requested that since it is a Deemed University it may also be given
development funds on the pattern of other Universities.  The Committee recommends that this may be considered.  He
further explained that in the routine grants, every year 10% growth is there and due to escalation of costs, they are not
able to meet the demand.  While the number of patients are increasing every year, the non-plan expenditure is kept at the
same level of 10% increase as per the Government norms.  Due to this, the Committee was told, the Institute has to keep
some posts vacant to have some non-plan money to spend for patient care.  The Committee is also constrained to note
that in view of this, it would be difficult to fill up all the posts and if all the posts are filled, there is no money for food
for patients, drugs and other hospital management.  The Committee feels that this would only hamper the activities of
the Institute from doing good work.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the full requirements of the Institute
may be taken care of by the Department of Health.  The Committee feels that NIMHANS, being the only National
Institute of its kind, should not starve for want of funds.  The Ministry should plead the case properly with the Finance
Ministry and Planning Commission for providing adequate funds.
Action Taken
            The Budgetary requirements of NIMHANS, Bangalore are met on a sharing basis by the Central Government
and the Government of Karnataka.  While the sharing of Plan funds by the Centre and State Government is 75% and
25%, for non-Plan funds it is 45% and 55% respectively.  Therefore, any increase in Central funds will have to be
matched by increase in State funds to the Institute.
            The budgetary allocation for NIMHANS, Bangalore during the last five years from Govt. of India has been as
under:

                        The Institute has been advised to take up the matter with the University Grant Commission for

Further Comments
            Clarifying the matter of  contribution by the Karnataka Government to meet the Budgetary requirements of
NIMHANS, the Secretary replied that earlier NIMHANS was a mental hospital under the Government of Karnataka
which was later taken over by the Government of India and upgraded as a National Institute.  It was further clarified by
the Secretary that as per the agreement at the time of taking over the Karnataka Government was to put in one third of
the money and the Government of India was to put in two third.  The Secretary also stated that NIMHANS being an
autonomous body did not require matching funds from the state government.  Furthermore, the Central Government has
been contributing larger percentage towards plan as well as non-plan budget over the years.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes that the Central Government is meeting its part of financial obligation, so far as
NIMHANS is concerned.  The Committee is of the view that since NIMHANS has been taken over by the Central
Government and  upgraded as a National Institute, it has, therefore, the sole responsibility to ensure its smooth and
proper functioning.  Efforts should by made to make required funds available for the  Institute.
Recommendations
The Committee was surprised to find that different methods were being followed in the case of committed
expenditure of the previous plan.  According to the understanding of the Committee, committed expenditure will not get
reflected in any shape or form in the subsequent plan.  What is termed as a non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan
becomes relevant only to the expenditure of new non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan period.  This applies in
the case of both autonomous as well as deemed university institutions.  In order to get further clarification in the matter
the Secretary and the Financial Advisor of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare were specially called to clarify as
to whether this view of the Committee is correct or not.  The Secretary could not come because of illness.  The Financial
Advisor appeared before the Chairman and he confirmed that the non-plan committed expenditure of the previous plan
should not get reflected into the non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan.  He also confirmed that they are not
making any distinction between the Government institution and other autonomous and deemed university institutions
which   naturally means that the confusion which is prevailing in some of institutions in treating committed expenditure
as part of the new non-plan expenditure should be clarified by the department concerned to all the institutions in the
country so that there should be uniformity in matters of procedure of not including the committed non-plan expenditure
in the subsequent plan’s non-plan expenditure.
Action Taken
            Specific guidelines of Planning Commission in this regard have been brought to the notice of all institutions
under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

98th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/98threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:14]
Recommendations
13.3     The Committee also noticed that in some of the Institutions where vacancies were available, they were utilizing
the funds meant for vacancies, for the purpose of non-plan expenditure, which according to the Committee is not a
desireable  feature.  Plan money can not be diverted for non-plan side or even the non-plan expenditure should not  have
any element of the scheme provided under the plan.  All the vacancies prevailing in different institutions will have to be
filled in against the non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan as the burden of the expenditure will not be there.
Action Taken
            The observations of the Committee have been noted for guidance.
Further Comments
            The Financial Advisor informed the Committee that in respect of transfer of committed liability, the Department
had taken up the matter with the Ministry of Finance and got the following response:-
“The proposal of the Department of Health has been considered and it has been decided with the approval of
Secretary (Expenditure), that a provision of additional Rs. 110 crores to the Department of Health under non-plan in lieu
of transfer of a committed liability of various Eighth plan schemes will be considered at RE stage by making an equal
cut in the Plan Outlay”.
            It was further clarified that in case of the Department of Health, the total committed liability of Rs. 110 crores
had been shifted from plan to non-plan side.  Out of this, the committed liability of NIMHANS was Rs. 5.13 crores
which had been shifted to Non-Plan side.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee expresses deep anguish at the entire approach, which is not only totally against the
recommendations of the Finance Commission but also against the mandate of the Constitution.  The Committee has
been repeatedly and strongly observing regarding committed liability but this issue has not been sorted  out as yet.  It
once again reiterates its earlier observation and hopes that the issue will be sorted out at the earliest in consultation with
the concerned Ministries/Departments.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT

Recommendation
3.1        The Committee is constrained to note that funds granted to the States are not utilized fully.   The matter of low
utilization of funds has been of grave concern at all  levels.  The main problem is that State AIDS Prevention Organisations
(SAPO) face a number of difficulties in receiving and utilizing funds due to the current financial system at the State level.   The
major hindrance is that they do not have the direct power to spend the money and yet are accountable for it under the project. 
This is  a peculiar system and needs to be changed immediately.   The country is facing such a gigantic task of dealing with the
problem of AIDS and frivolous matters such as delayed release of funds etc.   should not hinder the implementation of the
project.   The Committee strongly recommends that the Centre in coordination with the States should take all required steps to
see that funds flow smoothly to the grass root level for successful implementation of the programme.   The Committee was
given to understand that the funds were released by State Finance Department at the last moment or sometimes at the end of the
current financial year.   The Committee feels that this kind of situation should not prevail any more.   The funds should be
released in advance, at least six months before, and on receiving the expenditure certificate, the next instalment may be released
immediately.
Reply of Government
3.1        In the initial years of the National AIDS Control Programme there was some problem in release of funds by the State
Governments to programme managers.  However, from the year 1996-97 an improvement was observed in utilization of the
funds as shown in Annexure-1.   From the year 1998-99 State AIDS Control Societies have been constituted by the States/UTs
as per directives of the Central Government.  Funds are directly released to State AIDS Control Societies without channelising
through the Finance Department of State  Government.   By this mechanism, the delay, which was caused in release of funds
from State Finance Department to programme management, has been eliminated.
Recommendation
3.6               The Committee was given to understand that the  IEC material for strengthening awareness programme was reviewed 
and revised material has been finalized.   The Committee desires that a local scrutiny should be kept on the IEC materials being
used and whenever any review is made the State Government concerned should also be consulted.   There is also a necessity of
training the people who handle the IEC material and also those involved in making the audio and video programmes.  
Specialized skills are required for this and Government should consider strengthening the training programmes for every group
including NGOs.
Reply of Government
3.6               Generic material such as posters, pamphlets, booklets, films has been designed at the central level and disseminated to
the States, UTs, NGOs and the media thus ensuring broad coverage and quality and the correctness of the messages.   All the
IEC material is pre-tested before use.
NACO has finalized a nation wide training plan for different functionaries in the health department till the sub center
level and NGOs.   A major component of this training is IEC with emphasis on developing communication skills on HIV/AIDS.
Recommendation
3.7               The Committee is given to understand that care, support and medicines for people living with HIV/AIDS  is very
inadequate.  This is particularly in view of the social stigma attached with this infection and the affected persons being treated as
social outcast by the community as a whole.   Infected persons are also required   to be counseled to ensure that they take all
precautions to avoid any further infection to others.   For this, the Committee feels, highly skilled and efficient counseling and
education are required.  The Committee has the evidence to note that very few counseling centers are existing in the country.  
This counseling should have been started much earlier and the Committee is pained to note that much effort has not been done
in this direction.   Therefore, much more emphasis should be laid on this aspect and also on educating the general populace
about their behavioural pattern with the infected people.   Similarly, as already recommended earlier, medicines to the infected
people should be regularly ensured and government should provide sufficient budget for this purpose and assistance from
foreign agencies may be obtained, if need be.
Reply of Government
3.7               NACO is setting up counseling services across the country on a top priority basis to provide information about
HIV/AIDS and related issues, and to provide psychological support to those already infected.
Counseling  services are being provided in the following ways:-
National Counselling Training Programme

Setting up a comprehensive counseling support programme, including training of a wide variety of health care workers
and social and community workers through standard training module and materials  is an important aspect of this programme.  
The trainers comprise of both government and non-government officials who can integrate counseling on HIV/AIDS with their
ongoing programmes.   Training is conducted at two levels: intermediate and grassroots.   The main objective of the training
programme is to create a cadre of counsellors at the grassroots level.

Telephonic Counselling Services
NACO has set up a National AIDS Help line on a toll free number 1097.   Callers can avail of counseling services round
the clock on this number.   The telephone is linked to a computerized voice response system which gives information on various
issues related to HIV/AIDS such as the general information on HIV/AIDS, symptoms of HIV infection/AIDS, testing of HIV
and care and support services for those infected and affected by HIV/AIDS.   Interested callers can also avail of personal
counselling.
            These services are very  useful since they maintain the confidentiality of the caller.
Such services have already been successfully implemented in Delhi, Calcutta, Hyderabad, Chandigarh, Guwahati,
Chennai and Patna.
Counselling Services in Government Hospitals
A model HIV councelling center has been set up at the Department of Skin and STD, Safdajung Hospital.  The project is
a joint collaboration of NACO, STD Department of Safdarjung Hospital and six Delhi based NGOs.   The counselling center,
the first of its kind to be set up in a government hospital, has the following objective:
Counselling Services in Voluntary Testing Centres
Voluntary testing Centres have been set up in all Government hospitals.   It would be mandatory to have pre and post
test counseling in these centers.   The counseling services would be provided by a trained NGO.         
Further Comments    

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/99threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
When asked by the Committee , whether the Department is taking any step to open such model counseling centers in
different parts of the country,     the Department replied that it is proposed to set up voluntary testing and counseling centers in
all the district hospitals in the country on the basis of the model counseling center at Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi.  These
voluntary testing and counseling centers would be run by qualified and trained NGOs and would be funded by the concerned
State/UT/Corporation AIDS Control Societies.   Protocols and guidelines are also being  formulated for such centers.
Recommendation
3.8               The Committee is of the firm view that much emphasis under the AIDS control programme has not been so far laid on
the high risk behaviour groups like sex workers and frequently travelling males and drug users.   These are main groups which
are highly vulnerable to HIV/AIDS infection.   Awareness and counseling are much more required on these people than on the
other group of the society.   They should be made to understand the danger of the STD/HIV/AIDS and the risk factor involved
in not using condoms and taking other precautions.  Special awareness programme should be taken up particularly for sex
workers and frequently travelling males.
Reply of Government
3.8               NACO is implementing targeted intervention programmes to prevent the spread of infection in the high risk
marginalized population.   A multi pronged approach has been devised to contain further transmission of HIV within this group
or to other strata of society through them, as also to give health care and support services to those already infected.   A
combination of IEC strategies, including counselling, and relevant service provision, such as STD care and condoms, can be
used to create an enabling environment for people to scrutinize their behaviour and effect a change to protect themselves.
NACO is working with donor agencies in cooperation with the State Governments to conduct pilot programmes with
identified groups using an integrated approach.  Examples of successful targeted intervention programmes include Sonagachi
intervention project in Calcutta, Kamathipura Intervention project in Bombay and Continuum of care project in Manipur.   In the
second phase of the AIDS control project these targetted intervention programmes would be scaled up to cover vulnerable
populations in all states.
Recommendation
3.10      The Committee has learnt that various international agencies are implementing various programmes in different parts of
the country for tackling the problem of HIV/AIDS.   In this connection the Committee is constrained to note that NACO is not
involved in the implementation of all the projects in all parts of the country.  For example even though many pilot programmes
are being implemented in Tamil Nadu, NACO is involved with the implementation of only USAID Project.   The Committee
recommends that  NACO should be involved in the implementation of all pilot projects in all parts of the country so that it has
complete information about the implementation of all the projects.
Reply of Government
3.10      A steering committee has been formed in all the states where bilateral agencies are implementing intervention projects.  
These steering committees have a representative from NACO as well as the Project Director of the State AIDS Societies as
members.   The steering committee meets regularly and all decisions are taken in consultation with the representatives of the
Central and State Governments.
Recommendation
3.11      The  Committee is constrained to note that many states were performing very slow and the World Bank Mission in its
mid term review in 1995 recommended discontinuance of credit to such states.   The Committee was given to understand that
the reasons for slow performance were non-adherence to action plan, non-availability of infrastructure, political and social
problems.  It also appears that many states do not perceive the AIDS Control Programme as their own concern.   The
Empowered Committees of the States have also not been effective and have little control over initiating activities.   The
Committee perceives that there is still lack of awareness and enthusiasm in the states.   If the State Governments do not rise to
the occasion and pool in all the sources and energies available with them, it would be difficult to tackle the problems of
AIDS/HIV either by the Central Government or any international agency.   It is the State Governments which are nearer to the
people and which implement the programme.   They should therefore, be more concerned about the problem.   The Central
Government should, therefore, seriously consider this aspect.
 
Reply of Government
3.11            In order to develop ownership of the programme in States/UTs, State AIDS Societies have been constituted under the
Chairpersonship of Health Secretary.   The Society also includes representatives of NGOs as well as other related departments

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/99threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
for effective coordination and implementation of the programme.   There is complete decentralization of the programme activity
to State level.   The role of the Central Government is only to provide technical expertise and policy guidelines.   The society
model will also ensure expeditious flow of funds from Central Government to programme implementation in the states.
Recommendation
3.12            The Committee was informed that efforts were being made to introduce AIDS education in the Schools.   It is true that
young people in India are equally vulnerable to HIV infection and they are also required to be educated in proper atmosphere.  
Inclusion of AIDS education as a part of the curriculum is of course one of the best alternatives to increase awareness about it.  
The Committee desires that it should be finalized as early as possible and it should be introduced from the academic year 1998-
99 onwards.
Reply of Government
3.12      Special programmes are being broadcast for the youth and rural/migrant populations on All India Radio FM and Vividh
Bharti respectively.   These programmes are in the entertainment mode with the objective of creating awareness and counseling
those who have specific queries or problems.   The programme on Vividh Bharti is broadcast in 11 regional languages.
A School AIDS Education Prograamme has been initiated to provide life skills education to high school students with a
component on HIV/AIDS.   The plan advocates a co-curricular approach in implementing School AIDS education.   It is
proposed to cover all the schools in a planned manner over the next five years.   The main components of the plan are advocacy
for opinion leaders, sensitization workshop for school principals, training of model teachers and peer education and school level
activities.
NACO  has also approached NCERT who have agreed to include information on HIV/AIDS in the curriculum.
Recommendation
3.14      The main concern facing the world community now is non-development of any vaccine for HIV/AIDS so far.   Many
countries are still in the process of research on this.   However, the Committee is constrained to note that no research on
development of vaccine for this has been initiated in India so far.   The Committee desires that our country also should
contribute its own mite, for it may so happen that the research conducted in India may ultimately lead to success.
Reply of Government
3.14      The Department of Biotechnology, Department of Science and Technology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences,
Delhi, National AIDS Research Institute, Pune and National Institute of Immunology, Delhi are involved in research in HIV
vaccine.   The Govt. of India encourages research in this field.
Recommendation
5.4         The Committee views with concern that mass awareness about Hepatitis B has not yet been taken up by the
Department.   People need to be educated about Hepatitis B virus the way it is being done in the case of HIV.   The IEC
activities in this regard need to be stepped up, and the Department should make use of all modes of IEC to spread the message
about Hepatitis B.   Special efforts need to be taken by the Department especially in the rural areas where people are still
unaware of it.  Steps should also be taken to print Pamphlets in the vernacular languages to address the issue among the rural
people.   NGOs can be successfully involved in this awareness campaign.
Reply of Government
5.4        Central Health Education Bureau, a subordinate office of the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health
and Family Welfare has undertaken a mass campaign to enlighten the public about the protection from viral Hepatitis (Jaundice)
by distribution of one lakh handbills to (1) State Health Education Bureau; (2)Directors of Health Services; (3) Department of
Prevention and Social Medicine (Medical Colleges); (4) Assistant Directors of Health Services; (5) National Medical Libraries;
(6) District Medical Offices; (7) Councils and Institute of India (Health); (8) Subscribers of Swasth Hind and Arogya Sandesh;
and (9) distributed to general public in the Family Welfare Pavilion during India International  Trade Fair 99. A press
advertisement on the subject was also given in the leading newspapers from 17th July to 3rd August, 1997 all over India.
Information, Education and Communication is an important component of the National AIDS Control Programme. 
Various communication media like electronic, print inter-personal communication and folk media etc. are being
intensively used for dissemination of information on HIV/AIDS.

Recommendation
3.5               The Committee is aware that there is no cure for AIDS.  Prevention is the only aspect which has to be strengthened. 
For prevention a large scale public awareness is required.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the  awareness
programme has not picked up in India.  Even though the problem of AIDS is enveloping the whole country, the Committee has
come to note that the literature prepared and the programmes initiated are neither related to the local needs of the people nor the
local dialects.  Half of India’s population is illiterate.  One aspect on which one can feel happy is that the AIDS syndrome has
not yet touched, in a bigger way, the horizons of the rural areas.  This is, therefore the area which is to be protected with very
well chalked out programmes.  The programmes to be launched should take into view the local people’s conditions, their
cultural behaviour and the language.  Unless the message transmitted is not properly received the whole effort will go waste. 
The Committee strongly recommends the Department to give a serious consideration on this.  The Committee is of the view that
in the awareness programme, participation of NGOs, students, local bodies etc. should be given preference to the maximum
extent because these are the groups which can effectively transmit the message through the language understandable to the local
community.

3.5        During the last five years, the National AIDS Control Programme has successfully created awareness among the public
about HIV/AIDS through mass media campaigns, community mobilization and HIV/AIDS education in schools and colleges. 
All media of communication, including interpersonal communication are being used to disseminate AIDS prevention messages
in rural and urban areas.  The State Governments conduct awareness programmes through mass media campaigns as well as
traditional art forms in order to ensure that awareness programmes are in the local medium and bear the regional sensitivities in
mind.
The National AIDS Control Organisation also provides budgetary support to the media units under the aegis of Ministry of
Information and Broadcasting, viz. Doordarshan, All India Radio.  Song and Drama Division, Directorate of Field Publicity,
Press Information Bureau and Films Division.

                      The Directorate of Field Publicity has a network of 260 Field Units spread over all States and Union Territories.  All

-                      The Song and Drama Division organizes dance-drama shows and folk media performances in rural areas through its
regional centres.
-                      The Directorate of Advertising and Visual Publicity (DAVP) produced more than a dozen video spots and jingles.

-
                      Generic material such as posters, pamphlets, booklets, films has been designed at the central level and disseminated to

-                      NACO is collaborating with the Department of Women and Child Development to integrate HIV/AIDS awareness with

Recommendation
3.2              The Committee is pained to note that a number of States have not filled in the sanctioned posts.   The reason given that
this has been done in view of the fact that the National AIDS Control Programme is a time bound project, is not convincing to
the Committee.   The Committee feels that this aspect could have been tackled by the Centre in a better manner by convincing
the states about the importance of the programme and the necessity of creation of the posts and a via-media for the continuance
of the posts created could have been found out.   It is surprising for the Committee that the Department has not done anything in

posts as are required.
Reply of Government
3.2        In the first phase of the National AIDS Control Programme, 17 posts were sanctioned in large states and 11 posts in
small states/UTs for programme management at state level but due to various reasons, these posts could not be filled by the
State Governments.   Government of India had reminded states/UTs in this regard from time to time.
For the effective implementation of second phase of National AIDS Control Programme, Government of India has
sanctioned 47 posts for major States, 39 for medium States and 27 for small States/UTs which also includes posts to be filled on
contractual basis.  The States are in the process of filling up these posts.   All the States/UTs have given an undertaking to fill up
the sanctioned posts.

The Committee was informed that out of 1143 posts sanctioned under NACP Phase II, which started in
November, 1999, 542 posts have already been filled up till June, 2000.  The Committee is, however, disturbed to note that
information with regard to vacancy position in respect of States/UTs like Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Tripura and D

medium states, number of posts filled up so far is very less.  The Committee has been given to understand that the main
reasons for vacant posts are non-availability of suitable candidates in some states as well as the time taken in filling up
the posts either through deputation or on contract.  There has also been some reluctance on the part of the States to fill

            The Committee feels that given the menace of AIDS, which will only increase in future, the approach of Central
Govt. would not do any good to the morale of the persons who are instrumental in the implementation of the programme
at grass root level.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier observation that this aspect could have been tackled
by the Govt. in a better manner by convincing the States about the importance of the Programme and the urgent

necessity of creation of posts.  The Committee once again emphasises that keeping in view the financial  status of State
Govts. a via-media for continuance of the posts beyond the Project Period has to be found out by the Govt. without any
further delay. 
 
 
Recommendation
3.3               The Committee was given to understand that IMA and NACO are making a combined effort to train general medical
practitioners for clinical management of AIDS  and HIV infected persons.   The training given is too less to cover a chunk of
general physicians in the country, particularly in the states where AIDS and HIV are rampant.   A large-scale training to the
physicians and nurses is required so that they may be able to effectively tackle the patients.   The Committee is also given to
understand that many physicians and nurses do not turn up or attend to the HIV and AIDS patients mainly because of the lack of
general awareness and the skills to treat and tackle them.   Therefore, the Department should chalk out a massive scheme to
cover, at least once, for some period for training most of the general physicians in the major cities of the country.   Nurse

Reply of Government
3.3        Government of India has chalked out a comprehensive training programme to cover medical and para-medical workers
including nurses to train them in prevention and control of HIV and AIDS.   A programme for training of General Medical
Practitioners was also developed for which a sum of Rs. 37 lakhs was sanctioned  to central office of Indian Medical
Association.  So  far, they have trained 7500 physicians in different parts of the country.   The association is being requested to
take up more training programmes.   Besides  Indian Medical Association, Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI) and
Voluntary Health Association of India (VHAI) had also taken up training programmes for general medical practitioners on HIV

AIDS cases and their counselling.   In order to update the knowledge of Medical Practitioners on management of Sexually
Transmitted Diseases, 1.5 lakh booklets on Syndromic Management on Sexually Transmitted Diseases have been mailed to all
the members of Indian Medical Association.
            During second phase of National AIDS Control Programme, three tier saturation Training Programme has been
initiated.  At tertiary health care line, which includes medical colleges/regional institutions, persons have been trained.  To each

Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been informed that during the IInd Phse of NACP, 4412 doctors(specialists/medical officers),
5874 nurses and 5948 para-medicals have been trained at various levels by States/UTs and other organisations like Steel
Authority of India Limited (SAIL), Railways, ESI Corporation etc.  The Committee also finds that in majority of the
States, medical personnel have been trained as `Core Trainers’.  However, as per the figures furnished to the Committee,
States/UTs like Andhra Pradesh, Lakshadeep, Maharashtra, Pondicherry, Tripura and West Bengal have not taken any
initiative in this regard.  What is more disturbing is that in States/UTs like Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, J & K, Karnataka,
Kerala, M.P., Meghalaya, Nagaland, Orissa, U.P., D & N Haveli, Damman and Diu, work of training of Medical
Peronnel seems to have ended with the grooming of Core Trainers.  Not only this, a very negligible number of
medical/paramedical personnel have been trained in HIV/AIDS so far and that too is concentrated in very few states of
the Country.  The Committee is constrined to observe that training which is the most vital component of AIDS Control
Programme seems to be still in the initial stages.  It is all the more essential and urgent in view of inherent reservations
in the minds of a large number of doctors and nurses to handle HIV/AIDS patients.  While appreciating the role of
Indian Medical Association (IMA), Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI) and Voluntary Health Association of
India (VHAI), the Committee strongly feels that private organisations alone cannot handle this massive programme. 
Co-ordinated effort with an active role to be played by both Central and State Govts. would be the ideal position. 
Monitoring of the training programme at regular intervals is bound to achieve the desired results.
Recommendation
3.4               The Committee understands that blood banks are the area which needs to be strengthened and modernized for securing
safe blood supply.  Blood banks are the place from where infected blood is donated and transfused.   The Committee is,

however, constrained to note that many blood banks in the public sector are yet to be taken up for modernisation to achieve the

supply of safe blood.   The Committee also feels the necessity of a regular monitoring of the public sector blood banks on any

3.4        Government of India has provided for modernization of 727 blood banks in public sector and 88 blood banks in
voluntary sector.   It is mandatory for all the blood banks to obtain license from Drug Controller General of India before making

donation since 1.1.98.   It is mandatory for each licensed blood bank to test blood units for HIV, Hepatitis B, Syphilis and
Malaria.   For the monitoring of the proper functioning of blood banks in States there is the Department of Food and Drugs,
which conducts regular inspections of these blood banks, and the renewal of annual license is recommended by them on the
basis of their inspection reports.   State AIDS Control Societies are also conducting regular visits of the blood banks in their
respective states to maintain the quality of these blood banks.
Further Comments
On a specific query about the number of blood banks, whose licenses have not been renewed during the last five years
and the nature of irregularities found during the inspection, the Committee was informed that in the last five years, 176 license

deficiencies/irregularities were : I) inadequate storage facility ii) deficiency in testing procedure and facility iii) suspected
dependence on professional paid blood donors iv) lack of qualified technical personnel, etc.
Comments of the Committee
While noting that blood-related infection has come down from 8 percent to 4 percent, the Committee is of the
view that the role played by blood banks both in public and private sector is very vital in the containment of HIV/AIDS. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that expeditious steps should be taken by the Department to modernize all the
licensed blood banks both in public and private sector.  The Committee, while appreciating the appointment of a Joint
Controller of Blood Safety on a full time basis in every AIDS Control Society in the Country, is of the view that an
effective monitoring mechanism needs to be built up without any delay.  This is all the more essential in the case of
private blood banks which are alleged to be entertaining professional donors in large numbers.  Both regular and
random checks should be carried out to be followed by remedial measures.  The Committee notes that voluntary blood
donation is increasing  gradually.  The Committee, however, feels that with the active involvement of voluntary agencies,
public awareness can be increased in this regard.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
take effective steps in this matter.
Recommendation

NACO also organized a National Workshop with NGOs on HIV/AIDS.  The workshop which was held on 15-16
th
January, 98 was attended by representatives of 150 NGOs, bilateral and UN agencies.  The main objective of this National level
workshop was to involve the NGOs inthe policy framework of the second phase of the programme by re-examining the

medicines that are available are only to give temporary relief.  Even those medicines are not available to a large number of

and Family Welfare that there is no company which is importing the drugs.  Even if the Government does not want to introduce
the drugs for treatment, efforts should at least be made to ensure the availability of the drugs in the market.   The Committee
recommends that the Government should consider this and see that medicines which are available in other parts of the world are

3.13            Under the National AIDS Control programme, funds are provided to states and UTs for the management of
opportunistic infections in HIV/AIDS patients.   As far as the Anti-Retro-viral drugs are concerned,  they are not provided under

market.
Government of India has provided funds to Central Council of Research on Homeopathy for conducting trials of homeopathy

The Committee notes that drugs like Azidothymidine, Lamivudine, Indinavir, Saquinavir and Ritonaviv etc. for
treatment of AIDS/HIV are available in the market. However, the Committee apprehends that these drugs due to their
prohibitive cost must be out of the reach of majority of patients.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that serious
efforts need to be made by the Govt. so as to ensure the availability of these drugs in India at a cheaper cost.  If need be,
Patent Laws should be looked into for finding a solution to this problem.
 The Committee notes that funds have been provided for conducting research to study the efficacy of
homoeopathy and Sidha drugs in management of HIV/AIDS cases.  The Committee hopes that this research work would
lead to some positive results for HIV/AIDS Patients.
Recommendation
5.1        The Committee is constrained to note that the country has 40 million carriers of HBV and the Government has not
woken up yet to meet the challenge.  Even though some steps have been taken by the Department, they are far from adequate. 
The Committee is of the view that prevention is better than cure.  During the course of its interaction with experts, it was
emphasised again and again that mass vaccination was the only foolproof method for eradication of this ever spreading disease. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be taken up by the Government, on a large scale and steps should be taken
by the Government to include it in the universal immunisation programme.  Taking into account the fact that WHO has
recommended that countries with a carrier prevalence of 2 percent and above should consider inclusion of HBV in routine
immunisation programme for infants and as India has a prevalence of 4 percent, the Committee feels that vaccination
programme should be started without further delay.

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
