Recommendation
5.2 This measure becomes all the more necessary keeping in view the fact that infants and young children who generally have
mild infection, can become life-long carriers without showing any symptoms all along.  And after 20-25 years about 25 percent
of chronic carriers can develop hepatitis cirrhosis (liver failure) and liver cancer.  The Committee feels that successful
implementation of pulse polio programme can be taken up as a role model for starting vaccination programme for Hepatitis B. 
The Committee is constrained to note that the proposal to include vaccination against Hepatitis B can only be implemented if
adequate resources become available during the 9 th plan.  The Committee feels that this is a sorry state of affairs.  Government
has to provide sufficient funds during 9th plan period, if future generations are to be saved. 
Reply of Government
5.1. Since health is a State subject, it is the responsibility of the State Government to take measures for the prevention of all
diseases.  However,  Hepatitis B was considered in the Department of Family Welfare for inclusion in the Immunization
Programme while formulating Plan of Action for the 9th Plan.  The initial estimate which was worked out is as follows:-
a.             Estimated no. of newborn - 2.5 crore
b.             No. of doses to be administered - 3 doses.
c.             No. of doses required including wastage - 10.00 crore
d.             Approx. cost per dose at international rate - Rs.50/-
e.             Total fund requirement - Rs. 500 crores/year.
 
However, the Planning Commission had indicated that additional allocation of funds will not be possible.  Therefore, the same
could not be included in the final plan of action of the 9
th Plan.
The Department of Family Welfare is still actively involved in the consultation process with experts, Indian Council of
Medical Research, International Organizations for modalities of introduction of the vaccine, and also looking for the funding
sources from World Bank etc.
Further Comments
            In reply to a question as to what efforts have so far been made by the Department to generate additional funds,   the
Department replied that introduction of Hepatitis B in the Universal Immunization Programme  (UIP) has not been possible due
to the enormous financial implication of such a step.   The Planning Commission has stated that funds will have to be found
within the existing plan resources of the Department of Health for the 9 th Plan.   While steps are being explored for formulating
a pilot project, including Hepatitis B under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) is a step which will require large
scale resource mobilization.   This does not appear to be feasible during the 9th plan period.
Comments of the Committee
 The Committee is of the view that Hepatitis B is even more dangerous that AIDS in terms of its             infectious
nature and spread amongst 40 million people.   Mass vaccination is the only fool proof method for preventing this ever
spreading disease.   The Committee, therefore,  reiterates its recommendation that the Department should not only
pursue this matter with the Planning Commission but it should also look for funds from other sources.
Recommendation
5.3        The Committee feels that apart from vaccination there are some other areas where there is a chance of spreading HBV
which cannot be ignored like rampant use of unsterilised syringes in hospitals.   This unethical practice was more rampant in
rural areas.   Mere issuing guidelines to state authorities for the use of a separate sterile syringe and needle for each injection
would not suffice.   The Committee feels that stringent measures are required to check this dangerous practice.   Steps should
also be taken to educate the general masses about fatal consequences of such use of unsterlised syringes.
Reply of Government
5.3        National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) has initiated a comprehensive training programme for all categories of
the Health Care Workers on universal precautions to prevent the spread of HIV, Hepatitis 'B' and other blood borne infections in
all Government hospitals/Health Centers.  Besides, the information on this aspect is also being disseminated to the community
through media.

Further Comments
TheCommittee specifically wanted to knowthe measures taken by the Govt. to ensure the use of separate sterile syringe
and needle for each injection.  The Department replied that the following two measures have been takenso far:-
-                      instructions issued  by DGHS toall Central Govt. hospitals as well as State Govts. for use of separate sterile
syringe and needle for each injection .
-                      Training of doctors , nurses and para-medical personnel of hospitals etc regarding the use of separate syringes
and needles for each injection under the AIDS programme.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the view that these instructions lack the necessary  teeth to stop the unethical practice of use of 
unsterilised syringes in hospitals. Moreover, the Committee also feels that merely by issuing instructions to the hospitals
or by training doctors and para-medicals, this unethical practice perhaps would not be contained.  Hence, it reiterates its
earlier observation that stringent measures are required to check this dangerous practice.    The Committee feels that
exemplary punishment to defaulters would set an example for others.  Steps should also be taken to educate the general
masses about fatal consequences of use of unsterlised syringes and needles.  The Committee is also of the view that an
effective monitoring mechanism of random checks to be carried out right from PHCs to big hospitals in the cities can
yield the desired results.

States, medical personnel have been trained as `Core Trainers’.  However, as per the figures furnished to the Committee,
States/UTs like Andhra Pradesh, Lakshadeep, Maharashtra, Pondicherry, Tripura and West Bengal have not taken any
initiative in this regard.  What is more disturbing is that in States/UTs like Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, J & K, Karnataka,
Kerala, M.P., Meghalaya, Nagaland, Orissa, U.P., D & N Haveli, Damman and Diu, work of training of Medical
Peronnel seems to have ended with the grooming of Core Trainers.  Not only this, a very negligible number of
medical/paramedical personnel have been trained in HIV/AIDS so far and that too is concentrated in very few states of
the Country.  The Committee is constrined to observe that training which is the most vital component of AIDS Control
Programme seems to be still in the initial stages.  It is all the more essential and urgent in view of inherent reservations

in the minds of a large number of doctors and nurses to handle HIV/AIDS patients.  While appreciating the role of
Indian Medical Association (IMA), Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI) and Voluntary Health Association of
India (VHAI), the Committee strongly feels that private organisations alone cannot handle this massive programme. 
Co-ordinated effort with an active role to be played by both Central and State Govts. would be the ideal position. 
Monitoring of the training programme at regular intervals is bound to achieve the desired results. (Para 3.3)
Comments of the Committee
While noting that blood-related infection has come down from 8 percent to 4 percent, the Committee is of the
view that the role played by blood banks both in public and private sector is very vital in the containment of HIV/AIDS. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that expeditious steps should be taken by the Department to modernize all the
licensed blood banks both in public and private sector.  The Committee, while appreciating the appointment of a Joint
Controller of Blood Safety on a full time basis in every AIDS Control Society in the Country, is of the view that an
effective monitoring mechanism needs to be built up without any delay.  This is all the more essential in the case of
private blood banks which are alleged to be entertaining professional donors in large numbers.  Both regular and
random checks should be carried out to be followed by remedial measures.  The Committee notes that voluntary blood
donation is increasing  gradually.  The Committee, however, feels that with the active involvement of voluntary agencies,
public awareness can be increased in this regard.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
take effective steps in this matter.       (Para 3.4)
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes that a directory of NGOs working on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Control has been
developed by NACO which is being continuously updated.  While appreciating the various measures taken by NACO for
participation of NGOs, the Committee has a word of caution.  It has been observed that NGOs are by and large
concentrated in Metropolitan cities so as to get wider publicity for their activities.  The Committee feels that NGOs
should also come forward to work in rural areas as the menace of AIDS has started affecting rural masses also.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made by the Govt. so as to encourage NGOs to work both in
urban and rural areas.  While encouraging the participation of NGOs in AIDS Prevention and Control Programme, an
effective monitoring mechanism for supervising their activities also needs to be evolved so that only those NGOs
performing well remain in the field.    (Para 3.9)
Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes that drugs like Azidothymidine, Lamivudine, Indinavir, Saquinavir and Ritonaviv etc. for
treatment of AIDS/HIV are available in the market. However, the Committee apprehends that these drugs due to their
prohibitive cost must be out of the reach of majority of patients.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that serious
efforts need to be made by the Govt. so as to ensure the availability of these drugs in India at a cheaper cost.  If need be,
Patent Laws should be looked into for finding a solution to this problem.
 The Committee notes that funds have been provided for conducting research to study the efficacy of
homoeopathy and Sidha drugs in management of HIV/AIDS cases.  The Committee hopes that this research work would
lead to some positive results for HIV/AIDS Patients. (Para 3.13)
Comments of the Committee
 The Committee is of the view that Hepatitis B is even more dangerous that AIDS in terms of its            
infectious nature and spread amongst 40 million people.   Mass vaccination is the only fool proof method for preventing
this ever spreading disease.   The Committee, therefore,  reiterates its recommendation that the Department should not
only pursue this matter with the Planning Commission but it should also look for funds from other sources.  (Para 5.1)
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the view that these instructions lack the necessary  teeth to stop the unethical practice of use
of  unsterilised syringes in hospitals. Moreover, the Committee also feels that merely by issuing instructions to the
hospitals or by training doctors and para-medicals, this unethical practice perhaps would not be contained.  Hence, it
reiterates its earlier observation that stringent measures are required to check this dangerous practice.    The Committee
feels that exemplary punishment to defaulters would set an example for others.  Steps should also be taken to educate the
general masses about fatal consequences of use of unsterlised syringes and needles.  The Committee is also of the view
that an effective monitoring mechanism of random checks to be carried out right from PHCs to big hospitals in the cities
can yield the desired results. (Para 5.3)

REPORT 
The Ministry of Human Resource Development was created in 1985 for integrating all 
efforts for the development of human potential in the areas of education, culture, youth and 
sports, women and children. 
The Department of Education is responsible for universalisation of Elementary Education 
(UEE) , adult education, equalisation of educational opp9rtunities, women's education and 
development , vocationalisation of school education, consolidation of higher education, 
modernisation of technical education, improvement of quality, content and process of 
education at all levels. 
The functions of Department of Education are to evolve educational policy in all its 
aspects and to coordinate and determine the standard in higher education including research. 
This Department is also responsible to expand and develop technical education, to improve 
quality of textbooks, to administer scholarships and other schemes, to foster and encourage 
studies and research in Sanskrit and other classical languages, to develop activities in the 
field of non-formal education , to promote adult education and to co-ordinate pro·grammes of 
assistance and other activities with UNESCO. 
The Department of Education had been classified under the following major heads:-
A. Elementary Education 
B. School and Physical Education 
C. University and Higher Education 
D. Adult Education 
E. Scholarships 
F. Book Promotion 
G. Hindi 
H. Modern Indian Languages 
I. Sanskrit 
J. Technical Education 
K. Indian National Commission for Cooperation with UNESCO. 
L. Education Planning. 
The Ministry has sought an outlay of Rs. 850.01 crore for non-plan expenditure and 
Rs. 1309.30 crore for plan expenditure making· a total of Rs. 2159.31 crore which accounts 
for 25.16 per cent increase in the revised estimates for the year 1992-93. For the educational 
development of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes about 13 per cent of the divisible 
outlay for the year 1993-94 has been allocated for special component Plan for Scheduled 
Castes and 10 per cent for special component plan for Scheduled Tribes. They account for 
5 per cent and 4 per cent of the total outlay of the Department of Education. 
Inspite of the efforts made in the field of education the country has not so far achieved 
the·set targets. Yet , there are some positive indicators which cannot be set aside. The 1991 
census results reveal a literacy rate of over 52 per cent, with a higher rate. of growth for 
female literacy. All necessary steps may be taken to achieve the broader goal of 'Education 
for All' (EFA) by 2000 A.D. 

DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION (1993-94) 
Demand No. 47 
The various heads of expenditure in the Demands for grants and relevant clarifications 
mentioned in the documents together with the views of the Secretary and other officials of 
the Ministry are dealt with in the succeeding paragraphs. 
I. ELEMENTARY EDUCATION 
The Schemes of Elementary Education are being implemented mainly through State 
Govern ments and Union Territories. 
Over the years, the Centre and the States have made considerable investments in 
promoting elementary educa tion. As a result 94.06 per cent of the rural population are being 
served with Prim ary Schools/Sections within a walking distance of 1 kilometer and 85.39 per 
cent of them are being served with middle school/section within a distance of 3 kms. 
The Eighth Plan outlay on Education (Centre and States) at Rs. 19599.7 crore is higher 
than the Seventh Plan expenditure of Rs. 7632.9 crore by 2.6 times. Within the 'plan outlay 
there is a marked shift in the inter se allocation of resources for education. The outlay on 
elementary education increased from 33 percent in the Sixth Plan to 37.33 per cent in the 
Seventh Plan and to 46.95 per cent in the Eighth Plan. 
A. Operation Blackboard 
The Scheme of Operation Blackboard which was started in 1987-88 was launched to bring 
about a substant ial qualitative improvement in the primary school environment. The Scheme 
was to be implemented in three phases and aimed at providing (i) a building comprising at 
least two reasonably large all weather rooms with a deep verandah and separate toilet 
facilities for boys and girls (ii) at least two teachers in every school, as for as possible one of 
them a woman and (iii) essential teaching-learning material including balckboards, maps, 
charts. toys and equ ipment for work experience. Funds .for construction of school buildings 
are provided mainly from rural development schemes. Funds for the other two components 
are provided by the Depart ment of Education. 
The first phase of the Scheme (1987-88) has been evaluated by various agencies. The 
findings reveal inter-alia that the Programme has resulted in the creation of better 
infrastructure. Woman teachers were fotlnd to be more knowledgeable and were using the 
aids more frequ ently than men justifying the important provision in the Operation 
Blackboard Scheme that the second teacher added to the Schoo l should prefe rably be a 
woman. However, the prescribed norms regarding classroom size, verandahs, toilets etc. 
have not been performed , there was also no quality check on the items that were supplied . 
The evaluation reports provided the following valuable feedback on which the programme 
is sought to be modified:-
(a) Flexibility in the Scheme for purchase of equipment. 
(b) Qua lity Control mechanism to ensure good quality material. 
(c) Strengthening teacher training programmes to maximise the utilisation of equipment. 
(d) Ensuring that 50% of the teachers are women. 
It is also proposed to expand the Operation Black Board Scheme towards the later part of 
the Eighth Five Year Plan period to provide three teachers and three rooms where 
enrolment exceeds 80. 
In order to achieve the objective Rs. 149.53 crores , 175.53 crores, and 175.17 crores have 

been spent in the years 1990-92, 1991-92 al)d 1992-93 respect ively and Rs. 179 crores have 
been allocate<:l during the year 1 993-94. 
Durin g the period from 1987-88 to 1991-92, 5376 blocks (84%) having 413546 (76.96%) 
primary schools in the country have been covered and 8% blocks would be covered in 1992-
93 and the remaining 8% are propo~cd to be ·covered by 1993-94. 
The Committ ee is of the opinion that the number of schools in rural areas may be 
increased. Proper buildings for schools, ade quate number of teachers and other essential 
facilities may be provided. 
The Committ ee also expresses deep concern over the high drop out rate of Scheduled 
Tribes and Scheduled Castes students, which is Scheduled Tribes 86.72%, Scheduled Castes 
79.88.% against the over all dro p out rate of 75.36%. 
The Commit tee is unhapp y over the situation that the sp irit of Operation Black board has 
not been fulfilled. 
B. Mid-day Meal Programme 
Mid-day Meal Programm e with varying degree of coverage either as a programm e to help 
the educationa l efforts or as an anti-poverty programme has been launched and is effectively 
working in various States. At present, 17 State Governments are implementin g Mid-day 
Meal Programme for primay school children of the age group 6-11 years. In the study 
conducted to fi nd out the impact of the Mid-da y Meal, it has been reporte d that the higher 
retention rate was not not iced in respect of districts with Mid-day Meal Progra mme t han 
those without them. The impact on girl students belonging to Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes Communities were also not found to be satisfactory. 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry during the course of 
oral evidence by the Secretary (Education) that the Primary School Teacher s and their 
organisations have been resentful of taking up Mid-Day Meal Programme on the ground that 
functions and responsibilities in this regard make serious inroad s into their teaching time. The 
Committee recommends that concerted efforts should be made to implement the programme 
in an effective way. 
The Committee also recommends that this work should be entrusted to some voluntary 
organisation as is being done in some Stat.es: 
C. Non-Formal Education 
In 1979-80, the Scheme of Non-forma l Education was introd uced as an alternative ) trategy 
. to impart education to childre.n, who, for various reasons , cannot attend formal schools. 
It is said that where there is abse nce of schooling opportunities this will be compensated 
by non-formal education. While non-for mal education may be a potent antidote to illiteracy 
at the above-15 s tage, for children under that age non-formal education cannot be a 
substitute for regular schooling. At most, it can serve as an entr y point to regular schooling 
system. There is also no provision in the demand s for enabling labouring children to be 
released from their boudge and be integra ted in the education system. The perception of 
non-formal education as a s ubstitute for regular schooling a t the primary and seco ndary 
stage fs an abd ication of responsibility on the part of the Gove rnment. 
The scheme was revised in 1987-88. Although its focus is o n the e ducation ally backward 
States , but it has been extended to cover urban slums, hilly tribal and desert areas and areas 
with concentration of working children in the other states as well. Und er the Scheme , 
financial assistance is given to the States/Union Territ ories in the ratio of 50:50 and 90:10. 
The Committee feels, that the grants are very meagre. Government must ensure that the 

funds allocated for the purpose should not be misused and there should be a proper 
monitoring. 
D. Teacher Education 
The Centrally sponsored Scheme of Teacher Education is being implemented since 1987-
88. Its main objectives are to impart suitable pre-service and in-service training to school 
teach ers so as to provide all-rou nd academic and resource support to the school. During the 
years 1987-92, 306 District Institutions of Education and Training have been sanctioned 
covering all States except West Bengal and Union Territorie s of Delhi and Pondicherry. 
During the same period , 43 Secondary Teachers ' Training Institutes have been up-graded 
and a sum of Rs. 164.36 crores has been sanctioned under this scheme to State 
Governments. 
The Committee does not understand under what circumstances West Bengal and Union 
Territories of Delhi and Pondicherry have been )eft out of the scheme and recommends that 
the same tnay be included in the next year positively. 
E. National A wards to Teachers 
The National Awards carry a cash grant of Rs. 5000/- to the recipients meant only to be a 
token grant; not a cash reward. The real prestige to the awardee accrues on account of the 
distinction that it is a National Award conventionally given away by the President of India. 
The budget grant of Rs. 27 lakh for 1993-94 to meet the cost of cash component of a total of 
295 National Awards to be given for 1992 and for the incidental expenditure in connection 
with Awardees TA/DA , function expenses etc. does not seem to be sufficient. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the grant as well as the number of Awardees 
should be increased so that more teachers are covered under the Scheme. 
. In Bihar Education Project the revised estimate for 1992-93 has been reduced to Rs. 6 
crores from the Budget Estimate of Rs. 12 crores and whereas in 1993-94 again it is being 
raised to Rs. 20 crores. 
The Committee is not convinced with the Demand for Grants on this account and feels that 
it should be at the level of last year Budget Estimate. 
The Committee is unhappy to note that in the year 1991-92 only Rs.2 crores were spent 
against the budgetary allocation of Rs. 6 cFores and again in the year 1992-93 budgetary 
allocation of Rs. 12 crores was reduced to Rs. 6 crores in the revised estimate. 
The Committee feels that budgetary allocations were not utilised properly. 
The Committee fails to understand the rationale for not allocating any funds for the 
Monitoring of Universalisation of Elementary Education, Operationalising Micro Planning and 
Improvement of Learners' achievement for which Rs. 86 lakhs, Rs. 3 crores and Rs.2 crores, 
respectively were allocated in the Budget Estimate of 1992-93. 

SECONDARY EDUCATION 
It has been the constant endeavour of Government to improve the extstmg education 
system and innovate further to make education socially relevant. In this field the main 
institutions are:-
(i) Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan. 
(ii) Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti. 
(iii) National Open School. 
(i) Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan:- Kendri ya Vidyalaya Scheme was started by the 
Department in the academic year 1963-64. The main objectives of the scheme are: (i) to 
meet the educatio nal needs of the children of transferab le Central Governme nt employees 
including defence personnel by providing common programme of edcuat ion; (ii) to develop 
the Vidyalayas as model schools in the context of the national goal of education; (iii) to 
initiate and promote exper imentation in education in collaboration with other bodies; and 
(iv) to promote national integration. 
The Budget Estimates (Non-Plan) of Kendriya Vidyalaya, was Rs. 163.01 crores for the 
year 1992-93, the Revised Estimate (Non-Plan) for the same year was Rs. 165.55 crores, 
while the Budget Estimate (Non-Plan) for the year 1993-94, is Rs.185.46 c rores. 
The Committee feels that there is a continuous backlog in providing good low cost school 
e~ucation which causes proliferation of private schools and creates pressure on Kendriya 
Vidyalayas which are basically meant for children of Central Government employees with 
transferable jobs. The capital outlay is not sufficient to make up for this backlog. This is 
likely to make the goal of universal education an everreceding one. 
The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the number of Kendriya Vidyalayas, and 
recommends that the allocation of funds be enhanced so that the number of Kendriya 
Vidyalayas be increased with a view to impart education to sufficient number of students. 
The Committee also recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of 
opening Kendriya Vidyalayas in those areas, where there is heavy concentration of Central 
Government employees for whom there are no sufficient educational facilities. 
The demand for opening more Kendriya Vidyalayas may be given top priority. 
(iii) Navodaya Vidyalaya 
In order to provide good quality modern education to the talented children predominantly 
from the rural areas Government of India launched in 1985-86 a scheme to establish 
Navodaya Vidyalayas one in each district. So far 280 Navodaya Vidyalayas have been 
established in the country. 
The specific objective of these Vidyalayas is to ensure that all students may attain the 
reasonable level of competence in three languages, and to serve as focal point in each district 
for improvement in quality of education through sharing of experience while availing the 
facilities. 
The budget allocation for Navodaya Vidyalayas has increased from Rs. 55 crores in 1990-91 
toRs. 131.71 crores in 1993-94 for plan expenditure. As on 31st March , 1992, 7,849 students 
were on the rolls of these co-educational Vidyalayas. Admission of children from urban areas 
is restricted to one-fourth and children belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
communities are admitted in proportion to their population. 
The Committee is constrained to observe that the Navodaya Vidyalayas are very few in 

. number vis-a-vis the rural population and feels that the Ministry should make sincere effortS 
·to establish Navodaya Vidyalayas atleast one in each district, on an average, as per their 
target. 
The Committee feels that the . budget allocation for vocationalisation of education and 
providing hostel and boarding facilities for girl students in the Navodaya Vidyalayas be 
substantially increased and the Ministry should be very careful in spending of money in these 
programmes. 
The Committee stresses that the scheme for migration of 30 per cent students for a period 
of two years at class IX level from one Vidyalaya to another in a different linguistic region to 
promote national integration, be implemented effectively. 
The Committee feels that no assessment of students coming out of Navodaya Vidyalayas and 
their positive contribution to society has been made so far. Therefore, proper assessment may 
be made whether the purpose of these Vidyalayas which are being give more and more 
financial assistance is being served or not. 
NATIONAL POPULATION EDUCATION PROGRAMME 
The National Population Education Project was launched in 1980 with the main objective 
of institutionalising population education in school education system. The Project is currently 
running in 29 States and Union Territories. The Committee feels that the Budget Estimates 
of Rs. 98 lakhs for 1993-94, for this Project should be increased as Government proposes to 
substantially increase the activities and expand its net work during the Eighth Plan. 
(iv) National Open School 
The National Open School was registered on 23rd November, 1989 to provide secondary 
education of quality to the disadvantaged sections of the society through Distance 
Education. 
The education is imparted through distance teaching methods with the help of accredited 
institutions all over India . In comparison to 143 accredited institutions in 1991, there are 303 
such institution s and the target for 1992-93 is to have 350 accredited institutions. 
The Committee is not satisfied with the outlay asked for in the Demands for Grants of Rs. 
3.24 crores, for the year 1993-94 from Rs. 1.54 crore (RE. 1992-93) and recommends that 
more realistic view should be taken in formulating and calculating the Demands for Grants, 
which may not result in substantial decrease in the Revised Estimates for 1993-94. 

1 IDGHER EDUCATION 
Higher Education is imparted through yarious universities and a large ·number of arts, 
science, commerce and professional colleges affiliated to them. The Demand for Grants 
relating to higher education for, the year 1993-94 is Rs. 161 crores (Plan) and Rs. 339.88 
CfOres (Non-Plan). The total Plan allocation for University anq Higher Education for 1993-
94 in relation to that of 1991-92 is as under:-

The Committee observes that the share of higher education in the· total allocation for 
iducation has gone down drastically in the seventh and the eighth plans. No alternative 
arrangement has been made for resource mobilisation in colleges and universities. Capital 
outlay for colleges and universities in the States has become so limited that it is impossible for 
the states to fulfil the demand for higher education. UGC is asking colleges and universities to 
mobilise their own resources from non-governmental sources. Taking this in view efforts may 
be made to fmd out and augment resources for higher education. 
INDIRA GANDHI NATIONAL OPEN UNIVERISTY 
The Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU) was established in September , 
1985 by an Act of Parliament for the introduction and promotion of Open University and 
Distance Education Systems in. the educational pattern of the country and for the co­
ordination and determination of standards in such systems. The University has set up 9 
Schools in various disciplines. 
The University spent Rs. 1.2 crore during 1991-92 and the budget allocation during 1992-
93 was Rs. 17.53 crores which has been increased to Rs. 21.9 crores for 1993-94. 
The Committee feels that the amount be increased so that more centres of learning can be 
opened benefitting larger number of students. 
B. Indian Council of Historical researsch 
Indian Council of Historical Research was set up in 1972 as an autonemous organisation to 
promote the objectives of research in and writing of history. 
In 1992-93, the Council sanctioned study grants including travel contingent grant to 97 
scholars. 
The Committee stresses that the funds allocated for the Council may be utilised in 
conducting research to find out solutions to Indian problems and it whould have an Indian 
Orientation. 
C. Book Promotional Activities by Voluntary Organisations 
Under the Scheme, grants are given on ad hoc basis to Voluntary Organisations, 
belonging· to writers, publishers, book-sellers, etc. for organising seminars, training courses, 
workshops, annual conventions, surveys, etc. related to Book Promotional Activities. 75% 
of the approved expenditure on an event is met by the Mini~try and the remaining 25% is 
met by the voluntary organisations concerned. 
During the course of delibarations the representatives informed that for the last 2 years, 
the Ministry of Finance has imposed a ban on the expenditure on seminars work-shops, 

training programmes, etc. For the year 1993-94 Rs. 5 lakhs have been demanded which the 
representatives informed are meant for meeting emergent demands in relaxatoin of the ban 
in consultation with the Ministry of Finance. 
The Committee recommends that the ban be lifted and budget allocations the revised 
accordingly. 
D. Setting up of National Society of Authors. 
There was a provision of Rs. 2 lakhs in the Budget Estimate of 1992-93 for setting up of a 
National Society of Authors. In 1993-94, the same provision of Rs. 2 lakhs has been made. 
The Committee sought to know as to whether the amount allocated for the purpose has 
been spent and whether the Society has been set up? 
It was informed by the Ministry that the Society has not yet been set up. The Budget 
provision for 1992-93, therefore , could not be spent. The allocation for 1993-94 is a token 
provision only, as final decision to set up the Society is yet to be taken. 
The Committee recommends that the setting up of Societies like National Society of Authors 
be expedited. · 

ADULT EDUCATION 
The National Literacy Mission was launched on 5th May, 1988 with the objective of 
functional literacy to 80 million illiterates in the 15-35 years age-group by 1995. The 
successful implementation of the Mission is evident from the emergence of a large number of 
neo-literates who needed to be guided from teacher dependent learning to self-guided 
learning. 
The literacy campaign is marked by characte.ristics like it is area-specific, time-bound, 
delivered through voluntarism, cost effective and outcome-oriented and .is being 
implemented by Zilla Saksharata Samitis constituted under the District Collector. The 
members of the Samiti are drawn from all sections of society, especially the women , the 
weaker sections of the society etc. 
56 total Literacy Campaign projects including 6 projects sanctioned during 1992-93 have so 
far been sanctioned to 46 voluntary . agencie~.: 
21 State Resource Centres continue to function to provide academic and technical 
resource support to the Adult Education Programme throughout the country. 14 of them are 
functioning in the voluntary sector, 3 in Universitie s and four in Departments of Adult 
Education in various States. 
In the Demand for Grants for the year 1993-94 for Adult Education Programmes an 
outlay of Rs. 177.97 crores for plan expenditure and Rs. 2.63 crores for non-plan 
expenditure have been asked. . 
During the course of evidence the Secretary (Education), was asked to state the reasons 
for curtailment in the plan allocation on Non-Formal Education for women and girls (Adult 
Education). 
The Committee does not understand the reasons for decline in the non-plan expenditure and 
suggests that like the preceding years the amount should be increased proportionately. 
The Committee was not satisfied with the reply given during the course of oral evidence 
that this allocation has been kept for activities implemented with UNICEF assistance and 
recommends that some more allocation should have been made for this. The Committee was 
also not satisfied with reply given by the Ministry regarding Budget Estimates for 1993-94 
which are on the lower side than the Revised Estimates of the earlier year, for the education 
of women and girls. 
NEHRU YUV A KENDRA 
The Nehru Yuva Kendras (NYK) have been undertaking Adult Education Programme 
since the launching of national Adult Education Programme for eradicating illiteracy during 
the specified period. 
The Committee feels that it should be ensured that the proper utilisation of funds be made 
and an assessment of the performance of these Kendras may be undertaken.

development of Hindi and other languages-listed in_ the VIII Schedule to the· Constitution of

on the other hand , received due attention.

With a view to assisting the States/Union Territories in imple_menting the three language

SAN~KRIT: In the year 1970 the Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan was established with the

VOCA TIONALISATION OF EDUCATION 
In pursuance of the National Policy on Education 1986, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of 
Vocationalisation of Secondary Education was started from February, 1988 under which 
financial assistance is provided to the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations 
for Introduction of Vocational Courses in schools at the + 2 stage. Assistance is also given to 
the voluntary organisations for taking up innovative programmes in the field of vocational 
education. 
The Committee feels that the involvement of voluntary organisations in the field of 
vocational education should be encouraged. More Centres of Vocational Education be set up 
and resources required by these organisations be augmented. 

GENERAL 
(A) QUALITY IMPROVEMENT PROGRA:\IME- COMMUN ITY POLYTECHNICS 
As regards Demands for grants under sub-head D .5(1 )-Grant for quality 
improvement programme-Community Polytechnics. the Committee feels that the amount 
of grant for community polytechnics and Centres for Development of Rural Technology 
be substantially increased so that more institutions are covered under the Scheme during 
1993-94. 
r (B) SANSKRIT EDUCATION 
The Committee sought to know why the nomenclature of budget head No.C.5.(3) is 
Sanskrit Education even though the grant is utilised for other classical languages also. 
During the course of evidence it was informed that under the provision made for 
Sanskrit education, assistance is given to · desen ·ing voluntary organisations and 
institution s engaged in teaching/promotion of other classical languages. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that henceforth the Head Sanskrit education be 
changed to Sanskrit and other Classical Languages Education. 
(C) COMPUTER EDUCATION 
For familiarising school students with computers and their use and "hands-on" 
experience, a project on 'Computer Literacy and Studies in School' is being 
implemented jointly by the Department of Electronics and Department of Education 
since 1984-85. 2598 Secondary /Se nior Secondary Schools were provided two BBC micros 
which was increased to five from 1987-88 onwards. An expenditure of Rs. 48.30 crores 
upto 1992-93 has been incurred on the implementation of the project by the 
Dapratment of Electronics and the Department of Education. 
The Committee is unhappy to note that in view of the resource constraints of the 
government, it is not possible to provide subsidy to individual students and recommends 
that government should find ways and means to help those students who intend to 
procure and install a computer at home. 
(D) FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL PROFESSORS 
The Government of India had instituted in 1949, a Scheme of National Profes sorship 
to honour distinguished scholars in recognition of their valuable contribution to 
knowledge. Persons of eminence who have attained the age of 65 years and who have 
made outstanding contribution in their respective fields and are still capable of further. 
productive research are considered for appointment as National Professors. 
The total number of National Professors that can be there at a time 12, as per the 
Scheme. 
The Committee was informed that at present there are only t\vo National Professors 
receiving honorarium. 
The Committee expresses concern in this regard and recommends that appointment 
for all the posts of National Professors may be expedited.

The Scheme of Introduction of Yoga in schools was started in 1989-90 but cou ld take

Scheme till now. The Committee was informed that the implementation is expected to

The Scheme of Integrated Education for Disabled Children provides 100% financial 
assistance to State Govts I UT Admini!:-.trations and voluntary organisations for creating

Voluntary organisations under the Scheme arc given financial assistance throu.gh the State 
Governments. These Organisations supplement the work being done by the State 
Government. 
In the Budget Estimate for the year 1993-94 the allocation is Rs. 40 lakhs. The Committee 
feels that this amount may be increased and the participation of voluntary organisations in 
this field may a lso be enco ura ged. 
(G) DELINKI NG OF DEGREE FROM JOBS 
The New Polic y on Education (N PE) 1986, as modtfied in 1992 visualises delinking of 
degrees from jobs in selected areas, especia lly in service~ for which a University degree need 
not be a necessary qualification. 
The National Evaluation Organbation (N EO) \\as registered in December, 1991, to 
facilitate the process of del inking. b] conducting test'> 011 a \ oluntar) basis to determine the 
suitab ility of candidates for specific jobs and to evolve norms of comparable competencies 
across the nati on and to bring about an overall improvement in tc~ttn g. and measurement. 
The Committee was informed that the National Evaluation Organisation is yet to become 
operational. The various steps for rendering NEO functional are under way. 
The Committee feels that there has been an enormou s delay and recommends that the NEO 
may be set up and made operational at the earliest. 
(H) ILLIT ERACY AMONG WOMEN AND GIRLS 
The Committee was informed that according to the 1991 census the rate of literacy amo ng

The Committee is unhappy with the present rate of literacy and recommends that all out

AN OVERVIEW 
There are two main components of the Department i.e. Cultur~ and Arts . . A . separate 
department, called the Department of Arts, was constituted in August, 1985 with the aim 9f setting 
up the Indir a Gandhi National Centre for Arts (IGNCA)-a major centre for Arts, Humanities and 
Cultural heritage . The vast treasure of our culture is being preserved, promoted and propagated 
jointly by the Central and State Governments and Union Territ ory Administrations through out the 
country. The Archaeological survey of India is the largest and most important part of the Department 
of Culture engaged in conservation and excavation of old historical sites and about 25 per cent of the 
total budget provisions of the Department of Culture goes to this institution. Awareness generation 
and dissemination of information about our glorious past is done through exhibition of antiquities and 
artefacts preserved in museum s spread thr oug hout the country. Different Academies, National School 
of Drama, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training , Zonal Cultural Centres: Libraries , Memorials 
like Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, Kalakshetra, Madras etc., functioning under the Depart ment 
of Culture, cater to the artistic and literary needs of the people. The Anthmpological Survey of India , 
a subordinate office of the Departm ent, has been carrying out researches on cultural aspects of Indian 
population. 
2. The total outlay on culture during the Eighth Five Year Plan (as initially approved for the

The Central sector share is Rs. 385.00 crores, supplemented by an additional allocation of Rs. 75.00 
crores, making it a total of Rs. 460.00 crores.

8. In order to give fillip to the culture and to restore and refurbish its dying facets, Govt. has 
drafted an Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture. Views/comments received from Members 
of Parliament, eminent person in the field of literature, arts and culture, critics and administrators,

Department. Presently, by the Draft Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture is under

REPORT 
9. The Committee, taking note of the revolutionary changes taking place in communications and 
mass media and threat to the Indian culture from outside, emphasises that culture should be seen in 
right perspective and stresses the need of countering cultural invasion from outside. The Secretary, 
during the course of his oral evidence before the Committee, while taking note of the concern of the 
Committee stated that efforts are being made to have parleys with the Secretaries of Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting and Department of Tourism in order to ensure better coordination 
between them in this regard. The Commmittee urges upon the Government to make all-out efforts to 
contain cultural invasion and to restore our cultural ethos, ideals and values. 
10. The Committee expresses its concern over the neglect of the rural areas due to the 
centralisation of programmes in the urban areas by the Department of Culture. More and more 
programmes of the department are concentrated in the major cities and the rural areas are being 
neglected in the process . It was admitted by the department that in our cultural programmes priority 
is being given to the urban areas due to reason that major cultural institutions arc located in the cities 
and there are better transport and other facilities available in cities for the foreign delegates and 
dignatries visiting these centres. The situation c~n improve only when more and more such facilities 
are provided in the rural areas to facilitate the establishment of cultural centres in villages or semi­
urban areas. 
The Committee was also informed that there is a provision with the Department to extend 
building grant of Rs. 10 lakhs to any organisation for setting up of auditorium at any place including 
the rural areas, if it has a piece of land and is ready to spend matching amount. During the year 1993-
94, fifty nine such institutions/organisations were given building grants to the tunc of Rs. 1.38 crores. 
But the logic of the Department does not appear to be sound enough in the sense that if the semi­
urban, under-developed and rural areas are neglected and rejected on this pretext, how the cultural 
needs of the vast majority of people living in these areas would be met. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the programmes and resources of the Department be considerably decentralised and 

taken to the backward, rural and und erdeve loped urban areas where ancient cultural heritage still 
holds appeal and requires to be galvanised by the centre. 
Archaeological Survey of Indi a (ASI) 
11. Archaeological Survey· of India, set up way back in 1861, is engaged in several activities, 
prominent among which arc conservation and preservation of ancient monuments, exploration and 
excavation of ancient sites, study of inscriptions, research and training in different areas of 
archaeology. etc. Povisions made for this head during the last two years arc given in the table.

12. There has been an increase of Rs. 1.90 crorcs this year, as against the revised estimates of the 
last year, which, in view of price esclation, is negligible. Therefore, the Committee feels that allocation 
for ASI should be adeq uately increase d because a large number of monument s are in dilapidated 
conditions and need urg ent repairs and a great number of monument s and sites remain unidentified 
and unprotected. Out of arou nd 8,000 monuments, about 3,500 are cent rally protecte d. The Committee 
expresses its concern over the fact that even the centrally prot ected monuments do not have proper 
maintenance and foolpr oof protectioq. Cases of larcen y of artefacts, idols etc. have been occuring from 
time to time. During the course of evidence the Committee came to know that the number of staff 
engaged in preservations and maintenance of monuments is so small that the ratio works out to 11h 
staff per monument. Therefore, the Committee recommen ds that staff st rength of the ASI engage d for 
protection and preservation of monuments be adequa tely increased and all other necessary measures be 
taken to check the increasing menace of pilferage. Some amount from the proposed National Cultural 
Fund may also be utilised for the purpo se. 
The Committee is also of the view that, as envisaged in the Eigh th Plan documen t related to the 
Department of Cultur e, volunta ry organ isations should be attracted and encouraged to take up the task 
of preservation and protection of monu.ments. 
13. Even after one hundred and twenty five years of its existence, ASI has not been able to cover 
all parts of the country as far as excavation and exploration of ancient historical sites are concerned. 
Nor it has been able to decipher all the inscriptions. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
network of ASI sho uld ha ve been extensively expanded and enlarged. It should also be well equipped. 
The scheme of village to village survev should also be undertaken and expanded. 
Anthropological Survey of India 
14. Researches in anthropology and allied disciplines and study of customs and traditions are 
some of the major functions undertaken by the Anthropological Survey of India. In the Eighth Five 
Year Plan document it was proposed to salvage and document those specimens of the tribal and folk 
art which face the threat of extinction. It was also proposed to study inherent socio-religious 
disabilities of the tribals, nature of transformation and mobilisation of their special skills in arts, dance 
and music and mastery over musical instruments. But, no follow-up action on these lines is found in 
the Annual Plans of the Department. Therefore, the Committee urges upon the Government to pursue 
vigorously those objectives. Reasons for decrease in the plan allocation of Rs. 140.00 lakhs from Rs. 
150.00 lakhs (Plan Expenditure Revised) of the year 1993;94 arc not tenable . Hence the Committee 
recommends that the provision shou ld be incr eased. Study and research in the field of conservation of 
environment, welfare of women and children, nutritional status of Indian population, etc. have also 
been added to its activ~ties, recently. 

15. In keeping with its aims and objectives, the Anthropological Survey of India took up a 
national project called 'People of Indi a' to analyse Indian population on the basis of bio-cultural 
variables and socio-cultural determinents like marriage, kinship, region, language etc. Out of the 
proposed 43 volumes of the prestigious National Project 'People of India'- three under national and 
two under State ser ies have so far been published. The remaining work should be expedited. 
Museums 
16. Museums play a vital role in the preservation of documents and objects of cultural antiquity. 
In this field, at present, there are ten premier institutions under Govt. of India, including the 
National Reserach Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural property located at Lucknow. Out of the 
ten institutions, three each are located at New Delhi and Calcutta and one each at Lucknow, 
Allahabad, Hyderabad and Bombay, all situated in major cities. To provide representation to cultural 
aspects of other states of Indian Union, a new scheme for Promotion and Strengthening of Regional 
and Local Museums has been mooted and is envisaged to be operationlised during the Eighth Five 
Year Plan period. Govt. is also providing assistance for opening private museums. Govt. proposes to 
intensify this scheme through a Committee which will look after them. But for this well conceived 
scheme a meagre amount of Rs. 10 lakhs has been provided for the year 1994-95. There has been no 
change in the allocations for the last three years. In such a situation the Committee wonders how the 
scheme contemplated for the Eighth Plan could be implemented within the time-frame with this 
insignificant budget allocation. As the Eighth Five Year Plan is left with only two financial years, the 
Committee strongly recommends enhancement of financial allocation to speed up the implementation of 
the scheme. 
National Council of Science Museums (NCSM), Calcutta 
17. It is an autonomous organisation engaged primarily in the task of popularising science and 
technology among the students in particular and the mas~es in general through a variety of interactive 
and innovative programmes and activities like science exhibitions, school centres, portable 
planetarium and national science seminars etc. and setting up of a Science City in Calcutta, is the 
highlight of the activities of the National Council of Science Museums. In the Eighth Plan document it 
was proposed to create 1000 science centres to reach the common man, five new regional centres, 20 
district science centres and 203 school science centres in the under privileged rural schools, 20 new 
mobile science exhibition buses, a science train, etc. The total out lay for the 8th Plan period of Rs. 
4500.00 lakhs for these ambitious proposals is too littfe. Slight increase in the allocation for this year, 
as against the last year's Budget Estimates, of around Rs. 161 lakhs and of Rs. 111 lakhs in Revised 
Estimates may not be said to be adequate in view of the rising prices. The implementation of the 
scheme has made very little progress and should be speeded up. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that additional grant be given for this scheme to increase scientific temper among the people. 
National Museum, New Delhi 
18. During 1994-95, the National Museum, New Delhi, proposes to organise exhibitions of 
Persian manuscripts in Teheran, an exhibition of Indian Art at Singapore and of miniature paintings 
at Tashkent. Apart from this, it is also proposed to introduce such new programmes as developing 
software for physically handicapped persons, lending consultancy services to the State and other 
museums, introduction of disc system for documentation of its huge collection, microfilming of 
manuscripts and computerisation of its library, etc. 
19. The provisions made for this year, as against last year, remain more or less the same. Plan 
provision has fallen from Rs. 200.00 lakhs to Rs. 190.00 lakhs and Non-Plan provisions has increased 
by only Rs. 7 lakhs in comparison to the Revised Estimates of the last year. Thus, there has been a 
decrease of Rs. 3 lakhs this year. The Committee is surprised to know as to how with this small 
allocation. It would be possible to achieve the targets set for this year. The Committee therefore, 
recomm ends that the allocation for National Museum be increased appropriately. 
Indian Museum, Calcutta 
20. The total provisions made this year for Indian Museum, Calcutta, arc less by 1.45 lakhs as 
agianst the Revised Estimates (both Plan and Non-Plan) of the last year. In this situation, apart from 

carrying out on-going functions the proposal to construct a new building for display of valuable 
artefacts may find itself in rough weather. It was also envisaged in the Eighth Plan document to set 
up new galler ies on textiles, folk arts, gems and jewelleries. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that sufficient grant should be provided to the Museum so that these schemes are completed. 
Institutes and Organisations of Tibetan and Buddhist studies 
21. There are. four autonomous institutes, namely, the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan 
Studies, VaranasC the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, Leh; the Sikkim Research Institute of 
Tibetology and the Library of Tibetan Works & Archives, Dharamsala, which are engaged in 
preservation and propagations of Tibetan culture and tradition, restoration of ancient Indian literature 
preserved in Tibetan language, imparting higher education in Buddhist philosophy and literature, etc. 
The Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Varanasi, enjoys the status of a 'Deemed 
University'. The Committee while expressing its satisfaction over the encouragement given to these 
institutes feels that they should be allowed to pursue their academic interest without any extraneous 
influences. 
22. The Committee feels that due attention is not being paid in these institutes to promotion and 
development of Pali, one of ancient language of India and, therefore, recommends suitable steps in this 
regard. 
Libraries 
23. The Committee feels that the reading habi!s of the general masses are on the wane, partly 
owing to revolutionary changes in electronic media, partly due to the shift in social values titled more 
to materialism, and partly because of high prices of books. In this situation, libraries have to be 
opened on a large scale with even distribution in urban and rural areas. 
24. There arc six major libraries under the Department of Culture. The total budgetary provision 
(lOth Plan and Non -Plan) for the year 1994-95 under this .head is Rs. 13.36 crores a total increase of 
Rs. 2.38 crores in comparison to the Revised Estimates (Both Plan & Non Plan) of the last year. In 
view of the rising prices of books and other allied items, maintenance cost of buildings etc. this 
increase of Rs. 2.38 crores in not enough. 
25. The tendency of centralisation is perceptible in the scheme of libraries also. The Committee 
feels that suitable scheme be devised to spread the network of libraries to District Headquarters and 
small towns. There is also a need to Interlink the major libraries with computer network. It will 
facilitate the research scholars and other persons desiring any information sitting in one library to 
gather additional information from all the connected libraries. 
26. The Delhi Public Library, established in 1951 with the assistance of UNESCO to provide free 
library service to the citizens of Delhi , has also now developed into a Metropolitan Public Library. A 
major portion of its activities is located in the affluent localities of Delhi and the rural and 
underdeveloped areas are being neglected . Therefore, -the Committee, recommends that Govt. should 
take adequate steps to spread it~ network of libraries and reading rooms in the slum and 
underdeveloped ar~as of the National Capital. More and more mobile library vans should also be made 
available. In view of all these, the Committee recommends that the budget allocation for Delhi Public 
Library be enhanced appropriately. 
Raja Ram Mohan Roy Library Foundation, Calcutta 
27. Established in 1972, it is an autonomous organisation fully funded by the Deptt: of Culture. 
The · main aim of the library is to support and promote library services in the country. 
28. Increase in its budget provision this year is welcome. However, some Irregularities in the 
fuQctioning of the lib_rary have come to the notice of the Committee. Guidelines on book purchasing are 
not being adhered to and books are allegedly being purchased at higher r~tes than the market rates. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that these matters be looked Into. 

Rural Library Scheme 
29. The Committee is happy to note that the Department of Culture has decided to focus its 
attention on the rural populace by deciding to set up rural libraries in villages. A teacher from the 
local school is proposed to be made in-charge of the library which will, in the incipient,have around 
300 books. The Committee "is of the view that these libraries should also ~ave such books which may be 
used by neo-literates in the post-literacy stage. It is, undoubtedly a well conceived scheme and generous 
funds should be provided for it. The Committee recommends that this scheme be made a pilot project 
so that about five and half lakh villages could be covered within a stipulated time-frame. The 
Committee also recommends that separate allocation be made for individual states. In consultation with 
the Ministry of Rural Development, the assistance of Panchayats may be sought to ensure speedy and 
effective implementation of this scheme. The Committee also recommends that the modalities for the 
implementation of this scheme be worked out as early as possible so that the scheme implemented in 
right earnest. 
Akademies and National School of Drama 
I. Sahitya Akademi 
30. The Sahitya Akademi was inaugurated in 1954 and registered as an autonomous society in 
1956 with the objective of working actively for development of literature and to foster and coordinate 
literary activities in all the Indian languages and to promote through them the cultural unity of the· 
country. To achieve these objectives, the Akademi is running programmes such as granting literary 
awards, translation and publication of books in different languages, etc. The Akademi also provides 
assistance to State Akademies. 
31. The Committee is not happy with the budgetary allocation made for the Akademi this year, 
which is only Rs. 57 lakhs more than the Revised Estimates of the last year :-

32. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that a premier literary institution like the 
Sahitya Akademi is made ·to curtail its activities due to lack of funds. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends strongly that more resources be made available to the Sahitya Akademi and the arrear 
payments, if any, should also be released forthwith. The Akademi should bestow more attention on the 
development of regional languages, in addition to Hindi. 
II. Sangeet Natak Akademi 
33. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, which come into being in 1953, is a national institution engaged 
in promotion and preservation of performing arts, extending financial assistance to cultural institution 
for training and production, undertaking inter-state cultural exchange programmes etc. Although 
there is an increase of around Rs. 27 lakhs this year, as compared to the last year's Revised Estimates 
(both Plan and Non-Plan) this is negligible in view of the price escalation. The Committee is of the 
view that the outlay for the Akademi may be appropriately increased. 
III. Lalit Kala Akademi 
34. The Lalit Kala Akademi an apex institution in the field of art was established in 1954 for the 
promotion and development of paintings, graphics, sculpture, ceramics, etc. in the country. The major 
activities of the Akademi are to organise exhibitions (in and outside the country), artists' camps, 
bringing out art publications, and implementing cultural exchange programmes. 
35. The allocation for the Akademi this year has come down from Rs. 2.85 crores (Revised 
estimates) of the year 1993-94 to Rs. 2.40 crores. The Committee urges upon the Govt. to increase the 
allocation appropriately. 

National School of Drama 
36. The National School of Drama, established in 1959, is a premier institution devoted to 
imparting training in the field of theatre and to propagate dramatics in the country. Increase in this 
year's budgetary provisions for the institution from Rs. 266.65 lakhs to Rs. 285.00 lakhs is welcome. 
The National School of Drama proposes to set up regional centres, which is a welcome step, and the 
Committee desires that these regional centres should enjoy due autonomy in their functioning and not 
made mere branches of the National School of Drama, New Delhi. 
Promotion of Art & Culture 
37. A number of organisations and institutions are active in promoting and disseminating 
different types of art and cultural activities in various regions and zones of the country. A brief sketch 
of their activities, objectives vis-a-vis provisions thereof is given below:-
/. Centre for Cultural Resources & Training 
38. The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, set up in 1979 with its headquarter in New 
Delhi, is doing a commendable job in the propagation of culture, especially among college and school 
students. One of the major activities of the Centre is to train inservice school teachers in the area of 
linkage between education and culture and to provide a cultural component in the curricula. The 
Centre also prepares audio-visuals and printed materials to be used in schools for cultural education. 
The centre also took over the scheme 'Cultural Talent Search Scholarship' from the Deptt. of Culture 
in 1982 under which 300 children in the age group of 10-14 years are awarded scholarships each year 
in various fields. 
39. The Centre has been entrusted with the task of interlinking culture with education, mass 
media and the scheme of the Deptt., bearing an identical nomenclature, has since been merged with 
the centre's scheme. 
40. The Committee is of the view that it is not practically feasible to cover whole country by the 
one and only Centre in New Delhi and hence feels the need to decentralise the activities of the Centre 
by opening sub-centres in various zones and regions. 
41. The provisions made for the Centre are not in consonance with the multifarious activities of the 
Centre. A comparative analysis of the allocation suggests that there has been a meagre increase of 
Rs. 20 lakhs in Plan and 0.65 lakhs in Non-Plan expenditure, as against the revised estimates of the last 
year. Since this is the only institution which is taking culture down to the general masses, students and 
teachers, the Committee recommends that more .resources should be allocated to the Centre, 
particularly keeping in view the Committee's recommendation for opening sub-Centres at various 
places. 
Zonal Cultural Centres 
42. At present, there are seven Zonal Cultural Centres which cover the entire country. The main 
functions of the Zonal Cultural Centres are to provide facilities for the creative development in the 
entire spectrum of culture, particularly in that of folk and tribal art. These centres are also 
implementing National Cultural Exchange Programmes, Republic Day folk dance festival and setting 
up Shilpgrams etc. For the year 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 200 lakhs has been earmarked for zonal cultural 
centres. During the year 1992-93 there was an under-utilisation of the approved outlay to the tune of 
about Rs. 175 lakhs, mainly because of the delay in allotment of land by Sta~ Government for setting 
up of Shilpgrams. The Committee, however, feels that such delays should be avoided so that funds are 
utilised in time. The Committee recommends that speedy progress be made in setting up Shilpgrams at 
the remaining six zonal cultural centres, particularly the one being set up at Thanjavur. The 
Committee also feels that centrewise allocation should also be reflected in the documents of the 
Department. 
43. Documentation and propagation of folk art constitute one of the main functions of Zonal 
Cultural Centres and as stated by the Secretary, Department of Culture, it is also one of the major 
thrust areas during this year. But the work being done in this regard cannot be said to be satisfactory. 
There is no indication as to how much money each Zonal Cultur al Centre spends on the propagation of 
the Jjving folk art forms at the grassroot level in villages where they are actually performed. Therefore, 

~he Committee is of the view that due emphasis of the Zonal .Cultural Centres should be on folk arts 
and necessary financial assistance should also be provided for the same. 
44. The Committee is constrained to note that the hopes generated at the time of establishment of 
Zonal Cultural Centres have not been fulfilled and realised. Because these centres are not pursuing the 
programmes and schemes fop which they were set up, therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
time has come for a high-powered Review Committee to be constituted to look into the working of the 
Zonal Cultural Centres. 
Dissemination of Tribal Folk Art & Culture 
45. Under this scheme, financial support is given to voluntary cultural organisations, institutions 
and individuals-both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small duration projects of around one year 
for preservation and development of tribal folk art and culture, conduct of tribal cultural activities, 
including their festivals and festivities. This year, there has been an increase of Rs. 10 lakhs for this 
scheme. But the Committee is not happy with the working of the voluntary organisations/institutions 
in this field because it is found that the assistance does not percolate down to the folk artistes, 
although the Secretary, Department of Culture, has submitted before the Committee that Gqvern­
ment is taking necessary steps to ensure that the artistes get the desired benefit. The Committee 
recommends the pro_gressive establishment of a network of organisations to ensure that folk artistes in 
villages are enabled to derive full advantage of the scheme meant for them. Assistance should also be 
given for opening performance centres or auditoria at the village and block level so that artistes could 
perform and interact with each other to improve their particular art forms. 
Multipurpo se cultural complexes at States & National Cultural Complex in Delhi 
46. Under this scheme, financial assistance is proposed to be extended to autonomous bodies for 
settmg up art complexes in the States to improve the quality of life among youth and students and to 
sensitize them to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society and also to expose them to the 
finest forms of creative expressions. 
47. The Committee is not happy with the progress made in the scheme and expresses its serious 
concern over the fact that almost two financial years have elapsed and the projects have not been 
finalised yet. The Committee is also not happy with the idea of creating more and more cultural 
infrastructure in big cities and towns at the cost of rural areas. However, the Committee is satisfied to 
note that multi-purpose complexes, are being set up in smaller towns, rural and backward areas and 
recommends that other schemes being formulated by the Deptt. should also be located in sucn art!aS. 
The Committee also recommends that the National Cultural Complex (Parisar), proposed to be set up 
in Delhi, be established in the trans-Yamuna or outer Delhi areas. 
48. The Committee is also of the view that instead of concentrating only on huge cultural 
complexes, Govt. should set up smaller units where the deprived, under privileged and unprivileged 
may have access to all forms of culture as well as to practice and promote their arts. The Committee 
also holds that the Department may construct multi-purpose stadia in smaller towns and cities which 
could be utilised for sports during the day and for cultural purposes in the evening and night. 
Asia'tic Society, Calcutta 
49. The Asiatic Society, Calcutta, is an institution of national importance involved mainly in 
oriental studies and research, research in humanities and science, publication of periodicals, books 
and other literature. At present, there are around 12 senior fellows and 30 junior research scholars 
attached to the Society. 
50. The Committee is surprised to note that a drastic cut has been resorted to in this year's budget 
allocation for the society. The plan provision has been reduced from Rs. 341.00 lakhs (Revised 
Estimates) during the year 1993-94 to Rs. 200.00 lakhs for the year 1994-95. The provision is 
understood to have been reduced in view of the opening of the Asiatic Society, Bombay. The Committee 
desires that the activities of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta should not suffer pending opening of Asiatic 
Society, Bombay. 

51. No financial assistance has been provided to the Asiatic Society, Bombay, during the Eighth 
Five Year plan. The reason behind this is stated to be that the Planning Commission has earmarked a 
provision of Rs. 200.00 lakhs to be given to the Society as corpus fund. But this fund also has not 
reached the Society so far as it is pending approval from the Ministry of Finance. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that government shotJd expedite the matter and release the amount without 
any further delay. 
Assistance to Cultural Organisations 
52. For promotion and dissemination of Cultur¢ the Department extends financial assistance to 
voluntary organisations under various schemes such as Scheme for Building grants to voluntary 
organisations, Scheme for financial Assistance to Dance, Drama and Theatre Ensembles, Financial 
Assistance for Research Support to voluntary organisations· engaged in Cultural Activities, Grants to 
Institutions I Individuals engaged in literary Activities. 
There' has been only marginal increase in allocations for these schemes and the Committee 
recommends that they should be enhanced adequately. 
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Centre for Asian Studies 
53. This centre, proposed to be set up in the wake of the centenary celebrations of Maulana Abul 
Kalam Azad, is still not complete. The Committee is surprised to note that this ·year budget provision 
for the Centre has been reduced by Rs. 5 lakhs, for the reasons not acceptable to the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that tLere should be no further delay in the setting up of this Centre. 
Indira Gandhi National Centn: for Arts 
54. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts was established in 1985 as an autonomous 
Trust. The Government had contributed to its Corpus Fund Rs. 46.75 crores between 1987-88 and 
1993-94. The balance of Rs. 3.25 crores of the Committed amount has been provided in this year's 
Budget. For the building fund, the Government has so far allocated Rs. 32.35 crores and in this year 
Rs. 16.75 crores have been provided. The Committee regrets to note that even after eight years or 
establishment of the Centre, its main projects including the building are yet to be completed, though 
requisite allocations are being made by the Government. The Committee has been told that work on 
the construction of the building has started in the real sense only in March, 1994. The other activities 
of the Centre like microfilming of unpublished manuscripts and creation and updating of data base are, 
however, in progress. The Committee feels that ~teps should be taken to utilise the funds fully and 
speedily so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
Memorials and Centenaries 
55. The Department of Culture proposes to commemorate this year the 125th birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi through Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti. But the allocation earmarked for the 
purpose is most inadequate. Also, in 'this year, the country will observe the 75th Anniversary of the 
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre but no budgetary provision has been made for this purpose. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the budget provision for celebration of the 12Sth birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi be increased and adequate funds be allocated for the observance of the 7S.th 
Anniversary of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.

I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population.  The census of 1991
had indicated the population of India as 846.3 million.  In the decade of 1981-91, 163 million persons were added to the
population of India.  On 11 th May, 2000, the population of India has already crossed 1 billion mark.   If the present rate
of annual growth of population  of 1.74% continues, India may overtake China in 2045 to become the most populous
country in the world.
1.2      With a view to check  the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was taken up with the
introduction of Planning in the country.  The objective of the Family Welfare Programme for the country has been to
stabilise population at a level consistent with the needs of national development.  To achieve this goal the Department
continues to implement the three-pronged strategy of :
(i)         improvement in the health status of women and children;
(ii)        fulfillment of the unmet needs of contraception with a special focus on widening the range of choice
available to the people; and
(iii)       professionalising and broad-basing the Information, Education     and Communication Campaign (IEC)
on Family Welfare, by not only using the mass media, but also involving the community, NGOs,
women’s organisations in the local specific IEC work at the district, sub-district and village level.

1.6.      The Committee notes that though there is a continuous decline in various demographic indicators over the years,
they are still very high in comparison to other developing countries like Sri Lanka, Indonesia, China and Cuba.  The
Committee, therefore, feels that rural and inaccessible areas are still outside the reach of Family Welfare Programme 
and unless these  areas are covered by the various Family Welfare Programmes, there cannot be any significant decline
in the abovementioned indicators and the growth of population will remain unabated.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee notes that the allocation for the Department has been reduced from Rs. 3541.47 crores in  BE
2000-2001 to Rs. 3221.37 crores at the RE stage.  However, a provision of Rs. 4232.28 crores has been made in BE
2001-2002 which represents an increase of Rs. 690.81 crores over the previous year.  
2.2       Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, it has been stated that in the Annual Plan proposal for
the year 2001-2002 sent to the Planning Commission, a requirement of Rs. 5922.72 crores was projected.   However, an
allocation of only Rs. 4210 crores  for 2001-2002 has been made by the Planning Commission.  As a result of the cut in
the Plan proposal, there is likely to be an accumulation of arrears and inadequate funding on infrastructure side of
various programmes and activities like RCH Programme, contraceptive supplies and maintenance of expenditure on
Rural Family Welfare Centres, etc.  
2.3       The Department has further informed that in the case of Rural Family Welfare Centres  the outlay proposed by it
was Rs. 700.00 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 430.00 crores.  In the case of Sub-Centres the outlay proposed
was Rs. 1237.00 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 675.00 crores.  In the case of maintenance of Urban Family
Welfare Centres, outlay proposed was Rs. 53.33 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 35.00 crores. 
2.4       The Committee notes that the Eleventh Finance Commission agreed with the views of the Committee that the
transfer of cost of maintenance of infrastructure under Family Welfare Programme to the States would impose
enormous liability on them and weaken their resources and also there is no guarantee that the transferred funds would be
used for Family Welfare Programme.   The Committee, therefore, reiterates  its earlier recommendation that status quo
in this regard should be maintained.
III.       RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
3.1       An enhanced allocation of Rs. 1105.00 crores has been made for Rural Family Welfare Services when compared
to BE provision of Rs. 921.00 crore in 2000-2001. The break-up of  total allocation for Rural Family Welfare Services is

3.2       There are at present 5435 Rural Family Welfare Centres functioning in the country which were established at all
the block level PHCs sanctioned upto 1.4.80.  These centres are entrusted with the responsibility for implementing the
Family Welfare Programme, i.e. planning, mobilisation, monitoring, administration and supervision in their areas.  
Block level PHCs have either replaced a PHC or got strengthened as CHC.   Besides that, to provide basic health and
family welfare services to the rural population, 1,37,271 Sub-centres are currently functioning, out of which 97,757 Sub
centres are funded by Govt. of India and the rest are funded under the State Minimum Needs/Basic Minimum Services
Programme.
3.3       Sub-Centres and PHCs provide basic health and family welfare services  and implement the Family Welfare
Programme in all respects.  The Committee observes that all India achievement level of targets set for 1999-2000 by the
Planning Commission in respect of Sub-Centres /PHCs / CHCs is as follows :-
