In this regard the Voluntary Agencies are funded for literacy projects in areas where the Total Literacy
Programme has not been sanctioned to the District for implementation through Zilla Saksharta Samities.  During the
Monthly Monitoring Meetings as and when the issue regarding covering the whole State for literacy Programmes is
taken up, the State Government can decide as to whether to take up to projects on Total Literacy or to promote
Voluntary Agencies.
Recommendation
19.       The Committee feels that libraries are a must for neo-literates if their interest in education is to be sustained. 
The Committee finds that libraries have played a very important role in spreading literacy in Kerala. Similar efforts are
required in other parts of the country.  Community libraries can be made use of in generating interest in reading among
the neo-literates.
Action Taken
The importance of providing facilities of libraries and Reading Rooms for generating interest in reading among
the neo-literates has been recognised and  adequate financial provision has been made in the non-recurring and recurring
grants for Continuing Education centres under the Continuing Education (CE) programme.
Recommendation
21.2     While appreciating the monitoring mechanism for Adult Education, the Committee feels that involvement of
local MPs/MLAs in this task will prove to be more effective
Action Taken
The literacy  campaigns launched by the National Literacy Mission are being implemented in more than 450
districts around the country.  These campaigns have  become a people’s movement and people from all walks of life are
actively involved in various activities like mobilising learners, volunteers, environment building, training, material
preparation, monitoring, evaluation and so on.
In many campaign districts the local MPs, MLAs and other political leaders are taking keen interest in the
programme and they are closely associated with the various activities under this programme.  As members of State
Literacy Mission Authorities and Zilla Saksharta Samities (ZSS) , the local MPs and MLAs keep a vigil on the
implementation of various schemes.
CHAPTER-III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
Recommendation
8.1  The Committee apprehends that until some radical measures are taken the target date may again have to be
extended.  There is a strong need of working out a mechanism of enrolment of adults, their retention and their
continuing education.  It must  be ensured that any adult enrolled is helped to reach the final stage of permanent
functional literacy.  Therefore, tracer study approach will have to be adopted.
Action Taken
National Literacy Mission has the objective of making 100 million persons literate in a time bound manner. 
Against this objective, the literacy campaigns, which is the principal strategy of the National Literacy Mission for
eradication of illiteracy, have been launched in 450 districts of the country.  As per the latest reports, approximately 130
million learners have been identified through survey, of which approximately 95 million persons were enrolled.  Out of
these, 73 million persons have so far been made literate under various schemes of the NLM.
The target of the National Literacy Mission which was set at 80 million persons to be covered in 345 districts by
1995 was revised to making 100 million persons functionally literate by the end of the 8
th   Five Year Plan i.e. the year
1996-97.  Keeping in view the progress made by the NLM, this target was reset in the year 1996 extending the date to
the year 1998-99.  Presently, the target stands reset to make 100 million persons literate in a time bound manner without
fixing any time schedule.

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
     Against the objective of 100 million, NLM has been able to achieve 73% of the target which could be termed as quite
satisfactory.  In addition, the learners attending literacy centres, are still in the pipe line and this figure is certainly going
to cross the 100 million mark very shortly.
To revitalise and revamp the literacy campaigns in different districts, special strategies have been evolved by the
NLM which include involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions with literacy campaigns, more effective and result-
oriented monitoring, transparent evaluation systems, non-cash incentives to volunteers to enhance their level of
participation and linkages of literacy with other development programmes as well as programmes for the economic
well-being  of  the learners. 
Further Comments
On a specific query about  the  reasons for revising the target of the National Literacy Mission again and again,
the Department simply informed that the goal has now been redefined so as to attain full literacy i.e., a sustainable
thresh-hold level of 75 per cent literacy by 2005.   The progress made against the latest target was that upto March 2000,
number of districts covered under Total Literacy Campaigns was 559.  The number of persons made literate under
different programmes upto March 2000 was 84.0 million.
 The Department further clarified that  the figures regarding number of persons made literate were based on data
collected from monitoring reports of the literacy projects.  In order to obtain real picture on the ground as far as the
Nation as a whole and for individual states is concerned, the Department commissioned NSSO to carry out the required
exercise and bring out a consolidated picture of literacy as from the time of the last decennial census in 1991.
         The data now released at the end of the 53
rd round of survey indicates literacy rates in  the 7 + age group between
1991 and 1997 as well as that projected for 1998 as  shown below:
                 Year                     Literacy Percentage
1991                                                    52
1997                             62
1998
                                                    64
               Secondly, the urban-rural differential in literacy rates has shown a marked decline to 24% in 1997 as against 
28.4% in 1991.   Thirdly, and vitally important, the rise in female literacy between 1991 and 1997 has been 11%
whereas the male literacy rate for the same period has risen by 9%.  In the previous decade too, the female rate of
literacy had grown faster than the male rate (9.6% as against 7.8%).         
Comments  of the Committee
The Committee expresses its serious concern over setting an unrealistic target at the time of launching  of
National Literacy Mission in 1988.  The target data had to be extended from 1995 to 1996-97, from 1996-97 to 1998-
99.  As per the Action Taken Note submitted by the Department in August, 1999, target was reset to make 100 million
people literate in a time bound manner without fixing any time schedule.   However, the Committee finds that the goal
has been yet again redefined  so as to attain full literacy , i.e. a sustainable thresh hold level of 75%  literacy by 2005,  as
indicated in the reply given by the Department to the Questionnaire on ATN in September, 2000.   The Committee is
constrained to observe that the initial target of NLM, i.e. 80 million people by 1995 could be achieved only by March,
2000 (84 million).    Not only this, out of total 588 districts in the country,  Total Literacy Campaigns are yet to be 
launched in 32 districts.   The Committee notes that 53
rd round of NSSO survey commissioned by the Department was
meant to bring out a consolidated picture of literacy i.e. of +7 age group as from the time of the last decennial census in
1991.   The Committee fails to understand  as to how this survey can bring out the achievements under NLM which
covers non-literate persons in the age-group of 15 to 35 years. 
Recommendation
8.2       Against the total allocation of Rs.1400 crores for adult education during the 8
th   Plan, actual expenditure was
only Rs.718.14 crores.  Similarly, for 1997-98 although there was an allocation of Rs.129.81 crores , expenditure was
only Rs.84,48 crores.  The Committee expresses its deep concern over underutilsation of funds. It is true that in some of
the educationally backward states like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, campaigns have lagged
behind leading to underutilisation of funds.  The Committee strongly feels that merely requesting such State

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
Governments to draw a time bound action plan for bringing uncovered districts under Total /Post Literacy Campaigns
will not serve the purpose.  What is required is a result oriented coordination between the Centre and the States.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should impress upon the States for effective implementation of
Adult Education Programme. The role of bureaucracy should recede and involvement of people should increase the
ownership level of the programme.  Strategy for this will have to be worked out.
Action Taken
In the report, it has been stated that against a total allocation of Rs.1400 crores,  only Rs.718.14 crores was
utilized.   Similarly for the year 1997-98 against an allocation of Rs.129.81 crores only Rs.84.48 crores was utilised.  It
may be submitted that apart from slow progress of the campaigns particularly in the Hindi speaking areas, the campaign
approach has reached a saturation  point where more release and /or utilization of funds may not help in the successful
implementation of the campaigns.   Of late, the National Literacy Mission has laid stress on consolidation of the existing
campaigns on ground rather than more and more expansion by way of more releases.  In addition to this community
participation has also gone up through contributions made to the implementing agencies by individuals as well as by
agencies in different areas for conducting various activities relating to the campaigns. This has a bearing on less
utilization of funds. 
As regards less expenditure by the National Literacy Mission, it may be stated that though Rs.1400 crores was
allocated for the 8
th  Five Year Plan , only a sum of Rs.953 crores was actually made available over a period of five
years.  In the case of less utilization of funds for the year 1997-98,  it may be submitted that due to non- finalisation of
revised enhanced norms for various schemes during the 9 th  Five Year Plan, the allocations had to be reduced at
appropriate stages of the financial year.  This resulted in less expenditure against the actual allocation.
The focus is now shifting towards decentralisation and devolving of powers on State Literacy Mission
Authorities (SLMAs) set up in different States.  The SLMAs  will be responsible not only for approval of literacy
projects like continuing education but also for actual implementation of the programme and its close monitoring .  State
level workshops have been held by the National Literacy Mission in several States to make aware the concerned
agencies of the role of SLMAs and clearly bring out as to how the literacy  programmes  would actually function.
Further Comments
The Department has informed the Committee  that in the revitalised National Literacy Mission, financial and
administrative powers have been decentralised to the State Literacy Mission Authorities (SLMAs).  SLMAs which have
been set-up in 18 States  have a two layer structure viz. Governing Council and Executive Council.  The State
Directorate of Adult Education serves as Secretariat.
           The State Literacy Mission Authorities are now specifically responsible for  the following:
-         Planning for literacy programmes in the State; fixing target dates for completing one phase of the programme and
launching new programmes.  Issuing guidelines for execution of State level.
-           Sanctioning Projects of Continuing Education: 
-           Sanctioning of Projects to NGOs:           
-           Monitoring of programmes:
-           Evaluation.
            The Department further informed that  the Director of Adult Education who is the member- secretary of the
SLMA in each State/UT is required to hold a monthly meeting on a fixed date.   The objectives of these meetings are to
review the progress of literacy campaigns and post literacy projects in various districts.  The focus of discussion is also
on assessment of qualitative aspects such as problems encountered in accelerating the pace of literacy campaign,
efficacy of corrective measures initiated in the past, activities planned for the coming month, and so on.   These
meetings are attended by secretaries of the Zila Saksharta Samities, Directors of State Resource Centres, State/Area
coordinators of the Bharat Gyan-Vigyan Samiti or representatives of the nodal voluntary agency and of Jan Shikshan
Sansthans. A representative from the National Literacy Mission or the Directorate of Adult Education is also present.
            The State Directorates scrutinise, analyse and compile the data from all the districts carefully and send
consolidated state reports to the central Directorate of Adult Education in the prescribed format.   National-level status
reports on literacy and post literacy are also compiled and published periodically.

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
.           The Committee was informed that  under the  three-step evaluation system of Literacy Programmes, self-
evaluation is a built-in feature of the literacy primers, concurrent and final evaluation is carried out by competent
evaluation agencies from outside the concerned district or State respectively.  The State Directorate is responsible for
nominating three evaluation agencies of which the district chooses one to conduct the concurrent evaluation.  Agencies
for external evaluation are nominated by NLM, but the SLMA keeps a close co-ordination and watch over progress and
results.
          As informed by the Department, recently, seven SLMAs- UP, MP, Rajasthan, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra
Pradesh & Maharashtra were visited by officers from NLM and qualitative and quantitative assessment of performance
made.  Criteria of performance appraisal were effectiveness of administration, management, planning, monitoring and
evaluation of the literacy programmes in the State.
Comments of the Committee
Despite the fact that the actual fund made available was less than that of allocated funds under 8th Five Year
Plan, the Committee finds that even the available fund  was not utilized upto the optimum level.    In Committee’s
view, major portion of allocation of funds under the programme is either wasted or misused.   The Committee,
therefore, feels that remedial steps need to be taken in this direction.  Decentralization of administrative and financial
powers to the State Literacy Mission Authorities (SLMAs) is a step in the right direction.    The Committee, however is
of the view that  the composition of SLMA  should be made in accordance with requirement of the state and  elected
representatives should  be involved in its activities. Besides, the monitoring of the programme in any state should be
done at the level of Chief Secretary periodically  and the D.C./D.M.  be made responsible for proper  implementation of
programmes under this scheme in his/her district.
Recommendation
9.1 The Committee, however is constrained  to note that PLCs have not taken off in the country in the real sense. 
Whereas 442 districts have been covered under TLC, Post Literacy Campaigns have been launched in only 229 districts
so far. 
Action Taken
            The progress of the literacy campaigns was not upto the mark in Hindi Speaking areas due to various factors. 
This has resulted in slow progress of post literacy campaigns throughout the country.  However, the present number of
districts where PLCs have been launched stands at 280 out of total of 450 districts.  In addition, 66 districts have also
launched the subsequent phase of continuing education after completion of the literacy phase.  It is expected to cover the
remaining districts under the PL as well as CE phase during the 9
th  Five Year Plan.  
 
Further Comments
In response to a query as to the factors responsible for the slow progress of literacy campaigns  in Hindi
speaking areas , the Department replied that  the reasons could be as follows:
1.         Low level of literacy: A small base to act as catalyst for Literacy Campaigns
2.         Lower Female Literacy Rates
3.     Inadequate Voluntary Teachers due to low literacy rate and social factors inhibiting Female       Literacy.
The Department also informed that  it has been indicated by the NSSO survey that during the period 1991-97, 
all the Hindi Speaking States have done exceptionally well. Rajasthan has shown dramatic improvement, pushing
forward from 38.55 per cent in 1991 to 55 per cent in 1997, a rise of 16.5 per cent. Uttar Pradesh registered a rise of
14.4 per cent, moving from 41.6 per cent to 56 per cent.  Bihar showed a gain of 10.5 per cent, rising from 38.5 per cent
to 49 per cent.  Himachal Pradesh has surged forward to take third position in the country, moving from 63.9 per cent to
77 per cent --a rise of 13.1 per cent.    The trend indicates that the Hindi Speaking States, though still below the National
average have been able to break the barriers and are surging ahead and it is expected that they would be able to match
the National level soon.
Recommendation
9.2  There is a gap of two to three years in the launching of TLC  and PLC in all the districts.  Thus the basic objective

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
of PLC to provide opportunities of continuing education  to neo-literates so as to facilitate retention of their literacy
skills and to enable the learners to continue their learning beyond elementary literacy stands defeated.  The community,
therefore, recommends that the Department should impress upon all the states especially the educationally backward
states to launch PLCs  in the remaining districts so as to ensure  that benefits of literacy are sustained by the neo-
literates.
Action Taken
NLM’s  policy is to avoid any time lag between the completion of TLC and the subsequent launch of a PLC in a
district.   In order to achieve this, the districts are expected to formulate a Post Literacy Campaign during the currency
of the TLC itself .   However, it is true that in some districts, delay in launching PLC has occurred due to various
unavoidable reasons.   The State Governments have been advised to launch timely PLCs in various districts.
Further Comments
On a specific query as to   what steps are being taken to launch PLC in the remaining districts and  which are the
districts where  formulation of the PLC has not been done during the continuance of the TLC, itself, the Department
informed that Post-Literacy Campaigns have been launched in 352 districts in the country. In the revised policy for
NLM an integrated approach to Literacy has been launched which would enable the enormous illiteracy problem to be
tackled in a holistic manner.  By treating the imparting of functional literacy as a continuum rather than as a one-off
benefit for the illiterate person, progress of literacy efforts would be made goal-directed.  Literacy campaigns would
continue to run in those areas where there are large pools of residual illiteracy.  At the same time, for those who have
crossed the basic learning phase, programmes of consolidation, remediation, vocational skills, integration with life skills
and such other aspects are considered the basic unit.
         A district, while submitting their initial project, now also submits their strategy for post- literacy on the basis of
their anticipated target and projections of achievement.  The integrated proposal seeks to effectively bring the activities
of literacy campaigns under one ‘Literacy Project’ to achieve continuity, efficiency and convergence and to minimise
unnecessary time lag between the two, the Committee was informed.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been given to understand that as per the findings of 53
rd round of NSSO  Survey, during the
period 1991-97, all the Hindi speaking States have done exceptionally well.   The Committee would however, like to
point out that the literacy rate under NSSO  Surveys are based on 7+age  groupwhereas targeted group of NLM is 15 to
35 years age group.   The Committee notes that although considerable progress has been made in the launching of Post
Literacy Campaigns, gap between launching of Total Literacy Campaigns (TLCs) and Post Literacy Campaigns (PLCs)
still persists.   Position as in March, 2000 is that TLCs have been launched in 556 districts, and PLCs have been lunched
in 352 districts.   The Committee is constrained to observe that nine districts of Bihar are yet to be covered by TLCs
inspite of the Department vigorously pursuing the matter with the State Govt. and earmarking funds specially for these
districts.   The Committee notes that besides wide gap between launching of TLCs and PLCs in educationally backward
States, in NE States of Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland and Sikkim and also in J&K, not even one
district has been covered by PLCs so far.   The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that all such States
should be impressed upon to launch PLCs at the earliest in the districts not covered so far.
Recommendation
14.  The Committee, however, feels that  Government proposal  to sanction at least one Shramik Vidyapeeth (SVP) to
each district would not have the desired results. There might be many districts where there is no industry at all .  What is
required is to make , in the first instance, the existing 58 SVPs more purposeful, based on the area specific needs of the
working class. Evaluation of SVP Scheme, if not already done , may be initiated by the Department before further
expansion of the Scheme.
Action Taken
It has been proposed to sanction Shramik Vidyapeeth (SVP) for each district in due course of time keeping in
view the shift of focus of the revised scheme of Shramik Vidyapeeths from urban industrial workers to the neo-literates
and semi literates  and deprived sections of the society. The Expenditure Finance  Committee in its meeting held on
18.12.1998 has approved opening of 50 SVPs during the 9
th  Five Year Plan .  The Shramik Vidyapeeths, at present,

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
functioning in the urban areas, will henceforth be  catering  to the needs  of the neo-literates, semi literates and other
deprived sections of people in urban and rural areas to help them acquire  some vocational skills or to upgrade their
vocational skill and income generating capacity . 
As per the revised scheme , the Shramik Vidyapeeths will concentrate more on continuing education in which
vocational education is a part. Enhanced role of the Shramik Vidyapeeths would be more or less to act as a district level
resource agency for vocational programmes.
The scheme has been evaluated by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences which gave valuable suggestions and
based on that a number of modifications have been carried out in the scheme.  As the scheme is in the threshold of a
change, further evaluation can be carried out after the scheme in the revised form is implemented  for some time.
Further Comments
         The Committee was informed that the Scheme of of Shramik Vidyapeeths was evaluated by the Tata Institute of
Social Sciences (TISS), Mumbai in 1993.  Some of the findings of the evaluation are as under:
·
        As long as the Sharmik Vidyapeeths remain committed to the deprived sections of the society with its tailor-made
programmes of polyvalent education, they have all the justification to exist as institutions outside the formal system
and deserve financial support from the Government;
·        The skill-oriented programmes of the Sharamik Vidyapeeths are largely directed towards enabling the beneficiaries
to be engaged in self-employment;
·        The Shramik Vidyapeeth scheme has the potential to equip individuals with the skills required to be gainfully
employed;
·        None of the existing organisational structures is in itself against the interests of the scheme of Shramik
Vidyapeeths.  Shramik Vidyapeeths can function effectively as autonomous, non-autonomous or semi-autonomous
institutions.
The Committee was further informed  that keeping in view the findings of the evaluation, scheme of  Shramik
Vidyapeeths has been  renamed as Scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) or Institute of People’s Education with
increased focus on imparting vocational training to neo-literates.  Area of Operation of the JSS has been expanded to
cover both the urban and rural areas in the entire district where it is located.   Activities have been enlarged to function
as district repositories of vocational and technical skills under the Continuing Education Scheme.     JSS are to provide
academic and technical support to Zila Saksharata Samitis in taking up vocational and skill development programmes
for neo-literates and to organise equivalency programmes through the Open Learning System.
Comments  of the Committee
The Committee is of the view that adult persons are not merely interested in learning their alphabets.   They
would be only drawn towards this programme if there is a provision of some incentives and their money earning
capacity is also increased. The Committee notes that the revamped scheme of Shramik Vidyapeeths, now renamed as
scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) approved by the Cabinet on 30.11.99 is under implementation  at present.  The
Committee has been given to understand that under this scheme, besides incentives, vocational education is being
imparted so as to enable the beneficiaries to get jobs.
The Committee finds that annual grants  for JSS have been considerably enhanced – from Rs. 12.30 lakh to Rs.
35 lakh for `A’ category city/ town, from Rs. 8 lakh to Rs. 30 lakh for `B’  category city/town and Rs. 25 lakh fixed for
`C’ category city/town.   Besides that considerable provision of non-recurring grant has also been made for vehicle,
equipment and building.  The Committee is of the view that due to the enhanced financial parameters laid down for the
scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan, an inbuilt effective monitoring mechanism with involvement of public
representatives is also required to be built up.  The Committee recommends  that evaluation of the scheme of JSS may
be carried out after some time so as to assess the impact of changes made therein.
Recommendation
17.1 The Committee feels that services of  VAs can be more gainfully employed if identification of really motivated
VAs is got done by State Governments.

Action Taken
In this regard in the EFC for the 9 th Five Year Plan it is proposed that 50% of the grants to the Voluntary
Agencies will be given by the State Literacy Mission Authorities for local projects.  State Literacy Mission Authorities
will be in a better position to screen Voluntary Agencies and also to monitor their performance.  At national level to
release the funds to Voluntary Agencies, the  credentials are checked and with lesser number of projects for monitoring,
the monitoring will be strengthened.
Further Comments
Since the scheme is implemented  with the support of NGOs/VAs , the Committee wanted to know as to what
were the sources of checking the credentials of voluntary agencies at national level.  In response,  the Department has
informed that  the credentials of voluntary agencies at national level are checked by following means:
·        Scrutiny of documents as to whether they have the requisite registration, constitution and experience.
·        Feedback from the State in which functioning regarding performance and credentials through SLMAs.
·        Feasibility study, especially in case of innovative projects by teams comprising of NLM, SLMA & established NGO
personnel.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the view  that most of the NGOs, particularly in the field of Adult Education, are not
performing well and all sorts of complaints have been received against them from various states.  The success of
implementation of a scheme/programme, to a great extent, depends upon the work done by good NGOs.   Therefore, the
selection of NGOs becomes very important.   The selection criteria for NGOs needs to be fool-proof so as to eliminate
fake NGOs without in anyway causing harassment to good NGOs.  The Committee is not sure about the effectiveness of
the above criteria in view of large number of complaints against NGOs.
The Committee  feels that high school students during their vacations can prove to be excellent instructors under
the Adult Education Programme.   The Committee has been given to understand that a special provision has been made
under the revamped programme to involve students as volunteers in Literacy Campaigns.   The Committee hopes that
this initiative would have a positive  impact.
Recommendation
20.1     The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps should be taken to ensure that Adult Education Programme is
taken up on a priority basis  by panchayats.  There is a specific responsibility of making the district fully literate as per
functional norms set by the NLM which may be given to Zilla Panchayats with total planning, implementation and
monitoring.  The funds for this as per requirements of the Zilla  Panchayat should be provided by the Central
Government from the Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  It must be made clear that this fund is in addition to the fund
allocated by the State Finance Commission.  The achievement of the target set by the Zilla Panchayat should be
externally evaluated and responsibility for any shortfall should be fixed on the concernedagency.  This will ensure the
responsibility and accountability coupled with decentralization of power and implementation.
Action Taken
Regarding the role of Panchayati Raj Institutions in the implementation of Literacy Campaigns, it may be stated
that wherever the elected Panchaytat Bodies exist, the implementing agencies  have been  advised to involve Panchayati
Raj functionaries in the actual implementation of the Campaigns.  Instructions have also been issued to reconstitute the
existing Zilla Saksharta Samities wherever PRIs  do not find a place in the Executive Committee  of the ZSS.  During
the 9
th Five Year Plan, the role of Panchayat Bodies in the implementation of Literacy Campaigns is proposed to be
specified more clearly so that they are made responsible for achievement of the overall objectives of the National
Literacy Mission.
Recommendation
20.2     The Committee was also given to  understand that there is a proposal to shift Collector Centric model to
alternative second – line of command to implement the campaigns,  through involvement of more and more non-
officials and voluntary agencies. The 

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
Committee in this connection would like to suggest that the Kerala model may be experimented by making District
Panchayat President as the Chairman and District Collector as coordinator.
Action Taken
Wherever the elected Panchayat bodies exist, like in the States of West Bengal, Kerala  etc., the District
Panchayat President/Chairman of Zilla Parishad have been made as the Chairman of the Zilla Saksharta Samities and
the District Collector as the Executive Vice-Chairman,. This practice could be followed in other States also.
Further Comments
Specifying the role of Panchayat bodies, the Department informed that after the 73
rd Constitutional amendment,
responsibility of Adult Education rests with Zila Parishad/Zila Panchayat.  Panchayat elections have taken place in most
of the States and steps have been taken to nominate the elected representatives of the Panchayati Raj Institutions to the
literacy programmes and to integrate the Panchayat Raj structure more meaningfully with the Zila Saksharata Samiti
(ZSS).  In newly sanctioned districts, representation of Panchayat Raj Organisations at various levels is being ensured. 
Zila Saksharata Samities which were constituted before the election, people’s representatives at Panchayat, Block and
District level are being inducted by reconstituting the ZSS.  Panchayati Raj representatives are being imparted
orientation and sensitisation through workshops being held by the State Resource Centres and the National Literacy
Resource Centre at Mussoorie.
In response to a further query as to whether  the practice of Kerala and West Bengal of making  District
Panchayat President/Chairman of Zila Parishad, the Chairman of the Zila Saksharta Samities (ZSSs) and the District
collector as the Executive Vice-Chairman has been followed in any other State, the Department informed that in the
revised scheme for the nine Plan, the Literacy Programmes will continue to be implemented by the ZSS headed by the
Collector.  However, a democratically elected Chairman of the Zila Parishad may also head the ZSS in a State where a
full-fledged Panchayati Raj system has been established. The Zila Saksharta Samities have complete freedom to adopt
either of the systems, but no other State except West Bengal and Kerala have yet adopted a different pattern.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee feels that the matter has not been taken up in the right earnest.   It recommends that the
experience  of Kerala and West Bengal could be discussed/shared with other States and they could adopt the same if
they found it convenient and useful.

Resource Development, having been authoris.ed by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Eleventh Report of the Committee on the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar University Bill, 1994, alongwith 
the Bill, as amended by the Committee. · 
2. The Bill, which was introduced in.the Rajya Sabha on.the 9th May, 1994, seeks to establish 
and incorporate a teaching and residential University in the State of Uttar Pradesh and to provide for 
matters connected thereWith or incidental thereto. In pursuance of the rules relating to Department­
related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred* .the Bill, to the 
Committee for examination arid report. 
3. A Press Communique, inviting suggestions from various individuals, organisations and 
institutions interested in the subject matter of the Bill, was issued on 24th May, 1994 (Appendix-I). 
4. Twelve memoranda, containing views, opinions, comments and suggestions on the various 
provisions and aspects of the Bill, were received by the Committee. (List at Appendix-IT)'. 
5. The Committee, in its meeting held on the 8th July, 1994, decided that the memoranda received 
by it be sent to the Ministries of Human Resource DevelopmenVLaw, Justice and Company. Affairs 
for obtaining their comments for its consideration. The comments from the concerned Ministries were 
received and considered by the Committee. · 
6. The Committee considered the Bill in seven sittings (Appendix-III) and heard the oral evidence 
of 8 witnesses, including the representatives of Ministries of Human Resource Development 
· (Department of Education) and Law, Justice and Company Affairs (Department of Legal Affairs and 
Legislative Department). Besides, the Committee also heard the views of some eminent Members of 
Parliament. 
7. In its meeting held on the 18th August, 1994 the Committee considered the Draft Report 
and adopted it for presentation/laying in both the Houses. 
8. The Department of Education,. in their detailed note on the subject sub~itted to the 
Committee, explained the need for introduction of the Bill and the circumstances under which the 
University, initially proposed to be set up as a State University, is now sougnt to be set up as a Central 
University. (Appendix-N) 
9. The Secretary, Department of Education, during the course of his oral evidence before t~e 
Committee, stated that one of the unique features of this University is to gives it a distinct bias in favour 
of science and key and frontier areas qf technology, as compared to any other University. 
10. However, some Members expressed the view that the objects of the University, as contained 
in Clause 4 and Schedule 1 of the Bill, do not provide for teaching of subjects near and dear to the 
heart of Dr. B.A. Ambedkar, on whose name the University is being set up. The Committee is of the 
view that a specific provision should be included on this so as to promote the study of the ideology 
and philosophy for which Dr. Ambedkar stood and strove throughout his life. 
11. The Clause also provides for promotion of educational and economic interests and welfare 
* Aajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin part II, Para 34509 dated the 19th May, 1994, 

of the people of Uttar Pradesh, etc. However, the Committee is of the view that the University, which 
is nar:ned after one of the great son of India, should not confine itself to Uttar Pradesh only, and it 
should promote the interests and welfare of the people of the entire country. The Committee has, 
therefore, decided to delete the words of 'Uttar Pradesh'. · 
. 
. 12. The Committee also had some apprehensions about the jurisdiction of the University which 
is mentioned in Clause 6 as Uttar Pradesh and also about admissions in the University. Some Members 
were of the view that a9missions in the University shall be open to students from all parts of the country. 
In this regard, th.e Chairman. U.G.C. clarified to the Commil1ee thaUhe jurisdiction has nothing to do 
· ·· . with admissions. Jurisdiction relates to opening of campuses, etc. It w~s also made clear that this 
University would admit students from all parts of the country. 
13. Members of the Comr:nittee felt that the 'Planning and Academic Committee', as provided 
in the Bill, which would carry out the functions of the Academic Council and the Planning Board during 
the first 10 years of the University, was superfluous and the Comfllittee felt that the provisions relati[lg 
to 'Planning and Academic Committee', wherever occurr~d in the Bill, be done away with. 
14. Some Members of the Committee expressed apprehensions over the possible implications 
of providinQ higher percentage of seats for SCs!STs in this University, on the ground that similar 
demands might be raised in future in the case of admissions to other Central Universities. The 
percentage of reseNations applicable in all the exis.ting Central Universities is 15 per cent for the 
Scheduled Castes and 71/ 2 percent for Scheduled Tribes. This is the first Act of a Central University, 
where the quantum of reseNation is being specifically mentioned. It is· done because this University 
is proposed to be set up for special reasons, which do not apply in the case of other Central Universities. 
Therefore, higher than normal reservation. is proposed in the Bill. 
15. The Committee also sought the views of the Law. Secretary on the legality of providing 
higher percentage to SCs/STs over and above the existing percentage. He stated that a higher 
percentage of seats for SCs/STs would not violate the provisions of the Constitution. He also agreed 
with the view that reseNation could also be provided to BCs, women and handicapped, besides higher 
reseNati<;>n to SCs/STs, subject to an overall ceiling of 50 percent. 
16. On the same issue of higher percentage of reservations to SCs/STs in this University, the 
Chairman, U.G.C .. , during the course of his evidence stated as under: 
• As far as reservation is concerned, there is a provision for reservation in Central Universities. 
But, it is not there in the AGts. This is the national policy ~hich the Central University are expeeted 
to follow." · ' · 
"The University Grants CommissiGn has advised all the Central Universities to implement. it ... 
Now with regard to this Bill, I think this is a departure from the National Policy. Wheri we say that more 
reseNation would be provided, it means that it would be more than 221/ 2 percent.This, naturally, would 
generate demand in other Central Universities as well. But, Ke~ping in mind the fact that this University 
is being named after one of the distinguished sons of this country, Dr. Ambedkar, the Government. 
probably, wanted that there should be more reservation for SCs and STs in this University: 
17. The Committee is of the view that since the University is being set up to perpetuat~ the 
memory of a great son of India, there should not be any reason for such apprehensions. H_owever, 
the ·committee decided to substitute ."higher percentage" by "adequat~ percentage". 
18. While considering Clause 19, some merDbers were ·of the view that the composition of the 
Board of Management had not been specified, either in the Bill or ·in the Statutes. Tl1e Committee 

i recommends that necessary steps should be taken to specify the details of the composition of the Board 
~ in the Statutes at the earliest. The Committee also suggests that ~ provision be made for the 
~ representation of Parliament, Government of India, U.G.C.,etc. in the Bill itself. 1 
19. Th.e Committee agrees with the views expressed by the Chairman, University Grants 
Commission, that whenever a new Central l)niversity is proposed to be set ·up, additional financial 
provision for the same should be made. Otherwise, the funds meant .to~. State Universities would have : 
to be diverted and the State Universities would face resource crunch. ·The Committee recommends 
that Government ·should take necessary steps in t~is regard. · ·

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
The Uttar Pradesh Dr. Shim Rao Ambedkar Act, 1989 (UP Act 25 of 
1989) was enacted by the State Legislature to establish and incorporate a 
unitary teaching and residential University at Lucknow as a memorial to the 
life and works of the late Dr. Shim Rao Ambedkar. However the establishment 
of the University under the State Act was not notified by the State G~vernment. 
2. The U,P. Government had requested that the Central Govt. should 
either convent the Dr. B. R. Ambedkar University of the State Govt. into a 
Central University or agree to bear 50 per cent of the projected cost for the 
establishment of the University. The Standing Committee for the celebration 
of Centenary Year of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar had resolved that this University be 
converted into a Central University and that it may specialize in technology 
courses and provide for higher percentage of seats for SCs/STs. 
3. The Bill Seeks to establish a teaching and residential University at 
Lucknow in the State of Uttar Pardesh. The University shall promote advanced 
courses in Science and key and frontier areas of teshnology and other allied 
· disciplines in the educational programmes of the University;. take appropriate 
measures for promoting innovations in teaching -learning process in inter-
. disciplinary studies and research and pay special attending to the improvement 
of social and economi Conditions and welfare of the people of Uttar Pardesh 
in general and to members belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled 
Tribes in particular by providing higher percentage of seats for SCs and STs. 
4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 
Clause 27 of the Bill provides that the first Statutes are those set out 
in the Sch ed1,.1ie to the Bill. It also empowers the Board of Management of the 
University to make a new or additional Statutes or amend or repeal the Statutes 
to the Univers.ity subject ot the assent of the Visitor. Sub-clause (5) of the 
aforesaid clause empowers the Visitor also to make new or additional St.atutes 
or amend or repeal the Statu tes of the University during the period of three 
years immediately after the commencement of the Act. Sub-clause (6) further 
empowers the Visitor to direct the University to make prdvisions in the Statutes 
in respect of any matter specified by hiin and if the Board of Management is 
unable to implement such directions within sixty days of its receipts, the Visitor 
may, after considering the request, if any communicated by the Board of 
Management for its inability to comply with such directions, make or amend 
the Statutes suitably. The matter in respect of which the Board of Management 
and the Visitor may make, amend or repeal Statutes include the constitution, 
powers and funcitons of the authorities and other bodies of the University, the 
appointment of officers and teachers of the University, the conditions of service 
of the employees of the University and other such matters. 
2. Clause 28 of the Bill empowers the Vice-Chancellor of the University 
to make the first Ordinances of the University with the previous approval of 
the Central Government and provides that the Ordinances so made may be 
amended. repealed or added to at any time by the Board of Management in 
the manner prescribed by the Statutes. The matters in respect of which 
Ordinances may be made, or as the case may be. amended, repealed or added 
to, relate to admission of students, Courses of Study, medium of instruction 
and examina tion. the establishment of Centres of Studies, Boards of Studies. 
Special Centres, Specialised Laboratories and the manner of co-operation and 
collaboration with other Universities and authorities. the management of 
Colleges and Institutions established by the Univesities and other such matter. 
3. Caluse 29 of the Bill enables the authorities of the University of make 
Regulations, consistent with the Act, the Statutes and the Ordinances for the 
conduct of their own business and that of the Committees appointed by them 
and not provided for by the . Act, the Statutes or the Ordinances. 
4. The matter for which Statutes, Ordinances or Regulations may be 
made pertain to matter of procedure of detail and it is hardly possible to provide 
for them in the Bill. The delegation of legislat ive powers is, therefore, of a 
·normal character.

APPENDIX-IV 
Note Necessitating the introduction of the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar University Bill, 1994 
In pursuance of the provisions of Clause (3) of Article 348 of the Constitution, the Governor 
of Uttar Pradesh promulgated on 11th April, 1989, the Uttar Pradesh Doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar 
University Ordinance , 1989 (U.P. Ordinance No.3 of 1989) for the establishment of Doctor Bhimrao 
Ambedkar University at Lucknow and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. 
Subsequently the Legislature of Uttar Pradesh Passed on 6th October, 1989 the Uttar Pradesh Doctor 
Bhimrao Ambedkar University Act. 1989 (U.P. Act No. 25 of 1989} to establish and incorporate a unitary 
teaching and research residential University at Lucknow as a memorial to the life and works of the 
late Doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar. The above- mentioned ordinance as also the Act, provided that the 
Ordinance or the Act would come into force on such date as the State Goverment might, by 
notification,appoint in this behalf. The State Government has reported that the Ordinance as well as 
the Act have not been brought into force by the State Government. As a conseq uence. no of­
ficer of the University, namely Vice-Chancellor. Registrar, Faculty members, etc. have been appoinfed. 
A limited staff headed by a Chief Administrator has. however, been appointed by the State Government 
in a project to ensure the establishment of the proposed State University. 
2... The State Government. of Uttar Pradesh had. constituted an Expert Committee in July, 1989, 
under the Chairmanship of Shri T.P. Tiwari, to give recommendations on the faculties and courses to 
be started in the University. The Expert Committee identified the following faculties with which the 
University could start operating with provisions for future expansion:-
1. Material Science & Technology . 
2. Bio-Sciences & Technology . 
3. Space Sciences & Technology. 
4. Instrumentation & Design Engineering (including Micro-Eiectronices) . 
5. Pharmaceutical Sciences. 
6. Management Sciences. 
7. Social Sciences & Technology. 
The University was proposed to have a Science & Technology orientation. 
3. In pursance of the above enactment the State Government has acquired about 244 acres ot 
.land on Lucknow -Rai Bareili H1ghway near Sanjay Gandhi Post Graduate lnstitrte of medical sciences, 
Lucknow. No. The cost of the project was estimated by the State Government at Rs.200.00 Crores. 
The State Government has already spent about Rs. 14.00 Crores on the Project. A boundary wall has 
been constructed around the campus of the University and a life-size bronze statue of Babasaheb 
Bhimrao Ambedkar was InStalled on 14.4.199~ . by Shri Mulayam Smgh Yadav, the then Chief Minister 
of Uttar Pradesh. Some other works , like temporary supply of electnc1ty. water supply and tree plantation 

in the campus have also been done. However. further work has not been carried out due to financial 
constraints. · 
4. Shri Mulayam Singh Yadav, the then Chef Minister of Uttar Pradesh has on 1.6.1990 requested 
the Prime Minister that in view of the limited resources of the State, the Centre should provide financial 
assistance to the extent of 50% of the estimated cost lor establishing the University. There were also 
requests from other quarters lor the conversion of the Doctor Bhmirao Ambedkar University into a ' 
Central University . Shri Kalyan Singh, the then Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh had on 18.5.1992 written 
to the Prime Minister that the Centre should either convert Doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar University into· _.:.:-. 
a Central University or agree to bear 50% of the projected cost for establishing the University. Requests •· 
from any eminent persons. including Dr. (Mrs.) Savita Ambedkar. Parliamentarians and publicmen were 
also recived for conversion of doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar University at Lucknow into a Central University. 
The Minister of welfare had also written to HRM on 22.8.1992 to consider the proposal of the State 
Government favourably. The Standing Committee for the Celebration of the Centenary year of 
Babasahib Or. B.R. Ambedka r had also resolved that this University be converted into a Central 
University and that it may specialise in Technology courses and provide for a higher percentage of 
seats for SCs and ST s. 
5. The r.aatter regarding the conversion of Doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar University into a Central • 
University was considered by the Cabinet in its meeting on 6.4.1993. It was submitted to the Cabinet 
that the conversion of Dr.B.R. Ambedkar University into a Central University cannot be considered at 
par with other demands for conversion of State Universities because of the uniqueness of this proposal. 
The fact that this will be a technological University and would make special efforts towards imparting 
of technical education. in particular to the weaker sections, makes this proposal unique. 
6. In pursuance of the above decision , the Department of Education processed the matter in 
consultation with the officials of the Government of Uttar Pradesh and of the Ministry of Law. 
7. The Governme nt of Uttar Pradesh have since sent their commitment to repeal the existing State 
Act. The State Government has also intimated that the assets to be transferred to Central University 
are being identified. 
8. The Cab1net at its meeting on 6th April. 1993 approved that the Qr. B.R. Ambedkar University, 
as a Central University. would be a technological University and w.ould make special efforts towards 
imparting technical educat1on m particular to the weaker sections. In keeping with this, it is proposed 
to provide authority to the proposed University for a higher percentage of seats for SCs and Sts. 
9 Since the Or. B.R. Ambedkar Un1vers1ty would be specialising in technology courses the cost 
of setting up this Umversity would be more than that of a conventional University. Though the cost 
of the project has been estimated by the State Government of Uttar Pradesh at Rs.200 crores, precise 
est1mates of funds requ1red for setting up the University is not possible as the development of any 
Univers1ty continues for 12 to 15 years. It has been decided that the UGC will approve developmental 
proposal of the proposed Un1vers1ty on a 5 year basis with a view to ensuring its optimum development.

EPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in its Seventy-fourth Report on the
Vocational  Education which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 8th December,1998. Action Taken Notes have been received
from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report.  They have been categorized as follows:-
(i)                  Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: Para 2.2, 2.6, 2.10, 2.12, 2.14, 2.16, 2.21, 2.23 and 2.28 (Chapter-
I)
(ii)                Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government’s replies: 2.3, 2.5, 2.7, 2.8, 2.17, 2.18,
2.27 and 2.29  (Chapter-II)
(iii)               Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted by the Committee : Para-2.1, 2.4, 2.9, 2.11,
2.13, 2.15,  2.19, 2.20, 2.22, 2.24, 2.25, and 2.26   (Chapter-III)
(iv)              Recommendations/Observations in respect of which  replies of the Government have not been received.  –Nil, (Chapter-IV)
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
2.2       The Committee is deeply anguished to note that only 5% of the targets fixed has been achieved.  The Committee is of the view that even if this figure is
to be relied on, there remains another 20% to be covered by 2000 AD for diversion of students at +2 level which stands as a tough task ahead.  The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the Deptt. should make serious efforts to give a meaningful thrust to the scheme.  The Committee also feels that the
programme needs to be totally reoriented.
Action Taken
            In 1999-2000, the programme was evaluated by the Centre for Planning, Research and Action and the Centre in its report emphasised that there should
not be any tie up of the educational plans with hypothetical targets of diversion at +2 level to the Vocational Education Programmes.  In fact,  the report termed
the NPE-1986 target of 25% diversion of students to V.E. stream as “absurdly unrealistic and should never have been included in the document.   Even 10%
target for the year 1995 was not achievable and has not been achieved.  It is necessary to examine this fetish of fixing targets in the cut and dry manner adopted
so far, and learn from the experience of  Family Welfare planners who also went on fixing unrealistic targets year after year till it was given up on the World
Bank initiative.”  However, as per the information available, the total enrolment under the programme is about 4 lakhs (23 states/UTs.) which works out 5.17%
compared to the figure of 3.18 lakhs (4.82%) given in ORG Report in 1995 (22 states/UTs.).  In real terms, the increase in enrolment for vocational courses
amounts to about 80,000.  Reorientation process, which includes exploring the possibility of linkages with Industrial Training Institutes and community
polytechnics for maximum use of infrastructure, has been initiated.
Recommendation
2.6       As the scheme of Vocational Education is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme and funds allocated depend on proposals received from the States, the
Committee is of the view that sufficient awareness is required to be created in this regard.  The Committee is also of the view that proper initiative is lacking on
the part of the Central Government due to which the problems are arising.  The Committee stresses that the Department should take all necessary steps to
activate the State Directorates and increase awareness among the States about the utility and importance of the scheme.

Action Taken

Secretaries in the near future.
Recommendation
2.10     The Committee feels that there is a necessity on the part of the vocational schools to formulate updated packages which must be multifunctional
through trades/specialised skills from secondary school level.  There is also necessity of a placement cell to establish, maintain and disseminate placement
status record at the school and provide a sense of direction to the students.  The Principals of the Vocational Schools and Heads of the respective Departments
should be in
constant liaison with sector specific industry personnel/ representative deputed by the collaborating industry.
Action Taken
Several states have made provisions for placement and Vocational Education Guidance Cells.  Through these cells, vocational pass-outs are counselled to take
apprenticeship programme under Board of Apprenticeship Training.  At the Central Government level, pilot project with NIFT and those in pipeline with
FICCI, CII will also help placement of Vocational pass-outs.
Recommendation
2.12     Looking at the present scenario, the Committee feels that there is a need to devise a system of imparting vocational education which while building a
sound theoretical base, could also ensure connectivity to the market and job security.
Action Taken
            Committee’s observations to the effect that vocational courses should ensure connectively to the market and job security will be considered at the time
of revising the existing scheme.   It may not be out of place to mention that the present curriculum has a component on entrepreneurial development, guidance
and counselling.   This step, to some extent, will obviate the need for job security.
Recommendation
2.14    Similarly, many students who are good at practical and vocational courses may be weak in the regular subjects such as language, mathematics, science
etc.  Such students may not be able to pass out the regular examination to get the schools certificate.  It is, therefore, necessary that a separate certificate for
vocational course is given to enable such students to get gainful employment.  In case a student could not complete the other subjects but secured good marks
in vocational papers, another year of practical training may be given and a certificate in vocational course could be given to him.  There could also be two
levels of vocational certificate course.  The lower level should cover the students who take up Vocational Education after class VII or class VIII and Higher
level certificate could be given to those who take up Vocational Education after class X.  The certificate from Vocational Education centres would act as a
proof of acquired knowledge in skill.  There can be separate institute or Board for issuing the certificate for vocational education.  The certificate can be
recognised one just like the ITI certificate.
Action Taken
New vocational courses are being designed in modular form.  In this format after completing each module a certificate indicating the competency will
be issued by the Central Board of Secondary Education.  National Open School also offers 49 vocational courses in 7 broad disciplines for different durations. 
Credit transfer is also being implemented by NOS for award of certificates at X and XII level.  The existing courses will be taken up for designing in modular
form at the time of their revision.  Plans are afoot to introduce multilevel entry and exit with certificate being issued for each course at all levels.
     A committee has been constituted to advise on vertical mobility of vocational pass-outs.  Representatives from NIEPA, UGC, PSSCIVE and this
Department’s technical bureau are members.  The committee had held its 1
st meeting and come out with its initial findings/recommended action.
Recommendation
2.16     The Committee is constrained to note that even if seats are reserved for the Dalits and other deprived sections in Vocational Institutes, many of them are
not in a position to finally clear the courses offered.  The Committee also observes that in rural areas, due to poor infrastructural facilities and lack of other
development facilities many a student fail to compete with the urban educated students.  Hence, the Committee is of the view that unless some sort of coaching
classes are provided to these groups, it would be difficult to achieve the desired goal.  The Committee,  therefore,  recommends that coaching classes be
arranged for the disadvantaged sections of society.
Comments of the Department
            The concerns of the Committee have been communicated to the State Governments for consideration while running vocational courses in schools and
other areas.
Recommendation
2.21     The Committee is of the opinion that Voluntary Organisations must submit their audited report year wise.  The Committee desires that the evaluation by
Joint Evaluation Team be conducted every year and voluntary agencies must be made accountable to the local community for their acts of omissions and
commissions.
Action Taken
            A copy of the sanction order is being endorsed to the local Panchayat, MLA, MP and state government concerned to keep a watch over thefunctioning
of these organisations. Release of grants to the NGOs (2
nd installment) is linked to the report from local District Magistrate or visit by Joint Evaluation Teams.
Recommendation
2.23     The Committee was given to understand that under the Vocational Education Scheme, Certificate is issued by the Board after the completion of two-
year course.  The Deptt., however, clarified that there were some courses which did not require two years to complete it.  The Committee is of the view that the
courses which can be completed in less than two years should not be prolonged purposelessly and permitted to be completed within the required period only. 
By putting a strict range of two years for Vocational Education for a course which could be completed much earlier, the scheme itself has created a barrier for
the students.  Hence, the Committee recommends that there should be flexibility in the term of the courses and necessary changes in the Vocational Education
scheme may be effected accordingly.
Action Taken
            Steps have been taken to introduce flexibility/modularity in the design of the vocational courses to provide for multiple entry/exit.  This flexibility will
enable those who want to upgrade their knowledge through studies after a break or who want to pursue the course in a limited manner for one reason or the
other.  Under the system, certificates will be issued for the courses successfully completed.  Steps are being taken to link the prior learning through issue of
certificates or equating them with the known standards.
Recommendation
2.28     The Committee is constrained to note that although physical achievements so far as training aspects of both the Schemes is concerned are quite
satisfactory, this is not the position if we look at the figures relating to number of Youths self-employed/wage employed.  The Committee would like to
emphasise that generation of employment, both self and wage-employment, is the ultimate objective of both these schemes.  The Committee, accordingly,
recommends that some pilot projects should be started on trial basis where all kinds of facilities are made available to trainees so as to make them gainfully
employed.

CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
Recommendation
2.3       The Committee is also not happy to note that in spite of 9 years of implementation of the programme, the need and area based approach has not yet
been strictly followed.  The Committee recommends that community participation and need and area based approach must be followed to accelerate the
process of diversion of students at the +2 level so as to achieve the target.
Action Taken
            So far, 320 districts have been got surveyed by various State/UT governments and vocational courses have been introduced on the basis of these survey
reports.  On their own assessment, they have introduced need/area based courses.  More projects in consultation with FICCI, CII, CBSE and other stakeholders
to develop and operationalise more need/area based courses are in the pipeline.
Recommendation
2.5       The Committee finds that in many a case, the Central assistance released for vocational education is used by the states as a ways and means expenses
and/or diverted for the purpose other than the one for which the assistance was released.  The Committee feels that this is not a healthy trend.  The Committee
is of the considered view that this problem can be tackled if separate funds are earmarked for Vocational Education  by the Planning Commission and it is
impressed upon the State Govts. that non-utilisation of funds for Vocational Education would be treated as misappropriation, for which the concerned State
Government would be held responsible.  The Committee also recommends that for proper monitoring, there should be a Joint Monitoring Mechanism which
would have representatives from Central Govt., State Govt. concerned, Members of Parliament from the particular State and MLAs of that area to ensure
successful implementation of the scheme.
Action Taken
            State Governments have been advised of the recommendation of the policy regarding diversion of funds for the purpose other than the prescribed one
and non-utilisation of funds for the allocated purpose.  The monitoring is done by the area officer scheme, personal visits of the officers concerned with the
scheme and review of the progress of each scheme, state-wise by the Secretary himself.  The details are given as under:
(1) Area Officer Scheme: Under this Scheme, each Deputy Secretary/ Director level officer has been allocated one or two states.  The Area Officer prior
to his visit to the state concerned collects information from the various divisions in regard to the issues to be sorted out with the State Government.
(2) Education Secretary has recently instructed all the Divisions dealing with the schemes to endorse a copy of the sanction to Block Development
Officer, Panchayat President, M.L.A. & M.P. representing the area and to the Webmaster for putting up on the website for the general information of
the public.  Accordingly, copies of sanctions have been endorsed.
 
Recommendation
2.7      The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the neglect of District Vocational Surveys.  These surveys are an important ingredient, because the
need and area based approach of the programme depends mainly thereon.  The yearly District Vocational Surveys should be made compulsory and community
participation in it should be encouraged so that assessment of manpower requirements of the area, range of available occupations, trend of emerging vocations
etc. are properly recognised.  Without this, it is difficult to introduce area and need based courses.
Action Taken
Realising the importance of District Surveys, effective steps were taken to ensure district surveys throughout the country.  Considerable progress has
been achieved, as survey has been completed in 320 districts.  State Governments have been advised to ensure the completion of surveys in the remaining
districts.
Recommendation
2.8       The Committee finds that the courses offered are generally not very popular in many of the states. If out-dated courses are offered, the people would
have very limited choice. Similarly, if a course which is not suitable to an area is introduced, students would not be attracted  by such courses. It is, therefore,
essential that the programme should include the courses which are useful in the tertiary sector. The Committee is,  however, constrained to note that the
approach of the Department is very peripheral in this regard. There are many examples such as plumbing, carpentry, agriculture related skills, pump set repairs,
para medical courses which can be introduced on requirements.  There is a tremendous scope and demand for such courses. The Department should keep  in
mind the fact that the vocational education programme is meant for improving the skills of the people who are not able to go for higher education, rather than
making people engineers/architects/scientists, etc. 
Action Taken
            The scheme requires only energisation through meetings/ conferences.  A committee has been constituted to review the linkages of the vocational
courses to the tertiary sector.  The scheme provides for periodical updating of vocational courses.  Pt. Sunderlal Sharma Central Institute of Vocational
Education (PSSCIVE) reviews the vocational courses in consultation with other agencies.  Several obsolete courses have been weeded out.  New courses in
several areas including Information Technology have been introduced.  Central Apprenticeship Council also reviews vocational courses periodically.  The steps
outlined above will hopefully rectify the situation.
Recommendation
2.17     The Committee is of the opinion that mentally and physically handicapped children and other deprived sections of  the society need to be given special
attention.  A more humanitarian approach should be followed while dealing with the neglected and disabled sections of society whereoutput need not be judged
by the adherence to law rather  than by the number of people benefited and settled.
Action Taken
            The State/UT Governments have been advised to remove infrastructural barriers and to provide special facilities like toilets, ramps etc. in the schools
for the welfare of the disabled children studying therein.  Under Integrated Education of Disabled Children (IEDC) scheme disabled children are provided
school uniform, books, stationery, equipment to overcome disability, transport allowance, hostel allowance, etc.  The IEDC Scheme endeavours to promote
inclusive education in general/mainstream schools.  A scheme of Community Polytechnics for persons with disabilities has been envisaged under the ambit of
Community Polytechnics to provide institutional, technical, vocational and educational support to children with disabilities.  Fifty polytechnics have been
selected which would benefit every year 1250 students with disability in diploma level courses and 5000 students with disability in short duration Technical/
Vocational courses.  Also after the promulgation of the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995,
all government educational institutions and other educational institutions receiving aid from the government, shall reserve not less than 3% of seats for persons
with disabilities.  The State/UT Governments, KVS, NVS, UGC, NOS and other Bureaux in the Ministry of HRD have been advised accordingly.  Relaxed
standards are also applied to such students taking examinations.  All sanctions to State Governments/NGOs would highlight and emphasis 3% reservation in
admissions for children with disabilities.
Recommendation
