 OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT GLANCE
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
            The Committee is aware that under the Constitution, Sports is a State subject and in the implementation of the
different youth and Sports related schemes, State Govts./ autonomous organisations/NGOs have to play a very active
role.    However, the Committee has observed that during the Ninth Plan period,  although the allocation has been
generally  less than the projected requirements, allocated funds after being reduced at the RE stage remained under-
utilised.   Another disturbing trend noticed by the Committee was non-uniform spread of expenditure during the year.  
Last year, the Committee had pointed out that the expenditure on different schemes should be planned in such a way
that last moment spending is avoided.   The Committee is, however, constrained to point out that the situation seems to
have worsened in 2001-2002.   Against a Plan allocation of Rs. 255.00 crore, expenditure reported as on 1.3.2002 is
only Rs. 155.84 crores.   Specially under  the Youth Welfare Schemes, expenditure reported upto 1.3.2002 is less than
half of the allocated funds (Plan allocation - Rs. 91.25 crores Exp. upto 1.3.2002 is Rs. 42.47 crores).    The Committee
strongly feels that the formulation of a quarterly annual action plan for 2001-2002 has failed to achieve the  desired
results.    The Committee would like to point out that instead of projecting higher requirements and launching new
schemes without completing the requisite formalities, focus should be on the judicious and optimum utilisation of funds

122nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/122ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:28]
allocated for various schemes.   The Committee is of the view that a detailed review of all the ongoing schemes should
be undertaken so as to assess the shortcomings being noticed and take remedial steps for removal of the same.   The
Department should endeavour to involve the State Govts. and various implementing agencies in this exercise. (Para 2.3)
III.       NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN
The Committee, however, notes that an expenditure of only Rs. 11.12 crores has been incurred upto 1.3.2002 against an
allocation of Rs. 23.23 crores in BE 2001-2002.   The Committee has been given to understand that during 2000-2001,
the last instalment  of GIA  was released to NYKS only in the last week of March, 2001 as the Utilisation Certificate
submitted by the Sangathan was not in an appropriate  format.   The Committee  apprehends that non-submission of
Utilisation Certificate and statement of  accounts within  the prescribed time limit must be one of the reasons for
expenditure of only one-third of the allocated funds under NYKS during 2001-2002.   The Committee would like to be
apprised about the factors responsible for such a discouraging trend.  (Para 3.8)
Annual Report for the year 2001-2002  highlights a variety of regular programmes like Youth Club
Development,  Awareness Generation, Vocational Training etc.    organised and seminars and workshops conducted by
various Nehru Yuva Kendras and on each programme/workshop etc.   funds ranging from Rs. 4,000 to Rs. 30,000 per
Kendra have been either allocated or earmarked.  The number of these programme/workshops must have increased by
the year end i.e. 31
st March, 2002.    The Committee strongly feels that either these achievements in majority of the
cases are on paper only or unspent balances are lying with  many Nehru Yuva Kendras.  Either way, it cannot be
considered an ideal position.    The Committee is of the view that the Department should not entirely depend on the
progress reports forwarded by the NYKS.   An effective  monitoring  mechanism  with an element of surprise 
inspections should be evolved.    It is understood that instructions have already been issued for associating the local
MPs/MLAs with the District Advisory Committee on Youth Programmes.    The Committee would like to be informed
within  a period of three months about the implementation of these instructions together with the details of the inter-
action with local MPs/MLAs.  (Para 3.9)
The Committee notes that a total of 492 district NYKs have District Advisory Committee for Youth Programme
(DACYPs) and for the remaining 8 districts, DACYPs are likely to be formed by the first quarter of 2002-2003.    The
Committee observes that against the prescribed 30% representation of women in DACYPs, national average comes to
36.47%.    The Committee is, however, constrained to point out that in some of the States/UTs, representation of
women  in DACYPs is much below the prescribed 30% .   For example in Lakshdweep, it is as low as 11.1% and in
West Bengal only 13.63%.    The Committee recommends that NYKS in such States/UTs. should be approached for
doing the needful in this regard. (Para 3.10)
The Committee hopes that these efforts would have the desired results. (Para 3.7)
IV        NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME (NSS)
The Committee would like to point out that although allocation of funds might have been less than the projected
requirements of the Department in 1999-2000 and 2000-2001, allocated funds had remained under-utilised.   Situation
seems to have worsened in 2001-2002.   Against allocation of Rs. 23.85 crores, only Rs. 9.15 crores have been utilised
upto 1.3.2002. (Para  4.3)
            While examining the Demands for Grants for 2000-2001, the Committee had expressed its serious concern over
non-settlement of accounts by a large number of States/UTs.  The Committee notes that since then, situation has
improved somewhat in respect of States like Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Mizoram, West Bengal,
Arunachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Chandigarh, Sikkim and Rajasthan.   However, in respect of the following
States, no improvement whatsoever has been made:
State A/cs. settled 1999-2000 A/cs. settled as on 15.2.2002
Assam 1979-80 1979-80
Delhi 1982-83 1982-83
Lakshwadweep 1983-84 1983-84
A.N. Islands 1979-80 1979-80
Jammu & Kashmir 1989-90 1989-90
The Committee observes that situation might have improved in respect of some States/UTs, but the fact remains
that pendency in settlement  of accounts is there more or less in respect of all States/UTs.   The Committee expresses its

122nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/122ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:28]
serious concern over this state of affairs specially in the case of above-mentioned States/UTs.   What is more shocking is
that implementing agencies under NSS are universities, colleges and +2 level schools and institutions of higher learning
and not NGOs lacking the required background.    The Committee finds it rather amazing that the Department has failed
to pursue the matter even with NCT of Delhi.  (Para 4.4)
             The Committee is constrained to note that unspent NSS Grants amounting to Rs. 25,12,84,195 are lying with
various State Govts./UTs  with Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, UP, Gujarat and Maharashtra
being the major defaulters. As per the accounting procedure under NSS, funds are transferred from Central Govt. to
State Govts.   The State  Govts. after adding their  share of funds transfer this amount to the Universities/+2 level
schools which, in turn, transfer this amount to the NSS implementing units in colleges/schools.   The States/UTs submit
their accounts in the prescribed proforma indicating the details of central share and matching state share grants.   The
Committee has been informed that the present accounting procedure is working satisfactorily and there was no proposal
to revamp it.   The Committee is, however, not inclined to agree with the contention of the Ministry.   Had it been so,
huge amount of unspent NSS Grants would not have been lying with many States/UTs.   The Committee is of the firm
view that there is an urgent need to review the accounting procedure under NSS and the Department should initiate
action in this regard. (Para 4.5)
V         NATIONAL SERVICE VOLUNTEER SCHEME
            The Committee notes that no unspent balance is lying with the implementing agencies for National Service
Volunteers Scheme, which are being instructed that no unspent balance will be adjusted as done in previous years and
fresh proposal for GIA will only be considered on refund of unspent amount in future.    The Committee, however, notes
with concern that even though EFC has given its approval for increase in honorarium for NSVS volunteer, it has
effectively reduced the impact of the scheme by stating that the increase has to be met within the available resources
which in turn will see a considerable reduction in the number of volunteers over a period of time. (Para 5.3)
VI        NATIONAL INTEGRATION PROGRAMME
The Committee  notes that out of 258 National Integration Camps held during 2000-2001, none was held in NE
States of Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura, only one camp was held in each of the State of Meghalaya,
Nagaland and Sikkim and two camps in Assam.   Manipur is the only state where eight camps were held during this
period.   The Committee notes with constraint that the situation has deteriorated further during 2001-2002  with only
one camp being approved for Assam in the entire NE region and Sikkim.   While noting that every year about  75%
camps are organized by NGOs, the Committee understands that the Central Govt. also organizes such camps through its
subordinate offices like the NYKs and NSS units and also in collaboration with State Govts.    The Committee fails to
understand the reasons for lack of initiative on the part of the Central Govt. in holding such camps in uncovered areas
like N-E region.   The Central Govt. should pursue with the concerned State Govts. and NYKs and NSS units for
holding the National Integration camps there.    The Committee also feels that this scheme should be reviewed so as to
assess its impact specially in States/UTs like Bihar, UP, MP and Delhi where a very large number of camps have been
held during 2000-2001. (Para 6.3)
VII       YOUTH HOSTELS
Undue delay in completion of construction process of Youth Hostels has been engaging the attention of the
Committee since last year.   From the details about 21 Youth Hostels under construction, the Committee is shocked to
learn that there are Youth Hostels approved as early as in 1986 where 1
st and even 2 nd instalment of central funds for
construction had been released at the earliest, with concerned State Govt taking ten years in identifying suitable land for
the Youth Hostel.   Construction of Youth Hostel in Lucknow was approved in principle  on 21.8.87, and State Govt
identified the land in 1998.   Three instalments of central funds amounting to Rs. 70.00 lakhs released so far, with the
first instalment released in March, 1988 and the construction is yet to be  completed.   Position with regard to the
remaining Youth Hostels is more or less the same.   So far as 23 Youth Hostels approved in principle are concerned, the
earliest dates back to 1986.   Not much progress, apart from correspondence with the State Governments,  has been
made.   It seems that these proposals will continue to remain for another ten years or so.   The Committee notes that a
number of steps like writing letters to concerned State Chief Secretaries and entrusting of constructing work only to
CPWD have been taken by the  Department.   But the Committee does not find any noticeable impact of the same so
far.    The Committee would like to emphasise that drastic measures are required to be taken in the matter as with the
passage of time, estimates for construction would also keep on steadily increasing, thus leading to criminal wastage of

122nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/122ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:28]
Government funds. (Para 7.2)
VIII      NATIONAL RECONSTRUCTION CORPS SCHEME (NRC)
            The Committee hopes that the  scheme would fulfill its objectives. The Committee has, however, a word of
caution in view of different schemes relating to different Departments and Ministries sought to be implemented under
the umbrella of one single scheme.  The idea is a laudable one.  But the Department will have to play a pro-active role
by having proper co-ordination with all the Departments/Ministries and acting as the main linking force between the
implementing agency and the concerned Department.  The Committee would like to point out that a strong monitoring
mechanism also needs to be evolved from the very beginning for effective implementation of  the scheme of National
Reconstruction Corps.  The Committee also recommends that instead of launching all the targeted schemes in a
particular district simultaneously,  assessment should be made about their requirement and only thereafter schemes
should be implemented on priority basis. (Para 8.3)
IX        PROMOTION OF YOUTH ACTIVITIES AND TRAINING
The Committee is, however, constrained to note that not much progress seems to have been made during 2001-
2002.  The Committee notes that the Planning Commission have approved the merger of these schemes as part of the
zero-based budgeting exercise and the Ministry of Finance are now being approached to convey their approval.  The
Committee urges upon the Department to expedite the completion of all the formalities so that the new composite
scheme could be activated during 2002-2003.  (Para 9.2)
The Committee notes that there is a long list of such NGOs having Govt. funds lying with them from 1997-98
onwards as detailed in the Annual Report of the Ministry for 2001-2002.  The Committee would like to quote two
examples.  Under the earlier scheme of `Financial Assistance to Voluntary Organisations working in the Field of Youth’
as many as 40 NGOs in Bihar are yet to submit Utilization Certificates pertaining to more then  Rs. 52.00 lakhs since
1999-2000.  Likewise from UP, 48 NGOs are having funds amounting to more that Rs. 75.00 lakhs with them since
1999-2000.  The Committee has been given to understand that action has been taken to stop further Grants to such
NGOs and the matter is being actively pursued with them.  The Committee does not have much faith in this exercise. 
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that all the inherent flaws particularly relating to handling of
earlier schemes by NGOs should not be reflected in the revised scheme.  At the same time, the Committee fails to
understand as to how NGOs not having the proper antecedents are released Govt. funds for running different schemes. 
The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for having an element of accountability at every level –
Centre/State/district.  Only then, things might improve.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a fool proof
mechanism for selection of NGOs should be put into practice.  Efforts should also be made to avoid concentration of
many NGOs in one particular  district. (Para 9.3)
The Committee hopes that all the preliminary formalities for these two proposed schemes have been completed.
(Para 9.4)
X         SPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA
The Committee hopes that allocation of Rs. 88.23 crores in BE 2002-2003 would not remain under utilised.
(Para 10.2)
10.3     The Committee hopes that all the infrastructure created would be optimally utilized and there should also be
proper plan for maintaining of the buildings/stadia constructed at huge cost. (Para 10.3)
XI        SPECIAL AREA GAMES (SAG) SCHEME
            The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made in this matter.  The Committee hopes that the
State Govt. of Orissa must have handed over the Sankara Sports complex for establishment of a full fledged SAG
Centre at Sundargarh during 2002-2003.  If not done, the Ministry should make all efforts to expedite the same.  The
Committee strongly feels that the Sports Authority of India should make a special endeavour to activate such proposals
whenever brought to its notice. (Para 11.3)
XII       ALL INDIA COUNCIL FOR PHYSICAL EDUCATION
The Committee is not in favour of allocating a token provision for a yet to be approved scheme.  General trend
noticed by the Committee in such matters is that token provision is made year after year with the scheme continuing in a
proposal stage.  The Committee is of the strong view that only after completing all the requisite preliminary formalities

122nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/122ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:28]
for launching a new scheme, provision of funds should be made  for the same. (Para 12.1)
XIII      INCENTIVE SCHEMES
It is understood that these schemes are proposed to be brought under one composite scheme.  The Committee
welcomes the initiative as, by and large,  these schemes have failed to achieve their targets during Ninth Plan period. 
The Committee strongly feels that there is a need for giving wide publicity to such incentive schemes so that the
targeted persons can get the maximum benefit thereunder.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that the Ministry
should make concerted efforts in this direction. (Para 13)
XIV     GRANTS TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS.
The Committee has been given to understand that these federations being autonomous organisations, Govt. have
very little say in their affairs.  The Committee, however, is of the view that as Govt. funding is there, there has to be an
element of accountability also.  Out of 50 federations provided financial assistance during 2001-2002, allocations range
from Rs. 23,750 to Rs. 1,91,17,000.  The Committee strongly feels that submission of quarterly progress reports should
be made a pre-condition  for further release of funds.  The Committee finds that School Games Federation of India and
Tug of War Federation of India were provided Rs. 18,72,809 and Rs. 10,00,000 respectively in 2001-2002.  The
Committee would like to have an idea about the activities of these federations.  The Committee recommends that an
exercise for reviewing and evaluating the work done by all federations should also be initiated.  Such an exercise is
likely to clear the picture about the inherent flaws in the system and also come up with suggestions for improvement.     
(Para 14.3)
XV       GRANT FOR CREATION OF SPORTS INFRASTRUCTURE
The Committee finds that the main reason for such a situation is that some States have not incurred their share of
expenditure with the result the Department could not release the Central Govt’s share as the scheme prescribes incurring
of State Govt’s share  first.  Last year, the Committee noticed that 274 sports infrastructure projects sanctioned from
1990 onwards till 28.2.01 were in various stages of construction.  The  Committee has been apprised that during the
period 1998-2001, 65 projects have been completed after a lot of persuasion and constant correspondence.  The
Committee, however, feels that this has not made any  significant change in the number of pending projects.  The
Committee is not aware about the number of projects completed during 2001-2002.  The Committee has been given to
understand that no time limit has been prescribed under the scheme for completion of projects, indication of one  to two
years’ time for completion indicated in the application form and provision regarding claiming assistance within two
years in the approval letter notwithstanding.  The Committee is of the firm view that adherence to the time limit by both
the implementing agencies and the Ministry would have shown a better record.  These over-delayed projects have
virtually defeated the very purpose of launching of the scheme for Creation of Sports Infrastructure. (Para 15.2)
XVI     GRANT FOR INSTALLATION OF SYNTHETIC PLAYING SURFACES
            During the Ninth Plan period, allocation of funds and utilization thereof under this scheme has shown a
declining trend.  The Committee observes that situation has been very discouraging during 2001-2002, the last year of
the Ninth Plan.  Allocation of Rs. 5.40 crores was reduced to Rs. 3.85 crores at the RE stage and expenditure reported
upto 1.3.2002 is only Rs. 43 lakhs.  The Committee notes that the main reason for under-utilization of funds under this
scheme has been the difficulty being faced in providing the matching in share as well as failure of user agencies
furnishing the progress report and utilization certificates of the already approved projects.  The Committee has been
informed that during Ninth Plan, 16 synthetic hockey surfaces and 6 synthetic athletic tracks in different parts of the
country have been approved with Central assistance of Rs. 20.22 crores and the balance of Rs. 9.66 crores payable for
these projects.  The Committee has no other alternative but to conclude that the approval of 22 projects under the
scheme of `Grant for Installation of Synthetic Playing Surface’ indicates a very dismal picture as apparently not even a
single could be completed and put to effective use during the Ninth Plan period.  The Committee strongly urges the
Ministry to expedite the completion of all these pending projects without any further delay. (Para 16.2)
The Committee hopes that there will be no further delay in the launching of the revised scheme pertaining
to infrastructure. (Para 16.3)
XVII    NEW SCHEMES
            The Committee appreciates the idea and hopes that State Governments/ Corporate Sponsors will be able to
contribute their respective share in due time to make the scheme of State Sports Academies a success.   The Committee

122nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/122ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:28]
feels that the Scheme for Dope Test should be operationalised and strictly implemented  if the country wants to have a
name in the international arena.  The Committee, however, has its doubts about the possibility of launching of these two
schemes during 2002-2003 due to various procedural formalities yet to be gone through.  The Committee, therefore,
urges upon the Ministry to expedite all necessary measures so as to ensure that the schemes are launched at the earliest.
(Para 17.2)

Supply and Distribution) Amendment Bill, 2002*. (Annexure-I)

REPORT
The Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods    (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution)
Amendment Bill, 2002, seeks to amend sections 2,3,4,5,7,9,20 and 24 of the Infant Milk Substitutes,  Feeding Bottles
and Infant Foods    (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, so as to encourage continued
breastfeeding and to prohibit all forms of advertising and promotion -- light, sound, smoke or gas or by means of
electronic transmission  by audio or visual transmission in relation to Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant
Foods.
2.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill  is placed at Annexure IV
:
The Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development in his presentation on the Bill inter alia  stated:
"Basically, the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods    (Regulation of Production, Supply and
Distribution) Act, 1992 was enacted with a view to ensuring that there is no misrepresentation by companies that these
milk substitutes are  better than breast milk because, scientifically, it has been established that from the nutritional point
of view, in the first few months of infancy, there is no substitute for breast milk.   There is a lot of international and
national evidence in this regard.   We started with an Indian National Code in 1983, but it was felt that this was not
adequate and that there should be a statutory basis.   Then, the Act of 1992 came.   Basically, this Act has a lot of
prescriptions and prohibitions, how this should not be permitted - infant food and  infant milk substitutes- to the

detriment  of breast milk.   There are restrictions on labelling, advertising etc.  In the last 10 years there have been
further studies within the country and outside and now the considered technical opinion is that breast milk is preferred
for the first six months, instead of four months earlier, and thereafter, as far as possible, it should be continued for a
period of two years.  After the first six months, complementary food should be provided.
Another major happening that has happened is  the definition of advertisement has changed in the light of the various
developments which has taken place due to cable T.V.,  Satellite channels and electronic transmission.  Similarly, in
actual practice, it was noticed that apart from the healthcare workers in the hospitals, in the pharmacies, a lot of
propagation was being  done in favour of Infant Foods and Infant Milk Substitutes.  Therefore, a lot of minor
modifications have been brought in, with reference to advertisement, with reference to supplies, and with reference to
taking part in promotion".

promoting breastfeeding and ensuring proper use of infant foods. While implementing the provisions of the Act over the

that ideally, the infant thrives best on exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, as well as continued

ANNEXURE IV
 
The Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods    (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution)
Act, 1992 was enacted with a view to protecting and promoting breastfeeding and ensuring proper use of infant foods.   
During the course of implementation of the provisions of the enactment over the years, it has been found that some
aspects have led to difficulties, which need to be clearly spelt out.   The recent developments and findings of
international agencies as well as researchers have revealed that ideally, the infant thrives best on exclusive breastfeeding
for the first six months of life, as well as continued breastfeeding together with complementary foods for the first two
years.   The World Health Organisation by World Health Assembly Resolution No. 47.5 dated the 9
th May, 1994 called
upon all Member Nations to aim at achieving this goal.   The said resolution, inter alia,  required Member Nations to
foster appropriate complementary feeding practices for the infants from the age of about six months and encourage
continued breastfeeding as well as proper feeding with safe and adequate amounts of local foods until the infant attains
the age of two years.
In order to review and suggest appropriate amendments in the said Act, the Department of Women and Child

INTRODUCTION 
  
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource 
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
Hundred-Twenty Fourth Report of the Committee.  The report is  on the Protection from Domestic 
Violence Bill, 2002*.  
2.         In 
pursuance of Rule 270 relating to the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committees,

The Committee considered the Bill in eight sittings held on 16th May, 25th June, 28th, 29th August, 9th

REPORT 
  
            The Protection from Domestic Violence Bill, 2002, seeks to protect the rights of women who are 
victims of violence of any kind occurring within the family and to provide for matters connected 
therewith or incidental thereto. 
The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill states as under:  
“Domestic violence is undoubtedly a human rights issue and serious deterrent to development.  The 
Vienna Accord of 1994 and the Beijing Platform of Action (1995) both have acknowledged this.  The 
United Nations Committee on CEDAW (Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination 
Against Women) in its general recommendation No. XII (1989) has recommended that State parties 
should act to protect women against violence of any kind especially that occurring within the family.  
The phenomenon of domestic violence is widely prevalent but has remained largely invisible in the 
public domain.  Presently, where a woman is visited with cruelty by her husband or his relatives is an 
offence under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The civil law does not address this 
phenomenon in its entirety.   
With a view to providing a remedy under the civil law, which is intended to preserve the family and at 
the same time provide protection to victims of domestic violence, legislation is being proposed.  The 
main features as contained in the Bill are as follows:- 
it is being provided that any conduct of relative of the victim, which subjects her to habitual assault, or 
makes her life miserable, or injures or harms, or forces her to lead an immoral life would constitute 
domestic violence; 
the Judicial Magistrate of the first class or the Metropolitan Magistrate may take the cognizance of 
domestic violence and pass a protection order requiring the relative of the women to refrain from 
committing an act of domestic violence, or pay monetary relief which is deemed fit in the circumstances 
or pass any other direction as the Magistrate may consider just; 
the Magistrate may even require as an interim and urgent measure from the relative of the woman to 
execute a bond, with or without sureties, for maintaining domestic peace; 
the violation by the relative of the order made by the Magistrate would constitute an offence punishable 
with imprisonment up to one year, or with fine, or with both; 
it is being proposed to set up an institution of Protection Officer to help the victim of domestic violence 
in making application to the Magistrate and in availing of her other legal rights; 
a provision is being made for the appointment of Protection Officers  by State Governments and they 
shall possess such qualifications as may be prescribed by the Central Govt., and 
Protection Officer shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian 
Penal Code, 1860 and if he fails or refuses to discharge the duties as directed by the Magistrate, his act 
shall amount to an offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or with fine, or with both”. 
  
NEW DELHI   
3rd December, 2002      
ARJUN SINGH 
 Chairman 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Human Resource Development

3.         The Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development deposing before the Committee 
put forward the Department’s view for bringing the Bill. 
3.1       Outlining the basic features of the Bill, he stated that the existing civil, personal or criminal laws 
leave certain gaps in addressing the issue of Domestic Violence.  Under criminal law, if a husband 
perpetrates violence on his wife, she may file a complaint under Section-498 A of IPC.  Similarly, under 
the civil law, if there is disharmony in a family and the husband and wife cannot live together, any one 
of them may file a suit for separation followed by divorce.  However, the present Bill addresses such 
situation where there is some disharmony in the family but the situation has not yet reached a stage 
where either separation or divorce proceeding has become inevitable and the aggrieved woman also for 
some reasons does not want to initiate criminal proceedings against her perpetrator.  Therefore, the Bill 
seeks to give the aggrieved woman an alternative avenue whereby she can insulate herself from violence 
without being deprived of the basic necessities of life and without disintegrating her family. 
4.         The Committee in its sitting held on 13th November, 2002, took up `clause-by-clause’ 
consideration of the Bill.  The clauses where amendments were suggested  by the Committee have been 
discussed in the succeeding paragraphs. 
            Clause 2 (i) 
4.1.      Clause 2 (i) deals with the definition of the term  `relative` in the Bill. 
4.2       The definition of  relative as given in the Bill has two requirements.  First, the person has to be 
related by blood, marriage or adoption and second, he/she should be living with the respondent.  This 
definition obviously excludes women whose marriages are legally invalid, women in bigamous relations 
and other consanguineous relations. When asked about the reason for not including such women, the 
Department stated that only those marriages recognized in law were covered under this Bill.  Such 
women as have been living in relationship akin to marriage without legal marriages, were not included 
simply because the prevailing cultural ethos of the nation did not encourage such relationship. 
 4.3      The Committee  is aware of the fact that in our society there are numerous cases  where a man 
and a woman, though not legally married, live together as husband and wife and their relationship has 
got social sanction too.  Moreover, the issue of  domestic violence is more proximate  with the basic 
human rights of a woman to live a dignified life.  Therefore, providing relief under the present Bill to a 
woman whose marriage is not legally valid won’t be in conflict with the existing laws and will not give 
any legal sanction to the illegal marriages.  The Committee, therefore, suggests that Clause 2(i) should 
be suitably amended to include those women  also who have been living in relationship  akin  to 
marriages and in marriages considered invalid by law. 
Clause 4 (2) 
5.         Clause 4(2) provides the right of self-defence to the respondent if the pursuit of his conduct was 
reasonable for his own protection or for the protection of his or another’s property. 
5.1       As per this clause,  no action of the respondent shall amount to domestic violence if it is done to 
protect himself or to protect  his property or  someone else’s   property.  Almost all the organizations/ 
associations which appeared before the  Committee were of  unanimous view that this provision is 
extremely dangerous and retrogressive as it provides an escape route for the man who commits acts of 
domestic violence.  On this issue, the Department replied that the right to self-defence is recognized in 
criminal and civil laws and has accordingly been provided in the Bill. 
5.2       The Committee does not agree with the Department’s views  . It is of the considered opinion that 
there are sufficient provisions in the existing criminal  and civil laws to take care of the right to defence 
and there is no need to provide the same in the Bill and unnecessarily overburden it.  In view of the 
above, the Committee concurs with the views of the  organizations/associations which appeared before 
the Committee and strongly recommends  that Clause 4(2) should be deleted from the Bill. 
Clause 9 (1) 
6.         Clause 9(1) provides that the aggrieved person who is a victim of domestic violence or any other 
person on her behalf or the Protection Officer, may present an application to the Magistrate for seeking 
relief under section 14. 
6.1       The Committee feels that clause 9(1)  needs to be made specific  in terms of laying down the 
Page 6 of 29124thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report124th.htm

territorial jurisdiction of the Magistrate in whose court the aggrieved person is competent to file an 
application seeking relief under clause 14,   though the same has been provided under the definition of 
‘Magistrate’ in clause 2 (c)  of the Bill.  Given that, in a number of cases where the woman who has 
been subjected to domestic violence either comes back to her parent’s home or finds some alternative 
accommodation, which may not be under the territorial jurisdiction of the same magistrate  where the 
alleged violence i.e. the cause of action has arisen.  The Committee is of the view that clause 9(1) should 
specifically provide for presenting an application in such courts under whose territorial  jurisdiction 
either  the aggrieved person resides or the respondent resides or the alleged violence has occurred or the 
aggrieved person is temporarily residing.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that clause 9(1) may 
be amended accordingly.  The Committee further recommends that necessary consequential amendment, 
if any, may also be made in the Bill. 
Clause 11(1) 
7.         Clause 11(1) provides that the Magistrate at any stage of the proceedings under this Act may 
direct the respondent or the aggrieved person, either singly or jointly, to under go mandatory counselling 
with any service provider. 
7.1       The Committee has been given to understand that counselling is one of the methods of 
behavioural  corrections and according to accepted principles of  counselling, it should be given only 
when the concerned parties either volunteer or are willing to receive it .  In other words, counseling 
should be voluntary and not compulsory.  In view of this, it would not be proper to empower the 
Magistrate to insist on  `mandatory’ counselling to either party.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the word ``mandatory`` should be deleted from  clause 11(1). 
Clause  (13) 
8.         Clause 13 lays down that the proceedings may be held in camera, if the Magistrate considers that 
the circumstances of the case so warrant, and shall be so held if either party so desires. 
8.1       A number of organizations which\ appeared before the Committee were of the view that in 
camera trials of rape cases are generally helping abusers more than the complainants because the abused 
women are mostly left alone in court with only their lawyers to support. Thus `in-camera trials`` which 
is meant to protect  the privacy of the parties, in fact, is being utilized to unduly favour the respondent. 
8.2       The Committee feels that  holding the trial of a case in camera is a procedural matter which 
should be left to the wisdom of the Magistrate.  However, the use of the word `shall’ in Clause 13 would 
leave the Magistrate with no other choice but  to hold the trial in camera if either party so desires.  The 
Committee therefore, recommends that the word `shall’  be substituted by the word `may’ so as to 
provide room for judicial expediency.  
Clause 14(1) 
9.         Clause 14(1) enables the Magistrate to pass Protection Order when he is satisfied that the 
aggrieved person is being subjected to domestic violence. 
  
9.1       The Committee has been given to understand that the range of protection order that can be 
passed  under the Bill is not exhaustive as it does not include the right to residence of the aggrieved 
person in matrimonial home.  A large number of cases of domestic violence remain hidden as the victim 
faces the threat of immediate ouster  from her matrimonial home. 
9.2       When asked to respond to this, the Department submitted that under clause 14(1) (b) of the Bill, 
the Magistrate is empowered to pass any other direction as he deems fit in the circumstances of the case, 
such as the aggrieved person should not be evicted from the household or her assets should not be 
disposed of etc. 
9.3       The Committee however, feels that there should be specific mention about the right to residence 
of the aggrieved person in matrimonial home in the Protection order passed by the Magistrate.  It, 
therefore, recommends that clause 14(1) be amended suitably.   
9.4       The Committee also feels that in appropriate cases where the Magistrate is satisfied that the 
aggrieved person is being subjected to domestic violence, it should be made obligatory on his part to 
pass protection order.  The Committee, therefore, further  recommends that in clause 14(1)(a) the words 
Page 7 of 29124thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report124th.htm

`may pass the protection order’ be substituted by the words “shall pass the protection order”.   
Clause 14 (5) 
10.       Clause 14(5) lays down that where the Magistrate is satisfied that circumstances stated in the 
application presented under section 9 are such so as to justify the immediate intervention of the 
Magistrate to restrain the respondent from committing domestic violence, the Magistrate may issue an 
interim protection order directing the respondent to restrain from engaging in any act of domestic 
violence, and the Magistrate may further require the respondent to show cause as to why he should not 
be ordered to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for maintaining domestic peace for such period as 
the Magistrate thinks fit. 
10.1     The Committee understands that the provision of Interim Protection Order has been made in 
clause 14(5) so as to ensure immediate  relief to the aggrieved person in appropriate cases.  The 
Committee feels that as domestic violence  may occur on any day and at any time, there should be a 
magistrate available  or approachable  round the clock to pass the interim protection order under clause 
14(5).  The Committee,  therefore, recommends that in order to further strengthen the provision of 
Interim Protection Order and making it more relevant, clause 14(5) should be suitably amended or a new 
sub-clause may be added to clause 14, so as to allow the filing of application seeking emergency relief 
both within and outside the court hours and on a day which is not an ordinary court day. 
Clause 21 
11.       Clause (21) provides protection to the protection officer from action taken by him in good faith. 
11.1     The  service providers, as defined in Clause 2 (k) of the Bill, are voluntary associations who have 
been entrusted with the task of protecting rights and interests of women by any means including legal 
aid, medical, financial or other assistance.   
The Committee has  been apprised  that under the present Bill where the service providers are expected 
to carry out a lot of duties , there is every likelihood  that they may be sued even for acts done by them 
in good faith.  The Committee feels that they need protection. The Committee , is therefore of the view  
that the service providers may be given similar protection under Clause-21 of the Bill  as given to the 
Protection Officers and recommends that suitable amendments may be carried out accordingly. 
12.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses  of the Bill, including enacting formula and the title 
without any  amendment.  
GENERAL OBSERVATIONS 
  
13.       It has been submitted before the Committee that there is acute shortage of trained and 
experienced Service Providers, especially women, in the country.  The Committee, is, however, of the 
view that since the Bill seeks to protect women against domestic violence, it would be proper if the 
service provider provided in the Bill is preferably, a woman organization.  It, therefore, recommends 
that a provision that a Service Provider may be a woman organization, to the extent possible, may be 
made in the Rules.  
14.       The Committee is of the view that excessive use of physical, psychological and verbal violence 
in TV serials tends to lend legitimacy to domestic violence.  Besides that, undue focus on bigamy and 
extra-marital relations has undesirable impact on children. On being asked whether it would be feasible 
to have a suitable provision in this regard in the Bill, the Department replied that the aspect of excessive 
use of physical, psychological and verbal violence in T.V. serials was being taken care of by other laws.  
Only legal marriages were covered under the Bill.  Over legislation had been avoided to the extent 
possible. 
15.       The Committee notes that despite several legislations, violence on women still continues to be 
shown most audaciously in visual media.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the existing laws are 
perhaps not being implemented properly.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
should strictly monitor the depiction of women in print as well as visual media and whenever a woman 
is being portrayed objectionably, it should immediately take up the matter with the appropriate 
authorities/departments. 
16.       Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the plight of NRI women who are victims of 
Page 8 of 29124thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report124th.htm

domestic violence. To a question, whether it would be feasible to include such victims under the Bill, 
the Department replied that the issue of providing protection to Indian girls who married NRIs staying 
abroad was being considered separately.  It would not be prudent to include all such issues in the 
legislation which was meant for protection of women from domestic violence. 
16.1     The Committee is sensitive towards  the cause  of Indian girls who are subjected to violence after 
marrying NRIs staying abroad and feels  that this is  a  very serious matter which needs immediate 
attention  and recommends that the Department should take appropriate measures in this regard. 
17.       The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendments 
suggested above.  The Committee also recommends that the observations made by it should be given 
due consideration by the Department. 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE 
  
            The Committee  is aware of the fact that in our society there are numerous cases  where a man 
and a woman, though not legally married, live together as husband and wife and their relationship has 
got social sanction too.  Moreover, the issue of  domestic violence is more proximate  with the basic 
human rights of a woman to live a dignified life.  Therefore, providing relief under the present Bill to a 
woman whose marriage is not legally valid won’t be in conflict with the existing laws and will not give 
any legal sanction to the illegal marriages.  The Committee, therefore, suggests that Clause 2(i) should 
be suitably amended to include those women  also who have been living in relationship  akin  to 
marriages and in marriages considered invalid by law. (Para 4.3) 
            The Committee does not agree with the Department’s views  . It is of the considered opinion that 
there are sufficient provisions in the existing criminal  and civil laws to take care of the right to defence 
and there is no need to provide the same in the Bill and unnecessarily overburden it.  In view of the 
above, the Committee concurs with the views of the  organizations/associations which appeared before 
the Committee and strongly recommends  that Clause 4(2) should be deleted from the Bill. (Para 5.2) 
            The Committee feels that clause 9(1)  needs to be made specific  in terms of laying down the 
territorial jurisdiction of the Magistrate in whose court the aggrieved person is competent to file an 
application seeking relief under clause 14,   though the same has been provided under the definition of 
‘Magistrate’ in clause 2 (c)  of the Bill.  Given that, in a number of cases where the woman who has 
been subjected to domestic violence either comes back to her parent’s home or finds some alternative 
accommodation, which may not be under the territorial jurisdiction of the same magistrate  where the 
alleged violence i.e. the cause of action has arisen.  The Committee is of the view that clause 9(1) should 
specifically provide for presenting an application in such courts under whose territorial  jurisdiction 
either  the aggrieved person resides or the respondent resides or the alleged violence has occurred or the 
aggrieved person is temporarily residing.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that clause 9(1) may 
be amended accordingly.  The Committee further recommends that necessary consequential amendment, 
if any, may also be made in the Bill. (Para 6.1) 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that the word ``mandatory`` should be deleted from  
clause 11(1). (Para 7.1) 
            The Committee feels that  holding the trial of a case in camera is a procedural matter which 
should be left to the wisdom of the Magistrate.  However, the use of the word `shall’ in Clause 13 would 
leave the Magistrate with no other choice but  to hold the trial in camera if either party so desires.  The 
Committee therefore, recommends that the word `shall’  be substituted by the word `may’ so as to 
provide room for judicial expediency. (Para 8.2) 
            The Committee however, feels that there should be specific mention about the right to residence 
of the aggrieved person in matrimonial home in the Protection order passed by the Magistrate.  It, 
therefore, recommends that clause 14(1) be amended suitably.  (Para 9.3) 
The Committee also feels that in appropriate cases where the Magistrate is satisfied that the aggrieved 
person is being subjected to domestic violence, it should be made obligatory on his part to pass 
protection order.  The Committee, therefore, further  recommends that in clause 14(1)(a) the words `may 
Page 9 of 29124thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report124th.htm

pass the protection order’ be substituted by the words “shall pass the protection order”.  (Para 9.4) 
            The Committee understands that the provision of Interim Protection Order has been made in 
clause 14(5) so as to ensure immediate  relief to the aggrieved person in appropriate cases.  The 
Committee feels that as domestic violence may occur on any day and at any time, there should be a 
magistrate available or approachable round the clock to pass the interim protection order under clause 14
(5).  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to further strengthen the provision of Interim 
Protection Order and making it more relevant, clause 14(5) should be suitably amended or a new sub-
clause may be added to clause 14, so as to allow the filing of application seeking emergency relief both 
within and outside the court hours and on a day which is not an ordinary court day. (Para 10.1) 
              The Committee feels that they need protection.  The Committee, is therefore of the view that 
the service providers may be given similar protection under Clause-21 of the Bill  as given to the 
Protection Officers and recommends that suitable amendments may be carried out accordingly. (Para 
11.1) 
12.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of the Bill, including enacting formula and the title 
without any amendment. (Para 12) 
            It, therefore, recommends that a provision that a Service Provider may be a woman organization, 
to the extent possible, may be made in the Rules. (Para 13) 
            The Committee notes that despite several legislations, violence on women still continues to be 
shown most audaciously in visual media.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the existing laws are 
perhaps not being implemented properly.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
should strictly monitor the depiction of women in print as well as visual media and whenever a woman 
is being portrayed objectionably, it should immediately take up the matter with the appropriate 
authorities/departments. (Para 15) 
            The Committee is sensitive towards  the cause  of Indian girls who are subjected to violence after 
marrying NRIs staying abroad and feels  that this is  a  very serious matter which needs immediate 
attention  and recommends that the Department should take appropriate measures in this regard. (Para 
16.1) 
            The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendments 
suggested above.  The Committee also recommends that the observations made by it should be given 
due consideration by the Department. (Para 17)

The Protection from Domestic Violence Bill, 2002,  as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 8th March, 
2002, has been referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development,  headed by Shri Arjun Singh, M.P., for examination and report. 
  
2.         As per the Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill, the phenomenon of domestic 
violence is widely prevalent but has remained largely invisible in the public domain.  Presently, where a 
woman is visited with cruelty by her husband or his relatives is an offence under section 498 A of the 
Indian  Penal Code, 1860.  The existing civil law does not address this phenomenon in its entirety.  
Therefore, the main objective of the Bill is to provide protection under the civil law to a victim of 
domestic violence.

The final replies in respect of the recommendations/observations made in Chapter IV of the Report are still awaited
from the Department.  The Committee may be apprised of the same as and when action is taken.
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
 2.2    The Committee is, however, not fully inclined to agree with the explanation given by the Department. The
Committee observes that the trend of under-utilization has continued during the Ninth Plan due to variety of reasons like
non-setting up of required infrastructure for implementation of various disease control programmes, non-release of
funds due to unspent balances lying with the implementing agencies, slow performance of district societies, less number
of proposals from NGOs, non-completion of required formalities etc.  During 2001-02, Plan allocation of Rs.1450.00
crores was reduced to Rs.1320.00 crores at the RE Stage, and anticipated expenditure at the end of the year is
Rs.1300.00 crores. The Committee hopes that all procedural formalities under ongoing and proposed
Programmes/Projects during Tenth Plan has been completed so that optimum and judicious utilization of allocated funds
is ensured right from 2002-03, the first year of Tenth Plan
ACTION TAKEN
The Committee’s observation regarding completion of all procedural formalities to ensure optimum utilization of 10
th
Plan funds right from 2002-03, the first year of the Tenth Plan, has been noted. All procedural formalities to the extent
feasible have been completed for various disease control programmes. For example, under National Tuberculosis
Control Programme, the State/District health authorities have been asked to complete the required procedural formalities
well in time, guidelines for NGOs have been finalised and widely circulated to ensure their effective involvement in the
Revised TB Control Programme and the financial ownership of the programme has been decentralised to the State level.
For National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP), all procedural formalities under the 2
nd NLEP have already been
completed. Under National Blindness Control Programme, EFC memo has been prepared and pending approval of EFC
memo, concurrence of the Finance Division has been sought to implement the programme as per the approved scheme
of the Ninth Five Year Plan so that the activities do not come to a halt. Under National Anti-Malaria Programme, some
of the States have constituted State Malaria Control Society and others are being persuaded to expedite formation of
such societies. In so far as National AIDS Control Project is concerned, the formalities for setting up the required
infrastructure for  implementation of the programme  have been completed and implementation of the programme is
proceeding smoothly.
Recommendation/Observation
3.6       It has been observed that the Medical and para-medical staff of CGHS dispensaries are not always responsive
and sensitive towards patients. Not only this, element of punctuality is generally lacking in majority of the CGHS
dispensaries. Instances have come to the notice of the Committee where medical/paramedical staff posted at a
dispensary remain absent from duty by having an internal adjustment with their colleagues. The Committee is of the
view that in addition to regular inspections, surprise inspections will bring out the ground reality. The Committee
welcomes the decision regarding formulation of guidelines for at least one inspection of each CGHS dispensary in the
country. The Committee hopes that these guidelines as and when formulated and implemented will help in the
improvement of functioning of CGHS dispensaries.
 
Action Taken
3.6       Instructions have already been issued vide letter No.H-11021/1/2001-CGHS/Desk-I dated 12/4/2002 along with
a detailed proforma covering all aspects of the CGHS dispensary services to all the CGHS units for conducting regular
inspections and surprise inspections of the CGHS dispensaries.
SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL
Recommendation/Observation
4.2       The Committee notes that the required faculty and infrastructure is being made available for the Vardhaman
Mahavir Medical College (VMMC). As the first session of the new college has already commenced, the Committee

125thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report125th.htm[01-07-2016 16:02:49]
urges upon the Department to make concerted efforts to make the college fully functional at the earliest so that the
students are not put to any problem.
Action Taken
Concerted efforts are being made to make the College fully functional. The infrastructure is being made available for the
Vardhaman Mahavir Medical College in Safdarjung Hospital itself. The facilities for teaching Pre-clinical subjects have
been developed. The requisite number of posts of the staff for the college have been created with the approval of
Ministry of Finance. The teaching faculty for the first session has already been recruited. The equipment for teaching
paramedical subjects are in process of procurement.
SAFDARJUNG  HOSPITAL
Recommendation/Observation
4.4       The Committee is of the view that procedural formalities should be expedited so that the 22 posts recommended
by the Screening Committee are filled at the earliest. Besides that, ongoing comprehensive review of various vacant
posts/likely to fall vacant by the Medical Supdt. Should not be unduly delayed in procedural wrangles. The Department
should also impress upon the Ministry of Finance the urgency for filling up the required posts of Safdarjung Hospital
which is the biggest Hospital in the Capital catering to the needs of not only local patients but also from the
neighbouring States.
Action Taken
4.4       After following due procedures, 22 posts have been advertised in the Employment News on 15.6.2002 and

NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
18.9     The Committee is of the view that there is apparent contradiction between the two clarifications given by the
Department. As per the ATN, the World Bank administration has agreed to reduce the requirement for production
capability from 25% to 10% of the tendered quantity. As per the second clarification, World Bank has raised the past
supply criteria to 50% from 25%. In the earlier reply, country has been divided into four regions. However, second
clarification mentions eight regions. The Committee would like to be enlightened in this regard.
Action Taken
18.9     The factual position is summarized below:
The National AIDS Control Organization undertakes bulk procurement of HIV Elisa and HCV Elisa kits as part of its
annual procurement activity. Some other kits are also procured, but they are in  smaller quantities, the largest orders
being the above two kits i.e. HIV Elisa and HCV Elisa. In the first year, kits for 35 lakh tests for each had been
procured. However, after assessing the consumption pattern, the total  requirement was reduced to 30 lakh tests for
subsequent procurement.
The World Bank’s policy on procurement has to be followed by the Project, as per the agreement agreed with it.
The initial tender for procurement of HIV Elisa kits for 3.5 million tests was floated in December, 1999 (inadvertently
mentioned as February, 2001 in the earlier reply). As per the prevailing Bank policy one of the eligibility criteria was
the past supply of 25% of the offered quantity in any one of the last 2 years. It was seen during processing of the bids
received in response to this tender that a large number of firms, including all Indian ones, could not meet this stipulated
criteria of 25% of past supply i.e. 8.75 million tests and were held to be in eligible. The order was ultimately placed on
M/s. Labsystems for a kit made in Finland.
Separately, a bid for procurement of the same number of HIV Elisa Kits had also been floated in March, 2000 with the
same qualifying criteria. However, none of the offers received in response to this bid was accepted and in October, 2000
it was decided to reject all bids and seek fresh invitation thereof. The fresh bid was floated in December, 2000. For this
revised bid, the qualifying criteria was changed in the light of the experience gained while processing the HIV Elisa bid,
and the past supply criteria was reduced to 10%. The entire requirement was also split up into 4 schedules, so that the
quantity of kits for each schedule would also be reduced. This was done with a view to enabling more firms to be
eligible for the bid. The first procurement of HCV Elisa kits for 3.5 million tests did go ahead with this stipulation of
10% of past supply and 4 region wise schedules.
In February, 2001, bids were invited for the next round of HIV Elisa test kits, and the same qualifying  criteria i.e. 10%
and 4 schedules were proposed therein. However when the bidding documents were submitted to the World Bank for
their clearance, it was pointed out by them that  as per the current requirement the past supply criterion had been raised
to 80% of the offered quantity. This issue was strongly taken up with the World Bank on more than one occasion,
pointing out that insistence on a very high qualifying criterion would result in elimination of competition from a large
number of bidders. The Bank however did not agree to relax this past supply criteria to below 50%. Since the Bank did
not agree to relax this criteria to below 50% of past supply despite constant follow up and interaction, it was decided to
divide the entire quantity of 30 lakh tests into 8 region wise schedules instead of 4 schedules finalized earlier. This was

125thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report125th.htm[01-07-2016 16:02:49]
done to ensure that the quantity required for each schedule would come down, and thus more bidders, including
domestic ones, would become eligible even with the criteria of 50% of past supply. Domestic manufacturers have been
awarded the contract for supply of kits for two schedules; and even in other they were not disqualified on this account.
The same eligibility criteria of 50% of past supply, with eight region-wise schedules, is being adhered to for the
procurement of HCV Elisa kits for 30 lakh tests also. The bids are being evaluated currently.
NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
19.3     The Committee notes that shortage of trained psychiatric manpower and lack of awareness regarding treatment
are the two main barriers to the provision of mental health services in the country. The Committee has been given to
understand that about 4000 clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers and psychiatric nurses are working in the
country which is inadequate to meet the total needs of persons with mental disorders in the country. The shortage of
psychiatric manpower is felt in all the States, specially in rural areas. The Committee strongly feels that there is a need
for having systematic evaluation regarding Statewise requirement of manpower. The Committee also observes that
mental health programmes are being implemented in a varying degree by different States. The Committee has been
informed that the District Mental Health Programme is to be enlarged and made more effective covering the entire
country during the Tenth Plan. The Committee feels that there is an urgent need for expanding the mental health
services. While appreciating the substantive allocation of funds for this programme for 2002-03, the first year of Tenth
Plan, the Committee would like to emphasise that there should be regular and extensive monitoring at all levels to
ensure optimum and judicious utilization of funds.
Action Taken
19.3     About 1-2% of the population suffer from major mental disorders and about 5% of the population i.e., 50 million
people suffer from minor depressive disorders. It is also estimated that 25% of people who attend primary health care
clinics suffer from various types of psychological problems. However, most of these patients do not require
hospitalization. There are presently 37 specialized mental hospitals in the country in the Government sector with a total
bed strength of over 18,000 beds. In addition, the various medical colleges and general hospitals in the country have
about 200 psychiatry units of varying sizes with bed strength varying 2-200, at an average of 20 beds. There are about
3,500 such beds available in such units. There are about 40 training centers for postgraduate study in psychiatry. In
addition, there are about 40-50 private psychiatric facilities in the country. Availability of psychotropic drugs is
satisfactory and the cost of such drugs is reasonable/affordable. Two mental hospitals namely NIMHANS, Bangalore
and CIP, Ranchi are under the administrative control of the Central Government.
A comprehensive study had been conducted in this regard by this Ministry in two workshops held in February 1999 for
the Medical Superintendents of mental hospitals and in June, 1999 for State Health Secretaries regarding the minimum
standard of care in mental hospitals. Further, the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-sciences, Bangalore an
autonomous body under this Ministry, also undertook a review of the functioning of all the State-run mental hospitals
and psychiatric units in a project commissioned by NHRC in 1999. Another detailed study of mental health care in the
country was also undertaken by this Ministry in November-December, 2001 and in June-July, 2002 by all the State
Governments on the direction of the Hon’ble Supreme Court.
The overall condition of mental health care delivery system in the country as assessed by Union Health Secretary on the
basis of affidavits submitted by all the State Chief  Secretaries, was placed before the Hon’ble Supreme Court. In the
affidavit it was pointed out that the Court’s direction to the Central Government to set up at least one psychiatric
hospital in each State for the purpose of making available increased manpower and facilities in the field of mental
health, may not be proper and be reviewed, since as per the new scientific thinking, community based treatment is
preferable and beneficial to the hospital based ones. The improved psychotic drugs can now be given in the community
itself and the family bond between the patient and family members  is maintained which results in quicker cure and
rehabilitation. The mental health programme will, therefore, popularize community-based treatment required for a large
number of cases of mental illness. It is in this context that the District Mental Health Programme will provide
community care with treatment shifting from custodial to therapeutic. It removes stigmatization and isolation of
mentally ill persons in society. The mental health programme will popularize community based treatment required for
large number of cases of mental illness. Under the District Mental Health Programme, the mental hospitals and medical
colleges which have professional expertise in the field are designated as nodal agencies to build a District Health Team
to provide service to needy mentally ill patients at their families in the district and adjoining areas. In service candidates
and personnel appointed as clinical psychologist, trained social worker, psychiatrist, psychiatric nurse on contract basis
are expected to perform the task of early detection of illness and quick treatment at the community level itself. There are
presently few people choosing the field of psychiatry as a career, but still with the limited availability of personnel,

125thReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report125th.htm[01-07-2016 16:02:49]
through District Mental Health Programme, the activities have been expanded to cater to larger population. As a sequel
to this approach, there is shift in emphasis from mental hospitals to upgrading psychiatric units in medical
hospitals/colleges closer to the community. Secondly, as to the States’ demand for overcoming shortage of trained
manpower in the categories of psychiatrists, clinical Psychologists, Psychiatric Social Worker and Psychiatric Nurses in
mental hospitals, it was suggested to the State Governments that one of the ways to tide over the problem is that in-
service personnel (Medical Officers, Social Workers and Nurses) may be detailed by the States/UT authorities
concerned, for short-term skill-based training in the disciplines at reputed institutions such as NIMHANS, Bangalore
and CIP, Ranchi.
With the up-gradation of infrastructure of mental hospitals, psychiatric units in medical colleges, expansion of District
Mental Health Programme from 27 districts to 100 districts along-with IEC activities and research in the 10
th Plan
period, the need for proper mental health services with sufficient infrastructure and manpower is expected to be
fulfilled.

3.4       The Committee was apprised that in places where there are no Central Government run hospitals, the
facilities provided for in-patient treatment to CGHS beneficiaries are woefully inadequate. Very few beds are
reserved for them. Consequently, the patients are put to avoidable inconvenience and have to seek treatment
through private facilities which are very expensive.  The Committee, therefore, would like the Ministry to look
into this aspect and furnish details of the facilities available to the CGHS beneficiaries in private-run hospitals
for CGHS beneficiaries and measures taken to augment the same.

Action Taken
3.4       Presently CGHS facilities are available in 22 cities. Out of these 22 cities, CGHS facilities to six cities namely
Trivandrum, Guwahati, Bhuwaneshar, Chandigarh, Bhopal and Shillong have been extended after 1977.
For the convenience of the CGHS beneficiaries and with a view to augmenting the inpatient facilities for CGHS
beneficiaries, it has been decided to recognise more private hospitals/diagnostic centres in various CGHS covered cities.
Orders recognising these private hospitals/diagnostic centres have already been issued in respect of the nine CGHS
covered cities  viz., Allahabad, Ahmedabad, Delhi, Jabalpur, Lucknow, Meerut, Mumbai, Patna and Ranchi.  These
orders also contain the rates of various treatment procedures and the facilities/specialities provided by these
hospitals/diagnostic Centres to the CGHS beneficiaries.  Process of recognition in respect of remaining CGHS coverned
cities is under way and the orders are expected to be issued soon.
Further Comments Of The Committee
            Out of 22 cities in which CGHS facilities are available, Committee notes with concern that the private  hospitals
have been recognized only in those cities which are comparatively  better placed as regards medical facilities are
concerned, and which are located in northern and western parts of the country.   The Committee, therefore, would like
the Department to recognize private  Hospitals/Nursing Homes in other States as well, particularly in the north-eastern
ones where sizeable number of CGHS beneficiaries are  residing.
            The Committee would also like to point out that whenever there is need for in-door treatment in these recognized
hospitals, particularly during emergencies, a Government servant is in a dilemma with regard to his entitlements in
respect of various  facilities, including boarding and lodging, treatment, pathological tests and food etc.   The
Government must ensure that no such questions arise at the time of admission of a Government servant  in these
hospitals.   Government hospitals should be asked to send the entire bill to the employee's office or CGHS for full
payment, thus taking of a burden for the mind of a Government servant of how  to arrange funds when he may have
none at his disposal or of deciding what in his case is admissible or not.

therefore, recommends that in-service training with special focus on work culture and approach towards patients may be

patient care. Doctors, Specialists etc. are regularly participating in the National/International Seminars/Workshops for

Comments Of The Committee
The Committee feels perturbed a the seemingly evasive reply given to its observation which was specifically

"work culture and approach towards patients" was being improved by subscribing research papers/journals for
them.
            Even if the reply given by the Government is relied, the Committee observes that at least this is not
reflected in the patient care being given in Central Government Hospitals.   The fact remains that a patient
cannot receive treatment, more so in emergencies, till he is accompanied by an attendant.   He is made to run
from pillar to post for registration, for obtaining a stretch  ( for which he as to pay whether he has money or not),
face rude or indifferent nurses or doctors, unhygienic beds, toilets and wards.   If what has been stated by
Government, the reality could have been different at least in some respects.

Recommendation/Observation
10.2     The Committee notes that out of sanctioned strength of 133 teaching posts, the number of posts lying vacant as
on 30.6.2001 was 32. Although the situation has improved somewhat, such a large number of teaching posts lying
vacant cannot be considered to be a healthy trend. The Committee has been given to understand that whenever the
requisitions are being sent to UPSC, the posts are being advertised indicating that the initial posting will be at JIPMER,
Pondicherry, with the liability to serve anywhere in India. However, even this initiative has failed to have the desired

impact. The Committee is of the view that some drastic steps need to be taken for having the required faculty at
JIPMER, a premier teaching institution in the country.
Action Taken
JIPMER, Pondicherry are being requested to take up the matter with all concerned for filling up the vacant posts at the
earliest keeping in view the observations of the Committee.
Further Observation By The Committee
            The Committee further observes that "the liability to serve anywhere in India'' could possibility be one of  the
factors to dissuade applicants to respond for the job advertisements. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that in the
application format candidates could be asked to indicate whether they would be willing to serve anywhere in India.  If
the applicant indicates "No" it should be clarified that efforts would be made by the Department to accommodate the
candidates, short time assignments in case of national calamities could not be ruled out.   This would encourage
candidates, at least in some cases for come forward.
 
NATIONAL T.B.  CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
15.2     Plan allocation under the T.B. Control Programme for BE 2001-02 was Rs. 122.00 crores which was
substantially reduced to 100.00 crores at the RE Stage. The Department has clarified that delay in the procurement of
anti-TB drugs to be supplied to various States/districts and non-procurement of binocular microscopes during the
financial year resulted in the reduction of funds meant for this purpose from Rs.44.43 crores to 32.55 crores. Allocation
for grants to State/District TB Societies was also reduced from Rs.56.00 crores to 42.50 crores. Reason being funds
meant to be released to the new 120 districts under the expansion plan could not be fully released due to delayed
approval of the EFC and CCEA. Surplus funds lying with some district societies was another reason for reduction. The
Committee observes that this trend has been there during the entire Ninth Plan period. As per the figures available with
the Committee, out of plan allocation of Rs.581.00 crores from 1997-98 to 2001-02, the total expenditure incurred as on
22.2.02 is only Rs.398.48 crores. The Committee finds that achievement level of Physical Targets under Sputum
Examination and Sputum Positive Detection has also been much below the fixed targets during the Ninth Plan period.
Action Taken
15.2     The Revised National TB Control Programme was launched in the country in March 1997 and the coverage
under the revised strategy was very low in the initial years. Under the conventional programme due to poor
infrastructure, the physical achievements remained below the targets as the targets were fixed uniformly based on the
population. As the coverage under the revised strategy in the later years of the 9
th Five Year Plan increased, the physical
achievements in the later years of the plan also improved.
further comments of the committee       
In view of the poor performance of the conventional T.B. control programme, the Committee apprehends that  the
revised programme also might meet similar fate.     The Committee would, therefore,  like the Department to make
earnest efforts in  implementing RNICP with a view to arresting the incidence of this infectious disease.
Recommendation/Observation
15.3     Last year, the Committee’s attention was drawn towards under-utilisation of funds released as Grants-in-aid to
some State Govts. for procurement of anti-TB drugs for sputum negative cases. The Committee apprehends that
situation may not have improved much. The Committee is constrained to note that Utilisation Certificates are still
awaited from some State Govts. in spite of reminders. Pending Utilisation Certificates, no further funds are being
released to the State Govts. for purchase of anti-TB drugs for sputum negative cases. The Committee views this with
serious concern. The Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the submission of Utilisation
Certificates with all concerned State Govts.
Action Taken
15.3     The State Governments from whom utilization certificates in respect of funds released for procurement of anti-
TB drugs for sputum negative cases are awaited are constantly reminded. Matter has been taken demi-officially with the
Health Secretaries of the concerned States for expediting the utilization certificates. Attention of Chief Secretaries of
concerned States has also been drawn.

Recommendation/Observation
18.2     The Committee in its last Report observed that in spite of  the foolproof procedure for selection of NGOs,
undesirable  activities are still continuing and,  therefore, recommended that regular and  intensive monitoring of NGOs
is very essential and stringent measures need to be taken.  The Department has informed that regular and extensive

information system has been established which includes regular monitoring of NGO activities by both the State AIDS

proposed to do a sample survey of  NGOs to evaluate their impact.
