in metropolitan cities, the Committee had recommended that the Department should conduct a survey so as to assess
which are the districts where NGO activity is simply not there and take up the matter with the State Society for
attracting NGOs towards this social activity. The Department has informed that under NACP-II, the identification and
funding of NGOs has been completely decentralized to the State AIDS Societies. At present 570 NGOs are being
funded under the Programme. State AIDS Societies have been advised to proactively identify NGOs in various districts
based on a mapping of the high risk behaviour groups among which NGOs are asked to implement the Targeted
Interventions Projects. The State AIDS Societies have also been advised to identify credible NGOs working in other
areas of development such as women’s empowerment, education, street children, rural development etc. to expand the
base of NGOs in NACP-II. The States of Gujarat, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal
have identified the NGOs for this purpose and other States are currently undertaking the same.

regard, the selection of an evaluating agency is under process  and the job of evaluating the NGOs would be taken up

1.7       The Committee understands that under the Community Needs Assessment Approach (CNAA) an action plan is
prepared each year at the district level based on the need assessment done by Auxiliary Nurse-Midwife of Sub-Centre at
village level. In the beginning of the financial year, the health worker will first complete the house-to-house survey.
Based on this survey, Eligible Couple Register is updated by the ANM. The Committee has been informed that the State
Governments are impressed from time to time to ensure that the Sub-Centre action plan is got prepared for each Sub-
Centre in the State. The Committee has its own doubts about the implementation of this annual exercise, which is most
essential for successful implementation of Family Welfare Programme, specially in the remote and inaccessible areas. 
The Committee strongly feels that surprise inspections in the performing as well as non-performing districts by Central
teams/dedicated NGOs/ Social Workers can bring out the ground reality. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department should initiate such an exercise in 2002-2003.
 Action Taken

visit Districts and to see themselves the functioning of various schemes of family welfare at the district, Community

the year 2001-02 have been organised in the  Empowered Action Group (EAG) States namely, Bihar, Chhattisgarh,
Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal.

RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
Recommendation/Observation
3.6       The Committee notes that 22842 Primary Health Centres exist in the country against the requirement of 25907
Primary Health Centres. However, there are only 5435 Rural Family Welfare Centres at present. Hence, there is a need

Planning Commission.

Recommendation/Observation
3.13     The Committee also observes that in many States, the number of established Sub-Centres exceeds the projected
requirements as per 2002 projected population. Financial liability with regard to all existing 1,37,311 Sub-Centres is to
be borne by the Central Government from 2002-2003. The justification of bearing the expenditure in respect of excess
Sub-Centres set up in different States by the Centre needs to be explored from all aspects, especially in view of the fact
that proposal of the Department for financing the establishment of new Sub-Centres under the 100% Centrally-
Sponsored Scheme is pending with the Ministry of Finance and shortage of Sub-Centres is there in large number of
States.
Action Taken
Sub-Centres are normally established by the State Governments as per population norms. However, the ground
realities in some areas make it imperative for the State Governments to establish more Sub-Centres than fixed as per
these norms. This may be due to difficult terrain, absence of roads, hilly regions, coastal areas or deserts etc. In these
areas, travel time and travel distance for a patient in a remote village to reach a health facility also becomes crucial in
addition to the population norms.
One Sub-Centre normally serves 4-6 villages. Ideally, Delivery Huts/Health Posts or some sort of health facility
for providing Reproductive & Child Health Services should be available in every village. Other facilities like Rural
Family Welfare Centres, ISM&H Dispensary and Primary Health Centres should also be there nearby. In the absence of
these facilities, Sub-Centres try to fill up their gap. However, due to financial constraints, establishment of all these
facilities may not be possible for several more decades. In the meantime, if surplus Sub-Centres have been established
by some States to provide services to the people and meet some of their unmet needs, Central Governments should not
hesitate to support the States in the maintenance of these surplus Sub-Centres which have already been created.

5.10     A scheme for holding RCH Camps at PHCs in remote and under served areas has been initiated during 2000-
2001. The Scheme is being implemented in 102 districts in 17 States. While appreciating the Scheme, the Committee
find that only 6 States have intimated that camps are being held in identified districts. The Committee recommends that

districts.
Action Taken
The scheme for holding RCH Camp at PHCs in remote and under-served areas was initiated during 2000-2001
for implementation in 102 districts of 17 States. Camps are being held regularly in identified districts of 12 States. The
scheme is being continuously monitored and discussed with the States. The scheme was reviewed in a meeting held on

STRENGTHENING OF IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME AND ERADICATION OF POLIO
Recommendation/Observation
6.2       The Committee is deeply anguished to find that a cut in the allocation at the RE stage was made due to delay in
procurement of equipment and stores. The Committee feels that such delays seriously affect the implementation of
Family Welfare Programmes. It, therefore, recommends that the Department should inquire into as to whether this delay
could have been avoided and if so, the responsibility should be fixed in this regard. It should also take extra precaution
so that such delays are avoided in future. 
Action Taken
The views of the Standing Committee have been noted for future compliance.
Further Comments
The Committee was informed that the delay in the procurement of Cold Chain equipment during the year was on
account of the following reasons:
1.         The procurement plans for all the three years under the Immunisation Strengthening Project were submitted to
the World Bank and approved in March 2000. However, World Bank in their review during 2001 suggested clubbing of
the procurement of cold chain items for year 2 (2000-2001) and year 3 (2002-2003).  This took some time and the
detailed consignee addresses and qualities could be made available to Hospital Services Consultancy Corporation
(HSCC), the National Procurement Support Agency (NPSA) in this case only in September 2001.
2.         After floating of the bids, World Bank insisted on changing the qualification criterion, i.e. the bidders experience
from an earlier 20% requirement to 50% requirement. This issue was taken up with the World Bank and after receiving
clarifications from World Bank, HSCC was advised in November 2001, to change the qualification criterion. As a result
of this change in qualification criterion, there was delay in opening of the bids. for various items of equipments.
3.         It will thus be seen that the delay in procurement of the various items for 2001-2002 was largely on account of
changes in conditions as laid down by the World Bank, firstly for clubbing the procurement for two years and secondly

Recommendation/Observation
6.3       In case of Pulse-Polio Immunization, the Committee notes that the All India achievement in 1997-98 was 93.9%
which increased to 98.2% in 2000-2001. However, in Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland, the achievement is
around 50%. In case of Measles Vaccination, the Committee is constrained to note that the All-India achievement in
2000-2001 is 92.1% but the States like Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland failed to achieve even 50%
of its target . In case of BCG vaccination and DPT Immunization the Committee is happy to note that the All-India
achievement is more than 100%. However, again Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland are the low-performing
States. The same can be said about DPT Immunization coverage.
 
The Committee observes that the States like Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland continue to
perform much below the national average over the years in all the immunization programmes. Another disturbing
feature noticed by the Committee is the downward trend in the percentage of coverage during the last three years of
Ninth Plan in respect of some States. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should identify such
States as are performing below the national average and take special steps to strengthen the immunization scheme in
such States.
Action Taken
As regards Pulse Polio Immunization, the States of Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland have also reported
near 100% coverage due to vigorous campaign.
The Committee has recommended that the Department should identify such low performing States and take
special steps to strengthen the immunization scheme in such States. In this connection, it is stated that such low
performing States have already been identified and steps taken to strengthen the immunization schemes in these States.
Under Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) Outreach Scheme, 50 districts in low performing 8 States were given
additional support in 2000-2001 to improve the quality of outreach vaccination sessions, social mobilization, mobility
support, alternate vaccine delivery system. This scheme was extended to additional 101 districts in various States in
2001-2002.  Under the Immunization Strengthening Project, funds have been given to all the States for improving
monitoring of the routine immunization programme, for organizing review meetings and mobility support. Various
training programmes have also been initiated to train State/district and field level functionaries to improve the
management as well as quality of implementation of routine immunization programme.

INTRODUCTION
Recommendation/Observation
1.6       The Committee notes that though there is a marginal increase in the case of sterilisation and C.C. users, the
number of IUD insertions and O.P. users has decreased in the year 2000-2001, in comparison to 1999-2000. The
Committee feels that in the case of sterilisation, the number of male sterilisation is much below the desired level and
recommends that the Department should take appropriate steps so that the participation of males is increased in Family
Planning methods.
Action Taken
To increase male participation in the family planning programme, the Department has introduced No Scalpel
Vasectomy (NSV) Programme. This method is an improvement over the conventional method with practically no side-
effect or complication. To ensure the availability of this new technique at the peripheral levels, efforts are being made to

have been trained in this technique. Of this, 1048 doctors have been certified  as NSV providers and 47 doctors have
been certified as NSV State Trainers. The training is still going on and proposes to cover all the States by the end of this
year.          
Moreover, during 2002-2003, a new scheme namely Male Participation has been included primarily for bringing
about gender equality since in most of the societies, men exercise preponderant power in nearly every sphere of life,
ranging from personal decisions regarding size of the families to the policy and programme decisions.  Under the
innovative new scheme of Male Participation, special efforts are to be made to emphasize men’s shared responsibility
and promote their active involvement in responsible parenthood, sexual and reproductive behaviour, including family
planning.  The budget provision for this scheme during 2002-03 is Rs.2.00 crores.

DISTRIBUTION OF CONTRACEPTIVES
Recommendation/Observation
8.3       In regard to the quality of Nirodh, the Committee has been given to understand that 19% users have rated it
under free supply scheme as okay, 75% as good and 6% have rated as very good. The Committee feels that the quality
of condoms goes a long way in its acceptance by the users.  The Committee is also of the view that poor quality may
lead to unwanted pregnancy and reproductive tract infections.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Departments should ensure that only the best quality of latex is used in manufacturing of condoms.
Action Taken
Department of Family Welfare entrusted a study on ‘Use and Wastage of Nirodh under Nominal Levy Scheme
in Certain States’ to National Institute of Health & Family Welfare (NIHFW), New Delhi in 2001.  The provisional
report mentions about the information the study collected about the quality of Nirodh under free supply scheme.   These
percentages are based on the provisional study report furnished to the Department in September 2001.
Department of Family Welfare takes care of the quality of condoms provided to the users under the Free Supply
Scheme as well as under the Social Marketing Programme.   To ensure the quality, the samples from each and every
batch are got tested from approved laboratories before supply is accepted from the manufacturers.   The condoms are
tested as per schedule ‘R’ of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, revised from time to time.   The condoms procured by
Government of India are of international standard and no compromise is done in the matter of quality.
Further, to ensure the quality, as the condoms have a shelf life of 4 years, special attempts are made to collect
samples of these Nirodh from the field by Regional Directors and get them tested in the approved laboratories only,
from time to time.  In case of any failure, the supply of that particular batch is immediately stopped and manufacturer of
the batch is asked to replace the whole batch immediately on his own cost.   Thus, the quality aspects are rigorously
observed and monitored in respect of condoms being supplied both under Free Supply and Social Marketing Schemes.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee observes that there is a need to develop a mechanism  to determine the extent of stocks of
condoms which remain unutilized or are wasted due to expiry of date in the various outlets in and outside 
Government Departments. Once this mechanism is developed, production lines could be oriented accordingly.
Quality of condom could also be improved by doing away with the wastages and without affecting the budget.   
The Committee further observes that certain percentage of condoms could also be sold at economical rates by
installing condom vending machines in public toilets, toilets of restaurants, cinema halls, theatres and such
other   public places.   Much more needs to be done to contain the rising population by devising incentives  in
every field of national life.
NEW INITIATIVES
Recommendation/Observation
The Committee feels that the problem of exponential growth of population is the mother of all the problems of
this country. No matter, howsoever high is the growth rate of national economy, it will be insufficient to meet the
economic needs of the people if the rate of population growth is not arrested. The Committee is of the considered view
that unless the factors which are contributory to the uncontrolled growth of population, such as illiteracy particularly in
women, poverty etc. are appropriately addressed, we will have no escape from this unfortunate situation. All the
political parties/groups owe their duty to the country to sit together and evolve a consensus in this regard. (Para No.
11.2)
Action Taken
The strategies in the National Population Policy 2000, are under implementation in consultation with the States

and other stake-holders.  Currently, all such schemes and programmes are being undertaken which attempt to achieve
the immediate objectives of the National Population Policy 2000, to address the unmet needs for contraception, health

            The Committee is constrained to observe that unless adequate steps are taken to contain the population,

CHAPTER I 
OPERATION BLACKBOARD 
Recommendations/Observation 
5.7       The Committee notes that against Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 1955.04 crores under Operation 
Blackboard, utilization figures upto 18.03.02 are only Rs. 1719.83 crores.  Trend of under-utilization of 
funds was due to unspent balance lying with various State Governments due to one reason or the other.  
The Committee has been informed that during 2001-2002, amount of unspent balance was brought down 
from Rs. 377 crores to Rs. 228 crores as a result of concerted efforts made by the State Governments.  
All the concerned State Governments have now been requested to liquidate the unspent balance by June, 
2002.  The Committee is of the opinion that large number of vacant posts of teachers and non-utilisation 
of funds for the various components of Operation Blackboard is a clear indication that the Scheme has 
failed to achieve the targetted results.  The Committee hopes that all these inherent shortcomings noticed 
under the Scheme over a period of time must have assisted the Department in taking all the corrective 
measures in the formulation and implementation of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA). 
Action Taken 
Against Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 1955.04 crore, a sum of Rs. 1751.27  crore (about 90%) has been 
utilized. 
            There has been unspent balances with States/UTs towards procurement of Teaching Learning 
Equipment (TLE).  The unspent balance is monitored regularly in meetings/conferences, etc. 
            The Department has taken into account the shortcomings found in the implementation of 
Operation Blackboard while formulating norms for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. 
Further Comments of the Department 
The Department has further informed that while implementing the Operation Blackboard 
through States/UTs, it noticed  two main problems- delay in the appointment of teachers, and slow 
pace of utilization of funds. 
            Under the scheme, salary payment was covered till the end of the Five Year Plan period in which 
appointments were made and the liability with regard to teachers’ salary was transferred thereafter to the 
States/UTs.   Under this arrangement, some States were getting financial assistance for teachers’ salary 
usually for 2-3 years, most of them were reluctant to create new posts of teachers even if they required it 
urgently.  In fact, States expected Central assistance for teachers’ salary for an assured longer period.   
This demand of the State Governments was kept in mind while formulating the norms for interventions 
under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan.  Under this programme, support for teachers’ salary could be shared 
between the Central Government and the State Governments in a ratio of 85:15 during the Ninth Plan, 
75:25 during Tenth Plan and 50:50 thereafter.   
            The slow pace of utilizing the funds sanctioned for Teaching Learning Equipment (TLE) under 
the scheme of Operation Blackboard could inter-alia be attributed to several factors, such as lack of 
sufficient flexibility; procurement procedure; mode of release of funds, etc.  These hurdles have been 
neutralized by effecting community ownership of school-based interventions through effective 
decentralization in SSA.  Further, funds under the scheme of SSA are directly released to the 
implementing agencies/societies for ensuring higher and timely utilization of funds.  
The constructions of school buildings under the scheme of Operation Blackboard were to be made under 
the programmes of Rural Development on sharing basis.  Often such funds were not available.  In SSA 
provisions have been made for utilizing funds on civil works upto 33% of the entire project cost 
approved by Project Approval Board on the basis of perspective plans prepared for the period till 2010.

CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
INTRODUCTION 
Recommendations/Observation  
An attempt to make  Elementary Education a Fundamental Right and justiciable under the Constitution 
by shifting it from Directive Principles of State Policy, which is non-justiciable, marks a bold initiative.  
It shows the commitment of the nation to provide `Education for All’, priority being free and 
compulsory elementary education, coverage of children with special needs, eradication of illiteracy, 
vocationalisation, women’s education and special focus on education of socially disadvantaged 
sections.  It is true that in the field of Elementary  Education, progress towards Universalisation of 
Elementary Education (UEE) has been made. Concerted efforts have resulted in the manifold increase in 
institutions, teachers, students.  National Family Health Survey-II (1998-99) indicates that 79 percent 
children in the age group of 6-14 are attending school.  Even though there has been considerable 
improvement in the participation of girl children belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, 
religious and linguistic minorities etc., the goal of UEE still remains elusive. 
Approach Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-2007) has also pointed out that our performance in 
the field of education is one of the most disappointing aspects of our development strategy.  Out of 
approximately 200 million children in the age group 6-14 years, only 120 million  are in school and net 
attendance in the primary level is only 66% of enrolment.  Therefore, it has been suggested that the 
Tenth Plan should aim at a radical transformation in this situation. ‘Education for All’ must be one of 
the primary objectives of the Tenth Plan. 
Action Taken 
1.1 & 1.2 :       The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan would cover all districts in the country and aims at providing 
universal enrolment by the year 2003.  The specific goals of SSA are : 
all children in schools  
Education Guarantee Centre 
Alternate schools  
Back to school camp by  2003.   
Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 and at Elementary level by 2010. 
           As on date, under SSA, 521 out of the 599 districts have been approved of their Annual Districts 
Elementary Education Plan for development of infrastructure in schools, proper distribution of teachers, 
provision of teacher training facilities and teaching learning equipment etc. 
            The SSA envisaged the constitution of a National Mission  whose Governing Council is headed 
by the Prime Minister and has representation of all stakeholders.  The Executive Committee of the 
Mission  is headed by Human Resource Development Minister.  The Project Approval Board is headed 
by Secretary (EE&L).  
Further Comments of the Department   
 To a query regarding the time by which the Annual Districts Elementary Education Plan of the 
remaining districts were likely to be approved, the Department informed that till 12/11/2002, Annual 
Plan 2002-03 of 362 districts had been approved, and plans of another 211 districts had been received 
which were being appraised. Only 39 districts had not been covered either in 2001-02 or 2002-03. Of

and the number of upper primary schools by about 15 times. Total enrolment at the Primary stage 
increased by 5.91 times, from 19.2 million in 1950-51 to about 113.61 million in 1999-2000.  Total

 In reply to a query as to the causes for deterioration in Pupil Teacher Ratio (PTR) both at primary 
education level as well as upper primary level and the  steps proposed to improve the same, the

teachers which has led to the deteriorating PTR. The States have been found to be reluctant to appoint

commitment of funds under SSA, though on a diminishing scale of 85:15 in 9th Plan, 75:25 in 10th Plan

Recommendations/Observation  
The Committee has been given to understand that under the Scheme of Operation Blackboard during the 
entire period of the Ninth Plan physical target fixed for third teachers for Primary Schools was 
1,58,000.  Against this, the posts of only 48,153 teachers were sanctioned.  Similarly, against the 
physical target of 1,23,624 upper primary schools, 90,420 posts of teachers were sanctioned.  As regards 
additional teachers for upper primary schools against the physical target of 1,23,624, only 40,730 posts 
could be sanctioned.  The Committee is disturbed to note that for the States of Haryana, Mizoram, 
Nagaland and West Bengal, even though 1204, 106, 161 and 2353 additional teachers, respectively, for 
upper primary schools were sanctioned not a single teacher was appointed in these States.  In the case of 
Assam, Maharashtra and Orissa against the sanctioned posts of 6730,10969 and 10023, only 2851, 7064 
and 7741 teachers, respectively, were appointed.  This shows that there has been a wide gap between the 
lofty targets fixed and actually achieved.   This calls for serious rethinking of our planning and 
implementation process. 
 Action Taken 
5.5       The initial physical targets were set subject to availability of funds in the Ninth Plan.    However, 
the Ninth Plan allocation was reduced to Rs. 1955.04 crore, out of which, Rs. 1751.27 crore (about 90% 
of the funds) has been utilized on the implementation of Operation Blackboard.  
            The scheme of Operation Blackboard covered all new posts for payment of salary till the end of 
the Five Year Plan period in which appointments were made.  At the end of the Plan period, the liability 
with regard to teacher salary is transferred to State Government.  Under this arrangement, States usually 
get financial assistance for teacher salary for 2-3 years and thus most of the States were reluctant to 
create new posts of teachers even when such posts are required urgently.  In fact, States wanted Central 
assistance for teacher salary for an assured longer period.  This demand of the State Governments has 
been kept in mind while formulating the norms for interventions under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan where 
the funding pattern will support the salaries of teachers on a long-term basis.

appointment of teachers was as per the policy adopted by the States. Government of India was only 
insisting that the NCTE guidelines were followed as far as the qualifications of the teachers were

            The Committee feels that under the National Literacy Mission, situation has not changed

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendations/Observation  
4.4       The Committee is of the view that successful implementation of a scheme can be undertaken 
with the partnership of both the Central Government and State Governments/UTs. If the funds are 
released by the Centre to the States/UTs and if the same are not utilized/spent by them, utilization 
certificates are not furnished, the Centre would have perhaps no option but to withhold  further release, 
resulting in under- utilization of funds.  However, in certain cases, the reason behind non-utilization of 
funds by some States/UTs may be genuine, particularly financial crunch.  In that case, the Committee 
feels that the Department will have to give a thought to it and find some way out for such States/UTs. 
Action Taken 
Non-utilization of funds by States /UTs, form a part of regular reviewing exercise and persuasive efforts 
have resulted in considerable utilization by States/UTs.  Currently, Education Secretary is reviewing the 
unspent balance available with the States by individually calling the State Education Secretaries.  
Proposals have been made to the States suggesting the ways of speedy utilization and removing of the 
bottlenecks.  
Further Comments of the Department  
            In reply to a specific query regarding the kind of proposals that have been made to the States 
suggesting the ways of speedy utilization and removing of the bottlenecks and their responses thereto 
the Department replied that the implementation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes were reviewed by 
Secretary, Elementary Education & Literacy as well as by senior officers of the Bureau of Elementary 
Education with Education Secretaries of States and State Project Directors by visiting the States or 
inviting them in the Ministry.  This provides an opportunity to gauge the status of implementation, 
implementing strategy, etc.  Suggestions were also provided for speedy utilization of the funds released 
to the States, if utilization was slow.   Meetings, conferences, workshops also provided an opportunity to 
exchange views / experience between Centre and State and among States. 
 Technical support from NIEPA and NCERT were also provided for developing a comprehensive 
District Elementary Education Plan (DEEP) (Both Annual Plan and Perspective Plans). 
Comments of the Committee 
            The Committee is of the view that the measures taken by the Department are routine exercises 
which have been going on  for a long time without any fruitful results, as far as fund utilisation is 
concerned.    The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should evolve suitable

MID-DAY MEAL SCHEME 
Recommendations/Observation  
8.12     The Committee had earlier been given to understand that the States, due to their poor financial 
condition, are not in a position to bear the conversion cost and hence cooked food is not supplied by 
most of them.  The Committee finds that implication of  the Hon’ble Supreme Court order is that States 
which currently do not have a cooked meal programme are seeking additional assistance towards 
conversion costs.   The Committee fails to understand, in view of provision of only Rs. 1175.00 crores 
for 2002-03, sufficient only for cost of foodgrains and transportation charges, how States will be in a 
position to implement the Supreme Court Orders.   Now, with the recent order of the Supreme Court, for 
distribution of only cooked meal, the Central Government will have to come to the rescue of the State 
Governments though the Committee had been recommending to this effect from the very beginning.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should apprise the Committee, within a period 
of three months, the manner in which it intends to implement the Supreme Court (SC) directive. 
 Action Taken 
The Department is in agreement with the observation of the Committee.  The Department had  proposed 
to Ministry of Finance to augment the allocation but the same has not received favourable response.  
Similarly, Planning Commission has also not considered Department’s request for higher allocation.  
There is also no opportunity for the Department to re-appropriate/re-allocate  funds  from within its own 
allocated budget. 
       States/UTs, therefore, have been already informed that under the Scheme the cost of conversion of 
foodgrains into a cooked meal is to be borne by the States/Implementing Agencies.  It is submitted that 
the Department would continue to support States/Uts with supply of foodgrains free of cost and 
admissible transportation charges.  The conversion of foodgrains into cooked meals as per the 
specifications of the Hon’ble  Supreme Court would be the responsibility of the Implementing Agencies. 
The Department would, however, be willing to support States with any other permissible item of 
expenditure provided adequate funds are made available for the same. 
Further Comments of the Department  
            To a specific query regarding  the steps taken to implement the Supreme Court’s order dated 
28.11.2001 the Department replied that it had convened a meeting of the Education Secretaries/Nodal 
Officers of all States/UTs dealing with the programme to review the implementation of the programme.  
They were requested to implement the programme as per the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court.  
The Ministry was committed to ensure supply foodgrains free of cost and admissible transportation 
charges to the implementing agencies. In addition, the Ministry of Rural development had also agreed to 
construct kitchen shed under their programme. 
  In addition to existing States namely Gujarat, Kerala, Orissa (rural areas of KBK districts & Boudh 
district and ITDA blocks), Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and Chattisgarh (Tribal areas), Karnataka (7 
educationally backward districts), Delhi ( ready to eat food )  and Pondicherry,  the State  of  Rajasthan, 
and   UTs of Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu have also started 
providing cooked meal. Chattisgarh, which was earlier implementing a cooked meal programme in tribal 
blocks, have now extended the said porgramme across the State. 
            The other States/UTs have not yet introduced a cooked meal programme mainly due to  financial 
constraints.   Ministry had also taken up the matter with Ministry of Finance for additional funds to 
implement a meal programme across the country with a proposal to bear the conversion cost with 
States/UTs on a 50:50 basis, but the same was not agreed to. 
Comments of the Committee 
            The Committee feels that it is perhaps due to resource- crunch, the Department was not able to 
get additional allocation from the Ministry of Finance as recommended by it.   The Committee is not 
inclined to agree that defaulting States were not able to implement cooked meal programme due to 
financial constraints particularly in States like Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Haryana etc.   In view of

cooperation of Panchayats. 
Recommendations/Observation  
9.8       The Committee observes that the funding pattern under SSA would be 75:25 in the Tenth Plan 
and 50:50 thereafter, between the Centre and the States.  The Committee has been given to understand 
that this pattern was fixed through a consultative process after extensive discussion with the States.  A 
large number of States have submitted their District Elementary Education Plans which indicates that 
these States have implicitly agreed to the above sharing pattern.  The Committee, however, is not 
inclined to agree with the contention of the Department that States will be better placed under SSA as 
compared to Operation Blackboard under which liability of teachers salary was transferred to State Govt 
at the end of the Plan period.  This is evident from the fact that already three States- UP, Assam and 
Tripura have requested reconsideration of the sharing pattern.  The Committee feels that more such 
requests are bound to follow.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that viability of this funding 
pattern may again be reviewed, particularly in the case of non-performing States, as observed during the 
implementation of Operation Blackboard. 
Action Taken 
This is the first year of the Tenth Plan.  Hence, it would be too early to review the sharing pattern. 
Further Comments of the Department   
            In reply to a specific query whether there have been any request from the states other than UP, 
Assam and Tripura for reconsideration of the funding pattern of SSA, and whether there has been any 
reconsideration on this issue, the Department replied that no other State has requested for 
reconsideration of the funding pattern and that no reconsideration on the funding pattern had been done. 
Comments  of the Committee 
            While the Committee agrees with the Department that it was too early to review the funding-
pattern under SSA during the first year itself, the Committee feels that the Department should analyse 
the reasons on the basis of which some States had requested reconsideration of the pattern to allay their 
fears, in the beginning itself, so as to  ensure a smooth implementation of SSA, particularly when we 
have had a bad experience of its precursor, the  Operation Blackboard.

Recommendations/Observation  
11.4     The Committee is, however, constrained to note that during 2001-2002, BE allocation of Rs. 
30.00 crores had to be reduced to Rs. 10.00 crores at the RE stage.  On a specific query in this regard, 
the Department has explained that the Project was having an unspent balance of Rs. 12.23 crores as on 
1.4.01 to be utilized during 2001-2002.  The State Government of Rajasthan was also not in a position to 
allocate more plan funds to the Project during the year.  The Committee would like to point out that this 
problem seems to have been there during the entire Ninth Plan period.  Against a physical target of 
coverage of 2,81,525 children during Ninth Plan, achievement level is 2,17,126 children.  Similarly, 
against a provision of Rs. 80.37 crores during this period, expenditure reported is only Rs. 53.74 crores.  
The Committee is aware that in view of post Pokhran developments, Swedish International 
Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA) declined to support the Project.  As a result, there was a 
break from 1st July, 1998 to 30th June, 1999.  The Committee, would, however, like to emphasise that 
there is scope for more effective implementation of the Programme, impressive achievements 
notwithstanding.   
Action Taken 
The  project is run in the State of Rajasthan Greater emphasis had been given by the State 
Government on the expansion of State funded Rajiv Gandhi Pathashalas, thereby limiting the 
expansion of Shiksha Karmi Day schools.  However, in the  year 2002-03, under the Shiksha 
Karmi Project, approx. 1021 new schools are proposed to be opened.  This will lead to an increase

REPORT

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this Thirteenth Report of the Committee on the Prevention of
Apartheid in Sports Bill, 1988.

2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary: Standing
Committees, the Hon’ble Chairman Rajya Sabha referred the Bill to the Committee for
examination and report.

3. The Committee considered the Bill in two sittings. (Annexure-I).

4, The Committee at its meeting held on 20th December, 1994 adopted the Draft
Report on the Bill.

5. India has always been a fore-runner in the international campaign against apartheid,
i.e., any system of institutionalised racial segregation and discrimination for the purpose of
establishing and maintaining domination by one racial group of persons over another racial
group and systematically oppressing them, as was done in South Africa. India was actively
involved in the drafting of the International Convention Against Apartheid in Sports, which
was approved and adopted by the UN General Assembly. Like other member countries,
India was required to accede to and ratify the Convention, which came into force on 3
April, 1988.

6. Since some of the provisions of the convention impinged on the normal legal rights of
the sports persons and their associations, the Government of India decided to have a
legislation to equip itself with the legal powers necessary for giving effect to those provisions
and, therefore, brought this Bill, which was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 7 December,
1988.

7, The prevention of Apartheid in Sports Bill, 1988, seeks to prohibit sports bodies,
sports teams and individual sportspersons to have sports contacts and enter into contract
with a country practising apartheid. The Bill provides for refusing to give financial or other
assistance to sportspersons who participate in sports activities in a country practising
apartheid or with teams or sportspersons selected on the basis of apartheid. It provides for
restriction on access to national sports facilities to such teams and sportspersons. It also
provides for penalty of imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine
which may extend to ten thousand rupees or with both, for violating the provisions
mentioned above.

8. The International Convention Against Apartheid in Sports, according to the
Statement of the objects and Reasons of the Bill, is a major step in the sustained efforts to
secure comprehensive boycott of the racist regime of South Africa, by the international
community, in respect of sports.

9. In view of the latest developments in South Africa, such as holding of elections based
on universal franchise after, dismantling the racist regime, series of cricket matches between

“Rajya Sabha Parhamentary Bulletin Part II, para 34730 dated the 28th September, 1994.


India and South Africa and participation by the latter in the World Cup Hockey
Championship held recently in Australia, the comments of the Ministry were invited by the
Committee on the following points:

1. whether the Government has acceded to the Convention;
2. whether the Bill still holds good; and

3. whether the Government wants to go ahead with the Bill in the light of the changed
scenario in South Africa.

10. The Ministry, in their note has informed the Committee that the matter was
examined by the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports, in consultation with the
Department of Legal Affairs and the Ministry of External Affairs. It was agreed that since
the Convention has lost its significance in the emerging new world scenario, no legislation
was necessary for implementing the provisions of the Convention any more. The note
further added “In our view, in the light of the latest developments in South Africa, it is not
necessary to proceed with the Bill”. A copy of the Ministry’s note is at Annexure-Il.

11. The Government, however, in the meantime had acceded to the Convention and the
Instrument of Accession was handed over to the UN on 12 December, 1990.

12. The Committee noted the latest developments and changes that have taken place in
South Africa, the fact that India has already acceded to the Convention, and the categorical
advice given by the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of Youth
Affairs and Sports that it was not necessary to proceed with the Bill, recommends that the
Bill be withdrawn.

The Prevention of Apartheid in Sports Bill, 1988.

This. pertains to the Prevention of Apartheid in Sports Bill; 1988. The Bill was introduced
in Parliament with a view to giving effect to the provisions of the International Gonvention
against Apartheid in Sports and for India to accede to the said Convention,. upon: the passing .
of such legislation. The Bill was not pressed for discussion as there was thinking in the
Department to move some official amendment with regard to the “Third Country principle
and this needed further examination

2. The matter was reviewed by the then Minister for Human Resource Development in
July, 1989 when it was decided to examine whether India could accede to the International
Convention without prior legislation. After consultation with the 1960 Legal Affairs and
Ministry of External Affairs, the following proposals were made to the Government:—

i) Mo External Affairs may be asked to go ahead and accede to the Convention without
waiting for legislation on the subject

ii) for further action in regard to the endorsement of Article 6(b) (c) and (d), the matter
would be examined a new in consultation with the Mo Law and M.E.A

3. Government decided to accede to the Convention and the Instrument of Accession was
handed over in the UN Secretariat on 12th September, 1990.

4. However, in pursuance of the decision of the Government, Department of Youth
Affairs & Sports persued the matter with the 1160 Legal Affairs as far as Article 6(b) (०) and
(d) were concerned. These are as follow:—

6(b): To restrict access to national sports facilities to such sports bodiesteamsSportsmen
that participate in sports in a country practising apartheid or with teams representing
a country practising apartheid 4

6(c): Not to enforce sports contracts which involve sports activities with a country
practising apartheido or individual sportsmen selected on the basis of apartheid.

6(d): To deny and withdraw national honours and awards in sports from such teams/
sportsmen that participate in sports in a country practising apartheid or with teams
representing a country practising apartheid.

5. Subsequent discussionconsultation with the Deptt. of Legal Affairs led to the
conclusion that there is no need for legislation to implement Articles 6(b) and (c). However,
the Law Deptt. was of the opinion that Article 6(d) may require legislation as it will not be
easy otherwise to recover the amount of the cash award.

6. It was noted by Deptt. of Youth Affairs & Sports that the rules for Arjun Awards etc.
provide for withdrawalcancellation of the award. However, in case of cash component of
Arjuna and Dronacharya Awards, it would be difficult to recover the amount even after the
award has been cancelled. Deptt. of Legal Affairs observed that the provisions of the rules


could be applied either to the cancellation of certificates or recorded entry relating to cash
award but it may be unreasonable to insist upon the refund of amount and compulsory
recovery of the same in case of refusal.

7, In the light of the opinion given by the Deptt. of Legal Affairs and views of the Deptt.
of Youth Affairs & Sports, Min. of External Affairs was consulted in the matter. That
Ministry agreed with the views that no legislation is considered necessary for implementing
the provisions of the Convention. Approval of the Minister for Human Resource
Development was, therefore, sought and obtained for approving the proposal for withdrawal
of the Bill. Globally also, it was seen that apartheid is getting dissipated. There has been
definite demolition of barriers in South Africa and racial discrimination is on the wane all
over the world. Therefore, the Convention has lost its significance in the emerging new
world scenario. The proposal for withdrawing the Bill was, however, not approved by the
Cabinet.

8. Thus, the present status of the matter is that Government of India has already acceeded
to the International Convention against Aparatheid in Sports. In our view, in the light of the
latest developments in South Africa, it is not necessary to proceed with the Bill.

9, This is to further inform that Smt. Asha Swarup, Joint Secy. Depit. of Youth Affairs &
Sports, Room No. 504, 8 Wing, Shastry Bhavan (Tel. 384441) is dealing with the Bill in the
Ministry.

DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME
Observation/Recommendation
7.1       The District Primary Education Programme was launched in 1994, as a major initiative to revitalize the primary
education system and to achieve the objective of universalisation of primary education.  It is a Centrally- sponsored
scheme with the Central Govt. contributing 85 per cent of the project cost and the State Governments contributing the
remaining 15 per cent.  The Central Government's contribution is resourced entirely through external funding.  17
districts of Bihar, 8 districts of Orissa, 56 districts of UP and 34 districts of MP are covered under  DPEP.   The
Committee was given to understand that the norms prescribed by the World Bank with regard to school buildings are
not flexible. The Committee desires that it  may be reviewed.
Action Taken
The World Bank and other funding agencies have not prescribed any norms for construction of school buildings.  The
design, specification etc. are decided by the project implementing agencies depending on the area of construction. Under
the DPEP guidelines, which were formulated with the approval of the Cabinet, the ceiling on civil works was prescribed
at 24% of the project cost. Keeping in view the demand from States, the ceiling has already been increased to 33%.
Since, for achieving the objective of universalisation of elementary education, other components like appointment of
additional teachers, teacher training, curriculum development, academic resource support, community mobilisation etc.
are also important, the above ceiling has been considered to be reasonable to keep the balance between the various
components. In fact, under the scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, the same ceiling for civil works has been fixed.

The main responsibility for the construction of primary school building, provision of amenities and infrastructure

repairs to school buildings and construction of toilets. The Operation Blackboard scheme has now been subsumed in
SSA.  Under SSA primary schools are provided with Rs. 5000/- per annum per school for repair and maintenance as per

carried out.  The  first  phase of the programme,  which  was  launched in November, 1994  in 42 districts  in 7 States
was  subjected  to an  In-depth   Review  during  September-October, 1997.  The 2nd In-depth Review was conducted in
November, 1999-2000.  The reviews and various evaluation studies of the programme have brought out that the
programme has resulted in significant increase in enrolment, improvement in learning achievement, reduction in
repetition rates/drop-outs with increased community involvement, improvements in classroom processes.
Regarding unspent balances with the project states, under the DPEP guidelines and agreements with the funding
agencies, funds are required to be released to the State Implementation Societies in advance to meet the requirements of
next six months.  The amounts shown as unspent funds in the beginning of the financial year also include the funds
released by the Government of India at the end of the previous financial year, which are actually received by the state
societies in the next financial year. Actual funds available with the concerned four states as on 01.07.2002 were          
Rs. 1.05 crores in respect of Bihar, Rs. 37.65 crores in respect of Madhya Pradesh, Rs. 16.45 crores in respect of Orissa

and Rs. 37.01 crores in respect of Uttar Pradesh.

Para 7.5 of the 114th Report.  
SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN
Observation/Recommendation
10.5   The Committee recommends that provision for girls hostels especially in far flung areas should be made one of
the components  of SSA before it is implemented.
Action Taken
Girls’ residential schools can be opened under the innovative component of SSA, under which the District can spend Rs.
15.00 lakhs on any activity for furthering girls’ education. Further, the Department is also examining the launching of
another scheme Kasturba Gandhi Swantantra Vidyalaya Scheme under which residential schools would be opened for
girls of SC, ST and OBC classes.
In Uttar Pradesh, provision of residential school facility has been made in the SSA plans of district, Allahabad, Banda &
Chitrakoot. Besides, Bridge courses/Residential camps have been provided for far-flung areas in each of 16 SSA
districts under Education Guarantee Scheme Alternative & Innovative Education Programme.
In Orissa, 369, out of 400 residential Girls’ Hostels have been opened in the tribal districts.
In Madhya Pradesh, the facility of girls’ hostels already exists in many parts of the tribal districts of the State. However,
the component of girls’ education has been given due consideration while formulating SSA perspective plan.
Comments of the Committee
            The scheme of opening more and more residential schools in remote/tribal areas is a good scheme which
would provide necessary ambience and amenities to the girl child from underprivileged classes.    What is more
important in this respect is the attitude/response of parents in sending girls to these hostels.   The Committee
hopes that this aspect also is being taken up simultaneously.

GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED
STATUS OF ELEMENTARY EDUCATION
Observation/Recommendation
2.2       The Committee observes that whereas overall literacy rate as per the Census 2001 figures in Madhya Pradesh
and Orissa is almost at par with the national average, Bihar and UP are much below the national average.   The
Committee is constrained to note that actually the situation is much worse and serious even in the states as mentioned in 
the Census 2001.  There is wide variation in male and female literacy rates in all the four states.   In Madhya Pradesh,
female literacy rate is 50.28 against the national average of 54.16.   There are 3-4 districts in the State where female
literacy rate is far below the State average of 50.28.   As per the information (NSSO 1997) made available to the
Committee, female literacy rate in Orissa is 38 per cent which might have somewhat improved in Census, 2001.  
However, the Committee during its visits of some districts in the State having a sizeable SC/ST population, found  the
situation  very bad.   The visit revealed out into the surface that actual literacy and female literacy  situation, in
particular, has been suppressed very conveniently in the NSSO figures. The figures were misleading.  Literacy rate in
these districts was nowhere near the State average.   The Committee was surprised to note that in certain tribal districts
in Orissa, literacy rate amongst tribal women was merely 1.8 percent which is perhaps the lowest in the entire country.  
Similarly in Bihar, the Committee observed that besides the overall literacy rate being much below the national average
as brought out in Census  2001, female literacy rate was a cause of serious concern.    Female literacy rate of 34 as
compared to the national average 50 (NSSO 1997)  is self-explanatory.   Committee's experience after visiting 4-5
districts in Bihar was very discouraging.   In all the districts, literacy rates, particularly female literacy rates were  very
low.
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee is noted.
ENROLMENT AND DDROPOUT
Observation/Recommendation
3.2       The Committee was informed that district-wise drop-out figures are  maintained  in respect of DPEP districts
only at national level.  The Committee observes that in quite a few districts covered by DPEP in all the four states, drop

132ReportofHRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/Report132th.htm[01-07-2016 16:10:53]
out rates in respect of both girls and boys was very  high and quite contrary to the perception indicated from the figures. 
The Committee notes that the main reasons for high dropouts, as assessed by the National Family Health Survey – II
conducted in 1998-99, are lack of  interest in studies,  private cost of education being too high and the need for them to
work - both in their own farms / business / households or outside for remuneration.  The Committee has been given to
understand that these reasons  constitute almost 75% of the cases of dropouts.  The Committee is not, however, inclined
to agree  with this assessment. 
Action Taken
The assessment of drop-outs has been made on the basis of the survey carried out by the National Family Health Survey
1998-99. However, to identify the exact reasons for such drop-outs, a study is being undertaken in 6 States of Assam,
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, where drop-outs have been found to be very high. The
study is expected to be completed by December, 2002.
 
OPERATION BLACKBOARD
Observation/Recommendation
4.4       The Committee categorically  records its reservations about the figures regarding status of primary school
buildings in these States. Its experience in respect of both primary and upper primary school buildings has been totally
different.  The Committee during its visits found most of the school buildings in dilapidated condition.   During its
unscheduled visits, it found that some of the Govt. Schools in U.P. existed on paper only.   At some places, the
classrooms had all the junk and broken furniture stored.   Most of the schools were found to be without a boundary wall
which made the retention of students in the school all the more difficult.   Toilet and drinking water facilities were
available  in very few schools.  Even in few schools where these facilities existed, toilets were found  to be stinking.  
They were not being properly maintained at all.   In many cases, water taps/ hand pumps were not working for a long
time and needed repair.
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee is noted.
RESTRUCTURING AND RE-ORGANISATION OF TEACHER EDUCATION
Observations/Recommendations
5.4       The Committee was  informed by the Department that in order to assess the technical and infrastructural capacity
of DIETs, a national evaluation was initiated by NIEPA in November 1997.  The draft reports for DIETs of all the
States including those in Bihar, MP, Orissa and UP, have been sent to the concerned States to obtain their comments/
observations before the final draft National Evaluation Report is prepared by NIEPA. The Department further submitted
that while modifications based on the reports of NIEPA  will be considered during the 10
th Plan period, some changes
like the norms for recurring and non-recurring financial assistance to the States have been revised upward by about 50%
in 1999 following past experience.   Memoranda of Understandings (MoUs) are to be signed with State Governments in
order to ensure more effective DIETs.
Action Taken
MOUs have already been signed by 11 States namely: Orissa, Tripura, Meghalaya, Karantaka, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil
Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan and Punjab.  Action is being taken to get the MOUs signed by
the remaining States/UTs.
Observation/Recommendation
5.5       As regards the general attitude and behaviour of teachers, the Department stated that a  training in the
behavioural aspects of teachers is included in all training programmes of DIET.  In DPEP, behavioural aspects involving
motivation, activity based and joyful learning, gender sensitisation etc., are covered under the Teacher Training
programmes.  Various measures have also been suggested in the ‘Curriculum Framework for Quality Teacher
Education’ brought out by National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) in 1998 which will be implemented in due
course.
Action Taken
The observation of Committee is noted.
Observation/Recommendation
5.6       The Committee, despite various training and sensitization  programmes for teachers, is deeply perturbed over the
general attitude and behaviour of teachers towards the students in recent times.     It regrets to note that there is a general
erosion in the devotion and dedication of teachers towards their duties as compared in the past.    The noble bond of
teacher and the taught is entirely missing and commercialisation and parochialism have now taken its place.   The

Committee feels that production of good teachers is a great challenge before the country.   Good teachers are the makers
of the country.    All concerned will have to put their heads together to face this challenge otherwise the future of the
country will not be so bright as hoped.

The observation of Committee is noted.
MID-DAY MEAL SCHEME
Observation/Recommendation
6.4       The Committee notes that a Sub-group was constituted under the aegis of Working Group on Elementary
Education and Literacy for formulation of Tenth Plan and it has suggested major changes in the scheme.  The

the Mid-day Meal Scheme should be restricted to the formal schools for the time being. Steps should be taken to
effectively implement this scheme.  Efforts should also be made to provide cooked meal only under this programme.

this Committee  be given due weightage when modifications under Tenth Plan are made. The State Governments/UT
Administrations also need to be taken into confidence before revision of the Scheme.

The observation of the Committee is noted.

VI        POOR CONDITION OF GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
6.1       The Committee had the opportunity to visit a number of State-run medical colleges, besides 
interacting with medical professionals associated with such colleges.  The Committee observed that 
overall condition of these medical colleges was very bad.  The Committee was given to understand that 
there had been no improvement in the infrastructure facilities  for the medical colleges established long 
time back.   Even though there has been  manifold increase in the number of undergraduate and 
postgraduate seats, the facilities remained virtually the same.    Not only this, many new  paramedical 
courses have also been started without going into the availability of basic  infrastructure.   No new 
classrooms have been added, labs have tremendous scarcity of space and classrooms were equipped with 
the minimum teaching aids.   Over the  years, what has happened is that all the modern technology 
developments have not reached such colleges and as a result both teachers and doctors are not fully 
exposed to the latest techniques.   General opinion was that there was a need for having a moratorium  
on establishing new medical colleges in States having large concentration.  Instead attention was 
required to be focuses on updating the infrastructure of existing medical colleges. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
6.2       The Committee is inclined to agree with this view-point.   The Committee  is of the view 
that there is an urgent need for undertaking a review of  infrastructure status of all state-run 
medical  colleges in the country.   Non-existence of required facilities tend to create an atmosphere 
which  has a de-motivating effect on the teachers/doctors/students.    The Committee understands 
that Central Govt. has  already launched a pilot project for providing financial assistance to some 
State Govt.  medical colleges/hospitals.   The Committee feels that a time-bound action plan for 
revamping the infrastructure facilities should be drawn by the Central Govt. which could be 
implemented by State Govts in active co-ordination with Central Govt. and MCI. 
ACTION TAKEN 
 6.1&6.2    Though the State run medical colleges are bound by the MCI Regulations on the 
requirements for a Medical College vis-à-vis the admission capacity, the facilities available in some 
of the Government Medical Colleges are in a poor state.  Presently, the Central Govt. has 
launched a pilot scheme for providing financial assistance to State Govt. Medical colleges for 
strengthening their diagnostic facilities.  
XI. TEACHERS 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
11.4     The Committee finds that in states like Maharashtra and Gujarat, shortage of faculty strength in 
Govt. medical college has been addressed to some extent by having two types of teachers -  Full-time 
and Honorary teachers.  Although divergent views were given with regard to honorary teachers, the 
Committee had a feeling that both the categories of teachers  were playing a complimentary role.   The 
Committee observes that in spite of there being a provision for only full-time teachers in MCI 
Regulations on the request of some State Govts., system of honorary teachers has been further extended

by the Central Govt.  upto 30th June, 2002.   The  Committee is of the view that Central Govt./MCI 
should undertake a detailed review of Honorary System of teachers in the concerned States.   The 
Committee is of the view that after removal of all the  loopholes in this system and also safeguarding the 
interest of Full time teachers, other State Govts. can be approached to take benefit of Honorary System 
of teachers to the extent possible.  
ACTION TAKEN 
11.4     Taking into account the dearth of experienced teachers, the Central Govt. has extended the 
system of appointment of honorary/part-time teachers in the medical institutions for a further period of 
five years i.e. October 2006. This communication has been sent to all the State Govts., Universities and 
the Heads of all medical institutions for appropriate action. The MCI is, however, of the view that the 
engagement of honorary teachers may be made only in addition to the regular teaching faculty as 
required to be provided under the Council's Regulations. 
Recommendation/Observation 
11.5     The Committee finds that the UGC guidelines regarding extension of retired medical teachers of 
all medical colleges/institutions on yearly basis upto the age of 65 years have been agreed to by the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 1997.   The Committee feels that this directive should be 
given wide publicity  so that the Govt. medical colleges may take benefit of the same.  Besides that, 
possibility of hiring the services of  medical professionals – Visiting Professors and practicing doctors 
without compromising the standard of medical education can also be explored.  
Action Taken 
11.5     The Council is of the view that the possibility of hiring the services of medical professionals, 
visiting professors and practicing doctors can be permitted only in addition to the prescribed 
requirement of full-time teachers by the regulations and without compromising the standard of medical 
education. 
XII       TRAINING 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
12.1     During its interactions, Committee’s attention was drawn time and again about there being need 
for having some kind of training for medical teachers.   The majority view was that it is not necessary 
that a good medical practitioner is also a good teacher.  The Committee observes that most postgraduate 
teaching programmes have a component of students taking classes of undergraduate courses and also  
conducting seminars as part of their training. In spite of that, it was emphasized that training to 
prospective teachers  specially for communication skills was very much required.  The Committee 
strongly feels that training in educational technology should be made the eligibility criteria for 
appointment of a medical teacher.   If that is not considered feasible, extensive training programme of 
short duration should be mandatory before   the prospective teachers join their duties.  
ACTION TAKEN 
12.1     The Council's regulations only prescribe the minimum qualification and experience to be 
possessed by the medical teachers in different specialities. While agreeing with the recommendations of 
the Committee, considering the shortage of teachers in certain specialities it is felt that the training in 
educational technology can be made compulsory for the medical teachers within a fixed time after they 
join duties. The State Governments and institutions can set up training centres for this purpose..  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
12.2     Committee’s attention was also drawn to the fact that there was also a constant need to have in-
service training programme/refresher course for doctors involved in teaching to update their knowledge 
especially during the present era when rapid scientific developments are taking place and a wide variety 
of  diseases are being recognized.   The Committee finds that Graduate Medical Education Regulations 
provide that Medical Education Units/Departments be established in all medical colleges for faculty 
development and providing learning resource material to teachers.   The Committee is, however, 
constrained to note that these directives are not being adhered to as only about 50-60 medical colleges in 
the country  have established such units so far.   The Committee is of the opinion that fulfillment of this 
condition should be pursued with all medical colleges, both Govt. and private.

XV       PROBLEM OF SHORTAGE OF DOCTORS IN RURAL AREAS – REMEDIES 
THEREFOR  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
15.4     The Committee has been given to understand that some State Govts. have  adopted the policy of 
making rural service compulsory in the initial posting of medical officers before they are transferred to 
urban areas or permitted to do postgraduate medical education.   There is no shortage  of doctors as 
such, but there is mal-distribution between the  rural and urban areas.   The Committee is of the view 
that compulsion alone will not have the desired results.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
alongwith compulsory rural service for a limited specified time, incentives like special allowance, better 
housing and other allied facilities and special relaxation for admission to postgraduate courses are also 
necessary for attracting young doctors towards rural areas. 
ACTION TAKEN 
15.4     As per the decisions arrived in the Central Council for Health & Family Welfare, the State 
Govts. have been periodically advised to take various incentive measures to attract doctors for rural 
service, such as improving infrastructure facilities for doctors to remove their hardships, making rural 
service obligatory for three years, reservation of 25% of Postgraduate medical seats in medical colleges 
for in-service candidates who have.worked in rural areas for at least three years with a bond that 
thereafter they will serve the Government for at least five years etc. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
15.6     There was also a need for developing proper infrastructure in PHCs.   The Committee is of the 
view that the Department should pursue this issue with the State Govts.  The Committee understands the 
limitations of the Centre, health being a State subject.   However, PHCs are being maintained through 
Central Grants.  Hence, the need for Central monitoring about upkeep of PHCs is also there. 
ACTION TAKEN 
15.6     Wherever schemes are running with Central grants, the Central Government is obliged to 
monitor the execution of such schemes. The recommendation of the Committee in this regard will be 
kept in view while providing grants to the PHCs.  
XX       POWERS OF UNIVERSITY/HEALTH UNIVERSITY 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
20.1     All medical colleges in the country are affiliated to one University or the other.  Besides that, the 
States of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Punjab have established Medical 
University/University of Health Sciences, affiliating all the medical colleges  and other teaching 
institutions in health sciences. The Committee had the opportunity to  interact with the  representatives 
of some of the Universities including Health  Universities of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka 
and Maharashtra.   The major issues/problems with regard to functioning of universities/medical 
universities can be enumerated as given below :- 
Besides allopathic system, institutions of other systems of medicine being brought under the jurisdiction 
of Health University in one or two states has created procedural problems due to proper infrastructure 
not being there for the management of such a large number of  institutions. 
Resource  crunch being faced as funds being provided by State/Centre  not adequate  enough.  Need for 
having a separate Commission like UGC emphasized  for universities/health universities. 
There was no provision for setting up a Senate in a Health University.   As a result, Health Universities 
being deprived of their right of representation in MCI. 
Need for involving representative of a University/Health University in the exercise of 
formulation/revision of curriculum for medical education related courses. 
Only exam-holding powers vested with University/Health University. Local University should also be 
involved in the exercise of opening of new colleges/increasing the intake capacity/starting of new course 
alongwith MCI/Central Govt. 
Page 6 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

Effective involvement of local universities in the inspection of medical colleges. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
20.2     The Committee notes that in the opinion of the MCI, the concerned University from time to time 
should carry out its own inspections to evaluate the facilities available at the affiliated medical 
college/institution.   The University should also intimate any deficiencies to the Council from time to 
time in order to maintain the standard of medical education.   In addition to this, the University should 
ensure the strict compliance of the regulations of the MCI for its affiliated medical colleges. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
20.3     The Committee apprehends that the ground realities are entirely different.  Although as per the 
IMC Act, 1956, all  Universities have a right to be represented in the Council, majority of them are not 
there for so many years due to prolonged procedural formalities.   Not only this, Health Universities, by 
virtue of their composition, are not being represented in the Council.    The Committee has been given to 
understand that  universities are not being involved  in any exercise undertaken for regulation of medical 
education. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
20.4     The Committee is of the opinion that observations of local University  should invariably  be 
obtained before permission being given for starting a new college/increasing the intake capacity/adding 
new courses.  Similarly, the Committee finds no harm if University  representative is also part of the 
inspection team.   The Committee has been informed that a Sub-Committee was constituted by the 
General Body of the Council to go into the establishment of Health Universities.    The Sub-Committee 
has recommended discussion by a broader group in a workshop.  The Committee hopes that the issues 
raised before the Committee with regard to Health Universities would also be taken care of and a clear 
perception of the feasibility of Health University  would emerge as a result of discussion to be 
undertaken by the broader Group. 
ACTION TAKEN 
20.1 to 20.4     The establishment of University of Health Sciences in States was envisaged with a view 
to bring in uniformity in the standards of medical education imparted and to work as a Centre for 
Manpower Policy Planning. So far only five States have established the University of Health Sciences.  
The policy of the Central Government is to persuade the remaining State Governments also to follow 
suit. The Universities are already empowered to inspect the facilities available in the medical colleges 
before granting and renewing the affiliation to them.  Though, as per the present scheme there is no 
representative of the University in the inspection teams of the Council as such, the MCI has been 
appointing the Vice-chancellors/Deans as their inspectors

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
22.2     The Committee is also of the view that a cell for receiving complaints and inviting suggestions 
from general public and affected persons should be set up in the MCI to work as a watch-guard and also 
facilitate the functioning of MCI.

XXIII. PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY STUDENT COMMUNITY  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
23.1     The Committee had very fruitful discussions with representatives of student community of all the 
medical colleges visited by it.   Various suggestions for improvement of medical education based on 
their experience were put forth before the Committee which are reflected in the Report.  Besides that, 
the students also drew the attention of the Committee to a number of problems being faced by them 
which are enumerated below :- 
Due to a prolonged admission procedure for MBBS, session for 1st year generally starts very late. 
Maximum publicity needs to be  given to the rules/regulations and conditions with respect to admission 
procedure for the convenience of students.
Page 7 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

Hostel accommodation satisfying the needs of entire student community not there.   Majority of the 
students have to travel a long distance daily for attending their classes. 
Lack of  hospital accommodation has resulted in tendency of students not attending their classes 
regularly.   In the process, there were frequent instances of shortage of attendance. 
Another peculiar development is students opting for private tuition. 
Students of private medical colleges/younger institution not having adequate library facilities. 
Very low rates of stipend being paid to trainee doctors.    Amount of stipend also varies from State to 
State, institution to institution. 
Foreign textbooks  not fulfilling the requirements of students. 
Complaints of biased attitude of external examiners  conducting practical exams were also there. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
23.2     The Committee understands that a specific  time schedule for admission  to MBBS has been laid 
down by MCI.   The Committee finds that due to  delay in the admission procedure, training schedule 
gets disturbed and as a result, instances are there that results are delayed.  The Committee, therefore, 
strongly feels that MCI should strictly monitor the adherence of  time schedule by medical  colleges all 
over the country. 
ACTION TAKEN 
23.2     The Graduate Regulations 1997 provides that the universities should organise admission timings 
and admission process in such a way that teaching in first semester starts by 1st August each year.  
Though the regulations are mandatory, instances have come to notice where these are not strictly 
adhered to.  The Hon'ble Supreme Court vide its order dated 11.9.2002  has also directed that there shall 
be no mid-stream admissions in the medical courses and the Council is at present drafting a guideline to 
be followed by all concerned fixing a time frame for conduct of entrance examination, counseling, 
commencement of the academic session and closure of the admission.  These guidelines shall be binding 
on all concerned in pursuance of the Supreme Court directions. 
XXIV    TEACHER-STUDENT RELATIONSHIP 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
24.1     There has been gradual erosion in the traditional relations between students and teachers in 
medical education.    Over the years, what has happened is that  with the increase in the intake capacity 
in medical colleges all over the country,  faculty strength with a few exceptions has continued to be the 
same.    The MCI ratio 10:1 for  student teacher  is nowhere to be seen.   The Committee has been given 
to understand that in the majority of the medical colleges small group teaching was being practiced only 
during tutorials, clinical teaching and  field visits.   The Committee feels that the situation should be  
such that the teachers are able to share their experiences with the students.   Teachers also  get an 
opportunity to evaluate the students better in such an environment.   The Committee finds that  
availability of video cassettes and internet access has vastly improved interactive learning wherever 
available.   The Committee is of the view that steps should be taken for compulsory introduction of such 
hi-tech facilities in all medical colleges  in the country. 
ACTION TAKEN 
24.1   The recommendation of the Committee in this regard will be intimated to all the universities and 
institutions for appropriate action by the MCI.
