II         OVERVIEW 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
2.1       The Committee observes that the amendments made in the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 in 
1993 by laying down very stringent norms for establishment of new medical college, increase in the 
intake capacity and introduction of a new or higher course of study  has  checked  the mushroom growth 
of  medical colleges in the country to some extent.   However, these norms need to be enforced 
Page 8 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

uniformly  and  with an objective approach.   Sporadic proposals for starting a very large number of 
medical colleges at a stroke  still continue to be noticed. 
ACTION TAKEN 
2.1       The Medical Council of India Regulations on Establishment of Medical Colleges initially 
notified in 1993 were reviewed and revised Regulations were notified in 1999 prescribing stringent 
conditions for opening new medical colleges.  The observations made by the Committee will be taken 
into account as these Regulations are subject to periodical review. At present, the Government proposes 
to review these Regulations in the light of the judgment of the 11-Judge Constitution Bench in the case 
of TMA Pai Foundations & Ors. vs. State of Karnataka and Ors. delivered on 31st October, 2002. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
2.2       The Committee had the opportunity to visit both govt. and private medical  colleges and interact 
with the management, faculty members and student representatives.   Feedback with regard to  
functioning of both govt. and  private  medical colleges was also received from different quarters.   
While it is true that  common parameters about the  two categories of medical colleges can not be drawn, 
the Committee  has the following observations to make. Private medical colleges, in the initial period, 
barely reach the standards and  norms set up by MCI  with regard to infrastructure, manpower etc.   
Similarly, in the Govt. medical  colleges set up in different parts of the country, with the passage of time 
there has been a steady deterioration in the infrastructure because of   inability of State Govts  to provide 
any assistance  whatsoever due to their very poor financial position.   Other major   constraints noticed 
in the smooth functioning of Govt. medical colleges are control of too many authorities, lack of 
accountability, prolonged procedure of recruitment  and promotion of teachers.   Inadequate  staff, 
unwarranted interference by management and manipulation in the admission of students can be said to 
be major drawbacks of private medical colleges.    The Committee also noticed that access to clinical 
facilities having large patient attendance was there in Govt. medical colleges.   In contrast in private 
medical colleges, in spite of having impressive hospital  buildings, required clinical material  was 
lacking. 
ACTION TAKEN 
2.2       The Regulations of MCI has prescribed the minimum clinical attendance for recommending the 
grant of Letter of Permission to a new medical college. Presently, these norms are being followed.  
VI        POOR CONDITION OF GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
6.3       The Committee has been given to understand that in the present set up, educational level of 
technical/Para-medical  staff is not appropriate to handle the hi-tech equipments and to pick up newer  
techniques.   An indirect fall-out of such a situation is that more and more work is being handled by the 
medical staff themselves at the   cost of time to be devoted for teaching and training of students.  The 
Committee is of the view  that against the backdrop of technological development, basic qualifications 
required for technical staff need to be reviewed.   Besides that, regular in-service training, workshops 
and Continuing Medical Education (CMEs) for technical staff should be made a regular feature.   The 
Committee also feels that feasibility of having Medical Learning Technique (MLT) colleges imparting 
diploma/B.Sc degrees being attached to medical colleges can be explored. 
ACTION TAKEN 
6.3       The Council is having a scheme for conducting CME programmes which can be availed by the 
institutions under the NRI/Non-NRI participation schemes. This is in addition to the CME programmes 
already being conducted by various professional bodies such as Indian Medical Association, National 
Academy of Medical Sciences, AIIMS and PGIMER, Chandigarh and specialist organisations.   The 
feasibility of having institutes imparting diploma/B.Sc. degrees attached to medical colleges needs 
extensive discussion with the universities and others concerned. 
VIII      NRI QUOTA IN GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
8.1       The Committee notes that the  Central Govt. in a communication dated 7th April, 1999 had 
allowed the State Govts to take   their own decision with regard to admission of NRI students in State

Govt. medical colleges up to 15% of the total intake capacity after  keeping in view the requirements of 
the local students and   subject to the condition  that there shall  be no commercialization of medical 
education and that their contribution of seats towards the All India Entrance Examination Quota will not 
be affected.   The Council has also no objection to this procedure  subject to  admission of 15% of the 
total seats by NRI/foreign students.   The funds collected by these admissions should be utilized for the 
development of the particular institution.  The Committee understands that in some of the States, this 
practice has been started which is likely to be followed in other States also.   The Committee has its own 
reservations about this Central Govt. directive.   While noting that contribution of seats towards the All 
India Entrance Examination Quota by the State Govt. medical  colleges will not be affected by this 
move, the Committee apprehends that requirements of local students are bound to be hit hard.   The 
Committee wonders as to how the interest of local students will be taken care  of with the  total number 
of seats remaining the same.   The Committee is of the view  that relaxation should only be resorted to if 
equal number of seats are increased.   In that event also, availability of additional required infrastructure 
will also have to be ensured.    The Committee also feels that there are little chances of funds thus 
generated being utilized for the development of a particular institution.  Instances  have already  come to 
the notice  of the Committee where initial understanding with State Govt. was  that money generated 
from NRI admissions was to be deposited with college and a special committee was to be authorized to 
utilize these funds.   However, subsequently, State Govt directions were given  that such funds are to be 
deposited with the State Exchequer to be allotted  afterwards to the college. 
ACTION TAKEN 
8.1       The option of filling up of 15% of seats in the State Govt. medial colleges by NRI/foreign 
students was allowed to the State Govts. in order to tide over the financial crunch in response to the 
requests received from some of the States.  The Communication sent by the Central Govt. to the State 
Govts. was advisory in nature and it is for the respective State Govts. to take an appropriate decision in 
the matter. 
IX        EXAMINATION PROCEDURE 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
9.1       MCI Regulations on Graduate Medical  Education, 1997 deal extensively with the examination 
procedure to be followed for obtaining MBBS degree.   Attendance, internal assessment and university 
examinations are the three basic factors on which performance of a student in essential components of 
training is to be assessed.   Detailed procedure for internal assessment and conducting university 
examination has been laid down.   Distribution of marks to various disciplines has also been specified.   
Criteria for appointment of examiners – both external and internal -  is   also there.   There is a separate 
chapter on ‘Internship’ outlining beside other aspects the specific objectives, distribution of compulsory 
and elective posting in various disciplines and the methodology for assessment of internship etc.    Even 
model time-table for different semesters has been given. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
9.2       During the course of its discussions with various authorities, the Committee had the opportunity 
to hear divergent views on various aspects of examination procedure for MBBS course.   Semester 
system was generally welcomed.   However,  there were views both in favour and against internal 
assessment.  One view was that internal assessment of students should be given due weightage as it 
would result in improved attendance.  However, apprehensions were also there as it was felt that element 
of partiality was bound to be there in internal assessment.   It was also pointed out that examiners were 
not being appointed as per MCI norms.   Views were also expressed both for and against multiple choice 
system in question papers. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
9.3       The Committee is of the view that MCI norms are not being strictly adhered to by many of the 
medical colleges.   Had it been so, there would not have been such reservations and also variations in 
examination patterns being followed by different institutions/universities.  The Committee would also 
like to point out that uniformity of examination pattern to the maximum extent possible can only be   
achieved if the teaching facilities and  courses are also uniform.  The Committee, therefore, is of the 
Page 10 of 36133rdReportofHRd
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report133rd.htm

view that steps need to be initiated for evolving a forum for interaction amongst medical faculties of 
different universities on this aspect of medical education. 
ACTION TAKEN 
9.1to9.3           The concept of uniformity in curriculum, required hours of teaching and training and 
scheme of examination has been achieved significantly through incorporation in the Regulations on 
Graduate Medical Education.  However, the Council has always provided a national forum for 
discussion, deliberation and decision on such wider academic issues through holding suitable national 
workshops periodically and implementing recommendations emanating therefrom. 
XI        TEACHERS  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
11.6     The Committee observes  that MCI has not made any Regulations regarding separation of 
teaching and non-teaching cadres.   The Council Regulations only provide for a required number of 
teachers and other non-teaching staff required for each department in the medical college and attached  
hospital  according to the seat intake capacity in MBBS course.   The Committee is of the view that 
practice of inter-change between teaching and non-teaching cadres is indeed creating problems for 
medical faculty in some of the States.   The Committee,  therefore, recommends that the MCI should 
examine this practice and make specific provision in the best interest of medical teachers in its 
Regulations.  
ACTION TAKEN 
11.6     The MCI does not permit computation of non-teaching experience in lieu of teaching experience 
and the Council has prescribed Regulations on Teachers Minimum Eligibility Qualifications to that 
effect. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
11.7     The Committee observes that the duties and responsibilities of medical teachers are different, 
immediate and exacting in nature when compared with other categories  of professions/govt. 
employees.    The Committee would like to emphasise that there is an urgent need for providing the  best 
possible service conditions to the medical teachers.   Their pay scales and other incentives need to be of 
a higher scale as compared to other teachers. 
ACTION TAKEN 
11.7     The service conditions of the medical teachers are governed by the respective State 
Governments. In the absence of any Central funding, it is not possible for the Central Government to 
prescribe uniform pay scale for medical teachers in the country. 
XIV     PRIVATE PRACTICE 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
14.1     The issue of private practice by medical college teachers was raised time and again during the 
deliberations of the Committee with all categories of medical professionals – doctors, teachers, state 
authorities, student community.   Besides that, the Committee also received lot of feedback on this issue 
from various parts of the country.   The Committee observes that at present, no uniform system with 
regard to private practice by teachers is prevailing in the various medical colleges.   There are colleges 
where teachers of clinical subjects  are allowed to do private practice and teachers of non-clinical 
subjects are eligible for non-practicing allowance.   Besides that, in some states, there is a total ban on 
private practice by medical teachers.    Instances are also there of teachers, in spite of  getting NPA,  
doing private practice. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
14.2     The Committee finds that there is no provision in the MCI Regulations on this issue except that 
all teachers should be full-time in medical  colleges and attached hospitals.   The Committee has been 
informed that in pursuance of Central Govt. directions, a number of state govts. adopted the policy of 
grant of NPA to medical staff  including the teachers and have abolished private practice.

3.5       In some states, a number of Universities now fall under the jurisdiction of Health Universities  
established in the recent years.   This development has led to a peculiar situation.   By virtue of coming 
under the jurisdiction of a Health University, such Universities   have lost their right of being 
represented in the Council.   On the other hand, Health Universities  cannot send their nominee to the  
Council as they do not have any Senate.   Thus, as many as 21 Universities over and above 56 eligible 
Universities are not represented in the Council.   Health Universities   having a  large number of medical 
colleges under their  jurisdiction, specially  in southern  and western states have no say in the decision-

entitled to send one member to the Council and this provision is also available to the Health Universities 
set up in some of the States.   
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee is  aware of the provision of Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, which lays down 
that any University having a medical faculty is entitled to send one member to the Council.   
However, the problem is that some Universities are still un-represented  in the Medical Council as 
they do not have a Senate in existence.   In view of this, the Committee recommends that sincere 
efforts be made for the constitution of 'Senate' in such Universities so as to enable them to be  
represented in the Indian Medical Council. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.11     The Committee is not inclined to agree with the viewpoint  of the Council.  In its all the study 
visits  and interactions with the various   functionaries comprising the entire medical education   
spectrum, one view  that has been consistently put across before the Committee, was that with the 
increase  in the number of medical colleges over the years, it is practically not possible for a centralized 
body like MCI to constantly monitor the standard of medical education.    The Committee observes that 
there is no regional council of the MCI.   The State  Medical Councils are autonomous bodies 
established by State Govts that too not by all the State Govts.    These  State Medical Councils have no   
authority in the maintenance of standards of medical education.   In such a  scenario with 183   medical 
colleges spread across the country with chances  of future expansion, the Committee strongly feels that 
regional  councils  with MCI continuing as the apex body need to be set up in the country.   The 
Committee is of the view that, both the Central Govt. and MCI should explore the possibility of setting 
up four regional councils  in  Southern, Northern, Eastern and Western parts of the country.   This would 
ultimately lead to better monitoring of the standard of medical  education as laid down in the IMC Act, 
1956,  and regulations made thereunder.     The Committee also desires that the Department may take up 
the matter of establishing  State Medical Council in the States where they are not existing.   Role of 
State Medical Council may also be reviewed so as to involve them in the exercise of maintaining the

Where there are more than one college in a state and only one university/board conducting the

A competitive entrance examination in the cases of Institutions of All India character.

10.1     MCI Regulations on Graduate Medical Education, 1997 deal extensively with the curriculum 
prescribed for the   MBBS course.   The entire course has been divided into three  phases.   Phase I (two 
semesters) consists of pre-clinical subjects i.e. Human Anatomy,  Physiology including Bio-Physics, 
Bio-Chemistry and introduction to Community Medicine  including Humanities.   Phase II (3 semesters)

Pharmacology, Microbiology, Forensic Medicine including Toxicology and part of Community 
Medicine.   Phase III will be of 4 semesters.   The clinical subjects to be taught during Phase II and III 
are Medicine and its allied specialties, Surgery and its allied specialties, Obstetrics and Gynecology and 
Community Medicine.

XV       PROBLEM OF SHORTAGE OF DOCTORS IN RURAL AREAS – REMEDIES 
THEREFOR  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
15.1     Acute shortage of doctors in rural areas is a problem being faced in the entire country.   No State 
can be said to be not facing this problem, only its acuteness can be varying in different states.   The 
Committee finds that the main reason for the paucity of doctors in rural areas is the lack or inadequacy 
of facilities available in PHCs/hospitals.   Nobody would deny the fact that almost all PHCs in the 
country are ill-equipped.  They lack necessary facilities for treating even minor ailments whereas ground 
reality is that generally very complicated cases are handled there.   Another de-motivating factor is the 
disparity in the living conditions in the rural areas vis-à-vis  urban areas.  Geographical location is not 
convenient, and  even basic amenities like  proper roads, electricity and water, education for children, 
entertainment etc. are not there.  The situation gets more aggravated because doctors who man the PHCs 
are generally young pass-outs possessing only theoretical knowledge, practical exposure of ground 
realities virtually being nil.

inclined to agree with this view mainly because equal standards are required to be maintained for both 
rural and urban areas.   One must not forget the fact that rural masses although generally illiterate are 
gradually realizing the harm caused by unregistered doctors  practising in rural areas.   The Committee 
strongly feels that creation of a class within a class will not be appropriate.  Such a distinction would be 
detrimental to the entire medical profession.

XVI     BRAIN DRAIN 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
16.1     The Committee observes that the problem of brain drain is being faced at two fronts – one being 
from one institution to another inside the country and the other being flight of young talent to foreign 
institutions.   The Committee has been given to understand that this malady has penetrated even premier 
medical institutions.   On the one side,  national level institutions like PGI, AIIMS are facing shortage of 
faculty strength due to faculty members joining foreign institutions primarily for job satisfaction.   The 
other cause of serious concern is the silent brain drain in the form of voluntary retirement or taking  up 
regular jobs by Govt. medical  college teachers in private medical colleges.   Better working conditions, 
monetary benefits and more opportunity for undertaking research activities can  be  cited as the main 
factors responsible for this phenomenon.   The Committee observes that there is another aspect of this 
problem.   Young pass-outs do not get to know all the opportunities  which are available in the country.   
There is a need for evolving a facility  on the pattern of Recruitment agencies coming to the campuses of 
premier technical institutions for placements.   The Committee is of the firm view that  remedial steps 
need to be taken for creating best job opportunities  thereby retaining our young talent in the country.  
The Committee also feels that if necessary, students may be asked to pay back in easy instalments, 
wherever Government  funding is there.    Modalities in this regarding may be explored. 
ACTION TAKEN 
16.1     At present, in terms of Emigration Act the doctors and nurses fall under the exempted category 
of 'Emigration Check Not Required'. However, the MCI is of the view in the last 10-15 years the exodus 
of doctors has come down considerably due to the expansion in the medical and health facilities in the 
country.  Some of the foreign countries have also imposed stringent conditions on recruitment of doctors 
from abroad which has further curtailed the problem of brain drain.  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE: 
            The Committee does not quite agree that exemption of `ECMR’ under the Emigration Act 
is a reason for the problem of brain-drain.   The Committee would like this to be substantiated 
with facts and figures that during the last 10-15 years, the exodus of doctors has come down 
considerably due to expansion in the medical and health facilities in this Country.   The 
Committee feels that brain drain is a serious malady and that in medical profession where lot of 
tax payers money is spent on the education and training of medical students.  Tackling this 
problem may be difficult but not impossible.  What is needed is to adopt a carrot and stick policy 
in curbing this malady; purely punitive measures would not do.  Department should with the help 
of Department of Science & Technology work out a multi pronged strategy for curbing the brain 
drain in a time bound manner.

III        MEDICAL COUNCIL OF INDIA (MCI) 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.1       Medical Council of India (MCI) is a statutory body which was established under the  Indian 
Medical Council Act, 1956.   It is a nodal body assigned the task of processing the proposals for 
establishment of a new medical college, starting  of a new or higher course of study or training and 
increasing of admission capacity in any course of study  or training.      Other major function  of MCI is 
regulating the standard of medical education by carrying out regular inspections of different medical 
colleges  located all over the country in accordance with the  provisions of the Act and Regulations 
made thereunder. The Council is also empowered to recommend withdrawal of recognition in respect of 
any college based on its inspections.   Thus, it can be said  that MCI acts as the watchdog  for 
maintaining  the standard of medical education in the country. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.2       MCI is composed of both elected and nominated members.   As laid down in Section 3(1) of the 
IMC Act, 1956 under the elected category, one member of the medical faculty from each university, one 
member from each State in which a State Medical  Register is maintained and seven members to be 
elected  from amongst themselves by persons enrolled on any of the State Medical Registers are 
included.   Under the nominated category, one member from each state is nominated by the Central 
Govt. in  consultation with the State Govt.  and eight members are to be nominated by the  Central 
Govt.   Thus,  composition of MCI was envisaged to be well represented having members from all the 
required  categories. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.3       The Committee has been informed that  as on 21st June, 2001, the  total membership of MCI is 
113 out of which 77 are filled  up and 36 are vacant.   Out of 77 members in position, 34 belong to the 
nominated category and 43 are from the elected category.    Out of the total number of 36 vacancies, 35 
are from the  elected category.   The Committee observes that the  present composition of  MCI cannot 
be said  to be of an All India  character.   This is all the more evident as only  fifteen members form the 
quorum  of the Council and all the acts of the Council are   decided by a majority of the members 
present and voting. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
3.4       The Committee notes that out of 36 vacancies in the  113-member Council, 21 are in the seats

IV        PROCEDURE/NORMS PRESCRIBED FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF A MEDICAL 
COLLEGE, STARTING A NEW  OR HIGHER COURSE OF STUDY OR TRAINING AND 
INCREASING THE ADMISSION CAPACITY 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.1       Section 10A of the IMC Act, 1956 deals with the procedure for obtaining permission for 
establishment of a new medical college, starting a new or higher course of study or training and  
increasing the admission capacity. There also exist Minimum Standard Requirements for a Medical 
College for 50 admissions annually, Regulations, 1999 and similar regulations for 100 admissions and 
150 admissions separately.   These regulations provide for a specific area requirement for various 
departments both in the medical colleges and teaching hospitals, staff strength required and equipment 
for various departments.    
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.2       By and large, the feedback which the Committee received with regard to the procedure and 
various norms/conditions prescribed for opening a new medical college, starting a new course and 
increasing the intake capacity emphasized their efficacy and necessity for checking the mushroom 
growth of medical colleges.  However, it was pointed  out time and again that these norms need to be 
implemented stringently and objectively.   Besides that, some reservations were also voiced about the 
practicability of some of the norms, like requirement of minimum land specially for hilly, tribal and 
metropolitan  areas, very high amount of bank guarantee, requirement of infrastructure in the medical 
college/teaching hospital etc.    The Committee recommends that  the MCI should undertake an exercise 
for reviewing the various norms so as to  examine their viability in the present scenario and bringing  
about necessary modifications therein without compromising the quality. 
ACTION TAKEN 
4.1&4.2           The minimum requirement for starting a medical college with annual intake capacity of 
50, 100,150 seats was worked out by the Council in consultation with all concerned and notified in the 
year 1999.  Similarly, the Council's regulations on starting new or higher course of study and increase in 
the admission capacity was notified in the year 2000.  As per the practice these regulations are normally 
reviewed after five and a half years trial time during which the first batch of students admitted under the 
new regulations complete their course. The Council thereafter obtains feedback from the Universities, 
State Governments and others concerned before making recommendation to the Central Government for 
effecting appropriate amendments in the regulations. Some of the regulations of the Council have 
become due for review in the light of the judgment of the 11 Judges Constitution Bench of the Supreme 
Court delivered on 31.10.2002.  The recommendations made by the Committee will also be considered 
during the review. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.4       It can be said that with  the final authority vested in the Central Govt and MCI, mushrooming of 
medical colleges leading to regional imbalance and commercialization of medical education has been 
checked considerably.   However,  the Committee observes that there are certain practical problems also 
which go against the student interest.   There are instances where medical college once started is not able 
to  fulfill the commitments made at the initial stage, thereby losing recognition and thus playing with the 
future of students enrolled in that college.   The Committee is of the view that there is a need for 
building up a mechanism whereby maximum standards are to be met at the very beginning.   Reports are 
there where college is started on the basis of Essentiality Certificate and conditional approval.   
However, in the very second year, conditions are not met.    In such a scenario, either the college is 
allowed to function so as to safeguard the interest of students or students are shifted to a recognized 
medical college.   Both the situations cannot  be considered to be desirable and this should not be 
allowed to happen. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.5   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that both the Central Govt. and MCI should have a more 
cautious approach while giving approval for a new medical college.   There is a need for assessing  the 
background of a  trust, specially its involvement in medical field and non-commercial approach before

grant of any permission.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that definition of the term ‘trust’ 
should be incorporated in the relevant provisions of the IMC Act, 1956.  
ACTION TAKEN 
4.4&4.5           The minimum requirement for starting a medical college with annual intake capacity of 
50, 100,150 seats was worked out by the Council in consultation with all concerned and notified in the 
year 1999.  Similarly the Council's regulations on starting new or higher course of study and increase in 
the admission capacity was notified in the year 2000.  As per the practice these regulations are normally 
reviewed after five and a half years trial time during which the first batch of students admitted under the 
new regulations complete their course. The Council thereafter obtains feedback from the Universities, 
State Governments and others concerned before making recommendation to the Central Government for 
effecting appropriate amendments in the regulations. Some of the regulations of the Council have 
become due for review in the light of the judgment of the 11 Judges Constitution Bench of the Supreme 
Court delivered on 31.10.2002.  The recommendations made by the Committee will also be considered 
during the review. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.6       The Committee has been given to understand that a general view of the requirement of medical 
manpower is taken by the State Govts  while providing for establishing a new medical college.   The 
prescribed form of Essentiality  Certificate included in the  Establishment of Medical Colleges 
Regulations, 1999 requires the State Govts to indicate details of existing medical manpower in the State, 
doctor-population ratio in the State and the justification for  opening of the proposed medical college. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
4.7       The Committee is not inclined to agree with the view of the Department that although it is 
necessary to have an All India assessment of medical manpower requirement, it cannot be made a  pre-
condition for starting a new college.   The Committee strongly feels that the responsibility of the Central 
Govt does not end with the production of Essentiality Certificate by State Govt.   The  Committee would 
like to refer to Sub-Section (7) of Section 10A of the IMC Act, 1956 which deals with recommendation 
of the Council and approval/disapproval by Central  Govt. for opening of a new college.   One of the 
factors to be considered as enumerated in clause (f) is the requirement of manpower in the field of 
practice of medicine.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that both Central and the State Govts 
should specifically ensure whether there is a requirement in the  real sense for establishing a medical 
college in a particular area before giving its approval for the same. 
ACTION TAKEN 
4.6&4.7           At present the need for establishing a medical college at a particular area is to be 
considered by the State Government at the time of grant of Essentiality Certificate to the proposed 
college and the MCI is also required to take into consideration the manpower requirement in the 
particular area before recommending for grant of permission to the new college.  The MCI would evolve 
an effective mechanism for strict adherence to these provisions while undertaking review of their 
regulations.

VIII      NRI QUOTA IN GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
8.2       As per the Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations, 2000, there is a  provision for adopting 
any of the following procedures for admission to PG courses :- 
(i)         On the basis of merit as determined by a competitive test conducted by the State Govt. or by the 
competent   authority appointed by the State Govt. or by the university/group of universities in the same 
state; or  
On the  basis of merit as determined by a centralized competitive test held at the national level; or  
On the basis of the individual  cumulative performance at the first, second and third MBBS 
examinations, if such examinations have been passed from the same university; or 
Combination of (i) and (iii).The State Govts. have the option to choose any one of the options for 
admission to PG courses.   
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
8.3       The Committee has been given to understand  that the present procedure of allocation  of seats in 
different disciplines of postgraduate courses was mainly based on an entrance examination conducted at 
the state or the national level.   Thus, the merit position decided the choice of discipline which was  not  
considered to be an ideal position.   It resulted in frustration among students as there was every 
possibility of students not getting the choice of their discipline  ultimately leading to lack of 
commitment on their part.   An indirect consequence of this system of PG admission was that an 
important component of MBBS training  i.e. internship was totally neglected by the students due to their 
remaining busy in the preparation for admission to Postgraduate course.   The  Committee, therefore, 
feels that alongwith entrance test, feasibility of having  individual cumulative performance at the first, 
second and third MBBS examination and also aptitude of the students being  made the criteria for 
admission to Postgraduate courses may be explored. 
ACTION TAKEN 
8.2&8.3           The Council's Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations were notified in the year 
2000 which also lays down the criteria to be adopted for selection of students.  These Regulations were 
finalised after obtaining the views of the Universities, State Govts. and others concerned. As  the 
recommendation made by the Committee calls for amendment in the Regulations, the same shall be 
considered in consultation with the Universities and others concerned..

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
13.1     During the course of its discussion with  both teaching and student community  and  also experts, 
one issue on which divergent views emerged was the need for assessment of medical college teachers by

XVIII  INDIAN MEDICAL SERVICE  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
18.1     The Committee observes that  teachers of Govt. medical colleges are governed by varying 
service conditions, by and large, dependent on the financial health of the Institution.  As a result, 
although MCI Regulations specifically provide for Full-time medical teachers, there are different 
categories  of medical teachers – Full-time, Honorary, teachers on contract, teachers entitled to private 
practice.   Salary  and other incentives payable to a  Govt. medical  teacher also vary from state to state.  
There are states where inter-change between teaching and non-teaching cadre is permissible,  other 
states are there where  district identity of teaching cadre is being maintained.   Besides that, Govt. 
medical college teachers  are also liable  to be transferred within the state.   Another problem pointed out 
is that these teachers are   under dual control – State Health Department and Directorate of  Medical 
Education. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  
18.2     During the course of its deliberations, the issue for having an Indian Medical Service on the lines 
of IAS/IPS was raised.   The Committee observes that although it is a welcome idea, there are some 
inherent problems which may arise later on.   First is the difference between  the nature of jobs.   
Medical Service is mostly research-oriented, teaching job whereas IAS/IPS   is administration based 
service.   Secondly, it may not be  feasible as regional interest are not likely to be served.   The 
Committee  would also like to point out that there were strong reservations about  transfer policy being 
followed in the States.   Feedback which  the Committee received during its study-visits was that 
teachers, by and large were not in favour of being transferred even within a  State.   Not only this,  
Health being a State subject, it will be very difficult to create such a cadre and its implementation would, 
therefore, be difficult for obvious reasons.   The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that this issue 
needs to be subjected to wide-scale discussions in the medical fraternity before taking any decision. 
ACTION TAKEN 
18.1&18.2       The suggestions of the Committee for placing the proposal for creation of Indian Medical 
Service for discussion among the medical fraternity will be taken into account for initiating such a 
discussion.

The Committee is  aware of the provision of Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, which lays down 
that any University having a medical faculty is entitled to send one member to the Council.   
However, the problem is that some Universities are still un-represented  in the Medical Council as 
they do not have a Senate in existence.   In view of this, the Committee recommends that sincere 
efforts be made for the constitution of Senate in such Universities so as to enable them to be  
represented in the Indian Medical Council.(Para No.3.5)  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

constraints of the government including that of the State Governments and with due regard to the 
judgments given by the apex court from time to time, the Committee feels that the process 
regarding admission needs to be made as fair as possible.  The role of money, whether it is in the 
form of the capitation fee or under the table or in any other form must come to an end.  It has to

CHAPTER  I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED 
BY THE GOVERNMENT 
PLANNED DEVELOPMENT – ROLE OF AICTE 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.4  The Committee is of the view that the Department and AICTE should make all conceivable efforts 
for encouraging both Govt. and private initiatives in setting up technical institutions in N-E region. 
Action Taken  
Setting up of institutes on self-financing basis by Trusts/Societies is being encouraged.  As of now, 
there are 26 polytechnics, 8 Engg colleges, 7 Management Colleges and 18 PG programmes in the 
North Eastern Region. During 2001-2002, out of 3 applications received for setting up of Diploma 
Level, 2 were approved; 1 application received for degree could not be approved as it did not meet 
norms and standards. Also, during 2001-2002, 3 PG programmes were considered and approved. 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.11     It has been further informed that in April, 2000, AICTE had written to each State Government to 
prepare a perspective plan for developing technical education in the state and for qualitative 
improvement of technical education.    However, none of the States has given any perspective plan for 
development of technical education and the Council has so far not been provided with any feedback 
from the State Govts. regarding the quality of technical education, manpower requirement, employment 
opportunities etc.   The Committee is of the view that AICTE should impress upon the State Govts. to 
furnish the required information at the earliest.  
Action Taken  
Noted for compliance. 
INCONSISTENCIES IN DIFFERENT PROCEDURES AND NORMS – REMEDIAL SUGGESTIONS 
THEREFOR 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.2       The Committee was informed that in spite of academic eligibility prescribed by AICTE for 
Degree and Diploma  level courses, different States follow different academic eligibility criteria 
and there is no uniformity in the minimum cut off percentage which creates confusion.  During  its 
study visit to Chennai, the Sub-Committee was informed that in Tamil Nadu a minimum of 60% 
in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry individually and an aggregate of 70% at the 10+2 level is 
considered as entry criteria into the Professional courses.   However, in other States like 
Karnataka, Kerala,  Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and UT of Pondicherry, they require a pass 
percentage of  50 % .   Due to this differential eligibility criteria and other reasons, nearly 20,000 
seats  in Tamil Nadu remained unfilled this year.  The Committee strongly feels that there should 
be  uniformity at all India level for selection/eligibility criteria for admission in different technical 
education courses as far as possible.   The Committee, therefore, recommends  that the 
Department  and AICTE, alongwith State Governments, should work out common modalities in 
this regard. 
Action Taken  
In order to ensure uniformity at the all- India level for selection / eligibility for technical 
institutions in the country, AICTE had framed regulations in 1994;  Norms and Guidelines for 
Fees and Guidelines for Admissions in Professional Colleges Regulation, 1994”. Most of the States 
conduct a common entrance examination for admission, and they are following the requirements 
of the AICTE guidelines.  From the academic year 2002-2003, a Common Entrance Test for 
admission in engineering colleges (AIEEE) has been introduced. More and more higher technical 
colleges, in consultation with the State Governments, will be included in the entrance examination 
in the near future.  AICTE is also in the process of evolving mechanism for conduct of a common 
Page 4 of 19134thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report134th.htm

entrance examination for MBA and MCA courses. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.3       The Committee's attention was drawn to the practice of different Universities in the country 
awarding degrees under different nomenclature and resultant difficulty in establishing their equivalence.  
A suggestion was, therefore, made that AICTE should publish a list of such degrees with their 
equivalence to Degree in Engineering, PG Degree in Engineering and Diploma in Engineering  which 
should be given wide publicity.   
Action Taken  
AICTE has communicated the approved nomenclature of Bachelors degree in Engineering & 
Technology, Pharmacy, Architecture, Diploma programmes, PG programmes and Ph.D programmes to 
all the Universities. This information is also included in the application forms for starting new technical 
institutions as well as the AICTE handbook for approval of courses.   
Observations/Recommendations  
The Committee is also surprised to note that discrepancy is also there in respect of career 
advancement for the faculty members of Engineering Colleges and Polytechnics.  Latest circular 
of AICTE recommending the new Pay Scales states that a Lecturer requires eleven years service 
to get the selection grade without improving any qualification, whereas a Lecturer in Diploma 
level institution requires a higher qualification, i.e. Master’s Degree in Engineering in order to 
become eligible for selection grade.  In other words, teachers who are teaching the diploma 
programme need higher qualifications as compared to teachers who are teaching the students in 
the Degree Colleges. 
Action Taken  
A review of the Career Advancement Scheme will be taken up and discrepancy, if any, will be sorted 
out. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.8       The Committee was also apprised that there was no uniformity in the admission schedules of 
different States.  As a result,  students face difficulty while seeking admission in  different states.   Not 
only this,  at present different  admission tests are conducted on different dates for admission to various 
technical institutions in the country.   Sometimes,  it is observed that various  entrance test dates clash 
creating problems for the candidates and also putting  a lot of financial burden on their parents.   In this 
context, it was suggested that a uniform/common entrance test may be held for students seeking 
admission to different institutions on All India basis. Another suggestion made was that only one 
combined entrance test for one stream of technical education may be conducted at All India level.   
3.9       The Committee, in this context, was informed that in the IIT, JEE, already IT-BHU and ISM-
Dhanbad are participating in addition to the IITs.  The ambit of IIT-JEE is being expanded from the year 
2002 to include three other premier national level institutions (NIFFI, IITT, IITM) that have been 
conducting their separate tests.  The Committee was also  informed that the  Government is planning to 
hold an All India Engineering Entrance Examination (AIEEE) for admission to undergraduate 
programmes in Engineering which will cover all Centrally funded technical institutions, including 
Deemed Universities in the field of technical education.  All other institutions in the States that agree to 
participate in this test may be included and gradually the Examination will be extended to all technical 
institutions in the country.  The Committee hopes that  more and more States would participate in the 
Test and the Test may be conducted at the earliest, preferably from 2002-2003 academic session.  
Action Taken  
            AIEEE has been started from the academic year 2002-03.  It is expected that more and 
more States/Institutions will participate in the coming years. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.10     As per Section 10 of AICTE Act, which defines Powers and Functions of the Council, there are 
varied functions to be discharged by AICTE.   However, it has been observed that AICTE basically 
keeps itself engrossed  with the function under section  10 (k) i.e. grant of approval for starting new 
technical institutions  and for introduction of new courses or programmes in consultation with the 
Page 5 of 19134thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report134th.htm

agencies concerned.   However, other equally important functions like undertaking surveys, coordinating 
for development of technical education in the country, promoting innovations, research and 
development, formulating schemes for promoting technical education for women, handicapped and 
weaker sections of society  have been neglected.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that AICTE 
should not restrict its activities to granting approval or fixing norms, formulating guidelines for fees etc. 
but it should discharge its other functions as well which are necessary for proper, coordinated and 
qualitative improvement of technical education in the country as prescribed in the AICTE Act.     
Action Taken  
AICTE is giving due importance to other activities of technical education such as Research and 
Institutional Development Schemes / Projects, Faculty Development Schemes / Projects and 
improvement of quality of education through Accreditation of programmes. Reviews of the existing 
schemes have been initiated and on the basis of these reviews, the recommended existing activities will 
be strengthened further, and new activities will be initiated. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.21     The Committee was further informed that accreditation has been made mandatory for all 
institutions from which at least two batches have passed out.   The grades awarded are put on web 
site of AICTE.  Steps have also been taken to caution the general public regarding the quality of 
grades assigned by the National Board of Accreditation through various other modes of 
awareness.   The Committee is of the considered view that accreditation and gradation of 
institutions should be given more coverage and wider area of operation so that general public are 
aware of the status of the institutions before they apply for it. 
Action Taken  
AICTE publishes the results of accreditation of programs of the various technical institutions in a 
Directory. This information is also available at NBA Website (www.nba-aicte.org) and AICTE Website 
(www.aicte.ernet.in). The Council has published in national newspapers information about the nature 
and scope of accreditation as an indication of Quality Assurance for the benefit of prospective students 
and parents. The Council is also bringing out posters for disseminating this information. 
TEACHERS 
Observation/Recommendation  
5.4       The Committee has also been given to understand that possibility of relaxing the Ph.D. 
qualification for Asstt.   Professor level, if there is evidence of quality R&D and Industry work is there, 
can be explored.    Inviting industry/ R&D personnel of Public/Private Sector as guest lecturers  and 
permitting personal consultancy were the other suggestions put forth  for solving the problem of faculty 
shortage.   The Committee recommends that feasibility of these suggestions should be reviewed and 
decision taken accordingly.   
Action Taken  
As per the existing AICTE regulations, candidates with Ph.D are eligible for appointment as Assistant 
Professor. However, considering the severe shortage of Ph.Ds in Technical Education, the concerned 
Boards are examining the possibility of relaxing Ph.D., if there is evidence of quality R&D activity.  
This measure is to be taken for a limited period till adequate number of Ph.Ds are available. Several 
technical institutions also invite personnel from industry and R&D institutions as visiting faculty. 
AUTONOMY 
Observation/Recommendation  
7.2       There is no denying the fact that granting autonomy will go a long way in accomplishing self-
reliance and would encourage healthy competition.  The Committee, however, feels that granting 
autonomy without judging the capability of institutions will degrade the quality of education.  Only such 
institutions which have proper track record and committed to quality should be given autonomy.    The 
Committee would, therefore, like to emphasize that autonomy should be given only to selected 
institutions that have consistently maintained excellent performance in the recent past. 
Action Taken  
Grant of autonom
y for technical institutions is  given as per set guidelines of AICTE Autonomy is 
Page 6 of 19134thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report134th.htm

accorded only to institutions possessing adequate infrastructure and competent faculty which are 
assessed through accreditation of the programmes and expert committee visits. 
TECHNICAL UNIVERSITY  
Observation/Recommendation  
10  The need for establishing a Technical University in each State under which all technical institutions 
in the State are affiliated  has been much talked about during the visits of the Sub-Committee.   The 
Committee finds that  some States have taken up the initiative for establishing  Technical Universities.  
As a result, some of the major concerns such as delay in admission, delay in  the beginning of academic 
session,  reduction in number of academic days required for a semester, non-uniformity in basic 
structure of  curriculum etc. have been alleviated.   The Committee,  therefore, recommends, that with 
the vast expansion of technical education in different States, the possibility of setting up of Technical 
Universities in every State or group of states may be examined by the Government.  However, it should 
be ensured that such universities are managed by experts in the field of technical education, so that 
professional approach of the management may help the university for proper growth of technical 
education and monitoring of technical institutions in the State.   
Action Taken  
            Technical Universities have been set up in several States in the country. They are headed by 
Vice-Chancellors who are eminent persons and experts in the field of technical education. 
FUNDING  
Observation/Recommendation  
The Committee feels that shortage of funds could be tackled through generation of resources by 
the Institutions themselves.   This could be done through Industry Institute contacts, generation of 
technology for the Industry, renting the labs, Consultancy and encouraging the alumni  who are 
abroad and are in a position to contribute towards growth of technical education in the Country.  
The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that Govt. has also to simultaneously continue 
funding technical education with increased allocation wherever feasible.  The Committee would 
like to point out that availability of infrastructure in most of the States needs substantial 
improvement.  Govt. may take some initiative in this regard specially in view of poor financial 
condition of majority of the State Governments.  
 Action Taken  
In the accreditation criteria, the National Board of Accreditation (NBA) has given importance to 
Industry sponsored research, continuing education and consultancy as important ingredients of 
institutional activities. It is observed that several institutions have initiated progress in all these areas as 
a result of NBA requirement. AICTE provides funding under the schemes of MODROBS, TAPTEC & 
R&D schemes for institutions on the basis of proposals made by them for improvement and 
modernization of infrastructure and promotion of R&D. 
CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
PLANNED DEVELOPMENT- ROLE OF AICTE 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.8       The Committee also observes that  with the ongoing recession in industry, demand for IT has 
shown a declining trend.  Quite a few  sanctioned  seats in IT and Computer Science are remaining 
vacant.  The Committee, therefore,  strongly feels that for a balanced development there should be a 
planned and coordinated development of every branch of technical education. Courses in core areas like 
Civil/Electrical Engineering etc are required to be continued and updated by introducing specialization 
in keeping with the changing technological scenario.  The Committee is of the opinion that while 
starting  Information  Technology and related courses, the requirements of various States need to be kept 
in view so as to remove regional imbalances and disparity. 
Action Taken 
Page 7 of 19134thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report134th.htm

The demand for particular courses of technical education mainly depends on the employment 
opportunities available in the States in respect of a particular branch of technical education. 
However, in the Regional Committee meetings, effort is made to point out to the State 
Government representatives that every branch should be given adequate consideration. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.17     During its study visits, the Committee was given to understand that a number of  schemes, such 
as Modernisation and Removal of Obsolescence (MODROB), Research and Development (R&D), 
Thrust Area Programme in Technical Education (TAPTEC) etc.  operate under AICTE through which 
financial assistance is provided to technical institutions.   However,  many of the Govt. as well as self-
financing institutions were  unaware of such schemes and consequently failed  to reap the benefits of 
such schemes.  On a specific query, the Council clarified that all possible attempts to give publicity to 
various Schemes of Staff Development,  Institutional Development, Research and Development through 
national and local newspapers,  AICTE  website and also through individual correspondence with the 
States, Universities and institutions are being made.  Every year, more than 40 to 50 crores of rupees are 
being spent under these schemes.   The Committee feels that AICTE should prepare a composite list of 
financial assistance schemes under separate heads such as Schemes for staff Development, Institutional 
Development, Research and Development and send it to various Institution directly.   In that way, it 
would give wider publicity to such schemes than what is practised now.  
Action Taken  
Information relating to the scope of schemes and the procedures for making applications by institutions 
is already in vogue.  In addition, advertisements are placed in national and local dailies (Hindi & 
English). Copies of booklets of the various schemes are available at the seven Regional Offices and 
information on these schemes are posted in the AICTE Website. This year the Council has prepared 
posters summarizing the salient features of the RID schemes and has despatched to the Technical 
Institutions in various States. 
BRAIN DRAIN  
Observation/Recommendation  
8.2       The Committee has been given to understand that better pay package, career advancement, 
conducive work environment, freedom to work to one’s full potential, job satisfaction and security may 
help curbing brain drain.    Another suggestion made  to the Committee was that it should be made 
compulsory for a Graduate /Post Graduate of technical education  to serve in India for a minimum  
period before going abroad.   In the event of his going abroad permanently,  he should be made to refund 
the amount spent on his education.   The Committee is of the opinion that work environment in  the 
country needs to be improved so that our students find it lucrative to be in their jobs in the country.  
Besides, gainful opportunities need to be  created in the country itself to reverse the brain drain.  The 
Committee feels that if necessary, students may be asked to pay back in easy instalments wherever Govt. 
funding is there.  Modalities in this regard may be explored. 
Action Taken  
Because of the liberalisation and global scenario, job markets have widened.  There are lots of 
opportunities available to the professionals.  The concept of brain drain has also changed. Many 
professionals get training or work abroad and come back to the country after some years of service.   
CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE 
GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
PLANNED  DEVELOPMENT – ROLE OF AICTE 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.4       The Committee in this context is of the view that for proper growth of technical education, focus 
of the Department and AICTE should be on proper planning and coordinated development.   
Concentration in certain pockets has already given  rise to regional imbalance.   Therefore, focus should 
be on the country as a whole.     
Page 8 of 19134thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report134th.htm

Action Taken 
The AICTE invites applications from all over the country through advertisements in national and 
regional dailies and also through its Website for establishment of new Technical Institutes and for 
introduction of new courses. It is for the concerned State Government to keep in view the requirements 
of different regions within the State while recommending such proposals to AICTE for its approval.  All 
the State Governments have been requested by AICTE to prepare perspective plans for planning of 
technical education in the respective State.  AICTE is proposing to hold National Consultation (NC)  
involving representatives from State Governments, Universities and also academicians of repute in order 
to discuss several issues relating to the planning of future growth of technical education in the country 
including issues of quality and regional imbalance.   Large number of self-financing private institutes 
were established mainly in the States of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh and 
thus there has been higher concentration of Technical Institution in these States as compared to the 
States in other regions, particularly in Eastern and Northern Regions.  AICTE is aware of such 
imbalances and is encouraging setting up of new Institutes in those regions having lesser number of 
Institutes so as to achieve a balanced growth. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee feels that the proper planning and coordinated development of technical 
education in the country leave much to be desired.    
Observation/Recommendation  
2.5       Another disturbing development as a result of concentration of technical institutions in a few 
states is that intake capacity in different streams of technical institutions is not being utilised fully.   
There are reports that a very large number of seats remain vacant every year.    In most of the States, 
admission is made through a common entrance test conducted by the State Govt.    On a specific query 
about the number of seats filled up during the last three years in the States of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, 
Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra, the Committee has been informed that data on vacant seats is not 
made available to the Council.   Hence, it is not possible to analyse the details in this regard.   
Expressing its serious concern on such a situation, the Committee would like to point out that an 
objective analysis of intake capacity and vacancy position in these States is very much required for 
checking mushroom growth of technical institutions. 
Action Taken  
An analysis on intake capacity and vacant seats during 2001-2002 in the States of Karnataka, Tamil 
Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra has been made and the position is as under:- 
  
  
State                           Total Seats       Seats  Vacant               % of    Seats Vacant 
  
Tamil Nadu                 48887              11583                  23% 
Andhra Pradesh            46147              493                     2%

In the ensuing meeting of the National Consultation, the issues will be discussed for eliciting views of 
the State Governments to take corrective measures. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            The Committee notes with concern that during 2001-2002, a large number of seats remained 
vacant, particularly in the States of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Maharashtra, thus giving  an indication 
that the seats were approved without properly examining the requirements of the States.   The 
Committee observes that there is need to take suitable remedial measures in this regard. 
INCONSISTENCIES IN DIFFERENT PROCEDURES AND NORMS – REMEDIAL 
SUGGESTIONS THEREFOR 
Observation/Recommendation  
The Committee has also been given to understand that  there is a lot of discrepancy in  AICTE norms 
Page 9 of 19134thReportofHRD
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/Report134th.htm

and standards in respect of educational qualifications  prescribed for various faculty positions in 
Engineering, Architecture, Pharmacy and Polytechnics.  It was informed to the Committee that a 
Lecturer in the Engineering College needs 1st class Bachelor’s Degree whereas a Lecturer in Pharmacy 
College & Architecture College needs 1st Class Master’s Degree in the same pay scale. 
 Action Taken 
The qualifications prescribed for Pharmacy and Architecture degree level institutions are based on the 
recommendations of the Board of Pharmacy Education and Board of Architecture Education. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
            The Committee feels that anomalies should be removed to the extent they place students of 
these disciplines at disadvantage.   There should be a level playing field in this regard.   
Observation/Recommendation   
3.22     It has been reported that many universities are not periodically updating curricula for  
different streams of technical education.   As a result,  curricula used for imparting training are 
not in tune with the requirements of industry.  The Committee notes that the Council does not 
have any mandate to revise the curricula which is the responsibility of respective universities 
which affiliate technical institutions.  The Committee is however, given to understand that Council 
has endeavoured to prescribe a model curriculum in various major branches of engineering, 
pharmacy, computer applications etc.   The Committee is of the view that  updated curricula in 
tune with the present  global scenario is the very basis for maintaining the required standard of  
all streams of technical education.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that a joint 
mechanism for periodical updating of curricula for different streams of technical education  
consisting of representatives of universities, State Boards of Technical Education, AICTE and 
industry needs to be evolved.   
Action Taken 
AICTE has been preparing model curricula for various programs / courses for technical education. 
These curricula have been prepared by Working Groups which included industry experts and have been 
coordinated largely by QIP centres. Many of these curricula have been updated by a panel of experts 
which include industry  professionals and academicians. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
            The Committee is aware that AICTE prepares model curricula for various 
programmes/courses of technical education.    However, it is of the view that this is not serving the 
desired objective as the universities affiliating various technical institutions are free to either 
adopt them or reject them.   This is why, the Committee had earlier recommended that a joint 
mechanism consisting of representatives of universities, State Boards of Technical Education, 
AICTE and Industry needs to be evolved for preparing/updating the curricula as per the changing 
requirement, which can be suitable to all concerned.   
Observation/Recommendation  
3.24     The Council further clarified that at the time of granting approval, the intimation is also 
given to the respective states and the affiliating University for ensuring the adherence to the 
norms and standards as set by the Council.   The Committee is of the view that requisite norms 
and standards are not being scrupulously adhered to on the part of the concerned authorities.  It, 
therefore, recommends strict adherence to the prescribed norms and standard.   
Action Taken  
Adherence to the prescribed norms and standards is monitored through visits of expert committee 
for extension of approval at regular intervals. Shortcoming/ discrepancies/ non-compliance of 
Norms and Standards noticed are brought to the notice of the institutes concerned for 
remedial/corrective action. Punitive action is taken including 'no admissions' and 'reduced intake' 
in case of non-compliance. 
Comments of the Committee 
            The Committee observes that the question of overseeing the entire process of entrance 
examinations to technical institutions is very important and crucial for students.   While AICTE

must take steps to ensure, by bringing more and more institutions in its ambit or otherwise, that 
no inconvenience  is caused to the students by clash of examination dates, costly and time 
consuming procedures, inconvenient and distant located examination centres etc. 
            At the same time AICTE must keep in view that not more than 20% of students are able to 
reach the university level of education.   It is, therefore, imperative that the system of education 
from the secondary level or even earlier must have ingredients in its syllabus that minimum 
reliance is placed on white-collar   jobs.    The syllabus should have vocational content so much so 
that after completing secondary education one must be able to reach the top levels in technical 
education though I.I.Ts., I.T.Is.  and such other institutions.    At the same time the aim should be 
to provide technical education and that too at the Government cost to all those who want to 
pursue this. 
TEACHERS 
Observation/Recommendation  
5.3       The Committee notes that through the Early Faculty Induction Programme, an amount of Rs. 
10,000 is provided as scholarship from Eighth Semester onwards to B. Tech students who are selected 
through a National Level screening.   1100 qualified, trained and committed  faculty members for 
technical education was the target fixed by AICTE by the end of Ninth Five Year Plan.   The Committee 
is, however, constrained to observe that this programme could be launched only in 1999-2000 due to 
non-availability of the approval of the Central Govt. 30, 92 and 40 students joined the programme 
during the years 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 respectively against 300 available scholarships 
provided by AICTE.   The Committee is of the view that wide publicity should be given to such 
programmes so as to attract student community towards teaching.    The Committee is perturbed to note 
that separate  budget is yet to be sanctioned for this Programme by the Central Govt.  Taking strong 
objection to such uncalled for delay, the Committee emphasizes that the needful should be done at the 
earliest.   The Committee also hopes that recommendations of the Committee on Post Graduate 
Education and Research in Engineering and Technology for doubling of annual out- turn of various 
programmes in PG courses in Engineering and Technology will be implemented at the earliest. 
Action Taken  
Based on the Report of the AICTE PG Review Committee, MHRD issued policy framework on PG 
Education and Research in Engineering & Technology. Accordingly, AICTE has issued notifications in 
the national newspapers on the increase of duration from 18 months to 24  months for all M Tech / M 
Pharm / M. Arch programmes as well as increase in the stipend from Rs. 2500 to Rs. 5000 beginning 
from academic year 2002-2003. 
AICTE has also set up a working group for preparing action plan for implementation of the other 
recommendations of the Committee. 
Comments of the Committee  
            The Committee notes the position and awaits further development.

the conducting and evaluation of training programmes.   The Committee feels that feasibility of 
attaching technical institutions with nearby industries  also needs to be explored.

Several schemes such as Industry-Institute Partnership Cell, National Facilities in Engineering and

PLANNED  DEVELOPMENT – ROLE OF AICTE 
Observation/Recommendation  
2.1  The Committee, after undertaking extensive field visits and discussing the status of technical 
education in the country with various experts in the field, is of the considered opinion that AICTE has 
failed to accomplish the mandate given to it under the Act.   The Committee has found that there is no 
proper planning, proper assessment of technical manpower, balanced development, coordinated 
approach, and quality maintenance regarding technical education.    
Observation/Recommendation  
2.9       Committee's attention has also been drawn to a recent decision of the Apex Court (Bharatidasan 
University vs AICTE and Others) which indicates that the Universities are not obliged to seek prior 
permission of AICTE to introduce any technical courses in their departments and constituent colleges.   
The Apex Court has further decided that the role of AICTE with respect to Universities imparting 
technical education is recommendatory in nature.   The Committee has been given to understand that 
this decision would lead to different norms for Universities and other Technical institutions, different 
quality parameters and, therefore, different standards of education which would eventually result in 
lopsided development of technical education.   The Committee feels that implications of the aforesaid 
judgement may be studied in their entirety and remedial steps, if required, may be initiated. 
Action Taken 
An Expert Committee has been set up to review the situation arising out of the decision of the apex court 
in this regard.   Based on the recommendations, remedial measures will be taken. 
Observation/Recommendation

2.10     The Committee is of the view that for planned development of technical education, accurate data 
regarding demand and supply of technical manpower is necessary.  As per Section 10 (a) of AICTE Act, 
the Council is empowered to undertake survey in various fields of technical education, collect data on all 
related matters and make forecast of the needed growth and development in technical education.  The 
Council has initiated a scheme for collecting data and forecasting the demand and supply of technical 
manpower in the country through National Technical Manpower Information System (NTMIS) which 
has established various nodal centres in the country.   The findings  of NTMIS are made available to the 
user agencies including State Governments.    The Committee is, however, constrained to note that at 
present NTMIS is not being effectively made use of  which  has  led to uncontrolled and imbalanced 
growth of technical institutions, many of them being sub-standard.

SUGGESTIONS THEREFOR 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.4       The Committee observes that  various Technical Institutes/Boards  award degrees in technical 
education.  It becomes difficult to establish the equivalence of such degrees for the purpose of admission 
and also for the purpose of recruitment.  It was suggested that a State Council of Technical Education be 
set- up in all the States of the country and the Engineers who qualify in various examinations should get 
registered with SCTE for the purpose of admission to Technical Institution for acquiring higher 
qualification as well as for the purpose of recruitment.  The practice which is followed by Medical 
Council of India (MCI), Council of Architecture and Pharmacy Council of India may be made 
applicable to the engineering graduates and Diploma holders. 
Action Taken 
Action may be taken only after discussion with the States.  The matter will be taken up in the National 
Consultation meeting. 
Observation/Recommendation 
3.11     The Sub-Committee, during its interaction with various experts, got an impression that AICTE 
has become highly centralised and there is need for decentralisation of its powers among its regional 
offices.  The Committee also feels that Regional Offices of AICTE  need to be strengthened by 
delegating more powers by the Head Office to avoid delay and for effective and smooth functioning of 
the Regional Offices.  However, it would like to point out that delegation of powers to the Regional 
Offices may be done only after sanction of permanent staff for the Council and its Regional Offices.  
The Committee would also like to point out that in view of tremendous increase in the number of 
technical institutions in the Country  in the recent years, required strength of staff should be sanctioned 
for Regional Offices.   
Action Taken 
AICTE has delegated the responsibility of approving Diploma Level Institutions to the concerned State 
Govts. On the basis of study by the Staff Inspection Unit (SIU), requirement of staff in Regional Offices 
will be determined. 
Observation/Recommendation  
3.12     The Sub-Committee  during its field visits after interacting with different functionaries gathered  
that the present norm of 5 acres land in metropolitan cities and 25 acres in rural areas for establishing an 
Engineering College does not seem to be practical.  In a Metropolitan City  like Mumbai it is very 
difficult to get the required land.  Even in rural areas, due to land ceiling, difficulties were being faced.  
It was suggested that the requirement of land at different places should be realistic.  In metropolitan 
cities,  where land is too scarce, vertical construction could be thought of which would require lesser 
land.    
Action Taken 
AICTE had constituted a EC Sub-Committee for review of norms and standards.  The report of this 
committee is now under consideration by the concerned All India Board’s (AIBs) and Regional 
Committees. The requirement of land in metropolitan cities is among  various issues considered by the 
Committee.  On submission of Report, the Ministry shall examine it for further necessary action.

PREFACE 
  
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Hundred Thirty Fifth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand 
No.46) of the Department of Health,  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2003-2004. 
  
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the 
Department of Health and also heard the Secretary and other officials of that Department on the said 
Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 26th March, 2003. 
  
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on  
22nd April, 2003. 
  
REPORT 
I           INTRODUCTION 
            The      Ministry of Health & Family welfare consists of three Departments viz. Department of 
Health, Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy and Department of Family 
Welfare. 
            The Department of Health deals with medical and public health matters including drugs control 
and prevention of food adulteration.  It is headed by a Secretary to the Government of India who is 
supported by two Additional Secretaries. The Department has an attached office i.e. Directorate General 
of Health Services. The DGHS renders technical advice on all medical and public health matters and is 
involved in the implementation of various health schemes.  
            The Central Government has the sole executive responsibility in respect of subjects included in 
the Union List such as port quarantine including hospitals connected therewith. In regard to items 
included in the State List, such as Public Health, Hospitals and Dispensaries, the Central Govt's direct 
responsibility is restricted to UTs without legislature and providing  enabling framework for 
development of infrastructures in respect of matter falling under the Concurrent List. 
            The Central Govt.  evolves broad policies and plans through the Central Council of Health, set 
up under Article 263 of the Constitution, arranges for collection and exchange of information and 
renders financial and technical assistance to State Govts., UT Administration and other bodies for the 
implementation of important health programmes and various centrally sponsored schemes, including 
control of epidemics throughout     the country. 
Main objectives of the Department of Health are : 
to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention, control and 
eradication of communicable diseases; 
to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the medical 
colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas; 
to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs; 
to provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people and to train the required number of 
personnel for this purpose; 
to take steps for better implementation of Health Care Programmes for tribal and other weaker sections 
of the Society; and 
to collaborate with member countries of United Nations and International Agencies like WHO, UNICEF 
in matters relating to health promotion.

The Department of Health incurs expenditure either directly or through various institutions and
