IX.            DISTRICT  PRIMARY  EDUCATION  PROGRAMME  (DPEP)
Recommendation/Observation
9.8       The Committee is perturbed over the drop out rates and recommends that in order to check such a tendency the
Department should try to involve the parents/guardians of the children in school in the gainful employment under JRY
and other similar schemes. The assurance of employment under different employment schemes to a family member of
those who are in school would be an incentive for the people to send their children to the schools. The Committee is also
surprised that even after three years of the above survey, the Department has not yet come out with the final diagnosis of
the reasons for high dropout rate and its remedial prescriptions.
Action Taken
9.8       The DPEP is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme in which 85% project cost is met by the Government of India and
the concerned State Government shares the remaining 15%. The Government of India share is sourced through external
agencies like EC, DFID, UNICEF and the Government of Netherlands. The Programme objectives of DPEP do not
envisage providing employment to parents/guardians of the children in project schools. However, as a step against
reducing high drop out rate among children, the community is being increasingly involved in providing land for schools,

144th Report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/144threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:21]
running of the schools, etc. The contribution made by the community towards school improvement in several States has
been remarkable. In addition to academic activities, non-academic activities have also been planned for
parents/guardians, Gram Panchayats, etc. With the increased community participation in the building and running of
schools, it is expected that the drop out rate would come down in the coming years.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee appreciates the concept of community participation but it would like to emphasise that the idea
of community having a stake in the school improvement may not be enough. Such an idea presupposes that drop-out
among children is the result of non-participation of the local community. Problem of drop-out in fact is a multi-
dimensional one, which therefore, has to tackled by adopting a multi-pronged strategy. The Committee feels that such a
holistic approach to this problem is yet to be chalked out.
Recommendation/Observation
9.9       The Committee also takes note of the fact that about 1,77,000 teachers, including para-teachers/shiksha karmis
are involved in teaching activities. The Committee believes that such teachers do not fit in the pedagogical calculus of a
great education system. The committee would like that these para-teachers/Shiksha karmis should be given necessary
training by Teachers Training Institutes before they make forays into the novel and pristine field of teaching the young
minds.
Action Taken
9.9       Para-teachers are being appointed by the States on a large scale to bring down the adverse pupil-teacher ratio and
to provide teachers in remote inaccessible areas. Training courses for such teachers have to be of longer duration and
more intensive. Under the DPEP Programme, teachers training has improved both quantitatively and qualitatively.
During the year 2002-03, 2 million teachers and 3 million community members were trained.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been informed by various experts from the field of education that the concept of the para
teachers was not working well as these teachers do not have any training or experience in teaching as well as child
learning methods. They do not take their work seriously. While the Committee appreciates the idea behind this scheme,
it also has apprehension about the quality of teaching by such underpaid and untrained teachers. The Committee
recommends that serious efforts be made for training these teachers appropriately.
X.            ADULT  EDUCATION
Recommendation/Observation
10.7     The Committee, while appreciating the progress made towards literacy, also expresses its serious concern over
the functioning of various schemes of Adult Education. At the end of Ninth Plan, NLM was expected to achieve around
70% literacy but as per census 2001, literacy rate is 65.38%. The Committee notes with dismay the cut in allocation in
the Ninth Plan outlay in priority schemes of adult education viz., Literacy Campaign and Operation Restoration have
been reduced to Rs. 32.00 crore from 140.00 crore. Even this allocation has been underutilized by 26 per cent. However,
for continuing Education for Neo-literates, there was an increase in the allocation of Rs. 261.57 crore from Rs. 229.39
crore. However, the funds under the scheme remained unutilized to the extent of 11 per cent. The Committee takes these
under-utilizations seriously and feel that these under-utilizations have come in the way of attainment of 70 per cent
literacy by the end of Ninth Plan. The Committee hopes that the Department would make concerted efforts for optimum
utilization of allocated funds under the various components/projects of Adult Education Programme.
Action Taken
10.7     As per the National Sample Survey Organization survey, Organization survey, the literacy rate was 62% at the
beginning of the Ninth Plan. At that time, the projected rate of growth was 1.5% per year. It was accordingly estimated
that at the end of the Ninth Plan, the projected achievement of NLM would be around 70%. However, as per Census
2001, the literacy rate increased to 65.38% as against 52.21% in 1991. During the Tenth Plan, the goal of National
Literacy Mission is to attain a sustainable threshold literacy level of 75% by 2007.
            The funds earmarked under various Schemes of Adult Education could not be fully utilized during the Ninth

144th Report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/144threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:21]
Plan due to various reasons, such as non-submission and audited accounts and utilization certificates of the earlier
grants, non-receipt of viable proposals, etc. Efforts are being made to ensure that the allocation made under the various
schemes is optimally utilized so that the goal of NLM could be achieved. To ensure effective utilization of the grants,
periodic review meetings are being held by Secretary (Elementary Education and Literacy) and DG (NLM) with the
States. The Area Officers also visit the States to monitor the implementation of the various programmes. The position
relating to utilization of funds has improved during the last two years. In the year 2001-02, as against the budget
allocation of Rs. 200.00 crores, an expenditure of Rs. 173.66 crores (86.83%) was incurred. Similarly, in 2002-03, as
against the budget allocation of Rs. 233.00 crores, an expenditure of Rs. 216.29 crores (92.84%) was incurred. The
expenditure in 2002-03 would have been higher but for the earmarking of 10% funds for North-East and suitable
additional schemes for North-East were not available in the year. In 2003-04, schemes would be formulated to spend
10% funds for the North-East.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes a gradual improvement in respect of utilization of funds under this scheme. It, however,
feels that increase in the rate of literacy remained so slow as it was 65.38% against the target of 70% during the Ninth
Plan. For Tenth Plan period this target has still been fixed at 75%. The Committee is of the opinion that unless all out
efforts were made to take NLM scheme as a movement, it would be very difficult to achieve the target.

to create infrastructure for this programme. The Committee feels that the Department laying the blame on to the States
can hardly be justified. It is of the opinion that the Department should make all out efforts to convince and persuade the
States that they will have to deliver. The Committee is strongly of the opinion that a carrot and stick policy be adopted
to convince/motivate the States and its officials. Further, roping in of local people, NGOs, teacher can be thought of in
case of indifferent response to State Government.            (Para 6.6 and 6.7)
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes the position; but it feels that basic conditions for the success of the scheme like proper
recruitment/deployment policy, facilitating linkages of DIETs with schools, etc. put the entire exercise back to square
one as these very pre-requisites have been found to be the stumbling block to an effective utilization of funds as well as
to an effective teacher's education. this aspect needs to be considered by the Department.            (Para 6.8 and 6.9)
VII.            SUPPORT  TO  PRIMARY  EDUCATION  (MID-DAY-MEAL  SCHEME)
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes the reply and finds that despite a gradual increase in the off-take of foodgrains per cent
wise, the number of children getting the benefit has been declining since 
2000-01. The Committee is concerned with this decline and feels that the aim of Universalisation of Elementary
Education may get defeated, if the trend continues. Moreover, the Committee fails to understand that while the number
of children covered under the scheme has come down, the lifting of foodgrains has increased, though marginally.
Further, the Committee notices a decline in expenditure due to reduced overall budgetary allocation, which is bound to
affect the lifting of foodgrains and its distribution, thereby affecting the scheme adversely ultimately.(Para 7.4)
IX.            DISTRICT  PRIMARY  EDUCATION  PROGRAMME  (DPEP)
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee appreciates the concept of community participation but it would like to emphasise that the idea
of community having a stake in the school improvement may not be enough. Such an idea presupposes that drop-out
among children is the result of non-participation of the local community. Problem of drop-out in fact is a multi-
dimensional one, which therefore, has to tackled by adopting a multi-pronged strategy. The Committee feels that such a
holistic approach to this problem is yet to be chalked out.            (Para 9.8)
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been informed by various experts from the field of education that the concept of the para
teachers was not working well as these teachers do not have any training or experience in teaching as well as child
learning methods. They do not take their work seriously. While the Committee appreciates the idea behind this scheme,
it also has apprehension about the quality of teaching by such underpaid and untrained teachers. The Committee
recommends that serious efforts be made for training these teachers appropriately.            (Para 9.9)
X.            ADULT  EDUCATION

CHAPTER I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICHHAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
I           INTRODUCTION
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
1.2       The system of education in India has broadly been divided in two categories: elementary education and
secondary and higher education.  It has been observed over the years that new initiatives are being taken to strengthen
school education.  Programmes like National Open School (renamed National Institute of Open Schooling) are being
strengthened to reach out more and more children in distant areas. National Council of Educational Research and
Training is playing an active role in providing resource support in the areas of education research and training at school
level.  The Navodaya Vidyalayas have been set up with the objective of providing a progressive and forward-looking
school system in the rural areas.
 
Action Taken
 
1.2       The National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) provides opportunities for continuing education to those who
have missed opportunities to complete school and developmental education through courses and programmes of general,
life enrichment and vocational education from primary to pre-degree level.
 
            The enrolment at Secondary and Senior Secondary stage is approximately nine lakh.  With enrolment of such a
magnitude, the NIOS is operationalising the largest open schooling system in the World. The NIOS has a huge
infrastructure comprising five Departments at the Headquarters, ten Regional Centres and more than 2100 Study
Centres in various States of India.  Some Study Centres are located outside the country also, particularly in Canada,
Nepal and Middle East.
 
1.Some significant initiatives taken by NIOS are as follows:
Development of New Curricula and Self Learning Materials for Secondary stage keeping in view the provisos of the
National Curriculum Framework (2000).  The new curricula for Senior Secondary stage are being prepared.
NIOS took a bold initiative of starting Open Basic Education (OBE) programme for (i) children below 14 years and (ii)
adults above 14 years.  For implementation of OBE programme, the NIOS is partnering with NGOs and the Zila
Saksharta Samities (ZSSs) respectively.
           
 
3.         The NIOS is conducting the Child Labour Project in collaboration with (i) Union Ministry of Human Resource
Development and (ii) Union Ministry of Labour.
 
The NIOS has introduced about 60 Vocational Education Courses in major areas of Agriculture, Business and
Commerce, Engineering and Technology, Paramedical and Health, Applied Science and Social Services.  Some more
need based Vocational Education Courses are in the pipeline.
5.         The NIOS is developing reading materials for Life Enrichment Programmes (LEPs) such as (i) Bharatiya Culture
and Heritage, (ii) Education in Human Values, (iii) Peoples of India, (iv) Lives of Great Personalities of India, (v) Yog
and(vi) Performing Arts (Music, Dance, Painting).
6.         In order to make the NIOS Examinations more transparent, the NIOS switched over from home evaluation to
spot evaluation and complete computerization of processing of results.  The Question Papers and Marking Schemes are
placed on the Internet (websites www.nos.org and www.nios.ac.in) immediately after the examinations are over.  The

145th Report of HRD

examination results are also placed on Internet.  At the time of examinations, observers are appointed at the levels of (i)
Regional Directors of NIOS and (ii) the Chairman, NIOS.  The observers send their reports daily by FAX which are
studied and suitable actions are taken. Under the Open Schooling System, the NIOS has envisaged an innovative ICT
based On Demand Examination System (ODES).  ODES envisages to give freedom to learner, to appear in examination
in the subjects of his/her choice whenever he/she feels confident of taking examination.  ODES has been started at Open
Basic Education terminal stage (equivalent to class VIII) in some Accredited Agencies.  Steps are being taken to launch
ODES at the Secondary stage from the academic session 2003-04.  Besides the registration of candidates for NIOS
courses through the Accredited Institutions (Study Centres), NIOS has started direct registration of candidates for its
examinations at Secondary and Senior Secondary levels from the academic year 2001-02.
7.         The NIOS has been organizing orientation programmes for the training of open schooling personnel at regional
level.  In order to make the orientation/training programmes more effective, training packages are being prepared.  The
NIOS has set up an International Centre for Training in Open Schooling (ICTOS).  This Centre is soon going to start
Certificate and Diploma Courses in Open Schooling for personnel from India and from other countries in collaboration
with Commonwealth of Learning (COL) and UNESCO.  The training of officials from Swaziland, Bangladesh and
Namibia is on cards.
 
8.         In its endeavour to promote open schooling in the country, NIOS has been persuading the States to set up State
Open Schools (SOSs).   Nine States (Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh,
Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana) have already set up State Open Schools.  A State Centre for Open Schooling has been set
up in Himachal Pradesh.  A National Consortium for Open Schooling (NCOS) has been set up for promotion of Open
Schooling in India as also for discharging coordination and clearing house functions.  The Headquarter of NCOS is
located in NIOS.
 
            Negotiations are under way with more States (Orissa, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Jammu and Kashmir, Delhi etc.,)
for setting up State Open Schools (SOSs).
 
9.         In order to provide forums for exchange of ideas and information among various Commonwealth Countries, the
Open Schooling Association of Commonwealth (OSAC) has been set up.  NIOS acts as the Headquarter of OSAC. 
NIOS has started publishing, since November, 2001, the half-yearly “OSAC Journal of Open Schooling” of
international standard.
            In order to give fillip to the programme of international relations, the NIOS in collaboration with UNESCO-
BREDA and the Commonwealth of Learning (COL) organized an Advocacy Meet of Senior Decision Makers from
eleven African Countries (Bostwana, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, Somalia, Swaziland, Tanzania,
Uganda, Zimbabwe) from 9
th to 13th September, 2002.  Besides detailed interaction with NIOS faculty members on
matters such as development of relevant and need based curricula and self-learning materials, modes of programme
delivery, teaching-learning strategies, training of personnel, methods of pupil evaluation and certification, life
enrichment programmes and innovative programmes like ICT based ‘On Demand Examination System’(ODES), the
delegates from the above mentioned countries prepared Draft Frameworks for Promotion of Open Schooling in their
respective countries.  A Memorandum of collaboration was also signed between NIOS and UNESCO-BREDA to
support development of open and distance learning at all levels of education and training in Sub-Saharan Africa.
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
2.3       In absence of any authoritative figures the Committee has taken the total outlay (plan and non plan) of Rs.4749
crores and maximum number of students who registered themselves for 2002 examinations i.e. 530401.  The total outlay
per head comes to Rs.9345 half of which is non-plan expenditure.  The Plan expenditure per student is thus Rs.4500/-
approximately which includes expenditure on creation of infrastructure, peripheral or administrative expenditure.  The
net available per student is thus a pittance.  The Committee, therefore, observes that there is a need to provide more
funds in this section as this is an investment to secure the future of our young generation.  Government must provide at
least six percent of the national income to this sector, which is much starved of funds.
Action Taken:
 
2.3       The Budget Estimates during 2002-2003 was Rs. 4886.85 crore (Plan Rs. 2124.24 crore and Non-Plan Rs.
2762.61 crore).

            The National Policy on Education envisages that the investment on education be gradually increased to reach a

Recommendation/Observation
2.4       At the same time in many of the schemes/projects, the Committee has observed that substantial funds are lying
with State Governments/NGOs and Utilization Certificates are not forthcoming from them for years together.  The
Committee does not know whether these funds have been utilized at all.  The Department must give a serious thought to
this aspect and take necessary remedial measures for optimum utilisation of funds.  
Action Taken
2.4       Under the Scheme of Educational Technology (ET), position regarding utilization of funds has not been
forthcoming from 17 States/UTs.  The matter is being vigorously pursued with the States/UTs.  As a result of the efforts
made by the Department, concrete action plan has been received from the States of Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh for revalidation of the Grant to enable the States to make the purchase of
Radio-cum-cassette-players (RCCPs)/ Colour TVs (CTVs).  Ministry of Human Resource Development has revalidated

defaulting States have been asked to refund the amount by 15
th August, 2003 failing which the funds will be adjusted
under other Schemes of the Department, as the ET Scheme has since been discontinued.
 
            The grants under Scholarship Schemes are released to the States/UTs after getting their realistic requirement and
the unspent balance if any, lying with them.  The unspent balance is adjusted while releasing funds.  Whenever unspent
balances are lying with the States for long periods, they are requested to refund the same to the Government of India. 
The States are also requested, from time to time, at various levels, to report the progress of expenditure.
 
            According to the information furnished by the University Grants Commission, UGC does not justify the release
of grant to those institutions which have not submitted the utilization certificate of earlier grant received from UGC.  
On the contrary, all the universities have been informed that their proposals for 10
th Plan allocation will only be
considered by the UGC when the utilization certificate for the grants released in earlier years are submitted and found in
order.  The recent judgment of Hon’ble High Court has further strengthened the hands of the UGC which directs that no
grant would be released to any institutions unless the utilization certificate of the earlier grant are received.  The stand of
the UGC has been made very clear to the institutions, receiving non-plan and plan grant from the
Commission

Recommendation/Observation
3.2                   The Committee notes with satisfaction that non-utilisation of funds has declined from 22.68 percent in
1999-2000 to about zero percent by 2002-2003.  In fact, the NCERT has asked for more funds than Rs.15.05 crore
which was allocated to it at RE stage for the financial year 2002-2003.  The Committee recommends that the
requirement of extra funds by NCERT must be looked into with a view to help the organization in its pursuits.
Action Taken
3.2                   The demand for grants for the year 2003-2004 has already been passed by the Parliament keeping in view
the requirement sent by the Council. If any additional funds will be required, the same will be considered at the time of
RE stage.
Recommendation/Observation :
3.4                   The Committee observes that there is need to cover more and more areas in a bid to vocationalise the
education.  At the same time, there is a need to introduce some ‘Earn and Learn’ kind of schemes to inculcate the
feelings of self-sufficiency among the students.
Action Taken
3.4                   New occupational areas are continuously being identified and curricula developed for the same.
                        Efforts are being made to encourage schools to start Production-cum-Training Centres (PTCs) wherein
the student trainees can get hands on experience of the work and have the opportunity of earning while learning. The

V         KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA SANGATHAN
 Recommendation/Observation
5.3                   The Committee notes with concern the tardy pace of land transfers. The Committee observes that certain
transfer cases have been pending for last twenty seven years. The Committee desires that these cases be looked into with
a sense of urgency.

5.4                   The Committee has been informed that Government have since decided not to open new KVs. While the

establishment of block-level vocational training institutes, treating vocational stream at par with other streams of
education, appointment of full-time teachers, coordination and utilisation of resources with other implementing
agencies/ departments/ ministries, development of national vocational qualification of development of a short-term
course and linkages with major industrial outfits.
Action Taken
7.1       Keeping in view the recommendations of the Working Group of NCERT and other review committees the
scheme of vocationalisation of secondary education is being revised. The proposed revised scheme will be implemented
through schools/polytechnics etc. For treating the vocational education and training at par with other streams of
education, National Qualification Framework is being prepared. There is a provision for setting up National
Competency Testing Agency (NCTA) for assessing the competencies. The proposed scheme envisages full participation
of the concerned agencies/departments/ministries in the implementation process and utilization of resources. The
revised scheme will take care of the national level issues including recognition of short-term courses, linkage with
industry etc. No temporary or permanent posts are proposed to be created under the proposed revised scheme but the
teaching staff will be hired on contractual basis depending upon the requirement of the activities. For practical training
staff from the local industry/ user organization will be engaged
 
Recommendation/Observation
7.2       The Committee appreciates the proposed changes. In fact, the system of education developed during British
period and still being largely followed aims at producing white collar jobs which are decreasing day by day because of
Government's policy of down sizing and right sizing the Departments. The students thus face a bleak future with
growing unemployment. The Committee observes there is thus a need to re-orient the system of education by making it
more vocational to suit the present day situation and at the same time ensure balanced development as envisaged by
Mahatma Gandhi. Vocationalisation of the education should ensure that after completing certain level of education
students can stand in the world on their own. This would inculcate the sense of self-sufficiency among students and
possibly help in reduction of white-collar crimes, which are the result of one's hunger and bleak future sofar as
employment opportunities are concerned.
Action Taken
7.2       The proposed revised scheme envisages training of students in such occupational areas wherein self or wage
employment opportunities are available. The selection of the courses will be done on the scientific survey for manpower
need.
            Service sector courses shall be given high priority, due to high employment opportunity.
            A few areas in which sizeable jobs have been created and a good potential exists for the next five years is
indicated in Annexure - II
 
Recommendation/Observation
7.3       The Committee also desires that the participation of NGOs and voluntary organisations for implementation of
specific innovative projects for conducting short-term courses should be encouraged more vigorously. The Committee
apprehends that grants given to many NGOs are not being utilized for the purpose for which these are given to them.
The Committee also apprehends whether the NGOs are pursuing the mission for which they have come up. The
Committee, therefore, feels the need for an effective monitoring system which can oversee the implementation of the
schemes and note the concrete achievements, if any, made by the NGOs.
Action Taken
7.3       Under the revised Scheme, it is proposed to strengthen the NGOs sector by selecting only the credible NGOs for
implementing the scheme. For an effective monitoring system, a standard monitoring mechanism, known as
Management Information System (MIS), which shall help in expeditious information gathering from institutions at
various management structures, is proposed to be developed.

1.         INTRODUCTION
 
Recommendation/Observation
1.3       Secondary Education is of crucial importance to our students who spend formative years of their life here.  The
secondary stage of Education gains more importance as hardly 19% students reach the university level of education. 
While changes have been made from time to time by the Government, fact remains that this stage of education does not
lead students anywhere.  In fact, on the other hand, the subjects like English, Hindi and mathematics (i.e. modern
mathematics) which has been introduced in the recent years etc. are beyond one’s comprehension and on an average
parents are not able to support their children financially.  These reasons alone have compelled students more so from the
vulnerable sections of the society to drop out at secondary level only.  There is thus a need to involve the school more
effectively to prevent drop-outs and reorient the education at this level, may be in the form of making it more vocational
and need based so that in case of students who are not able to enter the university stage, at least the secondary education

145th Report of HRD

helps them to stand in the world on their own account.
Action Taken
Keeping in view the needs and requirements of students, the NIOS has given complete freedom in choice of subjects
whatsoever at both Secondary as well as Senior Secondary levels.  A decision has been taken to remove all restrictions
and allowing the students to choose any five subjects.  NIOS will award a certificate as per the achievement of the
students in the subjects chosen.  Although NIOS gives full freedom in choice of subjects, yet if the candidates wishes to
use NIOS certificate for higher studies, it is in his/her interest that he/she will have to keep in mind the requirement of
Board/University etc., he/she wishes to enter.  Thus sovereignty of the learner is recognized in matters of what (s) he
wishes to learn.
In tune with the philosophy of open schooling where flexibility and choice are important, a student of NIOS is also
allowed to take as many additional subjects as he/she desires at Secondary as well as Senior Secondary levels.  This will
also meet requirement of certain State Education Boards for equivalence.
At the Secondary and Senior Secondary Stages,NIOS has made provision for flexibility in choice of subjects, self-paced
learning and transfer of creditsfrom other Boards and State Open Schools.  A student can avail as many as nine chances
to appear in public examinations spread over a period of five years.  The credits in subjects are accumulated till the
student clears required subjects for certification.  In order to expand the outreach of its Secondary and Senior Secondary
programmes, NIOS has inter aliaprovided for direct registration of candidates for appearing in examinations. 
NIOS has made provision of flexibility in selecting Academic and Vocational Courses.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee appreciates the flexibility and range of subject being offered by the National Institute of Open
Schooling at Secondary as well as senior Secondary level. However, similar position does not exist for those enrolled
for regular courses. Further, the Department should endeavour to introduce rational and scientifically developed
curricula which is comprehensible to the children for whom they are prepared.   The Committee also believes that the
Department should take measures to make Secondary education more relevant, practical and career-oriented.
Recommendation/Observation
1.4       More so, vocationalisation of education is the need of the hour as the country faces a paradox of more and more
number of children at entry level and corresponding flow of students at exit level of secondary and university stages
with meagre opportunities in the development of one’s career, or, for that matter, employment.
Action Taken
1.4       Based on the recommendations of the various review groups/committees, the existing scheme of
Vocationalisation of Secondary Education at +2 level is being revised.  The proposed Vocational Education Scheme
shall be a distinct stream intended to prepare students for identified occupation spanning several areas of activity.  It
envisages training of students in such occupational areas wherein self or wage employment opportunities are available. 
Under the proposed revised scheme, the industry and user organizations will be involved at all stages of implementation
of the scheme from identification of courses, preparation and design of curriculum to actual on-site training.  The
courses shall be competency based, modular in nature and demand driven based on the need based surveys to make
them employment oriented.  Opportunity for acquisition of multiple skills shall be available to students to improve their
employability.
            The UGC has already launched many programmes to make the education more relevant to the needs of the
society.  The major scheme of Vocational Education at the Undergraduate level has been designed to equip graduates
with necessary add on skill for gainful employment with major emphasis on self-employment.  Since the introduction of
the Scheme in 1994-95, 2162 institutions (2124 colleges and 38 universities) have been identified by UGC to provide
assistance under the Scheme on selective basis.  UGC has identified 38 vocational subjects under the Scheme.  UGC
during the X Plan has also decided to permit the students to have dual degrees at the Undergraduate level whereby they
shall be entitled to an additional certificate/diploma/advance diploma in conjunction with the regular degree. 
            The National Institute of Open schooling (NIOS) is gearing its programmes to offer relevant and need based
vocational courses.  Entrepreneurial skills are being integrated in all Vocational Courses in a phased manner.  The
emphasis is on development of non-traditional technology oriented vocational courses and making the students value
oriented entrepreneurs and job providers and not simply the job seekers.  The NIOS has visualized offering some
vocational education courses on-line.  The Certificate in Computer Application Course is already available on-line.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee appreciates that vocational courses are being promoted at various levels and it desires that all out efforts
be made so that vocational education gets a real push.  The Committee notes that the revised programme of vocational
education at different levels still remain to be implemented.

Recommendation/Observation

X         UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
Recommendation/Observation
10.18   The Committee is also of the view that UGC should encourage genuine research activity and develop a
mechanism for encouragement of only genuine research so that nation can make use of such research both commercially
and academically.  In fact, R&D sector of our nation continues to be under developed.  The Committee feels concerned
over the position and desires that it must change for the better.  The universities should have inter-disciplinary approach
in its research activities which should commence from undergraduate stage.
Action Taken
10.18   The UGC continuously encourages general research activities in the universities.  To uplift the research activities
of the universities, the UGC has schemes at three levels (i) at institutional level (ii) at departmental level and (iii)
individual level.
            At institutional level, UGC has schemes like ‘Universities with potential for excellence’ under which universities
are identified based on their merit and accorded the status of University with potential for excellence and enhanced 
level of funding to these universities is given to further upgrade their research and academic activities. 
            At departmental level, UGC has schemes like Special Assistance Programme and ASIST under which the
departments of the universities receive special funding.  In the ASIST programme, funding is given for strengthening of
infrastructure in science & technology for acquiring highly sophisticated and expensive equipment to enable them to
become internationally competitive in the key areas of PG teaching and research.  Under Special Assistance Programme
(SAP), the assistance is provided at three levels (a) Departmental Research Support (b) Department of Special
Assistance (c) Centre of Advance Studies.  The assistance is provided to the departments to achieve excellence in 3-4
identified thrust areas and also to improve the quality of teaching and research in the department.
            At individual level, the UGC gives major & minor research projects to the university and college teachers to
enable them to take up high level work in specified area.  Apart from this, the UGC has Junior Research Fellowship
(JRF) to enable young students to avail fellowship for pursuing PhD. Degree programme.
 
            As far as Inter-disciplinary approach is concerned, the UGC is encouraging the universities to start more & more
courses in inter-disciplinary areas.  In fact, this has been kept one of the parameter to evaluate the performance of the
universities through development radars, which would determine the performance related grant of the university.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee feels that despite the institutional mechanism for carrying out research activities, there are very few
research projects, which have created waves in their areas of study. The Committee desires that UGC should push the
matter with vigour and zeal and should also come up with a system which can tap existing potential instead of confining
itself to a system which only allows patronage and recommendation.  
Further, the Committee believes that UGC should help the universities to market their research findings which in turn
would help them financially and also fuel their
research activities on full swing.

lines of Mahatma Gandhi’s revolutionary ideas on education and to consolidate, network and develop institutions
engaged in programmes of Gandhian Basic Education and Nai Talim.

stage. It has been functioning without a regular Chairman, a regular member Secretary and without any regular staff.
The proposal for creation of post of a regular Chairman has been sent to the Cabinet Secretariat for seeking approval
from the Cabinet. A proposal is being processed in the Ministry of HRD for obtaining approval of Expenditure Finance
Committee for the continuation of NCRI in 10
th Plan. It, inter-alia, involves creation of 31 posts which are considered
the barest minimum for undertaking activities of NCRI.

brought to the notice of the Minister and ensure that this unhappy state of affairs is brought to an end.
Action Taken
(11.1 to 11.3) After the NCRI was set up by the Central Govt. in October, 1995 at Hyderabad to promote rural higher
education on the lines of Mahatma Gandhi revolutionary ideas on education and to consolidate, network and develop
institutions engaged to programmes of Gandhian Basic education and Nai Talim, its progress has remained slow
primarily due to functioning with the help of temporary Advisors/consultants and officials for short period of time. The
Council has an honorary Chairman and part-time Member Secretary (Deputy Secretary/Director, M/o. HRD was given
additional charge of MS, NCRI).
            The Ministry of HRD had sent a proposal for creation of post of a regular Chairman to the Cabinet Secretariat
for seeking the approval of Cabinet. The proposal was considered by the Cabinet in its meeting held on 18.03.03 and has
deferred its decision. Further a proposal to create 15 regular posts, which are considered the barest minimum for the
functioning of NCRI has been mooted as a part of EFC Memorandum and has been circulated among concerned
Ministries for their concurrence/comments. The matter is also being brought to the notice of Hon’ble HRM. After EFC
approves the continuance of NCRI and creation of post is obtained, the Council could be made fully functional.

The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department for making the NCRI functional but given the fact that
this issue has been hanging in air for some time, it is desired that the Department should make vigorous efforts to obtain
necessary approvals from concerned ministries to make the NCRI fully functional.

Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in its One Hundred-
Fortieth Report on Demands for Grants (Demand No.58) of the Department of Women and Child Development,
Ministry of Human Resource Development for the year 2003-2004.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
II            BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee expresses its serious concern over reduction in allocation of funds for 2003-2004. It observes
that the Planning Commission should take a realistic view of the basic requirements of various Schemes before
restricting the allocation of funds from the projected Demands. The Committee recommends that the Department should
make all efforts to achieve the targets both physically as well financially and also utilize the existing allocation
judiciously and should not allow any scheme either being dropped or left neglected due to this curtailment in allocation.
 
Action Taken
 
This recommendation of the Committee has been brought to the notice of the Planning Commission.  The
Department makes every effort to ensure that no scheme suffers for want of funds within the available resources.
 
VI        DAY CARE CENTRES
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee feels there is tremendous need to introduce ISO standards. At the same time, it is necessary to
keep these crèches free from all kinds of infection for which utmost cleanliness is necessary as children are more prone
to infection. The Committee, therefore, recommends that top priority be accorded for maintaining cleanliness.
 
Action Taken
           
The recommendation of the Committee has been noted and the implementing agencies –2 NGOs (Bhartiya Adim
Jati Sevak Sangh & ICCW) and the CSWB have been  suitably advised
 
IX            BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA (BSY)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee observes that the overall performance under this Yojana has been very poor. This sends a signal
that the State Governments are not concerned with the welfare of the vulnerable sections of the society. The Committee
recommends that the Department must take up the matter with the States to see whether they can sincerely implement
the Yojana and review the same in light of their response.
Action Taken
 
A Study has been entrusted to NIPCCD to evaluate the working of the scheme, and to come out with such
recommendations as necessary to improve its efficacy at the grass root level.
 
XI            SHORT STAY HOMES

146th report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/146threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:22]
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
While the Committee appreciates the concept of Short Stay Homes, it appears not much publicity is given to
their locations for intended users. The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate publicity be given in this
regard. CSWB should also make special efforts to run the Scheme. Besides, the cooperation of trustworthy
organizations or NGOs could be enlisted in the field.
 
Action Taken
           
This recommendation has been noted for guidance.
 
XIV            SWAYAMSIDDHA
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee disapproves the decision of the Department to rename and recast the scheme every year.  In
2001-2002, the scheme of  Indira Mahila Yojana was renamed as Integrated Women Empowerment Programme.  In the
year 2003-2004, it has again been renamed as `Swayamsidha’.  The Committee recommends that efforts should be made
to improve the contents rather than the title under which they work.       
 
Action Taken
Noted
 
 
XVII            TRAFFICKING IN WOMEN AND CHILDREN
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee recommends that preventive measures should be undertaken in accordance with the following
strategies:
 
(i)
                 Prevention of trafficking through the legal and criminal system, training of law enforcement officers,
(ii)                Control and suppression of prostitution through  legal system,
(iii)              Rescue and rehabilitation for women and girl victims of trafficking,
(iv)              Protection for and awareness-raising among women and girls to prevent trafficking,
(v)               Enhance public awareness, particularly in relation to forced and child prostitution and other measures,
(vi)              Awareness-raising among parents and guardians,
(vii)            Provision of alternative employment and income-earning opportunities for women and girls, and
(viii)           Through campaigns targeting parents on the long-term advantages of girls’ education.
 
Action Taken
 
The strategies suggested by the Committee have  been noted for guidance.   The steps taken by the Department
of Women and Child Development to prevent trafficking of women and children are given as follows:  Helpline
services  are also being provided from 54 centres all over India.
 
The Government has taken the following steps to prevent trafficking of women and children.
 
(i)
                 Drawn up a National Plan of Action (1998) and constituted a Central Advisory Committee to combat
trafficking, rescue and rehabilitate victims of trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation, and activate
legal and law enforcement system to strengthen implementation of the immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act,
1956.
 

146th report of Committee on HRD

(ii)                Set up State Advisory Committees on Trafficking for the same purpose, devolving authority and
seeking of mobilise  greater state resources in the fight against trafficking.
           
(iii)              The Department of Women & Child Development (DWCD) has issued guidelines to the States for
effective implementation of the Plan of Action and regularly reviews State action.
 
(iv)              The DWCD is at present reviewing the existing legal framework including the immoral Trafficking
(Prevention) Act.
 
(v)               DWCD has undertaken regional efforts, in alliance with NGOs, to create greater awareness of the
dimensions of trafficking and increase sensitivity to victims among Government Departments, the Police
and judiciary, as well as within civil society at large.
 
(vi)
              The National Commission for Women is conducting active advocacy against trafficking in partnership
with NGOs. It has conducted 20 workshops all over the country and has prepared a comprehensive
Report on subject.
 
(vii)
            The concerned State Governments have enacted legislations to prohibit Devdasi and prevent Jogin
traditions of sexual  exploitation.
 
(viii)           Profiling NGOs that are engaged in tackling trafficking and helping to rehabilitative victims.
 
(ix)              The DWCD has initiated a new scheme called SWADHAR for women in difficult situations applicable
to victims of trafficking also. The scheme provides for shelter, counselling, medical assistance,
vocational training to rescued victims.
 
(x)
               The DWCD has formulated a model grant-in-aid scheme for assistance to NGOs  to combat trafficking
in source areas, traditional areas and destination areas through prevention, rescue and rehabilitation.
Emphasis is placed on counselling, non-formal education and vocational training.
 
XVIII            GENERAL
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee notes that every year new schemes are being added/ modified for the welfare of Children and
Women. However, the Committee recommends that instead of framing new schemes every year the Department should
concentrate on strengthening the existing ones with a view to enhance their utility and acceptability. 
 
Action Taken
 
            The recommendations of the Committee has been noted for guidance.
 
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENTS’ REPLY
II            BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee notes that the trend to utilize the funds in the last month of financial year is a regular feature and
observes that it is not a healthy trend and reflects adversely on the credibility of planning to utilize about 3% of the total
allocation in 15 days or a month before the close of the financial year despite the fact that the Committee recommended
in its earlier Reports that the Department should take corrective measures to avoid last moment spending so that the

146th report of Committee on HRD

funds could be judiciously utilized.
 
Action Taken
 
            The first instalment would be released at about 30% of approximate annual requirement of States without taking
into account last year’s savings (+/-).  The second instalment, at about 80% of approximate annual requirement, duly
adjusting last year’s savings would be released only after receipt of Statement of Expenditure (SOE) in respect of funds
released last year and utilization certificate(UC). The third instalment, at about 100% of approximate annual
requirement of States, duly adjusting last year’s savings, would be released after receipt of utilisation certificate of the
first instalment.  Normally, during the financial year, the first instalment would be released in   April -May, the second
in August-September subject to receipt of SOE and UC of last year and the third in December-January during the year
again subject to receipt of UC of first instalment.
 
III            INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee notes that there has not been any significant improvement in the number of Projects, which were
operationalised.  The states of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal have not shown any increase in the
number of operational projects even after gap of an year.  This shows the indifferent attitude of the State Governments
towards the operationalisation of the sanctioned projects.
           
The Committee recommends that the Department must renew its efforts and approach the State Governments to
persuade them to operationalise these projects. 
 
Action Taken
 
In Andhra Pradesh, the number of operational Projects became 347 as on 31.12.2002, as against 251 reported
earlier.  This error occurred on account of Andhra Pradesh not having reported   projects operationalised  with the
 assistance of  World Bank.  For Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal 215 and 45 Projects respectively were permitted for
operationalisation in 2001-02. As far as Bihar is concerned, there has been constant emphasis on the State Government
to accelerate the pace of operationalisation.
 
IV            WORLD BANK ASSISTED  ICDS PROJECT       
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee takes a serious note of under utilization of resources placed at the disposal of the Department
and impresses upon the need for proper monitoring of the Schemes by both the Central and State Governments in future
and ensuring effective implementation.
 
Action Taken
 
During the year 2002-03, Rs.378.74 crore was  released against the budgetary provision of Rs.378.77, which
shows a utilization of 99.99%.
 
The  Project  is regularly monitored by the Department.  In addition to  periodic review meetings, Quarterly
Progress Reports received from the States are consolidated and analysed.  Based on the analyses, quarterly
communications are sent to the States on action points requiring  their attention.

CHAPTER-III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT  BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
 
 
III            INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
            The Committee notes with concern the findings of the Report which indicate that the maximum benefit of the
proposals made by the Department is almost out of reach of the targeted sections of population as it is evident from the
low rate of utilization of facilities by the beneficiaries. The Department should find out the reasons for the reluctance of
the people to avail of benefits of Schemes and take remedial steps accordingly.
The Committee recommends that there is an urgent need to sanction additional ICDS projects for the uncovered
blocks/urban slums.  In addition to this more anganwadi centres should be opened and feasibility for relocation of
existing centres should be explored.
 
Action Taken
 
One of the important components of the ICDS Scheme, to ensure optimum coverage of the targeted
beneficiaries, is adequate provision for supplementary nutrition at the Anganwadi Centres to all eligible beneficiaries as
per prescribed nutritional norms. Provision of supplementary nutrition is the responsibility of the State Governments. It
has been repeatedly emphasized upon the State Governments to earmark sufficient funds for supplementary nutrition
and ensure implementation of this component as per the prescribed nutritional norms. In this regard, elaborate
guidelines to clarify the basic financial, nutritional and registration norms under ICDS Scheme were circulated  by this

146th report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/146threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:22]
Department in consultation with the Planning Commission. The Planning  Commission has also been requested to stress
upon the State Governments to make adequate provision of funds for supplementary nutrition under the ICDS Scheme
during the States’ Annual   Plan discussions. The States have also been requested to make full use of the funds available
under the  nutrition component of Prime Minister Gramodya Yojna.
 
2.         In addition, the Department has  taken a number of steps to make the ICDS Scheme more effective and result-
oriented, which includes decentralization of Medicine Kits and Pre-School Education Kits at the State level; effective
training of ICDS functionaries and Anganwadi Workers; revision of  training syllabi/curricula with a provision of 25%
State-specificity to be incorporated by the State Governments themselves;   improvement in the working conditions of
Anganwadi Workers and Helpers and substantial increase in their honoraria; constant emphasis on States to make
adequate budget provision in the State Plan Outlays for supplementary nutrition to all eligible beneficiaries; issue of
instructions/guidelines to States, in consultation with the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare for proper coordination
and convergence of health inputs; issue of instructions, in consultation with the Department of Elementary Education &
Literacy, to strengthen synergy between Early Childhood Care and Education under District Primary Education
Programme and Early Childhood Education under the ICDS Scheme; issue of instructions to States to relocate
Anganwadi Centres, wherever appropriate, within the overall ceiling of existing Projects and Centers to optimize
coverage of beneficiaries within the available resources; etc. 
 
3.         Various steps taken by the Department have shown positive results including increase in the number of
beneficiaries utilizing various services under ICDS Scheme. This would be evident from the fact that the supplementary
nutrition beneficiaries have increased from  2.90 crore  in March 2001 to 3.88 crore in March 2003, with  the number of 
beneficiaries per Anganwadi Centre  increasing from 70 in March 2001 to 83 in March 2003.
 
            The Plan allocation of the Department (and ICDS Scheme) was not increased in view of resource constraints. 
Therefore, no expansion activities under the ICDS Scheme are contemplated during the X Five Year Plan.  However,
with a view to optimizing  coverage of beneficiaries within the available resources, States have been requested to review
and relocate the Anganwadi Centres, wherever appropriate, within the overall ceiling  of existing Projects and Centres.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee notes various steps being taken by the Department to make ICDS Schemes more effective and
result-oriented.  But these efforts have not yielded any tangible results so far.  For example, increase in number of
beneficiaries per Anganwadi workers of supplementary nutrition from 70 in March, 2001 to 83 in March 2003 can
hardly been said as significant, looking at the number of targeted beneficiaries.  The Committee, does appreciate the
problem that the Department is facing in persuading the States to adopt/implement laid down norms, financial and
others.  The Department must be under severe resource constraint due to non - increase in its plan allocation.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should concentrate in strengthening, streamlining the existing
Schemes under ICDS so as to cover more & more beneficiaries during the year.
 
VII            OTHER SCHEMES (CHILD WELFARE) 
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee feels that the welfare of Children is an important one and requires intensive research so that
efforts may continue to be made to brighten the future of Children. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts
be made to encourage studies and research work in the area of child welfare, if  possible with the help of international
agencies or bona fide NGOs, if any, available in the field.    
 
Action Taken
 
This issue will be addressed with the setting up of the National Commission for Children
Comments of the Committee

7.     NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME (NSS)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee observes it is necessary to have another look on the three tier system to determine the extent to
which it has helped.  The Committee notes that the utilisation of allocated funds under NSS continues to be the
optimum.  The Committee is surprised to learn how in the absence of audited accounts/utilisation certificates, allocation
of funds has been continuing for years together.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that before going for
enhancement in the scale of assistance for regular activities and special camps under NSS, it is necessary to develop an
effective monitoring system to curb the misuse of expenditure, if any.
 
Action Taken
 
It is through the ‘Three Tier Monitoring Mechanism’ only that NSS programmes are being  monitored 
successfully  at Universities, Colleges and Schools at  +2 level.
 
  The Three-tier Monitoring Mechanism is as under:-
At Ministry level:
         
Every year NSS Grants are released to various States/U.T.s.  The State Govt. is required to furnish the Statement
of Accounts to the Ministry, annually, showing details of NSS Grants (Central + State share) released to various
Universities/Colleges falling under the jurisdiction of respective State/UT.   Ministry is entrusted with the examination
of the statement of accounts furnished by each State/UT and only after having satisfied itself with the performance of
each State/UT, further Grants are released.
 
At the level of Programme Adviser’s Cell:
 
            The Programme Adviser’s Cell is entrusted with the monitoring and implementation of NSS programme in
various States/U.T.s by examining the periodical (quarterly/half-yearly/annual) reports received from the State level
NSS Cell of various States/U.T.s
 
At Regional Centre’s level:
 
          There are 15 NSS Regional Centres covering the entire country which are entrusted with liaison between the
Centre and the State.  These Regional Centres also monitor the release of NSS Grants to various
Univerisities/Colleges/+2 schools by respective States/U.Ts.
Apart from this, officers of the NSS Regional Centres, State Liaison Cells, NSS Programme Co-ordinators visit NSS
Programmes/camps falling under their jurisdiction and send feed-back to NSS Programme Adviser’s Cell/Ministry on a
regular basis. 
 
 Since the inception of the National Service Scheme(NSS) in 1969, with 37 Universities involving 40,000
students,  it has now over 19.00 lakh student
volunteers spread over  more than 176 Universities and 22 Senior Secondary Councils. Since the existing monitoring

mechanism is  working satisfactorily, no need is felt to switch over to some other mechanism.
 
 As a corrective measure, however, NSS grants are now released only to those States/UTs  who regularly  furnish
their statement of accounts to the Ministry in time. From 2001-02,  grants are not being released  to those  States/UTs
who do  not submit the statement of accounts  in  time  and  those  who have sufficient  unspent funds lying with them.
Usually, a two years’ grace period    is given to the States/UTs   for settlement of Accounts.
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should realize the importance of sports and take necessary steps
towards utilization of vast potential manpower of students gainfully either in sports or in completion of projects of
national importance during holidays in forms other than NCC camps.  If dedicated efforts are made, the country can go a
long way in bringing about a change in the sports scenario.
 
The Committee also recommends that purposeful activity should be under taken in these camps so as to prove the
theme of NSS i.e. “Development of the Personality of the Students through Community Service” and also ensure the
physical as well as mental development of participants.  Besides Programmes under NSS should be constantly reviewed
with a view to develop the personality and promote meaningful interaction among students.
 
Action Taken
 
The aim of National Service Scheme(NSS) being “ personality development of students through community
service”,  and keeping in view
academic compulsions, NSS volunteers are engaged in Regular Activities and Special Camping Programmes for a
specific duration only.
 
            Under “Regular Activities”, volunteers are expected to work for a continuous period of two years, rendering
community service for a minimum of 120 hours per annum.    Under “Special Camping Programme”, a camp of 10
days’ duration is conducted every year in the adopted villages/ areas on specific themes like “Youth for Afforestation
and Tree Plantation”, Youth for Mass Literacy”, “Youth for Rural Reconstruction”, “Youth for Development”, “Youth
for Social Harmony”, Youth for Haryali”, etc.  The theme for the current year i.e. 2003-04 is “Youth for Swacchta”
(Cleanliness).
 
            In addition, the volunteers are also made to participate in various  community development  programmes and
activities  which provide them ample opportunities for group-living,  collective experience sharing  and constant
interaction with different communities. Such programmes/activities really help the students  in grooming their
personalities  and channelling their energies in a constructive manner for integrated national development.
 
NSS programmes  are constantly monitored/reviewed  under the‘ Three-tier monitoring mechanism’.  Review
meetings of Heads of Regional Centre/State Liaison Cells are also organized regularly.

5.            YOUTH AFFAIRS PROGRAMMES
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee observes that there is an urgent need to address the existing scenario of youth problems which is
reflected in the unlawful activities of misguided youth of the country. Youth power, if directed properly, can change the
socio-economic scenario of the country .Added to this lack of adequate employment opportunities, lack of direction
because of uncertain education system, inability to pursue education because of financial constraints are compelling
youth to take to the crimes to find some easy money to sustain life. In these circumstances, the Committee is constrained
to note that the achievement of targets, both financial and physical, by the youth wing has not been satisfactory. Infact
the budgetary support during Ninth Five Year Plan remained unutilised. Against the approved outlay of Rs.352.24 crores
for the Ninth Plan expenditure incurred amounted to Rs.336.94 crores, The Committee agrees with the view expressed
by the Approach Paper to the Ninth Plan that the social sector programmes have not performed upto the mark. The
Committee is therefore of the view that the monitoring and evaluation system either does not exist and even if it exists,

million non-student rural youth enrolled through village-based Youth Clubs.  These Youth Clubs work in the areas
covering education and training, awareness generation, skill development and self-employment, entrepreneurial
development, thrift and co-operation, besides development of the body through sports & adventure and of mind through
sustained exposure to new ideas and development strategies.

Recommendation/Observation
 
9.3   The Committee feels that programmes of interest to the youth be devised with a view to promoting community
living and sharing of common experiences.
 
Action Taken
 
The objective of the National Integration Scheme is to provide the youth from different parts of the country and
from diverse religious and cultural backgrounds a common platform to interact with each other, know each other’s
customs and life styles, to work together in community welfare projects and, in the process make them aware of the
underlying unity amidst diversity.  By living together in the national integration camps albeit for a limited period, the
youth develop better understanding of different perceptions, beliefs, faiths and life styles.  During inter-state youth
exchange programmes, youth visit different States with marked cultural differences.  During their visit, they familiarize
themselves with the environment, family life, social customs, understand historical and cultural heritage of the country,

19.            GRANTS FOR CREATION OF SPORTS INFRASTRUCTURE
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
            The Committee reiterates the need for creation of adequate infrastructure and that too of an international
standard.  This should be thrown open to all and sundry individuals as well as groups on moderate charges.  This would
facilitate the encouragement for sports.
 
Action Taken
 
 ‘Sports’ is a State subject and it is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments to create various sports
facilities including sports infrastructure of international standards to promote sports at all levels. However, in order to
supplement the efforts of the State Governments in this direction, Central assistance is provided to State Governments 
and others  for creation of sports infrastructure under the above scheme , in  accordance with the approved pattern. The
projects of Indoor Stadium  category-I and Swimming Pool  category-I under the above scheme are of International
Standards  and it is for the State Governments and others to submit viable proposals for grant of admissible Central
assistance. As regards making available the sports projects to individuals / groups on moderate charges , this condition is
already included in the prescribed proforma and   the concerned State Governments/grantees have to give an
undertaking  that “the facilities of the projects will be made available for bonafide  purposes to the general public free of
cost or on nominal/token payment only”. 
    
2.         The response to this scheme was quite encouraging during 2002-03, resulting in requirement of additional funds
to meet the demand for release of assistance to various approved sports projects. Against the BE of Rs.8.90 crores
(including Rs.1.00 crore for NE States) during 2002-03, 85 projects were assisted with total Central assistance of
Rs.10.58 crores.
 
3.            Keeping in mind the financial crunch of the State Governments,  particularly NE States , and with a view to
lessening  the burden of the States, the Ministry has proposed increase in the sharing pattern alongwith  ceiling of
financial assistance for various sports projects, in the revised Scheme,  which is being posed to the EFC and will  be
implemented after obtaining its approval. With the liberalization/introduction of new components in the revised scheme
which includes extension of financial assistance to projects involving construction of artificial surfaces for a number of
sports other than athletics and hockey, and a provision regarding meeting the cost of repairs, etc., it is expected that more
sports infrastructure, including those of international standard, will come up all over India.

2            BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
 
While the role and contribution of youth is of vital importance in all countries, it is particularly significant in a
country like India where the proportion of the youth in the country's overall social and demographic profile is
continuously increasing. According to the 2001 Census, there were approximately 355 million people in the 15 to 35 age
group, 74 per cent of whom lived in rural areas. The number was expected to rise to approximately 510 million by 2016.
Both Central and State governments need to harness the energies of this large group, providing them with adequate
infrastructure of world standards for excellence in sports at national and international levels.
 
The Committee is constrained to observe that no organized effort appears to be forthcoming over a national scale

147th report of Committee on HRD

to tap the potential of the Youth. Youth are the foundation for the development of the country and unless emphasis is
laid on youth programme and put the youth on the right track and right direction, the ultimate goal of nation building can
not be achieved. The Committee feels that in order to develop the youth, a yoga programme should be started throughout
the country for different age groups with a definite capsule of different sets of exercises provided for different age
groups. It should be as near to the homes of the people as possible. Adequate number of volunteers should be trained for
the purpose who may conduct the exercises in Yoga suited to different age groups.  These exercises may be conducted in
an hour say between 5 to 6 a.m. throughout the country. It should be designated a national hour. The trained volunteers
may be paid an allowance for the purpose. This would infuse new energy & fitness among the people and help build a
strong nation. Further modalities, if any, could be worked out services of any existing organization could also be utilized
for the purpose.
 
Action Taken
 
The Committee’s observation regarding youth being the foundation of national development is acknowledged. 
Subject to constraints of funds, it has been the endeavour of the Ministry to mobilise and expand the youth network in
the country and to provide for them an outlet for contributing towards the development of the country.  The scheme of
National Reconstruction Corps was one such attempt through which efforts were made to tap the potential of the youth. 
It is hoped that the scheme would be extended in due course to cover all the districts of the country so as to afford an
opportunity to the youth to render service to the community and the country at large.  As regards the suggestion of the
Committee to start a countrywide programme of Yoga, while the Ministry accepts the same as laudable, it has to be
pointed out that under the Government of India Allocation of Business Rules, promotion of yoga is a subject allocated to
the Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homeopathy. However, the recommendation of the Committee is
being forwarded to the nodal department, as well as the Ministry of Human Resource Development for appropriate
action.  Nonetheless, to begin with, the Ministry is also issuing instructions to the Nehru Yuva Kendras and the National
Service units to promote yoga, as far as feasible, in all their programmes.  
 
Comments of the Committee
 
Challenges being faced by the young people are complex and wide-ranging.  Therefore, the programmes and
projects meant for the youth should be integrated, community driven, people-focussed and result oriented  with a
distinct  aim of  improving the quality of their life while also involving them in the development process of the
community. All Youth programmes, the Committee feels, should be aimed at promoting their welfare and development.

nationwide Yoga programme should be started under the supervision of trained volunteers in a morning hour say
between 5.00 to 6.00 a.m. as already mentioned in the foregoing paragraphs, in order to harness the energies of youth.
The Committee hopes that efforts would commence in right earnest. This is expected to energise the nation and also help
promote unity.

12.            SPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA (SAI)
 
Recommendation/Observation
 
 
The Committee observes that SAI is required to be a purely professional entity devoid of bureaucratic control
and solely devoted to its objective of promoting sport so that country finds an honoured place in the comity of nations.
 
To that end, among other things, the Committee observes that it is absolutely necessary that there is not only
adequate infrastructure in the matter of sports and also whatever infrastructure is created it should be of international
standard.  Besides, it is equally necessary to maintain it and providing timely renewals, repairs and replacements which
is generally not forthcoming.
 
Action Taken
 
SAI is a professional organization consisting of Sports Administrators (48 outstanding sportspersons including
Olympians, Arjuna Awardees/Ex. Internationals), Sports Scientists (46), Coaches (1523), Doctors, Physical Education
Experts, Teachers, Engineers(Civil/Elect), Academicians, Grounds men  and other administrative/accounts staff.  There
has been a continuous endeavour on the part of SAI to bring professionalism in its sports promotion activities.  The
implementation of various SAI Schemes is done by adopting systematic and scientific approach towards sports
promotion.  More and more sportspersons and other experts are associated from time to time for implementing
schemes/programmes of SAI which are implemented by it through its Regional Centres in collaboration with the
concerned State Govt./UT Administration.
 
One of the major objectives of the Sports Authority of India is to bring in excellence in sports training with the
allocated funds under the Plan Schemes.  Presently SAI is running 57 SAI Training Centres, 17 Special Area Games
Centres, 8 Centres of Excellence and also training children in 83 schools and 7 Akharas.  A total of about 8000 children
are undergoing training in these training units.  However, the number of children being trained is very small compared to
the population of the country.  More infrastructure needs to be created at Village  Panchayat level in every State and
more funds need to be allocated for creation of infrastructure and training of elite sports persons to bring in Excellence.
 
All the trainees are trained by the professional coaches who have represented the state or nation during their
playing years.  In addition, foreign coaches/experts are invited from abroad to provide coaching to our sports persons. 
During 2002 Commonwealth/Asian Games there were 42 foreign coaches in different disciplines to train the national
team for different disciplines.  This apart sports scientists/experts are  also associated with the preparation of the national
team and progress thereof is reviewed periodically by Govt./Expert Committee(s) and remedial action thereon  taken.
 
In the XVIIth Commonwealth Games held at Manchester (England) in 2002, India secured fourth position in the
overall medal tally by winning 69 medals consisting of 30 Gold, 22 Silver and 17 Bronze.  This was for the first time in
the history of Indian sports that such a large number of medals were ever won by Indian Team in any mega international
event.
 
In the Busan Asian Games 2002, India secured seventh position in the medal tally by winning 36 medals
comprising 11 Gold, 12 Silver and 13 Bronze.

The stadia which were constructed/renovated for the IXth Asian Games held in 1982 are being maintained and
utilized by SAI on behalf of the Government. These stadia are of international standard and were renovated/upgraded in
2001.  However, none of the stadia is financially self-sustaining and their day to day maintenance cost is quite huge even
as per CPWD norms.  Hence, these stadia could not be maintained as envisaged.  Efforts are being made to generate
more income from the Stadia and to increase the budgetary support for their maintenance.  
 
The National Camps for preparing teams in different disciplines on behalf of Government in collaboration with
concerned sports federations  are held at SAI Regional Centres/Academic Wing located at NSNIS, Patiala where
requisite sports infrastructure/sports science set up of international standard is available.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee appreciates the trend of increasing the number of medals in international sports including the
recently held Afro-Asian games in Hyderabd.   But it feels that it is not enough and India has a long and arduous way to
go in this area.   Our infrastructure and outreach is highly inadequate which need to be improved/increased manifold.
 
14.            RURAL SPORTS PROGRAMME
Recommendation/Observation
 
The Committee recommends that Sports activities need to be encouraged keeping in mind the facilities available,
particularly in rural areas and the need to keep in youth fit and keep them engaged in sports activities.  As far as
possible, disciplines which did not require much equipment such as Kho-Kho, Kabaddi, volleyball, track events and long
jump in athletics should be encouraged.  Efforts should also be made to enlist the cooperation of the Ministry of Rural
Development in the promotion of sports in rural areas.  The Ministry should extend assistance to the panchayats for the
creation and maintenance of play fields and for providing sports equipment.
 
Action Taken
Under the scheme of Rural Sports Programme, rural sports tournaments are organized in selected sports
disciplines viz. Athletics, Tug-of-war, Archery, Hockey, Kho-Kho, Kabaddi, Weightlifting, Volleyball, Wrestling,
Football (Boys only), at Block, District, State and National levels. Besides, the State Government may organize
tournaments in any other indigenous sports, popular in the area. While National level tournaments are organized by the
Sports Authority of India (SAI), the other level tournaments, i.e. Block, District and State/UT level tournaments are
organized by the State/UT Governments. These tournaments are organized where the facilities are available.
2.         As regards involvement of the Ministry of Rural Development in promotion of sports in rural areas, this Ministry
has already written to the Ministry of Rural Development in this regard. 
3.         As regards involvement of Panchayat Raj institutions, in the New National Sports Policy which has been
announced in 2001, emphasis has been given to the involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions, Local Bodies,
Educational Institutions, Sports Federations/ Associations, Clubs and Industrial Undertakings in the creation, utilization
and proper maintenance of the sports infrastructure. Accordingly, action will be taken by the Ministry to extend
assistance to the Panchayati Raj Institutions.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
Around three-fourth of the youth live in rural areas. While it is the responsibility of the Ministry to harness and
develop the full potential of the youth as partners in nation-building, majority of them still remain unaware of these
sports activities.   Involving PRIs in holding/organising rural sports as well as in maintaining infrastructure may provide
adequate boost to sports in these areas.  The Committee reiterates that organized efforts need to be made at the national
level for this purpose.

Recommendation/Observation
