all the villages 100% enrolled under the SKP.
X.     ADULT EDUCATION
10.1  The Total Literacy Campaign (TLC) has been the principal strategy of National Literacy Mission for eradication
of illiteracy. The TLC is area-specific, time-bound, participative, delivery through voluntarism, cost-effective and
outcome oriented. The campaigns are implemented through Zilla Saksharata Samities (district level literacy committees)
as independent and autonomous bodies, having due representation of all sections of society.
10.2  The Committee was informed that no targets are fixed from the top for this; targets emanate from the grass-root
level on the basis of a survey, which also serve as a tool of planning, mobilization and environment building. Though
the TLC is meant to impart functional literacy, it also disseminates a ‘basket’ of other socially relevant messages such as
enrolment and retention of children in schools, immunization, propagation of small family norms, women’s equality and
empowerment, peace and communal harmony etc. On conclusion of TLC, Post Literacy Programme (PLP) is taken up
specifically aiming at consolidation of literacy skills and integration of skill development programmes to enable the
neo-literates to acquire skills for their economic self reliance. The normal time-span for TLC and PLP is 18 and 12
months respectively. The funding pattern is in the ratio of 2:1 and 4:1 between Centre and State Governments for
normal and tribal districts respectively. The learning cost per head for TLC and PLP is Rs. 90-180 and Rs. 90-130
respectively.
10.3  It is noted that out of 600 districts in the country, 596 have since been covered under Adult Education Programmes
- 167 under Total Literacy Campaigns, 191 under Post Literacy Programme and 238 under Continuing Education
Programme. About 106.77 million persons have been made literate as on 31.3.2003. About 60% of the beneficiaries are
women, while 22% and 12% belong to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes respectively.
10.4  In case where for reasons beyond the control of the local ZSS, such as natural calamities, absence of political will,
transfer of Collector, lack of grass root mobilization etc., TLC has stagnated; area-specific strategies are formulated for
restoration of these campaigns.
10.5  Under the scheme of Continuing Education for neo-literates, the main thrust is given to setting up of Continuing
Education Centres which function as a focal point for providing learning opportunities such as library, reading room,
learning centres, sport centres, cultural centres and other individual interest promotion programme centres. Continuing
Education Centres are set up to .serve a population of 2000 to 2500 with a relaxation in the population criteria in
sparsely populated areas. One Nodal Continuing Education Centre (NCEC) is set up for cluster of 8-10 Continuing
Education Centres (CECs) to oversee and monitor the activities of CECs. The Scheme of Continuing Education also
provides the opportunity to undertake other diverse activities such as equivalency programmes, quality of life
improvement programmes, income generating programmes and individual interest promotion programmes involving
alternatives and innovative approaches to cater to the need of the learners besides providing facilities for basic literacy
for the dropouts as well as new entrants. The programme of Continuing Education is being implemented under the aegis
of Zilla Saksharata Samiti (ZSS).
10.6  The Committee notes that Continuing Education of neo-literates is an important scheme under adult education
which has shown a good performance. Department wanted more funds for increasing its coverage further. The
Committee recommends that additional allocation be made for this programme so as to keep its pace.
10.7  The Committee would like to place on record its appreciation for the efforts made by the Department in
accomplishment of adult education programmes, particularly, its continuing education component. However, it feels that
literacy rate achieved i.e. 65.38% (as per census 2001) in comparison to the target fixed (i.e. 70%) by the end of Ninth
Plan, should have been achieved. The Committee notes that only 77% of the allocation could be used. The Committee is
dismayed at the underutilization of funds for different schemes of adult education. The Committee is concerned over the
issue of underutilization of funds and feels that such a tendency need to be checked and problems identified to be
removed at the earliest.
10.8  The Committee notes that in light of its recommendations in its 144th Report, the Department had allocated
Rs.250 crore to Adult Education for the year 2004-05 in comparison to Rs.233 crore provided during 2003-04. The
Committee feels that even this increase of mere 17 crore would not be adequate in the face of gigantic task that is before
the Government.
XI.    JAN  SHIKSHAN  SANSTHAN

149th Report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/149threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:19:24]
11.1  The Scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) or Institute of People’s Education (formerly known as Shramik
Vidyapeeth) aims to provide polyvalent or multi-faceted adult education programme by improving the vocational skills
and quality of life of it beneficiaries, which are mostly neo-literates, semi-literates and non-literates. It concentrates on
the socio-economically backward and educationally disadvantaged groups of urban/rural population, such as
neo­literates, semi-literates, SCs, STs, women and girls, slum dwellers, migrant workers, etc.
11.2  Till the end of Eighth Plan, the scheme was restricted to urban/semi-urban areas. With the emergence of missions
of neo-literates due to the total literacy campaigns throughout the country and the transformation having taken place in
the economic and social set up over the years, the role and scope of these institutes have widened manifold. During the
9th five-year plan the scheme has been strengthened with enhanced funding, widened scope and area of operation. In the
changed scenario, the focus of JSS is now shifting from industrial workers in the urban areas to the numerous neo-
literates and unskilled and unemployed youth both in urban and rural areas throughout the country. These Sansthans act
as district level resource support agencies especially in regard to organization of vocational training and skill
development programmes for the neo-literates and other target groups of the Continuing Education Scheme. At present,
there are 122 Jan Shikshan Sansthans in the country. In brief, the main objectives of the scheme are:­
(i)    To improve the occupational skills and technical knowledge of the neo-literates and other disadvantaged
groups.
(ii)    To provide academic and technical resource support to Zilla Saksharata Samities in Literacy, Post Literacy
and Continuing Education Programmes.
(iii)   To serve as nodal continuing education centers and to coordinate, supervise and monitor 10-15 continuing
education centers/nodal centers.
(iv)   To undertake innovative programmes and to organize training and orientation courses for key resource
persons and master trainers under the Scheme of Continuing Education.
11.3  The Committee has been informed that during 2002-2003, the JSSs offered around 225 different vocational
training programmes from Candle and Agarbatti making, sewing and embroidery to computer courses. During the year
2002-2003, about 20,074 programmes were organized and 2,83,931 persons were benefited through vocational and
other courses.
11.4  All the JSSs are encouraged to generate their resources through appropriate course fee for certain courses not
strictly meant for non-literates, neo-literates and weaker sections. They can also mobilize resources through ZSS and
other such agencies for conducting training programmes for resource persons and Preraks, etc. The JSSs are allowed to
utilize the resources thus generated for expanding their programme activities.
11.5  At the end of Eighth Plan, 58 JSSs were functioning while during Ninth Plan, 50 additional JSSs were set up
raising the number to 108. During 2002-2003, 14 additional JSSs were set up and during 2003-2004, it was proposed to
add another 15 JSSs.

experience and their funding pattern is as follows:­

11.7  The Committee is of the view that the vocational courses carried out by the JSS should be increased in number and
frequency. The committee finds that despite its mandate to concentrate on socio-economically and educationally
backward groups of urban and rural population, including neo-literates as well as unemployed youth, (through its 126
Sansthans) the total number of persons benefited through the courses of JSS in the year 2002-03 was 2,85, 979 which is
abysmally low, given the large number of people who are to be brought under the ambit of this programme. Further the

Committee is concerned over the underutilization of funds as only 81% of the total allocation could be utilized and it
emphasizes that every step should be taken to curb such a recurring tendency.
11.8  The Committee has been informed that according to 2001 census, 45 districts in the country, majority of them
concentrated in Bihar, Jharkhand, UP and Orissa have female literacy rate below 30 per cent. The Committee notes that
8 low female literacy districts in UP have been brought under an accelerated programme of female literacy which is
being implemented through a network of about 100 NGOs. 24.79 lakh women are expected to be made literate under the
programme. In Bihar, 15 low female literacy districts are being covered with the involvement of Panchayati Raj
functionaries, women volunteers teachers and self help groups. 24.03 lakh non-­literate women were identified, out of
which 19.69 lakh have already been enrolled in the programmes. While appreciating the initiative taken by the
Department, the Committee would like  to point out that the Department should take all steps to ensure that only NGOs
of proven track record are involved in this ambitious initiative.
XII.  PROBLEM OF DROPOUTS
12.1  The Committee notes that various schemes are being run by the Department of Elementary Education & Literacy
with the ultimate aim of achieving 100% enrollment so that no children in the country remained out of school. Not only
that efforts are also being made to retain them as also to provide quality education to all the children between 6-14 by
the 2007. The aims of innovative schemes under SSA can particularly be mentioned in this regard. The Committee is
concerned that implementation of even these schemes does not inspire enough confidence. The problem of dropouts, it
appears, has not been given due importance even under the SSA. The dropout rate, the Committee notes, has come
down just by 3.5% during the last decade from 42.6% in 1991 to 39.1% in 2001. The Committee observes that drop-out
rates in classes I-V for the year 2002-03 as per the provisional figures supplied by the Department are quite high in
respect of some of the States as indicated below ­
Bihar               61.64
Meghalaya                   56.96
Mizoram                      59.31
Rajasthan                    60.43
Sikkim             61.76
 
What is more disturbing is that except Rajasthan (2002-03), school data in respect of other States pertains to 2001-02.
The reasons given for this dismal performance are - existence of teachers’ vacancies, teachers’ absenteeism (39%),
particularly in rural areas inadequate involvement of community, difficulty in covering children from inaccessible areas.
This gives a very grim view of the state of affairs which exposes all the claims made by the Department. If the dropout
is taken as indicator, it appears that all the efforts and resources spent on achieving universalisation of elementary
education had gone down the drains. It is a sad reflection on the performance of the Department as well. This points out
towards an urgent need for having a serious look on the causes that are responsible for this. While doing so the states
should also be consulted because education is the concurrent responsibility. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department should look into this and submit a note to the Committee within three months of presenting this Report.
12.2  The Committee is of the opinion that the children who have dropped out can be integrated with the Continuing
Education Programmes of adult education so that they are able to undertake activities relating to income generation
providing skills in area specific activities.
12.3  The Committee feels that a ‘Learn & Earn’ scheme could be an effective measure for retaining the students in the
schools. It therefore, recommends that Government should consider the proposal of providing suitable vocational
education to desirous children at the upper primary stage so that those who cannot for any reason pursue education
beyond class 8, enter the world and earn their
livelihood.

         The SSA is, in fact, the flagship Scheme of the Department to pursue elementary education in mission mode. The
goals before it are laudable, yet highly ambitious ones. The Committee could see that the goal of having all the children
aged 6-14 in schools, Education Guarantee Centres/bridge course by 2003 could not be achieved. As per information
made available by the States, number of out-of school children was 2,30,34,518 as on 1.4.03 which stands reduced to
61,61,104 as on 31.12.03 (not including Goa, Sikkim, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.) The
Committee is not inclined to believe these figures specially in respect of Bihar, UP & West Bengal as indicated below
:­
 1.4.2003 31.12.2003
Bihar 44,30,140 7,46,000
U.P. 43,00,00 2,10,000
West Bengal 39,50,239 4,39,602
 
         The Committee finds it quite baffling that within a span of just nine months such a tremendous improvement had
taken place. It appears to the Committee that these figures may not be real. When asked about the channel of
information on the performance of this scheme, the Committee was informed that it is through official channel - from
District level to State level and to the Centre. The Committee was given to understand that 42 national research and
resource institutions with a proven track record have been involved with monitoring at different levels. Further
independent evaluation is provided through monitoring by independent external audit organizations. The Committee
would like to be apprised about the latest feedback provided by independent external audit organizations. These
information are crucial because they indicate health of a particular scheme based on which effective remedies can be
suggested.

Approval Board (PAB) was going to consider more plans thereafter. The Committee is aware that part of the gap in
resources is going to be met by collection from the educational cess levied this year. But even this would not be
adequate to fill the gap. The Committee, therefore, recommends that demands/needs of the Department for the SSA
should be reconsidered and additional allocation provided at appropriate stage so that such an important scheme does
not suffer and its goals were attained.     (Para 3.6)
         The Committee notes that there had been some underutilization of funds during the Ninth Plan. Underutilization,

in Committee’s view, is a cause for serious concern. It points out more towards the laxity on the part of the
implementing authorities than anything else. Such a performance does not inspire confidence as to the success of this
programme, hence it should be avoided at every cost.                                                                                      (Para 3.7)
         The Committee notes that assistance under the programme is on a 75:25 sharing arrangement between the Central
Govt. and State Govts. The Committee is not aware about the acceptance level of this distribution by the States already
burdened by financial constraints. The Committee apprehends that proposed 50:50 sharing between Central and State
Govts. after Tenth Plan may not find favour with majority of the States. The Department may need to have a re-
assessment of this funding pattern by having a Mid­-Term appraisal of Tenth Plan during the current year, 2004-
05.              (Para 3.8)
         The Committee also observes that although an impressive number of additional classrooms and new school
buildings were sanctioned by the PAB during the last two years, not much progress seems to have been made. Out of
79,766 additional class rooms sanctioned, construction of only 12,516 class rooms could be completed, as many as
62,275 class rooms remained under construction, and details about 5,375 sanctioned class rooms are not available.
Similarly, out of 40,944 new school buildings sanctioned, only 3547 school buildings could be completed, 32093 school
buildings were still under construction. Fate of 5504 new school buildings is not known. The Committee, therefore,
emphasizes the need for taking all measures so that situation improves in non/under-performing States in
SSA.                      (Para 3.9)
         The Committee is dismayed to note that of the 4,06,148 teachers sanctioned to be appointed, only 1,38,090 (i.e.
33%) could be appointed during the last two years. Against the fixed target for recruitment of teachers, States like Bihar,
U.P. and West Bengal could achieve zero percent, 22 per cent and 21 per cent of the target respectively. These States
constitute a large proportion of children between 6-14 years. Such a dismal performance in the bigger States does not
augur well for the future of this programme.                                                                                                         (Para
3.10)
         The Committee is concerned over the quality of education imparted under the Abhiyan. The Committee is little
apprehensive about the feasibility of appointing education volunteer/para teachers for imparting quality education to the
children. The Committee strongly feels that a child needs to be tended under well-trained hands to initiate him into the
art of learning. The Committee is aware of the fact that there was problem in getting regular teachers in remote and
inaccessible habitations. It, however, emphasizes the importance of trained teachers for child education. The Committee
is happy to know that the Department had made a provision of pre-service induction/training as well as in service
training of Education Volunteers even at Block/Cluster levels. But the Committee finds that due to shortage of teachers,
not to speak of trained teachers/qualified resource persons at block and cluster levels, aims of the Programme are not
being achieved.   (Para 3.11)
         The Committee also takes note of the evaluation study on Alternative Schooling (AS) conducted by the Central
Institute of Education, Delhi University in the year 2002-2003, which broadly revealed that a majority of teachers in the
Alternative Schools were first generation learners and the community was satisfied with their functioning. The
Committee is of the view that the community in remote areas may not be capable for making a correct assessment of the
functioning of AS teachers. But it is really encouraging that the communities were participating in the education of their
children. The Committee also takes notice of the study which revealed that the AS learners performed better on tasks
involving learning by doing. In view of the socio-economic context of the parent and the children themselves, the
Committee recommends that learning by doing should be emphasized in the syllabi while taking due consideration of
the child’s psychology and his surroundings. The Committee feels that agencies involved in the framing of syllabi
should ensure that at elementary level, to say the least, child’s creativity should be
promoted.                                                                                                                (Para 3.12)
         The Committee welcomes that the Government has approved a new programme for Education of Girls at
Elementary Level (NPEGEL). The Committee desires that funds for the programme be released to all 2656 selected
blocks as early as possible so that the gender differential in literacy rate in various Sates as well as at national level can
be lessened to such an extent as to achieve the goal of gender equity under SSA.                                               (Para 3.13)

V.     NATIONAL PROGRAMME OF NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT TO PRIMARY EDUCATION
         (MID-DAY MEAL SCHEME)
         The Committee however, observes that out of the seven States claimed to be implementing the Programme
partially, five States i.e. Bihar, Punjab, West Bengal, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh are distributing foodgrains with
percentage varying from 92 to 99 per cent. The Committee therefore, is of the view that in the major States, some of
them educationally backward also, Mid-Day Meal Scheme still remains to be implemented in the true sense and as per
the Supreme Court directive.                                                                                                                         (Para 5.4)
         The Committee notes that against an allocation of 1,33,84,064 MTs of foodgrains during Ninth Plan only
79,54,426 MTs of foodgrains were lifted, which is approximately 60 per cent of the allocation. However, against a
financial target of Rs. 6,50,177 lakhs fixed for the Scheme during Ninth Plan, a financial target of Rs. 6,49,980 lakhs
has been achieved, which is 99.96 per cent. The Committee is at loss to understand that despite a 100 per cent utilization
of fund there has not been a commensurate off take of foodgrains. The Committee is constrained to say that it is a result
of a weak planning for the effective implementation of the Scheme. The chances of pilferage/financial mismanagement
can also not be ruled out. The Committee, therefore, would like the Department to make the monitoring mechanism of
this scheme more comprehensive and effective by holding District Collectors responsible for such lapses. It could also
go in for an evaluation of the scheme with a view to tackling the problems faced in its implementation. The Committee
feels that State Governments are needed to be sensitized.         (Para 5.5)
         The Committee finds that the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, no doubt, was a noble scheme, which not only motivates the
children to come to school and remain there but also takes care of the problem of malnutrition, particularly, in the rural
areas. The Committee finds that the main problem is cooking and serving the food. It would require huge funds, should
the Centre decide to support this as well. Given the ground realities and financial constraints of some States, covering all
the children under this Scheme in near future appears to remain a distant dream. The Committee hopes that 15% of
additional central assistance under PMGY earmarked for meeting the cooking cost under MDM and additional
allocation that MDM was likely to get from the cess being collected from this year, will alleviate resource constraints to
a great extent in providing hot cooked meal to the children. The Committee recommends to allocate funds to meet at
least the gap between what is given and what is
required.                                                                                                                         (Para 5.6)
         The Committee though appreciates Government’s move for mobilization of additional resources for this Scheme
and extension of the scheme upto upper primary stage. The Committee, however, feels that it might put extra burden on
already cash starved scheme. It can be taken up only after the coverage of MDM is 100 per cent at primary stage.       
(Para 5.7)
         The Committee has been informed that teachers were being involved in cooking food in some States. It deplores
this practice which affects studies in the school. The Committee feels that, at the most, teachers can do only quality
checking. As an alternative, the Committee feels that involvement of NGOs as well as Self Help Groups in providing
cooked meal to the children would facilitate this scheme in a big way. In places where Self Help Groups may not be
available, the youth clubs and volunteers of Nehru Yuvak Kendras may also be involved for cooking and serving the
meals to students. The Committee has been informed that the Department had issued guidelines in 2001 whereunder
State Govts. may select NGOs for taking the responsibility of serving cooked meal to school children. States like
Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh have actively involved well-established NGOs in this matter. The Committee feels that
the Department should take the initiative in motivating the States lagging behind to follow the example of these
southern states.                                 (Para 5.8)
         The Committee’s attention has been drawn to media reports about children falling ill after taking cooked meal

provided in schools. The Committee feels that these media reports about contaminated food being served under Mid-
Day Meal Scheme in different States need to be taken seriously. The Department should make an effort as far as
possible to check with the concerned State authority about the veracity of such reports and if found true, implementing

the children as a part of MDM with a view to supplementing then nutritional requirements.      (Para 5.9)
VI.    STRENGTHENING OF TEACHERS TRAINING INSTITUTIONS
         The Committee is happy that the teachers’ training had caught attention which has been made as an integral
component of SSA. The Committee emphasizes on the need for an effective teacher’s training programme and is of the
view that the Government still has a lot more to do in this regard. The Committee is concerned that against a target of
establishing 20 new DIETs and upgradation of five institutions as CTEs/IASEs, only six DIETs could be sanctioned in
2003-2004. This situation becomes grim in face of the fact that a large number of trained instructors for elementary
education were required for the successful accomplishment of the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan apart from the requirements
in regular schools.            (Para 6.4)
         The Committee further notes that against a target to set up 100 new DIETs, 125 CTEs and IASEs, only 39 DIETs,
9 CTEs and 4 IASEs could be established during the Ninth Plan and actual expenditure against the total allocation of Rs.
976.53 crores have been to the tune of 763.06 crores, which is 78 per cent of the allocation. The Committee expresses
dissatisfaction over the progress made in the physical achievements and also the underutilization of funds more so in
face of the fact that there is a severe shortage of qualified teachers and this aspect is evident from NCTE’s directive of
raising the limit of DIETs intake to 200 seats to solve the problem of trained teachers.                                                      
(Para 6.5)
         The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by NCTE in encouraging State Govts. in developing special
training programmes in distance made for the training of untrained in service teachers. During 2003-04, a large number
of primary/upper primary teachers of Sikkim, Assam, Tripura have been covered under a six month programme
developed by IGNOU. The Committee hopes that other north-eastern States, and States like Bihar, MP would also take
benefit of this programme.                                                                                                                     (Para 6.6)
         The Committee has learnt that to meet the requirement of additional elementary teachers due to implementation of
SSA, NCTE has permitted increased in-take of DIETs to the extent of 200 seats and encourage recognized B.Ed
colleges to start elementary teacher training course, waiving the requirement of NOC from State Government. The
Committee feels that it could be only a stop-gap arrangement in teacher’s training programme. Moreover, abjuring the
requirement of NOC might result in the fall in standards of infrastructure and may also become the breeding ground of
education mafias apart from producing sub-standard, elementary education teachers. The Committee strongly
recommends that all out efforts be made to make all the sanctioned 498 DIETs, 86 CTEs, 38 IASEs functional as soon
as possible. Moreover, the new scheme allowing flexibility but increased accountability of the states in making teacher
education institutes functional, productive and qualitative appears to be good one. It, therefore, be implemented with all
sincerity and responsibility.                      (Para 6.7)

education had gone down the drains. It is a sad reflection on the performance of the Department as well. This points out
towards an urgent need for having a serious look on the causes that are responsible for this. While doing so the states
should also be consulted because education is the concurrent responsibility. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department should look into this and submit a note to the Committee within three months of presenting this Report.
                                     (Para 12.1)
         The Committee is of the opinion that the children who have dropped out can be integrated with the Continuing
Education Programmes of adult education so that they are able to undertake activities relating to income generation
providing skills in area specific activities.                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                     (Para 12.2)
         The Committee feels that a ‘Learn & Earn’ scheme could be an effective measure for retaining the students in the
schools. It therefore, recommends that Government should consider the proposal of providing suitable vocational
education to desirous children at the upper primary stage so that those who cannot for any reason pursue education
beyond class 8, enter the world and earn their livelihood.                                                                                 (Para 12.3)

REPORT

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on
its behalf, present this Fifteenth Report of the Committee on the Constitution (Seventy-

ninth Amendment) Bill, 1992.

2. The Bill, which was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 22nd December, 1992, seeks to
amend the Directive Principles of State Policy to provide that the State shall endeavour to
promote population control and to include in the Fundamental Duties a commitment to
promote and adopt the small family norm. It is also proposed that a person shall be
disqualified for being chosen as and for being a Member of either House of Parliament or of
the Legislature of a State, if he has more than two children. This will, however, have
prospective effect. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamen-
tary Standing Committees, the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred” the Bill to the
Committee for examination and report.

2.1 A Press Communique, inviting suggestions from various individuals, organisations
and institutions interested in the subject matter of the Bill, was issued on 20th June, 1994. A
copy of the Press Communique is placed as Annexure I.

2.2 The Committee also invited written views from leaders of the political parties in
Parliament and State Legislatures. A list containing names of persons from whom views
were invited and the names of those who responded is attached as Annexure II.

2.3 The Memoranda containing views, comments, opinions and suggestions received on
the Bill are attached as Annexure III.

2.4 The Committee considered the Bill in eleven sittings (Annexure-IV) and heard the
oral evidence of witnesses, including the representatives of Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare (Department of Family Welfare), and Ministry of Law, Justice and Company
Affairs (Department of Legal Affairs). The Committee also had the benefit of views of a
cross section of non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs), important women’s organisations
engaged in the promotion of family welfare schemes, besides views of some eminent

Members of Parliament.

2.5 In its meeting, held on the 3rd January, 1995, the Committee considered the Draft
Report and adopted it for presentation/aying in both the Houses.

*Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, para 34548, dated June 14, 1994.

1


Background

3. The Department of Family Welfare, in its background note on the subject submitted
to the Committee, has stated that in pursuance of. a decision taken by the National
Development Council (NDC), in its meeting of 23rd/24th December, 1991, the Planning
Commission constituted a Committee of the NDC on Population in February, 1992. The
Committee of the NDC on Population was chaired by Shri K. Karunakaran, Chief Minister
of Kerala.

3.1. In the Meeting of the Committee of the NDC on Population, held on 12th
November, 1992, under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister, it was decided that a
proposal be moved for disqualifying person violating the small family norm from holding
elective office, prospectively and not retrospectively.

3.2. It was in pursuance of this decision, the Constitution (Seventy-ninth Amendment)
Bill, 1992, was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 22nd December, 1992.

3.3. The Report of the Committee of the NDC on Population was considered by the
NDC in its 46th meeting on 18.9.1993 and endorsed.

3.4. The Department of Family Welfare, in its note, has further stated that tackling the
growth of population, which is currently of the order of 17 million per year on a population
base of 846.3 million, as per 1991 census, requires a national consensus, with the
participation of all citizens, backed by strong political commitment. Elective representatives
have to set an example and demonstrate political will and commitment for population
control.

4. The Committee also took note of the following documents while considering the Bill:-

(i) Report of the Committee of the National Development Council on Population
(The Karunakaran Committee Report); and

(ii) Draft National Population Policy (The Swaminathan Committee Report).

4.1. The Karunakaran Committee had made the following recommendation in respect of
the people’s representatives: P

“Amendment to Panchayati Raj Act, brought by the Rajasthan Government, is
recommended to be emulated. The Central/State Governments should consider
bringing similar legislation for disqualifying the people’s representatives at different
levels if they violate small family norm after getting elected. Such a step would have
useful, demonstrative efiect on the people at large.” (para 5.8, page 80 of the
Report).

4.2. The Swaminathan Committee, in its Report, has also made recommendation in

respect of the People’s representatives, which is as under:-

“Rajasthan and Haryana have enacted laws which debar, prospectively, persons who
do not adopt two-child family norm from contesting elections for Panchayats, Zila
Parishads and Nagarpalikas. This reflects political commitment. Even if such
legislation does not exist, there should be a code of conduct which enjoins on all
elected representatives of the people, from Parliament to Panchayat, to adopt,

2;


3

voluntarily, the small family norm. Elected people’s representatives will then become
role models for the public to emulate. Future legislation in this area at Central or
State level should, however, safeguard the interests of women, particularly those
belonging to the socially and economically under privileged sections of society.”
(para 13.1. page 40 of the Report)

5. The Secretary, Department of Family Welfare, in the course of his oral evidence
before the Committee, recapitulated the background leading to the introduction of the Bill
in the Rajya Sabha in December, 1992. He stated that even before the Karunakaran
Committee was set up, there was discussion in the NDC meeting in December, 1991, and
some chief ministers had voiced the opinion that those who were elected to Parliament or to
the State Legislature should set an example by restricting the number of their children to
two. He added that it was in pursuance of this that this Bill had taken shape.

Need for Constitutional Amendment

6. Explaining the background, as far as the restrictive nature of the Bill was concerned,
Secretary, Family Welfare, mentioned that the Constitutional amendment was being sought
in case of elected representatives because a disqualification of this nature could only be
passed through a constitutional amendment. He added that there was some thinking going
on in the Department of Family Welfare to enlarge the scope of the Bill and bring in other
categories of people, such as civil servants, etc. as per the recommendations of the
Karunakaran Committee. He further clarified that in the case of other categories of people,
constitutional amendment was not required and the objective could be achieved through an
amendment of the relevant service conduct rules. While talking about the incentives and
disincentives, he mentioned that the Swaminathan Committee on the Draft National
Population Policy has suggested that those who have more than two children should have
more severe liabilities. In this connection, he drew the attention of the Committee to para
9.1 of part B IL of the Draft National Population Policy which reads as under:-

“The employees of the Central Government, State Governments, Municipalities, as
well as employees of various public sector undertakings, must give the lead in
adopting the small family norm. The service rules in the central and state
governments and their undertakings: would be suitably. modified to ensure that the
small family norm is adopted by their employees. Similarly, all new entrants to the
government, who are married before the age of 21 years in the case of boys and 18
years in the case of girls, will be debarred from recruitment. Promotion policies
should be such that the adoption of small family norm is encouraged. ............ कर

6.1 The Secretary, Department of Family Welfare, in response to certain queries from
some Members of the Committee, informed that apart from these measures, the Govern-
ment had also been taking certain other steps to achieve the objective of slowing down the
population growth and the Government was not depending upon legal measures only. The
main programme was the programme of providing contraceptives to the 154 million couples
who were in the reproductive group.

6.2 As regards incentives and disincentives, as suggested by the Karunakaran and
Swaminathan Committees, the Secretary stated that the whole issue would be placed before
a conference of Chief Ministers for a decision.

6.3. While making a distinction between a coercive method and disincentive, the
Secretary stated that the Government’s policy in this regard could, in no way, be regarded as
coercive.


7. In regard to the necessity of a constitutional amendment as proposed, the Committee
considered the legal opinion given by the Legislative Department (Ministry of Law, Justice
and Company Affairs) (Annexure V). The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, during
the course of his oral evidence, was specifically asked, by the Committee to clarify as to
whether a Constitutional amendment was necessary and what advice was given to the
Department of Family Welfare on this subject. He was further asked to clarify as to whether
a stipulation of a disqualification, either in the Constitution or in the Representation of
People’s Act would violate the fundamental right of a citizen to contest elections. Clarifying
the position, Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, said that it was true that a
Constitutional amendment was not strictly a legal requirement, but it was the intention of
the. framers of the Constitution that certain things should be declared in the Constitution
itself as being of fundamental importance.

7.1 The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, further stated that in the advice given
to the Department of Family Welfare, they had advised that a constitutional amendment was
not a strict legal requirement. However, the Department of Family Welfare explained to
them that the amendment would lend moral authority to the programme of population
control, and as the matter would be placed on the priority agenda of the nation, it would
help in the emergence of a national consensus. Therefore, it became a matter of importance
that, from policy angle, certain provisions be incorporated in the Constitution on the subject.
It was in this context that amendment of the Constitution had been proposed.

7.2 The Secretary was also of the view that the provisions dealing with the disqualification
could be justified on legal grounds and would be perfectly in keeping with the letter and
spirit of the Constitution.

Evidence of NGOs etc.
8. The Committee also heard some eminent experts and Members of Parliament.

8.1 It was contended by one of the Hon’ble Members of Parliament that the number of
children in a family was related to the level of education and the economic condition of that
family. Achieving the goal of small family norm, he argued, depended mainly on literacy,
economic condition and propaganda compaign run by the State and voluntary organisations.
He apprehended that the provision of disqulaifying a person having more than two children,
if given effect to, might give rise to some kind of a class-bias as it would prevent women
from poor families from getting elected to the representative bodies. He, therefore,
suggested that people adhering to small family norm should be given certain positive
incentives instead of providing for disincentive to those who did not adhere to it. He
emphasised the States’ role in spreading education, improving the economic condition of the
people, particularly in the rural areas of the country. He described the idea of creating a
role model in this regard as a ‘wrong notion’ which would not work in India.

8.2 Representatives of the women’s organisations, which appeared before the Commit-
tee, expressed certain doubts about the Bill. They pleaded that disqualifying women having
more than two children from contesting elections did not seem to be a fair proposition, more
so, when they had the-least say in deciding the number of children they should have,
especially in villages. This apprehension is relevant in the context of reservation of 30 per
cent seats for women in the Panchyat Raj institutions.

8.3 The witnesses also felt that such a legislation did not tackle the basic problem of

population control. They suggested that, instead of enacting such a legislation, it would be
better if certain positive measures, such as better education, health facilities and adequate


5

employment opportunities, were provided for women. They also. expressed their doubts
whether the role, model concept would achieve the desired objective. In their view, it would
work only when it was supported by many other positive measures.

8.4 However, many witnesses belonging to non-government organisations, who
appeared before the Committee, were in general agreement with the main thrust of the Bill.
They felt that if the citizens were to be asked to control the number of children, there had
to be a role model from the top. They felt that the Bill was a step in the right direction.

8.5 Referring to the success of the family planning programmes in Kerala and Tamil
Nadu, one of the witnesses stated that these examples could not be applied to other parts of
the country, as there were multiple factors responsible for the success of the programme in
these two States. For example, if one were to tour Kerala, one would not normally find
highly underdeveloped villages such as those found in other parts of the country. More
thrust is laid in Kerala on literacy and the expenditure incurred by the State on health care
is higher as compared to other States. Furthermore, there are various voluntary organisa-
tions, which are very actively engaged in popularising family planning. Similarly, in Tamil
Nadu, the achievement was made mainly through better political will and committed
workers.

8.6 Some of the witnesses were of the view that a holistic approach needed to be
adopted, It was necessary to provide health-care particularly to women and children. Unless
literacy was improved among women to make them aware of their rights and the necessity
for adopting a small family norm, it would be difficult to achieve results.

8.7 The witnesses also generally agreed that the voluntary nature of the family planning
programme should not be watered down. It was felt that the programme should be
restructured in such a way that it would be closely inter-linked with developmental
programmes, with emphasis on decentralization.

8.8 However, many of them were of the view that in order to make the family planning
programme a success, the disincentives should also be extended to people in all walks of life,
particularly those in government, public sector undertakings, autonomous bodies and
organised private sector, as well as professionals, etc.

8.9 The Committee also took note of the fact that the State governments of Rajasthan
and Haryana have already amended their respective Panchayati Raj Acts to provide for
similar disqualification for contesting the Panchayat elections. The provisions made in the
Haryana and Rajasthan State Panchayati Raj Acts are at Annexure-VI.

8.10 The representative of the State government of Haryana, during the course of his
oral evidence before the Committee, stated that the spirit behind the amendment of the
Haryana Panchayati Raj Act was small family norm. Elections to Panchayats in Haryana
have since been held in December, 1994.

8.11 During the course of his oral evidence, the representative of the State government
of Rajasthan stated that Rajasthan had played a pioneering role in giving a new shape to
Panchayati Raj system in the State. The amendment relating to small family norm was made
in the Rajasthan Panchayati Raj Act in 1992. The amended Act came into effect from April
23, 1994. However, the Government of Rajasthan promulgated an Ordinance on December
30, 1994, which stipulates that the date of commencement of this provision would be 27th
November, 1995. According to the State Government, elections to Panchayats are scheduled
to be held during January-February, 1995.


Views of Political Leaders

9. The Committee also received written views of leaders of various political parties.
While some of them supported the proposed amendment to the Constitution for adoption of
small family norm by the Members of Parliament and State Legislatures, some others
expressed their reservations. They felt that the provisions of the Bill would erode the basic
democratic right of the people to choose freely any one as their representative, who was
otherwise qualified under the Constitution. It would also take away the basic right of any
voter, who has more than the prescribed number of children, to contest in an election. It
was also suggested that the Clauses 4, 5 and 6 should be deleted. They felt that what was
required was social education, as well as positive incentives.

Conclusions

10. Majority of Members of the Committee were generally in agreement with the
provisions of the Bill. The Members, while supporting the Bill, stated that this measure
would send out the right signal to the people and that it had to be enacted as early as
possible. Members also observed that although the country had been implementing several
voluntary family planning measures since 1951, not much headway had been made in this
regard. The proposed measure, would, therefore, go a long way in creating awareness
among the people for adopting a small family norm. The Members also expressed the view
that the Bill should not be opposed on human rights considerations.

10.1 Some of the Members said that they had serious reservations about this Bill, and
were opposed to it. They were of the view that this amendment would not stand the scrutiny
of a court of law and the evidence tendered before the Committee by the Law Secretary did
not convince them that such a provision would be upheld by the judiciary.

10.2 Referring to the good performance of Kerala, Goa and Tamil Nadu in regard to
the family planning programme, it was argued that one important reason for this success was
good education and the various incentives given to girl children, so as to encourage them to
attend school. It is this kind of incentives and schemes which should be given priority in'the
family planning programme and not the kind of ‘tokenism’ which characterised the present
Bill.

10.3 The Bill was also opposed from the angle of human rights, in general, and women’s
rights, in particular.

10.4 As regard human rights, a reference was made to the specific statement made at
the recent Cairo Conference on population that coercion should not be used in this area and
India was also a party to this. Members opposing the Bill felt that the proposed legislation
amounted to coercion and as such ran counter to the spirit of the Cairo Declaration.

10.5 Disagreeing that the Bill would establish a role model for the general public to
follow, it was pointed out that when a person became a Member of Parliament, he got
certain privileges and facilities which the general public did not enjoy. There could not be
any comparison between the mode of life of a Member of Parliament and that of an
ordinary citizen in the country. The question of role model, therefore, did not arise at all. It
was, thus, argued that there was no relationship, either casual or statistical, between the
family planning practices of the legislators and that of the society at large. Therefore, these
Members were opposed to the Bill.

10.6 Some of the Members felt that the Bill should have been more broad based to
include government servants, educationists, professionals, etc.

“~


10.7 In conclusion, an overwhelming majority of Members of the Committee wholehear-
tedely supported the provisions of the Bill. They felt that despite the fact that the country
had been independent for over forty years now, yet the standard of living of the common
man had not improved. Almost half of the population of the country was still below the
poverty line. The prime cause for this state of affairs was over-population which was
increasing unabated.

10.8 The Members supporting the Bill were of the view that the provisions of the Bill
should be applied irrestpective of caste, creed and religion. They were also of the view that
the Bill would send a positive message to the people at large and would thake the public
figures as role-models for the people to follow.

10.9 Those who were in favour felt that the Bill was not discriminatory against women.
Women who wished to contest elections, the Members felt, were enlightened enough to
follow the small family norm. In any case, contesting elections was purley voluntary and
there was no compulsion.

10.10 These Members were of the view that the Bill would have qualitative importance
and was in the country’s interest. In. totality, the Bill would create the necessary climate for
a small family norm and would establish the credibility of the people’s representatives. Thus,
the majority of the Members supported the Bill in toto.

Observations and Recommendations

11. The Committee notes with concern that the population of the country is growing at
a very rapid pace. As per the estimates of an Expert Committee of Planning Commission,
India’s population is expected to reach the one billion mark by the end of the current
century and double the present population by the year 2035 A.D. by which time it would be
the most populous country in the world.

11.1 The rapid growth of population has serious implications for economic develop-
ment and preservation of environment. The country, inspite of four decades of concerted
developmental efforts, has found it difficult to provide adequate food and nutrition, housing,
education, health care, employment and other basic amenities of life to millions of people.
The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the adoption of a small family norm should be
given the utmost priority and population stabilisation at the replacement level should be our

target.

11.2. The Committee notes that though it may be contended that an amendment of the
Constitution may not be necessary and the object of the Bill of debarring a citizen from
becoming either Member of Parliament or a State Legislature can be achieved by simply
amending the Representation of People’s Act, considering the fact that political leaders of
the country should serve as role models and that such a measure would lend moral authority
to the programme of population control, demonstrate the commitment of the political
leadership of the country and help in emergence of a national consensus, it would be
appropriate to amend the Constitution, as proposed in the Bill.

11.3 The Directive Principles of State Policy were embodied in the Constitution with
the objective of spelling out, expressely, the high ideals the nation should pursue and the
Fundamental Duties specify the obligations of the cititzens. The’ Committee, therefore,
endorses the proposed amendment to the Constitution, as embodied in the Bill, which
provides for disqualification and seeks to amend the Directive Principles of State Policy to
provide that the State shall endeavour to promote population control and small family norm
and also to include the same in the Fundamental Duties.


8

11.4 The Committee feels that if the political parties were to include the small family
norm in the code of conduct for their members, it would give an added impetus to the
family planning programme.

11.5. The Committee also took note of the Swaminathan Committee Report on the Draft
National Population Policy. The Committee recommends that the Government should take
an early decision on the report and come out soon with the final draft of the National
Population Policy.

11.6 The Committee also recommends that the incentives and disincentives, as suggested
in the reports of the two Committees, namely, the Committee of the National Development
Council on Population (The Karunakaran Committee) and the Draft National Population
Policy: (The Swaminathan Committee) should be implemented immediately and cover all the
sectors, such as government servants, teachers, professionals, organised groups in the private
sector, etc.

11.7. The Committee approves the Constitution (Seventy-ninth Amendment) Bill, 1992,
without any change and recommends that the Bill be passed.

11.8 The Committee, however, suggests that the Government might consider convening
a meeting of the leaders of the various parties in Parliament for further consultations on the
Bill so as to arrive at a consensus and ensure its smooth passage. This has become all the
more necessary due to the failure of a number of parties to respond to the Committee's
invitation to give their views on the Bill, in person or in writing.

(a) that this would be mere tokensim and would have little effect on the people so far 85

women in politics is sought to be enhanced, this proposed act which is prelude to extension

no empowerment in their own reproductive life, also from political empowerment; this was

ANNEXURE-I
The Constitution (Seventy-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 1992

The Constitution (Seventy-Nonth Amendment) Bill, 1992, as introduced in the Rajya
Sabha on the 22nd December, 1992, has been referred to the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Human Resource Development, headed by Shri P. Upendra, M.P., for
examination and report.

The proposed Bill seeks to generate awareness about the country’s population problem
and to contain the adverse impact of the unchecked population growth of the country on its
socio-economic development. It reflects the State’s endeavour to promote population control
and small family norm. It is proposed to amend the Directive Principles of the State Policy
and to include in the Fundamental Duties, a duty to promote and adopt the small family
norm. The elected representatives are expected to set an example and demonstrate political
will and commitment for population control.

It is proposed in the Bill that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for
being, a member of either House of Parliament of either house of Legislature of a State, if
he has more than two children. The proposed amendments will, however, have prospective
effect and will not apply to any person who has more than two children on the date of
commencement of the proposed amendment or within a period of one year of such
commencement. However, if such a person has another child after the said period of one
year he will incur the disqualification. Similarly, in the case of a person having only one
child on the date of commencement of the amendment or within a period of one year of
such commencement, it is proposed to provide that if a subsequent child birth results in the
birth of more than one child, he will not incur any disqualification. It is also proposed to
provide that mere act ef giving a child in adoption will not enable a person to escape
disqualification.

In this connection, it has been decided to invite memoranda, containing the views of
individuals, organisations, institutions, etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bill.
Accordingly, all the interested persons, organisations, institutions, etc. are requested to send
their views by the 4th July, 1994 to the Under Secretary (CHRD), Rajya Sabha Secretariat,
Parliament House Annexe (Room No. 539), New Delhi-110 001.

Copies of the Bill can be obtained on requisition from the Committee on Human
Resource Development, Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Room No. 228, Parliament House
Annexe, New Delhi.

Arrangements have also been made to keep copies of the Bill in the libraries of the
State Legislative Assemblies and Union Territory Legislatures, for reference purposes.

according to facts and circumstances of realities we face. Now the question is : Should we
amend the Constitution to include these amendments in Chapters which are not enforceable?
I strongly feel that it is not necessary—more so as the norms are likely to very according to

pleasure of the majority and this is one such case. Even if the Government wants to add the
proposed Thirteenth Schedule in the Constitution, it can do so without amending the
Directive Principles of State Policy and the Fundamental Duties. If we add every ‘over-
riding national priority’ in the Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Duties
arising now and then, then our Basic Law would become the nation’s diary of over-riding
national priorities.

3. The proposed Thirteenth Schedule implies that the “small family norm” means
“having two children” per couple, even though it is only mandatory for the Legislator, he
being an M.P. or M.L.A. or M.L.C. - The ‘two children norm’ cannot be a fixed norm. We
have now reduced the norm to a lesser figure from three. It is pertinent to point out that
China, with its 1.2 billion people, is selectively moving away from its 1979 official “one child
per couple” policy and is permitting some couples, especially in rural areas, to have two and
three children without economic penalty or forced abortion. Therefore, | think that it will be
rather unrealistic or even absurd to fix the norm of two children for a legislator-couple and

for a legislator-couple alone.

4, Whether the Thirteenth Schedule imposing a two-children norm to the Legislator-
couple is ultravires of the Constitution or not is itself a moot point because the Bill selects a
particular class of citizens and imposes a heavy punishment leaving others scot free. Even if
it is intra vires, this does not go with the principle of democracy. 1 do not think that in any
democratic country in the world, such constitutional provision exists. It can, at its worst, be
described as coercion and therefore a draconian measure,

5. 1 am afraid that th ue treads into the mine field of human rights. The Chinese
statement in the preparatory conference of the recent United Nations International
Conference on Population and Development (1994) in Cairo, Egypt says:

“Coercion in family planning programs, whether physical, economic or psychological,
is a breach of human rights and can never be acceptable; all in uals have the basic
right to choose when and if they will have children.”

6. The statement of objects And Reasons says that “India’s population may cross one
billion by 2000 A.D.”. But, how many Legislators are there in India to whom the Bill is
applicable? Only a few thousands! Attempting to control by coercive measures, the increase
of population by a few thousands of legislator-couples is definitely a drop in the ocean and
an exercise in futility.

7. Mr. John Rogosch, an expert on health and family planning at the USAID in New
Delhi s: ..-most children are born to mothers who are between the ages of 18 and
30—what we call the high fertility age group"—How many mothers of that fertility age
group are there among the Legislator-couples in India? It would be very few. To bring a
constitutional amendment to achieve that negligible target would be really ridiculous and not
worthwhile.

8. Why does this Bill choose the Legislator-couples for this coercive measure? Because
the law-makers think that the “Elected representatives have to set an example and
demonstrate political will and commitment for population control."—I am unable to
subscribe to this view. The purpose of any law is its utility—greatest advantage to the


20

greatest numbers and its basis is equality—not legislators—first. Any attribute of ‘responsible
citizenship’ may not and need not stop with legislators alone.-—I have a lurking fear that in due
course of time, the list would be enhanced to cover other ‘responsible citizens’ like the
Government Employees, Employees of Public Sector Undertakings and Defence Services etc. This
reminds me the days of ‘Nuys Bandhi’ during the days of Emergency and it is my firm opinion that
this Bill would breed negative massive reaction.

9. To seek to achieve the objective of “stabilisation of the population at the replacement
level” the answer lies elsewhere. The justification offered for having a large family hay its own
myths and truths. The developing nations have been urging that large families are a result of
poverty rather than a cause of it. Therefore, the slogan made famous at the U.N. Population
Conference in 1974 was, “Development is the best contraceptive.” The bumper sticker of Cairo
Conference might be “Women's empowerment works.” Then comes the preference for a boy-
child. Cultural factors and perceptions of economic advantages favour sons above daughters.
Experience in countries around the world has shown that birth rates drop and health and
economic conditions improve. Where once there was disagreement whether family planning or
economic progress was a pre-requisite to progress in either area, there is now a broad
recognition that both are important in their own right, but they work best when pursued
together. Therefore, it requires a holistic approach and it should go hand in hand with
community development, education, better health services for all age-groups, a social
revolution to raise the status of women, environmental protection etc.

10. India is not in a helpless position in population control and already the states of Tamil
Nadu and Kerala have achieved dramatic decline in birth-rates. Their fertility rates are at, or
close to, the levels in industrialized countries and it is pertinent to note that Kerala achieved a
low birth-rate with very low levels of contraceptive prevalence.

11. Therefore, | would advise that this legislative step may be dropped once and for all as it
serves no useful purpose and does not go into the heart of the problem itself. This Bill is nothing
but sound and fury that signifies the return of an internationally discredited Malthus. And it
disguises the malevolence of coercion under a paean to “political will and commitment” for
population control. If a stabilised population is such a good thing, why aren't a substantial
number of Indians stabilising their family numbers? Is it mere ignorance and lack of education
or are there compelling psycho-socio-economic forces that make large families a more rational
and beneficial proposition for large sections of the Indian rural poor? Unless we understand

MEMORANDUM NO. 11
Submitted By:— SYED SHAHBUDDIN, M.P.

While fully endorsed the Sections 2 and 3 of the draft, I consider Sections 4, 5 and 6 as
misconceived and inconsequential in controlling population or in establishing the small

family norm.

The Statement of Objects and Reasons include, in para 3, only one sentence to establish
a nexus between the object of legislation and its provision : “Elected representatives have to
set an example an demonstrate political will and commitment for population control”. This is
a very wide concept. There are many provisions under Directive Principles of State as well
as Fundamental Duties and 1 do not see any reason why only one of them should be singled
out for political disqualification.

Secondly, representation in the Legislature is not to serve only one specified purpose. A
legislator acts on behalf of his Constituency on all questions of public interest to the best of
his ability just as a lawyer pleads the case of his clients. In choosing a lawyer (or a doctor), a
person does not go into the question of whether the lawyer or the doctor practices family
planning or how many children he has. In the same way, most voters are not aware of nor
they particularly want to know, the number of children that a candidate has. Therefore, to
my mind, there is no nexus between the object and Reason of the Bill and the proposed
qualification for membership of the legislatures. In my view, such a provision could erode
the basic democratic right of the people freely to choose anyone as their representative, who


22

is otherwise qualified under the Constitution. What is worse, it shall take away the basic
right of any voter who has more than the prescribed number of children to stand for

election.

Needless to say that the proposed measure will not have any measureable impact on the
growth of population.

What is needed is social educational as well as positive incentives. Both these should be
covered by the National Population Policy.

There is yet another reason to oppose this provision. In our society, legislators alone do
not carry social prestige. In fact, they command less prestige than the wealth, the senior
Civil Servants and even top academicians. Are we going to prescribe a small family norm for
the top management, Civil Servants, bankers and academicians? I would, therefore, suggest
that the Bill should be trimmed by the Consultative Committee of this of its existing Sections
4, 5 and 6.

While appreciating the spirit and intensions behind the proposed legislation | would like

more accurate as well as technically correct.

people serving in state politics shall be mentally prepared by that time. Similar provisions
should be enacted for the persons engaged in local self Govt. bodies and other elected
bodies.

Ministry of Law, Justice & C.A.
(Legislative Department)

The proposals contained in D.O. letter No. 230225992-PLY, dated 13.11.1992,
received from Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (Department of Family
Welfare) and the note containing the views of Mr. Justice Retd. V.R. Krishna lyer have
been examined, The proposals, in brief, relate to —

(a) amending Part IV of the Constitution relating to directive principles of State
policy so as to insert a new article to cast a duty on the Government to take
measures to reduce the rate of population growth and make available medical,
economic and other facilities to promote small family norm;

(b) to amend Part IVA of the Constitution relating to fundamental duties so as
to cast a duty on every cititzen to actively promote and practice the small family
norm,

(c) to amend articles 102 and 191 of the Constitution so as to disqualify a
person, having more than two children, for being chosen as, and for being, a
Member of either House of Parliament or a Member of the Legislative Assembly or
Legislative Council of a State.

2. In so far as proposals (a) & (b) of the preceding paragraph are concerned, the matter
was examined in this Ministry in 1990 and the then Minister of Law and Justice (Shri Dinesh
Goswami) in his minutes, dated 20.9.1990 observed that “though I feel that the amendment
is not necessary yet when the administrative Ministry is keen for it, I will have no objection,
as no constitutional or legal point is involved”. The administrative Ministry finally insisted
for clearance of the Note for the Cabinet and it was cleared by this Ministry on 11.12.1990
and the same was considered by the then Cabinet and the proposal was not approved as per
minutes of the meeting of the Cabinet held on 23rd January, 1991. In case the administrative
Ministry want to persist with the said amendment in Parts IV and IVA of the Constitution
from policy angle, we may not have any legal and constitutional objections.

3. In so far as proposal (c) of paragraph 1 is concerned, it may be mentioned that sub-
clause (e) of clause (1) of articles 102 and 191 already provides that further disqualifications
can be laid down by or under any law made by the Parliament. Further Entry 20A of List
Ill of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution enables Parliament to make a law on
“population control and family planning.” In this view of the matter, the Constitution
amendment may not be strictly necessary for disqualifying people’s representatives in
