XVII. OVERLAPPING OF SCHEMES
17.1  The Committee notes that there are two similar schemes for women’s welfare, one is Swawlamban Scheme whose
objective is to promote women development through provision of employment by training them in traditional and non-
traditional trades such as computers, electronics, embroidery and weaving etc whereas the objective of the scheme of
Support to Training and Employment Programme (STEP) for women, is to provide training for skill upgradation in
traditional sectors like agriculture, animal husbandry, handlooms, handicrafts khadi and village industry etc.
Implementing agencies for both the schemes include Women Development Corporation, Public Undertakings,
Cooperatives, Women Development Centers of Universities, Voluntary Organizations etc.
17.2  On being asked about the rationale behind having two parallel schemes with identical purpose, target and
implementing agencies, the Department informed that both the Swawlamban, earlier known as NORAD, and Support to
Training and Employment Programme (STEP) Schemes aim at providing training and skill upgradation to women to
facilitate them obtain some kind of employment or self employment. The two schemes, however, differ in the following
aspects :
(a)   Unlike the Swawlamban Scheme which is a kind of stand alone scheme for training of women for a fixed
period ranging from 3 months to 12 months, STEP is a more comprehensive programme which is usually
undertaken on a project basis for a period of 2-3 years (b) The number of beneficiaries in a training project
under Swawlamban Scheme ranges from 30 to 100. Whereas the STEP Scheme, produces between 500 to
1000 beneficiaries in a single project. (c) The Swawlamban Scheme caters to both traditional and non-
traditional sectors on the one hand, the STEP scheme covers only the traditional sectors.
17.3  The Committee reiterates that the Department should revisit the schemes having overlapping objectives with a
view not only to avoid inevitable confusions but also to have focused and optimum utilization of the scarce resources.
XVIII.  FUNCTIONING OF NGOs
18.1  The Committee was informed that some of the schemes of the Department were being implemented through
NGOs. Idea of NGOs involvement, no doubt, is a noble one, functioning of some of the NGOs, however, leaves much
to be desired. Complaints of misuse/ misappropriation of government grants by some NGOs are reported from time to
time. There are allegations that in some cases different organization were being run by one person and same NGO was
receiving grants under different names. The Committee is aware that not all NGOs were defaulters and many of them
were rendering yeoman service. Department gave a list of NGOs blacklisted by it. The Committee feels that simply
blacklisting such NGOs would not deter the delinquent ones and they might come back with change names/address.
Government needs to streamline the procedure of their selection as well as regular monitoring of their work. We should
have penal provisions for recovering the grants given to defaulting NGOs. The NGOs doing good job needs to be
suitably rewarded so as to motivate others.
18.2  The Committee feels that there exist no restriction for having a maximum number of NGOs in a particular area.
The Committee has noticed that out of 60 NGOs provided financial assistance amounting to Rs. 2.53 crores under the
National Creche Fund during 2003-04, 31 are from Andhra Pradesh with 18 NGOs based in one district alone. The
Committee is of the view that there should be specific guidelines whereunder number of NGOs in a district (subject to
area) should be indicated.
18.3  The Committee has also observed that out of 463 NGOs provided financial assistance under Swawlamban Scheme
during 2003-04, 98 were provided funds for running computer institutes and 55 for readymade garments. The
Committee is of the view that NGOs involved in imparting technical education, even though of a very low standard
should be certified for running such courses.
18.4  The Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the fact that feedback from NGOs implementing various
schemes of the Department is not being received on a regular basis. The Department itself had admitted that under

proposals, and to recommend only good and viable proposal to the Department. Universities/colleges/local urban bodies
have also been made eligible. In order to attract good and viable proposals, the scheme is being publicized in the
national/regional newspapers.         (Para 8.4)
         The Committee finds this was yet another good scheme which somehow was not being successfully operated.
After so many years of its existence, there exist only 914 Working Women Hostels with 56,214 beneficiaries in such a
vast country by the year 2003-04.                                                                                                           (Para 8.5)
         The Committee notes that the scheme is under a process of revision which is at an advanced stage of
consideration. The Committee hopes that the revised scheme will be implemented in the current year, attracting a good
number of viable proposals. The Committee has been given to understand that there exist a system whereunder
performance of implementing agencies is reviewed through periodical reports from State Govts., review meetings and
field visits by the area officers. The Committee is of the view that surprise visits /inspections will strengthen the
monitoring mechanism.(Para 8.6)
IX.    SUPPORT  TO  TRAINING  AND  EMPLOYMENT  PROGRAMME  FOR  WOMEN  (STEP)
         The Committee did not find any reasons for reducing the RE in any document supplied to the Committee including
Performance Budget. The Committee recommends that the Department should be careful in furnishing the reasons for
variation and should give substantive reply in support of reduction/enhancement of allocation.          (Para 9.4)
         The Committee is baffled to see that achievement in the year 2001-02 and 2002-03 were many time more than the
target fixed. Whereas in the year 2003-04, it was just other way i.e. against the target of 40,000 only 16,650 could be
achieved. Confusion is worse confounded to see that in years 2001-02 and 2002-03 when achievement was shown
manifold, were the years when the funds utilization was weak. A convincing explanation for this would certainly make
the Committee wiser next time.(Para 9.5)
         The Committee recommends that random checks should be made to verify the authenticity of figures and also
recommends that efforts should be made to implement the scheme in all the States/ UTs without fail.(Para 9.6)
X.     NATIONAL  COMMISSION FOR WOMEN
         The Committee notes that a large number of complaints were pending over the years as shown in the table above
— “Complaints on which no action was found feasible /necessary or under process/pending”. It would have given a true
picture had complaints on which no action was found feasible/necessary been put separately from those under
process/pending. Reasons for delay in processing should be identified and removed at the earliest.             (Para 10.2)
         The Committee recommends that all the States should be pursued to set up Women
Commission at the earliest.                                                                                            (Para 10.3)
         The Committee believes that these amendments were long over due. It, therefore, recommends that immediate
steps be taken to complete consultations and other formalities for bringing drafts of these laws before Parliament with
no loss of further time.(Para 10.5)
XI.    SWASHAKTI
         It is baffling to the Committee again that under this scheme also achievement far exceeded the targets in the year
when funds could not be utilized. The Committee has been informed that the reason for under-utilisation of funds was
the proposal for restructuring/strengthening of women development corporations/societies in nine project States being
not approved by the World Bank and IFAD, the funding agencies. The Committee expresses its serious concern over
this development which indicates that the funding agencies were not apprised about the anticipated/proposed measures
for the smooth running of the scheme at the initial stage itself. The Committee hopes that such instances will not occur
in future.(Para 11.3)
XII.  SWADHAR
         The Committee is not happy to note that the scheme was limited to only ten States/UTs and the Central Social
Welfare Board. It appears that the scheme was not getting good response despite the three tier monitoring mechanism.

The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made to popularize such useful scheme in all States/UTs. A
wide publicity campaign should be launched across the country to highlight the activities and benefits under the
scheme.(Para 12.3)
XIII. RESCUE OF VICTIMS OF TRAFFIKING
         The Committee finds this scheme as need of the hour. With the changing scenario all over, cases of commercial
exploitation of women and children are being reported frequently on unprecedented scale. The Committee would like to
caution the Department to take up its implementation seriously in the light of experiences it might have had with the
Swadhar.
                                                                                                                                     (Para 13.3)
XIV.GENDER BUDGET ANALYSIS
         The Committee expresses dissatisfaction over the indifferent attitude of the Department towards this aspect. It is
sad state of affairs when the Department whose mandate is to analyse women specific schemes is not reflecting it in the
Budget, the effort to analyse budget from a gender-based perspective by all the Ministries will be just eyewash. If the
Department is sincere in achieving its objective, the Committee recommends that it should figure out the gender-­based
allocation/targets prominently in its Budget. The Department may also take up the matter with other Ministries on the
issue.           (Para 14.3)
XV.  INSURANCE FOR WOMEN WORKERS
         The Committee observes that Insurance is an essential economic support to women during crises and recommends
that efforts should be made to link insurance with health programmes. The Committee would like the Department to
explore feasibility of linking insurance to other financial services - savings and credit - which promotes long-term
insurance coverage and work out the modalities in consultation with some renowned NGOs who have already started
this exercise.  (Para 15.2)
XVI.NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR CHILDREN
         The Committee was informed that the Bill needed some revision with a view to strengthening the Commission.
The Committee recommends that the revision of the Bill be expedited at the earliest and introduced as soon as
possible.        (Para 16.2)
         The Committee feels that formulation of the National Plan of Action for Children is a very important document
which includes not only goal & objectives but strategies as well for the current decade for improving nutritional status
of children, reducing IMR and MMR, increasing enrolment ration, reducing dropouts, increasing coverage of
immunization etc. Formulation of this has taken a long time since it was announced in August 2002. The Committee
recommends that all the formalities relating to this document should be completed at the earliest and brought before the
Parliament for its approval.         (Para 16.3)
         The Committee finds that the National Children’s Board was formed for the planning, review and proper
coordination of the multiplicity of services aimed at improving the needs of children and is headed by none other than
the Prime Minister himself. The Committee is not aware of the reasons as to why the Board could not be constituted
after its term expired in May 1999. And despite this, a token amount of Rs. 1 lakh is being made every year thereafter
including 2004-05. It sufficiently indicates that there is no idea for doing away with this body or shifting its
responsibility to some other body. The Committee would like to be apprised of latest position on the constitution of the
National Children’s Board.(Para 16.4)
XVII. OVERLAPPING OF SCHEMES
         The Committee reiterates that the Department should revisit the schemes having overlapping objectives with a
view not only to avoid inevitable confusions but also to have focused and optimum utilization of the scarce
resources.       (Para 17.3)
XVIII.  FUNCTIONING OF NGOs
         The Committee was informed that some of the schemes of the Department were being implemented through
NGOs. Idea of NGOs involvement, no doubt, is a noble one, functioning of some of the NGOs, however, leaves much
to be desired. Complaints of misuse/ misappropriation of government grants by some NGOs are reported from time to
time. There are allegations that in some cases different organization were being run by one person and same NGO was
receiving grants under different names. The Committee is aware that not all NGOs were defaulters and many of them

151st Report of Committee on HRD

were rendering yeoman service. Department gave a list of NGOs blacklisted by it. The Committee feels that simply
blacklisting such NGOs would not deter the delinquent ones and they might come back with change names/addresses.
Government needs to streamline the procedure of their selection as well as regular monitoring of their work. We should
have penal provisions for recovering the grants given to defaulting NGOs. The NGOs doing good job needs to be
suitably rewarded so as to motivate others.    (Para 18.1)
         The Committee feels that there exist no restriction for having a maximum number of NGOs in a particular area.
The Committee has noticed that out of 60 NGOs provided financial assistance amounting to Rs. 2.53 crores under the
National Creche Fund during 2003-04, 31 are from Andhra Pradesh with 18 NGOs based in one district alone. The
Committee is of the view that there should be specific guidelines whereunder number of NGOs in a district (subject to
area) should be indicated.                                                                                                                      (Para 18.2)
         The Committee has also observed that out of 463 NGOs provided financial assistance under Swawlamban Scheme
during 2003-04, 98 were provided funds for running computer institutes and 55 for readymade garments. The
Committee is of the view that NGOs involved in imparting technical education, even though of a very low standard
should be certified for running such courses.                                                                                                     (Para 18.3)
         The Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the fact that feedback from NGOs implementing various
schemes of the Department is not being received on a regular basis. The Department itself had admitted that under
‘Swawlamban’ and ‘STEP’, feedback regarding status of employment of the training after the completion of the training
programme has not been forthcoming. Under ‘Swawlamban’ 1650 utilisation certificates and under ‘STEP’ 60
utilisation certificates are awaited which confirms Committee’s apprehension. The Committee strongly feels that
besides strengthening the monitoring mechanism, there is a need for making the sanctioning/approving authority
accountable for the non-performing/under-­performing NGOs.   (Para 18.4)

PREFACE
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Hundred Fifty-
second Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 105) of the Ministry of Youth Affairs and
Sports for the year 2004-05.
2.
                        The Committee considered the various documents and  relevant papers received from the Ministry
of Youth Affairs and Sports and also  heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Ministry on the said
Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 11th August, 2004.
3.     The Committee considered the Draft Report  and adopted the same in its meeting held on 
25th August 2004.
 
NEW DELHI;
August 25, 2004
Bhadrapada 3, 1926 (Saka)
VAYALAR RAVI
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Human Resource Development.

REPORT
I.      INTRODUCTION
1.1    The primary responsibility of the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports is to ensure qualitative and quantitative
improvements in Youth Programmes and also to broad base and bring about awareness about sports and physical fitness
amongst school children and youth.  The Programmes undertaken by the Department are mainly categorized
under ‘Youth Welfare’ and Sports and Games.

152nd Report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/152ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:26]
1.2   The  Ministry has formulated the National Youth Policy which redefines the age group  of youth
from 13 to 35 years and recognizes four thrust areas i.e.  (i)  youth empowerment (ii) gender justice, (iii) inter-
sectoral approach and (iv) information and research network. The policy identifies eight key  aspects like
education, health, environment, sports and recreation, art and culture, training and employment of youth. It also seeks
to accord priority to the groups of youth-rural and tribal youth, out of school youth, adolescents particularly female,
youth with disability and those under difficult circumstances.
1.3    The Committee notes that most of these programmes are implemented by the State Governments, UT
administration statutory/local bodies, autonomous organizations of the Ministry as well as the NGOs.
II.     BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
(Rs. in crores)

2.1   The Ministry submitted that its Plan allocation of Rs. 385.00  crores in B.E. 2003- 04, was reduced to
Rs. 310.00 crores at R.E. stage by the Ministry of Finance as a general cut in expenditure. The Non-Plan allocation for
BE 2003-04 was Rs. 55.30 crores. The provision  available for Afro-Asian Games was only Rs. 9.32 crores on
Plan side. Additional allocation of Rs. 55 crores was obtained through supplementary grant on non-plan side, for
providing grant-in-aid to State Government of Andhra Pradesh for meeting the expenditure on these games. In addition
to this, an amount of Rs. 8.00 crores was re-appropriated from  Plan side to the newly opened head for giving
grants to State Government on Non-Plan side. Due to this additionality of Rs. 63.00 crores (Rs. 55.00 crores (Plan) +
Rs. 8.00 crores (Non-Plan), the Non-Plan RE 2003-04 was enhanced to Rs. 118.00 crores. On Plan side, the Planning
Commission recommended an allocation of Rs. 400.00 crores for B.E. 2004-05 against the Ministry’s projected demand
of Rs. 448.91 crores.
2.2    The  Committee notes that initially, Rs. 9.32 crores was earmarked for the Afro-Asian Games in BE
2003-04 on the plan side and subsequently Rs. 55 crore was obtained as supplementary grant for this purpose, but on
non-plan side. The Committee also notes that Rs. 8.00 crore was re-appropriated from plan side to non- plan side for a
newly created head. In view of  this, the Committee feels that assessment about Afro-Asian Games
requirements was highly unrealistic, because ultimately, a total Rs. 64.32 crores had to be given (Rs. 9.32 + Rs. 55
crore) for this purpose, instead of Rs. 9.32 crore originally provided for. Secondly, the re-appropriation of funds from
plan to non-plan, according to the Committee, is not a healthy practice, which leaves less money for the schemes which
are already cash-starved.
2.3    The Committee notes that the allocation of the  Ministry for the year 2004-05, has been marginally
increased and believes that  it would hardly suffice to implement the ongoing projects, leave alone new
initiatives proposed by the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should place its
requirements for this year, before the Ministry of Finance/Planning Commission justifying its need for higher
allocations at the RE Stage.
2.4    The Committee, at the same time, would impress upon the Ministry to ensure that allocations were properly and
fully utilized.
III.      GENDER BUDGET ANALYSIS OF BUDGET ALLOCATIONS
3.1    Women empowerment without gender equality would be nothing but an illusion. The Gender based analysis
of the budget allocations under different  schemes of the  Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, it is learnt, was
initiated during the year 2003-04 only.  Gender based analysis of Budget allocations for the year 2003-04
under its different schemes has been done.
3.2    The Committee notes that percentage of funds spent on women component is not upto the mark under various
schemes of the Ministry, except the NSS, NSVS and sports scholarship. In some schemes, specially those run by SAI, it
is very low. It is matter of great concern to the Committee that only 33.60% of the total allocation of the Ministry was
spent on women component during  the year 2003-04. The very fact, that data have been assumed for some
schemes, shows that gender analysis of its scheme is being done neither systematically nor regularly. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the gender-based analysis of the allocations of the Ministry should be done regularly, as it
would provide an idea about the percentage of funds being spent on the women who constitute about half of our
population.

152nd Report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/152ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:26]
3.3    The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to take interest in the development of sports among
the Indian women who have brought laurels to  the country in the past and have shown good potential for
sports like  athletics, weightlifting, hockey and swimming etc. Incentives and cash awards would ensure motivation
and active participation of women in various sports activities.
IV.    YOUTH PROGRAMMES
         Following Youth schemes are being administered and implemented by the Ministry:-----
            1.    National Service Scheme
            2.    Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan
            3.    National Service Volunteer Scheme
            4.    Promotion of Adventure
            5.    Promotion of National Integration
            6.    Assistance to Youth and Sports Clubs
            7.    Financial Assistance for Promotion of Youth Activities and Training
            8.    Youth Hostels
4.1   The  total outlay, both plan and non-plan, for the Ministry under youth welfare scheme for the year
2003-04, was Rs. 136.54 crores (Rs. 109.23 crores plan and Rs. 27.31 crores non-plan). This was reduced to Rs. 100.38
crore (Rs. 73.94 crores plan and Rs. 26.44 crores non-plan) in the Revised Estimate 2003-04. Provision for the year
2004-05, is Rs. 137.27 crores (Rs. 107.50 crores plan and Rs. 29.77 crores non-plan).
4.2    The Committee again notes that against an allocation of Rs. 352.24 crores made under youth welfare schemes for
the Ninth Plan, an expenditure of only Rs. 336.94 crores (including Rs. 6.35 crores for NER) could be incurred, leading
to a balance of Rs. 15.30crores.
4.3    The  Committee notes with concern that the allocations for youth welfare schemes could not be utilized
during the entire Ninth Plan period, despite the fact that the main thrust of the Ninth Plan was on harnessing the Yuva
Shakti. Tenth Plan outlay for Youth Welfare Schemes has substantially increased to Rs. 677.64 crores, as
compared to only Rs. 352.24  crores in Ninth Plan. The Committee, however, observes that position
remains unchanged during the first two years of Tenth Plan. During 2002-03, against an allocation of Rs. 106.98
crores, expenditure incurred was Rs. 98.70 crores. Enhanced allocation of Rs. 121.98 crores in BE 2003-04 had to be
reduced to Rs. 82.20 crores at the RE  stage and even that remained underutilized. Low utilization of
funds, the  Committee feels, should be viewed seriously because it reflects nothing but the lack of sincerity and
determination in implementing the Youth Welfare Schemes.
4.4   The  Committee notes that the Tenth Plan proposed to target the adolescent youth in  the 
10-19 years age group which is 230 million, accounting for 22.8%, through specific intervention strategies
that will focus on their power, gender justice, health and responsible living.
4.5   The  Committee is of the opinion that for achieving these avowed objectives youth will have to be
provided proper educational and training opportunities, access to information on employment opportunities including
entrepreneurial guidance and financial credit, proper platforms for developing qualities of leadership, tolerance and
open mindedness, patriotism, etc. But with this financial performance, the Committee feels, the Ministry will hardly be
able to achieve these targets. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the  Ministry to play a more pro-active
and catalytic role in optimally utilizing the allocations in various youth-related schemes in the coming years.
V.     NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME
5.1    National Service scheme popularly known, as NSS is a Centrally sponsored scheme, which is being implemented
through universities, colleges and other institutions of higher learning.
5.2    Today, NSS has more than 20 lakh student volunteers on its roll spread over 178 Universities and 39 (+2)
Senior Secondary Councils and Directorate of  Vocational Education covering more than 8600
institutes/colleges of higher  education and 6350 Secondary schools all over the country. Since its inception,
more than 2.51 crore students from universities, colleges and institutes of higher learning have been benefited under the
NSS activities.
5.3    The Ninth Plan outlay of Rs. 104.56 crores has been enhanced to 172.00 crores in the Tenth Plan. During the
Ninth Plan, the actual expenditure incurred under the scheme was Rs. 96.51 crores.
5.4 Allocation  of Rs.25.20 crores (Plan) has been made under the scheme for 2004- 05. It was 23.40 crores
at BE 2003-04 which was reduced to Rs. 20.59 crores at RE. The allocation in BE 

152nd Report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/152ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:26]
2004 -05 is higher, the Committee was informed, due to the increased enrollment of students in the universities and
colleges under the NSS.
5.5    The Committee was informed that during the year  2003-04 against a target to enroll 20.82 lakh
students, 20.30 lakhs were enrolled and against a target to enroll 78.94 lakhs volunteers, 77.93 volunteers were enrolled.
5.6 The  Committee after having seen the achievements, both physical and financial, describes the
performance of the scheme as satisfactory. The Committee, however, feels that the Ministry should not be complacent
in respect of this scheme. It, therefore, urges the Ministry to see that the money is released in time and every effort
should be made to utilize the funds allocated in the same year for achieving the targets.
5.7    The Committee was informed that two major constraints being experienced in the implementation of the NSS
were; delay in the settlement of accounts by the States/UTs; and non-functioning of State Liaison Cells in some
States/Union territories.
5.8   It  appears to the Committee that the Ministry does not have any mechanism to expedite delayed
settlement of accounts by the States/UTs. As regards the State Liaison Cells, it is the same story. The Committee is not
aware of the efforts made by the Ministry to find out the reasons for these phenomenon. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should pursue with the States and find out the problems and try to remove the same. It is
basically the responsibility of the Ministry to see that NSS was implemented effectively at the national level, of course
with the cooperation of the States.
VI.     NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN
6.1 Nehru  Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS), an autonomous organization of the Ministry caters to the needs
and concerns of more than 8 million non-student rural youth enrolled through more than 2 lakh villages based Youth
Clubs. Five hundred districts have a network of trained cadre of District Youth  Coordinators, National
Service Volunteers and members of Youth Clubs/Mahila Mandals. The activities of the NYKS are organized through
two categories of programmes, regular programmes and special programmes.
6.2    The plan allocation for NYKS in BE 2003-04 was Rs 31.18 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 29.75 crores at RE
stage. It has been further decreased to Rs. 28.97 crores in BE 2004-05. On a specific query about the reason for
decreasing the allocation for NYKS in 2004-05, the Ministry gave the following reasons :
           1.     Deen Dayal Upadhyay Swawlamban Yojana was on a pilot project basis and ended on March 2003.
           2.     During 2002-03 and 2003-04 payment of arrears were made to the employees of NYKS on account of the
benefit of Assured Career Progression (ACP).
           3.     The allocation was pruned as there is a ban on filling up of posts and the resultant vacancies on account of
retirement, death etc. are not being filled in.
6.3    The Committee notes that out of 500 posts of district youth coordinators, 134 posts are lying vacant. The
Ministry has set a target to expand its activities to all the districts in the country. The Committee finds the
Ministry in the catch-22 situation. Funds have been reduced and there is ban on filling up the posts, let alone
creating new posts. Then, there is the target to cover the remaining districts also. The Committee is dismayed at
the casual manner the scheme is being run with such a less number of District Coordinators and how the targets
were going to be achieved. The NYKS having all India network, the Committee feels, its volunteers can play vital
role in areas like literacy, family welfare, health awareness, national integration, gender equality etc. in rural
areas. The Committee feels very much concerned at the way  this scheme is sought to be implemented. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to initiate effective measures for improving the situation and taking this
scheme out of the morass it is presently in.
6.4    Committee has been given to understand that a recruitment process to fill up the vacancies of District Youth
coordinators was initiated sometimes back. The Committee is not aware of the final outcome of the process. The
Committee would like to have a status note on the same.

VII.NATIONAL RECONSTRUCTION CORPS
7.1    The National Reconstruction Corps, which was launched as a pilot project on 30.6.1999, aims at providing
opportunity to youth who have completed their matriculation to participate as volunteers in the process of nation

Rs. 14.41 crores.

against Rs. 10.90 crores in the previous year. The scheme has been evaluated and its continuance is under consideration
in consultation with the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission.  The Committee notes that in the

the Department to expedite its evaluation as well as decision to continue/discontinue this scheme at the earliest so
that it could be implemented timely and effectively.
VIII.    NATIONAL INTEGRATION PROGRAMME
8.1    Under this scheme, assistance is given to voluntary Organisations, educational institutions, NSS and NYKS for
organizing National Integration Camps in different parts of the country, for interstate visits, seminars, conferences,
research, publication, youth festivals, cultural programmes and other activities, all of which aim at combating
communalism, regionalism, linguistic chauvinism and other divisive tendencies. The scheme was revised in 2001, and
the organisation of the National Youth Festival and celebration of National Youth Day and also National Youth Awards
have been made integral part of it.
8.2    The budget allocations made during last three years were fully utilized except, the year 2001-02. The Ministry
explained that this shortfall was due to non-submission of documents by some implementing organisations. The
allocations in the RE 2002-03 were increased as more proposals were received and most of them were found viable and
were approved. An increased amount has been sought for the year 2004-05. The Committee is happy that
the scheme appears to be picking up after facing some initial teething problems. Now, the number of viable proposals
were increasing. The Committee, however, wonders as to how the scheme of such a great national significance could be
successfully operated with a marginal enhancement of Rs. 0.45 crores in the year 2004-05. The Committee is of
the view that a scheme  for promoting national integration should not suffer due to financial constraints. The
Ministry should, therefore expand this scheme, by encouraging more and more organisations to operate it. Financial
allocations also for this scheme need to be suitably enhanced.
8.3The  Committee observes that voluntary agencies play a vital role in organizing both National Integration
Camp and Inter-State Youth Exchange Programmes. The Committee would like to be apprised of the assessment of
work done by them under these Programmes, specially of those agencies being allocated the maximum grants.
IX.   YOUTH  HOSTELS
9.1    Youth Hostels are built to promote youth travel within the country. While the Central Government bears the cost
of construction, the State Governments provide fully developed land, free of cost, with water, electricity,
approach road and staff quarters. After completion, Youth Hostels are handed over to the State
Governments for management. As of December 2003, 65 Youth Hostels have been constructed and 20 are under
construction.
9.2    The Committee notes that the allocation under this scheme in BE 2003-04, was drastically reduced at RE stage
from Rs. 260 lakh to Rs. 60 lakh. The reason given for this was that there was reduction in the overall allocation of the
Ministry made by the Ministry of Finance. This year’s allocation has been Rs. 270 lakh to meet the expenditure on the
pending proposals which could not be cleared in 2003-04 due to paucity of funds. The Committee is surprised to see that
due to overall reduction of Ministry’s allocation, share of this scheme was drastically reduced from Rs. 260 lakh to just
Rs. 60 lakh. This general reduction in Ministry’s allocation, committee feels, should have been evenly spread to the

other schemes as well.
9.3    The Committee notes with concern that out of Rs. 14.93 crores for the Ninth plan outlay, the actual expenditure
was only Rs 9.65 crores i.e. only 67%.
9.4    The Committee notes that performance of this scheme is not satisfactory, in view of the expenditure pattern
in the entire Ninth Plan period as well as 2003-04. The fact that the allocation of the Ministry was
reduced from Rs. 260 lakhs to 60 lakhs last year, gives an impression that this scheme was not given the
priority that it deserved. Just 85 youth Hostels upto December 2003, in a country of continental dimensions, the
Committee feels, is highly inadequate which needs to be increased in the coming years. The Committee notes that
the spread of these 85 hostels state-wise is also highly uneven. In view of this, the Committee recommends that
the Ministry must try to see that this scheme picks up and gets adequate resources so that the pending
projects are completed in time. It is also necessary to fix physical targets for this scheme every year.
9.5    On being asked about publicity of the scheme, the  Ministry replied that the relevant information
pertaining to youth hostels was available on Internet and the Youth Hostels Association of India had been
bringing out a booklet providing  necessary information in respect of youth hostels. The Committee
feels that this scheme lacks adequate publicity, as a result, youth, particularly from rural areas, were not
able to make use  of hostel facilities. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that  existence of
youth hostel facilities should be given wide publicity particularly  by Akashvani which has large
audience in rural areas. It also recommends to strengthen the scheme as the present coverage of the scheme was
too less to show any impact.
9.6    The Committee does not know how much of the existing facility of youth hostels was being
utilized by the women youth. Generally women, particularly from rural areas, do not come out due to reasons of
security and safety. The Committee, therefore, recommends that separate girls hostels should also be constructed
on the lines of youth hostel.
X.    NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR YOUTH
10.1 The Commission was set up in March, 2002 for a period of six month to study the problems of youth and suggest
remedies. Initially, an allocation of Rs. 40.00 lakh was provided for it in 2001-02, by way of supplementary grants. In
2002-03, no provision was initially made for the Commission. However an amount of Rs. 100.00 lakh was obtained
later from the Contingency Fund of India. Since the Commission could not even start its work due to various
constraints, its tenure was extended for a period of one year i.e. upto 15 th September 2003. A provision of Rs. 150.00
lakhs was provided by way of re-appropriation in the year 2002-03, as the Ministry of Finance had not agreed to provide
any additionality for the Commission. In 2003-04, a sum of Rs. 100.00 lakh was provided for the Commission in the
budget to meet its requirements upto 15 th September, 2003. The tenure of the Commission was extended further in the
middle of the financial year. However, no budget was available for it. The Ministry of Finance also did not agree to
provide any additionality. An additional amount of  Rs. 306.00 lakhs was therefore, arranged by diverting
funds from other schemes of the Ministry. In 2004-05 (Interim Budget), only a token provision of Rs. 10.00 lakh was
made, as there was no request from the Commission for any further extension. However, in 3 rd week of March, on
request from the Chairman of the Commission, its tenure was again extended upto  30 th September 2004 and
so a total provision of Rs. 193.00 lakh has been made in the regular budget to meet the expenses upto September 2004.
The Commission has now submitted its report and the process of its winding up is underway.
10.2 The Committee gets an impression from what has been stated above that the Commission was not taken with due
seriousness although it had laudable mandate. Its initial tenure of six months, the Committee feels, was not realistic and
the Commission was not provided with the necessary wherewithal and assistance for starting its work in time. The
Committee disapproves this ad-hocism as also the manner in which funds were arranged first by re-appropriation and
then from the Contingency Fund. The Commission has since submitted its report after two years and four months which
it was to submit within 6 months initially. The Committee expresses its unhappiness at the manner everything was done.
However, it would like to have a note on the report of the Commission at the earliest.

XV.SPORTS AND PHYSICAL EDUCATION
15.1  Sports activity is integral to the allround development of the human personality. Achievements in sport have a
considerable bearing on the national prestige and morale. International sports events have become a showcase of
national pride and power. Considering the importance of sports and games, the Government of India has taken a number
of initiatives to improve the standard of sports in the country. The Government has evolved a new National Sports
Policy which envisages broad-basing of sports, achievement of excellence in international sports events, provisioning of
modern sports infrastructure, upgrading skills of our coaching fraternity, more efficient functioning of national sports
federations, adequate sports-science back-up and active involvement of business and industry in promotion of sports.
15.2The  Committee notes that against an allocation of Rs. 472.61 crores made for entire Ninth Plan Period
under Sports and Physical Education, an increased expenditure of Rs. 558.50 crore was incurred at the end of the Plan.

Rs. 13 crores (against BE) is proposed  for Sports Authority of India for promotion of sports

which Ministry requested additional allocation to the tune of about Rs. 134 crores. This additionality, it was argued,

XVI.SPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA
16.1   Sports Authority of India is the apex body in the country, which is responsible for the development of sports.
A number of schemes for  spotting and nurturing of sports talent, promotion of sports in special areas,
women’s sports, rural sports etc. are implemented by the SAI. It is also responsible for maintaining and utilizing
stadia in Delhi. SAI has six Regional Centres and four Sub-Centres. SAI also has two academic wings-one for training
of coaches and research and development in sports at the Netaji Subhash National Institute of Sports, Patiala and the
other for physical education at the Lakshmibai National College of Physical Education, Thiruvananthapuram.
(i)     Budgetary Allocation
         An allocation of Rs. 123.83 crore has been made in BE 2004-05 for the ‘Sports Authority of India’ as against BE
Rs. 110.50 crore in 2003-04, which was reduced to Rs. 98.50 crore at RE stage. This reduction was mainly due to
general cut applied by the Ministry of Finance. When asked to comment on the increase in the allocation for 2004-05,
and the thrust areas for which the Ministry proposes to spend the enhanced allocation, the Committee was informed that
main works to be taken up in 2004-05 are: replacement of ACs in IG Stadium and Dr. S.P. Mukherjee Swimming Pool;
upgradation of the fire-fighting system in all the SAI Stadia; installation/replacement of the synthetic surfaces; creation
of Fitness Centres in all SAI Stadia and outstation units/regional centres of SAI where National Coaching Camps are
held; and purchase of sports scientific equipments required for the training of the National teams.
16.2   The Committee notes that the budget allocation for SAI had been increased over the years, in order to meet
the costs for  upgradation of facilities for coaching camps, purchase of equipments, upgradation of stadia and
infrastructure etc.
16.3The Committee, however, observes that in 2003-04 BE allocation of Rs. 110.50 crores had to be reduced to Rs.
98.50 crores in RE, whereas actual expenditure was only Rs. 97.00 crores. The Committee feels that the pace of
expenditure of the SAI allocations does not present an encouraging picture. The Committee would like the Ministry to
ensure optimum utilization of funds by the SAI for its programmes in 2004-05.
(ii)    SAI Sub-Centres
         In response to a query about sub-centres of the SAI, the Committee was informed that three more sub-centers at
Hazaribagh, Lucknow and Nagercoil were approved. While the sub-centre at Lucknow has been commissioned with
most of the infrastructure in place, the construction work in respect of the 
sub-centre at Hazaribagh is in progress. No construction has been started at Nagercoil since the land for the project is
yet to be handed over by the State Government.
16.4   The  Committee finds that the SAI Regional Centres at Sonepat, Gandhinagar, Bhopal, Kolkata, Imphal
and Bangalore are not evenly distributed as regards different regions in the country. So is the case with the sub-centres
also. The Committee feels that the creation of the regional as well as sub-centres should be based on performance of the
region as well as the States. It appears that this has not been the case so far.
16.5    The Committee recommends that the construction work at sub-centre at Hazaribagh  may be completed at
the earliest. State Government should be persuaded to hand over the land at a suitable place so that the
construction of sub-centre at Nagercoil could be initiated without further loss of time.
(iii)     Scheme for Dope Test
           The anti-doping programme in the country is managed by SAI through the Dope Control Centre located at the
JLN Stadium, New Delhi and is funded under the Central Sector ‘Scheme for Dope Test’ launched during the 10 th Five
Year Plan. The Committee is happy to learn about the temporary accreditation by the IOC to Dope Control Centre run
by the SAI. It has got ISO 9001:2000 & ISO: 17025 Certificate and efforts are on for permanent accreditation for its
laboratory by the IOC and World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).
16.6    Last few years have seen a number of sportspersons specially the weightlifters and athletes testing positive for
banned drugs. These instances have brought shame instead of fame to the nation. Our scheme for dope test was
launched only three years ago. The SAI has anti-doping lab set up a decade ago in New Delhi, it has still not acquired
the requisite international certification to gain legal sanctity. So, even if anybody fails a test, he or she can successfully
challenge it in a Court. Such a situation allows the over-ambitious ones to take the easy route.
16.7    In view of cases in Athens Olympics and earlier experiences, the Committee notes that our weightlifters are most
hit by the scourge of doping. Every time an Indian contingent prepares to leave the country for a mega event, doping
tests are hastily conducted and surprisingly they do not test positive here but fail the test in International events.

16.8   The  Committee was surprised to know that nobody seems to take the responsibility for the same. Even
the Sports Ministry and SAI claim that it is not their duty to conduct dope tests on athletes who are under
control of  IOA and various federations. Federations have a ready   excuse about the high cost of
conducting dope test. Thus, at the  end of the day nobody is ready to own the responsibility for the bad name
that a few athletes bring to the nation.
16.9    The Committee feels extremely unhappy about the continuing indifference shown by all sports bodies - the
Ministry, IOA, Federations and the SAI about the serious malaise. They appear to be passing the buck to each other and
no serious attempt has been made so far by them to clean the mess that has plagued our sports persons.
16.10   The very fact that sportsperson after having been cleared by our test, get caught during the events shows how
rudimentary or outdated procedure we adopt about this testing. It means lab at SAI does not have the necessary facility
for this test. The Committee was informed that the procedure allows for tempering of the samples also.
16.11  The Committee, therefore, recommends that more sports scientists should be deputed by SAI to efficiently put all
sportspersons to dope testing. It should evolve some mechanism so that the samples could not be tempered. The entire
procedure should be transparent and the punishment has to be as per international  norms. Though there is a
provision for withdrawal of grants and facilities to the offender, but that of course, is rarely resorted to. The coaches and
doctors of Sportspersons testing positive should be made liable because during the training they are in-charge of their
trainees. Blaming the sportsperson alone will not be fair.
16.12The  Committee recommends that the Ministry should make efforts to streamline the procedure for dope
testing, upgrading the test facilities, employing experts in the area for making the test results foolproof. Involving many
agencies in this, Committee feels, would only complicate the  matter. Only SAI and IOA, therefore, should
be made responsible for this work. And they should put necessary guidelines in tune with World Anti-Doping Code.
16.13  The Committee also emphasizes an urgent need for educating our athletes, coaches and other supporting
personnel about the harmful effects of dope; conducting in-competition and out-of-competition dope tests on
sportspersons; and promoting research and training in the area.
(iv)     Scouting and Nurturing talents
16.14   The Committee notes that the schemes such as National Sports Talent Contest, Army Boys Sports Companies
(ABSC), Special Area Games (SAG) and Sports Promotion Development Area Centres basically for scouting
and nurturing sports talent in the country. While first two schemes target the children between 8-14 years, the third
one is meant for youth between 14-20 years. Committee feels that objective of these schemes is very good which aim at
spotting the talent at younger age, and nurture them by giving every support including scientific training. But the
Committee finds that the impact of these schemes is not visible at any level, despite these being implemented for a very
long time. Coverage of these schemes is highly inadequate. Besides, the instances of bad upkeep and lack of hygiene in
the hostels where these boys stay are reported every now and then. The medical facilities for them are also poor. All this
presents a very dismal picture of these schemes.
16.15   The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that performance of these schemes should be evaluated and
problem identified with a view to strengthening and  expanding them to more and more areas of the
country. These schemes be implemented with full vigour so as to bring out our talented children and youth to the
forefront.
16.16   The Committee agrees with the Ministry that sporting standards in country have not declined. It, however,
believes that it  cannot be said to have improved either. Our performance in international sports is not at
all satisfactory and commensurate with the size of our country as well as the population.
16.17The Committee  is of the opinion that training is the core aspect of good performance.  Rigorous
training for years together for producing champions is required. The Committee opines that sports training
should be properly planned and managed for getting the best results. The Committee recommends to draw-out scientific
training modules for our sportsperson in different disciplines after consulting coaches, federations and experts in fields
like sports medicine and sports psychology.
16.18  It is a fact that qualified persons in sports medicine and sports psychologists are not available in our country. SAI
has at present only four qualified sports psychologists and services of eminent sports psychologists from abroad are also
being hired as and when needed.
16.19   The overall  performance as well as functioning of the SAI, the Committee feels, has been far from
satisfactory. Our performance in international sports as it is, is highly disappointing. The SAI obviously has not
been able to make any significant impact as was initially visualised when it was set up. It is said to have developed
into an unwieldy bureaucratic organization, which is not being managed by sportspersons themselves. The Committee

152nd Report of Committee on HRD

feels that there is a need to have a re-look on both its mandate as well as organization with a view to bringing in this
organization professionalism, dynamism and efficiency so that it becomes a think tank in the sports arena.
XVII.GRANTS FOR CREATION OF SPORTS INFRASTRUCTURE
17.1    Under this Scheme, grant is given to State Government/UT administrations, local statutory bodies such as
Municipalities, Municipal Corporations/Notified Area Committees/ Cantonment Boards and Registered Voluntary
Organisations, for development of playfields, construction of indoor/outdoor stadia, swimming pool, water/winter sports
infrastructure, shooting ranges and additional facilities in existing sports projects. In addition, State/UTs are also
assisted for construction of District/State level sports complexes. Financial assistance is rendered subject to the cost
being shared between the centre and the sponsoring agencies/State Government on 75:25 in respect of special
category States, hilly/tribal areas and 50:50 in case of other areas. Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya
Vidyalayas are also eligible to avail assistance upto Rs. 5.00 lakhs for construction/improvement of certain facilities in
their schools. The scheme is proposed to be merged with the umbrella scheme relating to infrastructure.
17.2    The Committee notes that BE allocation for this scheme was 13.00 crores during 2003-04, which was enhanced
up to Rs. 15.00 crores at RE in view of the large number of pending projects being approved. For NE States also BE
allocation of 3.00 crores was raised up to 11.06 crores (Rs 2.00 crores at RE  stage and Rs. 9.06 crores
through re- appropriation).
17.3    During the last financial year, assistance of Rs. 10.58 crores was released for 85 sports projects. During the
current year, 182 projects were assisted all over India with expenditure of Rs. 14.99 crores for general category States
and Rs. 14.06 crores forNE, States. An outlay of Rs. 34.08 crores was made for Ninth Plan period whereas the actual
expenditure incurred was only 32.82 crores. Tenth Plan outlay for the scheme is Rs. 160.51 crores.
17.4   More provision  was made in RE 2003-04 due to receipt of large number of proposals. Similarly, more
amounts has been provided in BE 2004-05 keeping in view the large number of viable proposals received and the
increased provision made by Planning Commission in the Tenth plan. The scheme is also under revision and it is
proposed to increase the scale of assistance. With revised eligibility condition, requirement of funds is expected to
increase.
17.5   The  Committee is happy to see that different schemes of infrastructural support  have been
proposed to be clubbed under two umbrella schemes on the pattern as was done for the schemes of promotion
of sports Awards incentives. The Committee feels that it would enable the Ministry to have a focussed and effective
implementation of scheme to create infrastructure  of a high standard in various parts of the country. The
Committee emphasizes the need for special focus on developing playgrounds in villages and providing sports
equipments to rural youth.
XVIII.    GRANTS FOR PROMOTION OF SPORTS IN UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES
18.1    The Ministry provides financial assistance to the universities/colleges for development of
playgrounds/construction of indoor stadia facilities in the ratio of 75:25 in the case of special category States and in the
ratio of 50:50 to all other States subject to a certain ceiling. Financial assistance is also given for purchase of sports
equipments upto a maximum ceiling of Rs. 3 lakh.
18.2    During 2003-04, budget allocation for this scheme was Rs. 9.00 crores. Keeping in view the large number of
proposals received, additional allocation of Rs. 1.00 crores was also provided at the RE stage. During 2002-03 227
colleges/universities benefited under the scheme and the expenditure incurred was Rs. 6.60 crores. During 2003-04(upto
31.3.2004) 413 colleges/universities were provided with grants under the scheme and an expenditure of Rs: 10.80 crores
plan was incurred (upto 31.3.2004).
18.3The  Committee observes that allocation as well as expenditure under this scheme has increased over the
years due to receipt of more and more proposals. It was able to utilize 
Rs. 32.78 crores as against Rs. 23.11 crores allocated during the Ninth Plan. The Committee urges the Ministry to see
that proposals received were processed and grant released within minimum possible time so that pace of its
implementation is not broken. The Committee  is, however, not satisfied with  the coverage of colleges and
universities under the scheme. It appears that proposals are coming from a few States, its benefit, therefore, are not
reaching to other States. The Ministry should take upon the responsibility of encouraging universities/colleges from the
areas where from the proposals are less or are not coming at all.

services/railway Sports Control Boards, local bodies and universities/colleges/schools, public/ private sector enterprises

XX.SCHEME RELATING TO INCENTIVES FOR PROMOTION OF SPORTS ACTIVITIES
20.1 The Committee notes that this is a package  incentive scheme in which the following five schemes
have been merged into  one:- Sports Fund for Pension to Meritorious Sport Persons; Rural Sports Programme;
Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools; Scheme of Sports Scholarships; and National Sports Development Fund.
Rs. 9 crores is provided for all these five schemes. The Committee notes that during 2003-2004, BE allocation of Rs.
15.06 crores was reduced to Rs. 9.76 crores in RE. The Committee expresses its anguish over the reduction under such
an important scheme having varied components for promoting sports activity.
20.2   The Committee finds that out of the five schemes, the financial performance in case of ‘sports scholarship scheme’
and ‘pension for meritorious sports persons’ has been good. In the case of other three, things were not that good. In the
case of Rural sports programme, for example, there were variation in allocation in BE 2001-02 and 2002-03. BE, 2003-
04 was reduced at RE Stage due to general cut in Ministry’s allocation. The Committee notes that the impact of this cut
was borne by this scheme meant for rural sports. Rural sports, the Committee feels, are not getting the required
attention.
20.3   Under the scheme of ‘promotion  of sports and games in schools’ assistance is given to States/UTs for
conducting school competition. The Committee notes that the allocation for this purpose had been reduced in 2002-2003
and at RE 2003-2004. Reason given was less number of proposals from State Governments and non-receipt of UCs of
grants released in the previous year. The Committee takes a serious view of the casual manner in which this scheme
meant for the school games is being implemented. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry should
vigorously pursue procurement of pending UCs and also try to simplify the procedure for it with a view to encouraging
States to come forward and send proposals.
20.4  Similarly, National Sports Development Fund could not pick up due to poor response from private/corporate units

XXI.SPECIAL AWARDS TO WINNERS IN INTERNATIONAL SPORTS EVENTS AND THEIR
         COACHES
21.1 Cash awards are given under this scheme for winning medals in the Olympics, World Cup/World Championship,
Asian and Commonwealth Games/Championships. Special Awards are also given to junior sportspersons for winning
medals in the World, Asian and Commonwealth Championships. Three hundred and twenty six sports persons/coaches
were given special awards during the year 2002-03.
21.2  An allocation of Rs. 9.00 crores was made in BE 2003-04, which was increased to Rs. 24.35 crores at RE stage.
The outlay has again been reduced to Rs. 5.00 crores for the year 2004-05. When asked, the Ministry explained that the
BE was revised upwards to meet the additional requirement of funds arising  out of the commitment made
by the Prime Minister to the gold medal winning Indian women’s hockey team in the Commonwealth Games, 2002,
and similar commitment made by the then Minister to all medallists of the Commonwealth and Asian Games, 2002. The
BE for the year 2004-05 has been reduced keeping in view the expected normal requirement of funds and the fact that
there was no major sporting events except Olympics.
21.3  The Committee is of the opinion that the pension scheme for sportspersons is a good scheme but it needs to be
further streamlined and strengthened. Besides, the Committee suggests that other facilities like CGHS benefits should
also be extended to them. It has come to the notice of the Committee that many cases of sportspersons for pension are
pending. The  Committee would like the Ministry to expedite the disposal of pension cases pending with it as
early as possible.
XXII.ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
22.1     Under this scheme National Sports Federations (NSFs), are provided assistance for conducting national
championships and international tournaments in India, organizing coaching camps, procuring sports equipments,
participation in international tournaments abroad, disbursement of salaries of their Joint/Assistant Secretaries and for
engagement of foreign coaches.
22.2   The Committee notes that BE allocation in 2003-04  for NSFs was Rs. 42.00 crores, which had to be
reduced to Rs. 29.00 crores at  the RE stage. This reduction, Committee was informed, was due to
general cut  applied in the Ministry’s allocation. Some funds had to be spared to provide funds for disbursing
special cash awards to medal winners in international events for which more funds were required due to enhancement of
the scale of awards.
22.3  For the year 2004-05, the allocation has been increased to 48.31 crores in order to meet some committed liabilities
of 2003-04; for disbursing the Commonwealth Games fee of Rs. 10.52 crores for holding the Games in 2010 and to
meet the additional demands from the NSFs towards preparations of team /sportspersons for the Athens Olympic.
22.4  The Committee was informed that pursuant to a recommendation contained in the 122nd Report of the Department
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development, a Committee was constituted by the
Ministry in December, 2002 under the Chairmanship of the Director General Sports Authority of India “to review and
evaluate” the workings of all the recognized Sports Federations. The move was opposed by the Indian Olympic
Association in their Annual General Meeting. The Minister in a reply to the IOA President had clarified the reason
behind the action of the Government and had assured that the concerns expressed by the IOA in their AGM would be
kept in mind. The Member Secretary of the Committee had written to the IOA to nominate its Member to the
Committee, but no reply was received. A Questionnaire was also sent to the National Sports Federations seeking
information about their functioning. However, only a few responded, and therefore, the Committee has not been able to
complete its task. The Ministry is proposing to hold meetings with main office bearers of National Sports
Federations.
22.5  The Committee is aware about questions being raised from different quarters particularly in media about the
functioning of National Sports Federations. While the Committee feels concerned about those questions, it,
however, thinks that National Sports Federations are the lynchpin in the entire sports structure of the
country. Organisations like Indian Olympic Association are under certain international obligations as well. While
recognizing the key contribution of the NSFs in the promotion and development of sports in the country, the Committee
is of the opinion that they should also see that their functioning does not leave any cause of complain. If some of the
NSFs were not functioning in transparent manner and the matter  is reported in the newspaper, it does not mean
that functioning of all the NSFs are questionable.

22.8The  Committee would like to mention about the alleged non-submission of UCs by some  sports

Besides, statement of accounts is also not  being published by some sports federations. The Committee
would like the  Ministry to ensure the financial accountability of these federations. The  Committee is
surprised at the silence maintained by the Ministry on this aspect. This approach ultimately would
hamper the development of sports. The  Committee would like the Ministry to adopt more pro-active

XXIII. STATE SPORTS ACADEMY
23.1 The main objective of this new scheme is to select the best talent in sports in the age group of 10-13 years and
groom them to achieve excellence at the national and international levels. A Sports Academy would be set up in every
state in partnership with the corporate sector and the cost of setting up of  the academy will be shared by the
sponsor, the Central Government and the State Government in the ratio of 51:25:24.
23.2To a  specific query about the progress made with regard to this scheme, the Ministry submitted that in
spite of wide publicity given to the scheme by writing to the State Governments and Chambers of Commerce and
Industry, no proposal has been received from any State Government or private  sponsor. A meeting was,
therefore, convened on 8.3.2004 under the chairmanship  of Secretary (YA&S) to discuss the problems and
difficulties in the implementation of the scheme. Based on inputs received from the representatives of State
Governments and industry, the scheme is proposed to be revised.
23.3  The Committee feels that this scheme has not taken off at all mainly due to poor response from the corporate
sector. The Committee appreciates the  efforts made by the Ministry to discuss the problems with the
private sector  and based on discussions held so far the scheme has been proposed to be revised. The Committee
therefore, recommends that the process of revision be expedited as early as possible.
23.4  The Committee calls upon the corporate houses to co-operate in this national endeavour as part of their social
responsibility. Any apprehensions/problems that they may be having in contributing for this noble cause, the Committee
feels, could be taken care of after mutual consultations with the Ministry as well as Federations.

XXVI.  MONITORING OF SCHEMES
26.1   The Committee notes that over the years, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has taken a number of new
initiatives and programmes in the field of youth development, sports and physical education. However monitoring in
respect of the youth programmes is not visible.
           On the other hand the progress and development of each discipline of sports is monitored by a Committee headed
by the Director General, Sports Authority of India and overall development of sports is monitored by a National Level
Monitoring Committee headed by the Union Minister of Youth Affairs and Sports.
26.2    The Committee is surprised to see that there is no permanent mechanism in the Ministry of its own to receive
regular feedback as well as to monitor various programmes, both under Youth Welfare and the Sports. This is an aspect
without which, it is not possible to know about the performance and success of the schemes run by the Ministry. The
Committee was informed that monitoring was being done basically by two Committees one formed under the DG, SAI
and the other under the Minister of Youth Affairs and Sports. The  Committee disapproves a monitoring
activity which is so centralised that it is being done from the Centre. Sports being the State subject, the Committee feels,
any mechanism which is not from down-to-the-top is bound to be ineffective. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Ministry should devise a decentralised mechanism of monitoring of its schemes at the earliest.

II.       BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
           The  Committee notes that initially, Rs. 9.32 crores was earmarked for the Afro-Asian Games in BE
2003-04 on the plan side and subsequently Rs. 55 crore was obtained as supplementary grant for this purpose, but on
non-plan side. The Committee also notes that 
Rs. 8.00 crore was re-appropriated from plan side to non- plan side for a newly created head. In view of  this,
the Committee feels that assessment about Afro-Asian Games requirements was highly unrealistic, because
ultimately, a total Rs. 64.32 crores had to be given (Rs. 9.32 + Rs. 55 crore) for this purpose, instead of Rs. 9.32 crore
originally provided for. Secondly, the re-appropriation of funds from plan to non-plan, according to the Committee, is
not a healthy practice, which leaves less money for the schemes which are already cash-
starved.                                         (Para 2.2)
           The Committee notes that the allocation of the Ministry for the year  2004-05, has been marginally
increased and believes that it would hardly  suffice to implement the ongoing projects, leave alone new
initiatives proposed by the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should place its
requirements for this year, before the Ministry of Finance/Planning Commission justifying its need for higher
allocations at the RE Stage.      (Para 2.3)
           The Committee, at the same time, would impress upon the Ministry to ensure that allocations were properly and
fully utilized.                                                                                                                                 (Para 2.4)

           The Committee notes that percentage of funds spent on women component is not upto the mark under
various schemes of the Ministry, except the NSS, NSVS and sports scholarship. In some schemes, specially those
run by SAI, it is very low. It is matter of great concern to the Committee that only 33.60% of the total allocation
of the Ministry was spent on women component during  the year 2003-04. The very fact, that data
have been assumed for some schemes, shows that gender analysis of its scheme is being done neither

to Rs. 677.64 crores, as compared to only Rs. 352.24  crores in Ninth Plan. The Committee,
however, observes that position remains unchanged during the first two years of Tenth Plan. During

BE 2003-04 had to be reduced to Rs. 82.20  crores at the RE stage and even that remained

provided proper educational and training opportunities, access to information on employment opportunities
including entrepreneurial guidance and financial credit, proper platforms for developing qualities of leadership,

Ministry will hardly be able to achieve these targets. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Ministry

         The Committee after having seen the achievements, both physical and financial, describes the

complacent in respect of this scheme. It, therefore, urges the Ministry to see that the money is released in time

           The Committee notes that out of 500 posts of district youth coordinators, 134 posts are lying vacant. The

Ministry in the catch-22 situation. Funds have been reduced and there is ban on filling up the posts, let alone

role in areas like literacy, family welfare, health awareness, national integration, gender equality etc. in rural
